text:
DOCUMENT: 1st Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Inside Information Definition and Criteria
ID: 10
CONTENT:
Inside information under REMIT must fulfill four criteria: (1) be of a precise nature, (2) not have been made public, (3) relate directly or indirectly to one or more wholesale energy products, and (4) if made public, would be likely to significantly affect prices of those products. Article 2(1), second subparagraph, of REMIT provides indications as to the notion of 'information'. Information shall be deemed to be of a precise nature if it indicates a set of circumstances which exists or may reasonably be expected to come into existence, or an event which has occurred or may reasonably be expected to do so, and if it is specific enough to enable a conclusion to be drawn as to the possible effect of that set of circumstances or event on the prices of wholesale energy products. The precise nature of the information is to be assessed by the holder of the information on a case-by-case basis and depends on what the information is and on the surrounding context.

text:
DOCUMENT: 1st Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Public Disclosure of Inside Information
ID: 11
CONTENT:
Inside information should be disclosed in a manner ensuring that it is capable of being disseminated to as wide a public as possible. The Agency prioritizes disclosure through platforms. If market participants are required to make information publicly available through a Transmission System Operator (TSO) platform (e.g. RTE-UFE transparency initiative) or a transparency platform of an energy exchange (e.g. Nord Pool Spot, EEX Transparency platform), in accordance with Regulations (EC) No 714/2009 and (EC) No 715/2009, market participants with inside information should use such disclosure mechanisms. According to Article 4(4) of REMIT, such publication of inside information, including in aggregated form, in accordance with these Regulations or guidelines and network codes adopted pursuant to those Regulations, constitutes simultaneous, complete and effective public disclosure.

text:
DOCUMENT: 1st Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Alternative Disclosure Mechanisms and Requirements
ID: 12
CONTENT:
If transparency platforms do not yet exist, market participants may be allowed, at least for an interim period and unless otherwise specified, to publish inside information on their own website. However, disclosure must enhance the level of transparency across the EU and not distort the dissemination of information. Inside information shall be disclosed by a market participant free of charge, in a non-discriminatory, user-friendly and quantifiable manner and, where appropriate, in a downloadable format that allows for quantitative analysis. The information should be published in the official language(s) of the relevant Member State and in English. Disclosure must ensure information is capable of being disseminated to as wide a public as possible, including the media.

text:
DOCUMENT: 1st Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Timely Disclosure Requirements
ID: 13
CONTENT:
If inside information has to be published in accordance with Regulations (EC) No 714/2009 and (EC) No 715/2009, including guidelines and network codes, the delay in publishing under these rules and regulations, including in aggregated form, is considered simultaneous, complete and effective public disclosure under Article 4(4) of REMIT. However, this does not necessarily constitute disclosure in a timely manner. Inside information must be published before the prohibition of insider trading ceases to apply. If inside information has not to be made public in accordance with these Regulations, it must normally be published, at least on the market participant's website, within one hour if not otherwise specified in applicable rules and regulations. In any case, inside information has to be published before the prohibition of insider trading ceases to apply. The Agency considers that market participants should develop a clear compliance plan towards real time or close to real time disclosure of inside information.

text:
DOCUMENT: 1st Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Exemptions and Reporting Requirements
ID: 14
CONTENT:
Article 3(4)(b) and Article 4(2) of REMIT provide for exemptions from the obligation to timely publish inside information and from the prohibition to trade on this information before it is published in a number of specified cases. In all these cases, however, the relevant information should be reported to the Agency and the competent NRA without delay. The Agency has developed a standard notification format, based on experiences in financial markets, and recommends its adoption by all NRAs. The Agency foresees to collect the notifications required by Article 3(4)(b) and Article 4(2) of REMIT mainly through an electronic format, especially when there are data standards relating to this information. The relevant electronic format is published on the Agency's website.

text:
DOCUMENT: 1st Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Significant Price Effect Criterion
ID: 15
CONTENT:
The criterion of significant price effect narrows the wide notion of information down to that information which is crucial enough to have a potential to significantly affect prices, thus excluding that any knowledge of non-public information which potentially has only marginal price effect shall prevent market participants from trading in wholesale energy products. According to Article 2(1) of REMIT, the likelihood to significantly affect the prices of wholesale energy products is already sufficient for the information to be qualified as inside information. No actual price effect is required; it is sufficient if the ex-ante available information is likely to have a significant price effect. Such assessment must take into consideration the anticipated impact of the information in light of the totality of the related market participant's activity, the market situation, including specificities of the market (size of the market, balance of demand and supply, steepness of the relevant offer curve, information on supply variation already published, time of day), and any other market variables likely to affect the related wholesale energy product.

text:
DOCUMENT: 1st Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Indicators of Significant Price Effect
ID: 16
CONTENT:
The Agency currently considers that the following should be taken into consideration as useful indicators of whether information is likely to have a significant price effect: (1) the type of information is the same as information which has, in the past, had a significant effect on prices; (2) pre-existing analysts research reports, price reporter publications and opinions indicate that the type of information in question is price sensitive; (3) the market participant itself has already treated similar events as inside information. These factors are only indicators and should not be treated as definitive in terms of meaning that the information in question will necessarily have a significant price effect. Ex-post information may be used to check the presumption that the ex-ante information has a significant price effect, but should not be used to take action against someone who drew reasonable conclusions from ex-ante information.

text:
DOCUMENT: 1st Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: REMIT Examples of Inside Information
ID: 17
CONTENT:
REMIT itself gives examples of inside information in its Recitals 12 and 15. The use or attempted use of inside information to trade either on one's own account or on the account of a third party should be clearly prohibited. Use of inside information can consist in trading in wholesale energy products by persons who know, or ought to know, that the information they possess is inside information. Information regarding the market participant's own plans and strategies for trading should not be considered as inside information. Information which is required to be made public in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 714/2009 or Regulation (EC) No 715/2009, including guidelines and network codes adopted pursuant to those Regulations, may serve, if it is price-sensitive information, as the basis of market participants' decisions to enter into transactions in wholesale energy products and therefore could constitute inside information until it has been made public.

text:
DOCUMENT: 1st Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Journalist Disclosure and Applicable Regulations
ID: 18
CONTENT:
The disclosure of inside information in relation to a wholesale energy product by journalists acting in their professional capacity should be assessed taking into account the rules governing their profession and the rules governing the freedom of the press, unless those persons derive, directly or indirectly, an advantage or profits from the dissemination of the information in question or when disclosure is made with the intention of misleading the market as to the supply of, demand for, or price of wholesale energy products. The definitions of Regulations (EC) No 714/2009 and (EC) No 715/2009 and Directives 2009/72/EC and 2009/73/EC, including guidelines and network codes adopted pursuant to those Regulations, apply. As regards wholesale electricity products, Regulation (EC) No 714/2009, including guidelines and network codes adopted pursuant to this Regulation, particularly the current 2006 Congestion Management Guidelines annexed to the Regulation, apply.

text:
DOCUMENT: 1st Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: TSO Information Obligations and Transparency Requirements
ID: 20
CONTENT:
TSOs are obliged to provide information on transmission infrastructure and its use, generation, load, balancing and wholesale market aspects. Market participants must provide TSOs with relevant data for publication. Information on network infrastructure includes capacity allocation, congestion management procedures, and operational and planning security standards. Classes of information published regularly (annual, monthly, week-ahead forecasts, daily day-ahead and intraday) include available transmission capacity, capacity used, aggregated commercial and physical flows, and planned/unplanned outages of generation units larger than 100 MW. Additionally, forecast demand and generation data, as well as realized values, must be published.

text:
DOCUMENT: 1st Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Inside Information Definition for Electricity Products
ID: 21
CONTENT:
Inside information for wholesale electricity products regarding a market participant's own business or facilities includes: any planned outage, limitation, expansion or dismantling of capacity of one generation unit that equals or exceeds 100 MW, including changes of such plans; any unplanned outage or failure of capacity that equals or exceeds 100 MW for one generation unit, consumption or transmission facility, including updates on such outages or failures; and any other information likely to have a significant effect on wholesale electricity product prices if made public. These definitions apply until the Comitology Guidelines on Fundamental Electricity Data Transparency are adopted and enter into force.

text:
DOCUMENT: 1st Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Transparency Requirements for Natural Gas Products
ID: 22
CONTENT:
Regulation (EC) No 715/2009, including guidelines and network codes, applies to wholesale natural gas products. Article 19 stipulates transparency requirements for LNG and storage facilities. The Gas Comitology Committee revised Chapter 3 of Annex 1 of Regulation (EC) No 715/2009. Legally-binding transparency requirements are most detailed for transmission systems, with basic requirements for LNG and storage facilities and entry points according to revised Chapter 3 and ERGEG Guidelines for Good Practice. The Third Package offers possibilities to develop comitology guidelines for storage and LNG transparency. Existing thresholds for publication of real time flow information or de minimis exemptions at national level may be considered for interim periods.

SECTION: Agency Guidance on Inside Information Evolution
ID: 23
CONTENT:
The Agency believes that respect of transparency requirements is essential to avoid breaches of inside information rules. Further guidance will be provided as more experience with REMIT application is gained, as the definition of inside information will evolve over time. Adoption of Commission guidelines on fundamental data transparency may alter the understanding of inside information definition and applicable disclosure mechanisms. The Agency will update its guidance as necessary and constantly review guidance on inside information, publishing revised versions as appropriate.

SECTION: Conclusions on Inside Information Definition
ID: 24
CONTENT:
The Agency considers that the notion of inside information should currently be primarily understood in relation to: information required to be made public in accordance with Regulations (EC) No 714/2009 and (EC) No 715/2009, including guidelines and network codes; information required to be disclosed in accordance with other legal or regulatory provisions at Union or national level, insofar as likely to have significant effect on wholesale energy product prices; and any other information likely to have significant effect on wholesale electricity product prices if made public. These considerations apply until more experience is gained about inside information in wholesale energy markets.

SECTION: Introduction to Market Manipulation Types
ID: 25
CONTENT:
Chapter 3 provides NRAs with examples of market activities that fulfill the definition of market manipulation stipulated in Article 2(2) and (3) of REMIT. The guidance and examples help NRAs develop common understanding of market manipulation and facilitate identification of relevant variables (diagnostic flags or signals) that could be monitored by competent authorities and market participants to detect or avoid engaging in market manipulation. Examples are deliberately described in non-legal technical terms, and descriptions are not intended to affect the scope of interpretation of REMIT.

DOCUMENT: 1st Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: REMIT Definition of Market Manipulation - Four Elements
ID: 26
CONTENT:
Article 2(2) of REMIT distinguishes four elements of market manipulation: (1) market manipulation through false/misleading transactions, (2) price positioning, (3) transactions involving fictitious devices/deception, and (4) dissemination of false and misleading information. These include entering into transactions or issuing orders that give false or misleading signals as to supply, demand, or price of wholesale energy products; securing prices at artificial levels; employing fictitious devices or deception; or disseminating false information through media or other means. The acceptable market practice argument can only be used for price positioning (Article 2(2), lit. (a)(ii), and (3), lit. (a)(ii)), not for other categories.

SECTION: Attempted Market Manipulation Definition
ID: 27
CONTENT:
Article 2(3) of REMIT defines attempted market manipulation as entering into transactions, issuing orders, or taking actions relating to wholesale energy products with the intention of: giving false or misleading signals as to supply, demand, or price; securing prices at artificial levels (unless legitimate reasons and conformity with accepted market practices are established); employing fictitious devices or deception giving false or misleading signals; or disseminating information through media or other means with intention of giving false or misleading signals as to supply, demand, or price of wholesale energy products.

text:
DOCUMENT: 1st Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: REMIT Examples of Market Manipulation
ID: 28
CONTENT:
REMIT Recitals 13 and 14 provide examples of market manipulation: actions that artificially cause prices not justified by market forces of supply and demand, including actual availability of production, storage or transportation capacity. Forms include placing and withdrawal of false orders; spreading false or misleading information or rumours through media or internet; deliberately providing false information to price assessment undertakings; and deliberately misrepresenting availability of electricity generation capacity, natural gas availability, or transmission capacity. Manipulation may occur across borders, between electricity and gas markets, and across financial and commodity markets including emission allowances. Examples include conduct to secure decisive position over supply or demand with effect of fixing prices or creating unfair trading conditions; and offering, buying or selling products with purpose of misleading market participants based on reference prices.

metadata.original_text: REMIT Recitals 13 and 14 provide examples of market manipulation: actions that artificially cause prices not justified by market forces of supply and demand, including actual availability of production, storage or transportation capacity. Forms include placing and withdrawal of false orders; spreading false or misleading information or rumours through media or internet; deliberately providing false information to price assessment undertakings; and deliberately misrepresenting availability of electricity generation capacity, natural gas availability, or transmission capacity. Manipulation may occur across borders, between electricity and gas markets, and across financial and commodity markets including emission allowances. Examples include conduct to secure decisive position over supply or demand with effect of fixing prices or creating unfair trading conditions; and offering, buying or selling products with purpose of misleading market participants based on reference prices.

SECTION: Market Abuse Directive and Wholesale Energy Products
ID: 29
CONTENT:
Area definitions are currently defined by Article 1(5) of Directive 2003/6/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 28 January 2003 on insider dealing and market manipulation (market abuse). These definitions may be adapted if that Directive is amended. Securing a favourable price for a wholesale energy product through legitimate market practices is an acceptable approach for market participants.

DOCUMENT: 1st Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: False/Misleading Transactions - Wash Trades and Matched Orders
ID: 30
CONTENT:
Wash trades involve entering into arrangements for the sale or purchase of a wholesale energy product where there is no change in beneficial interests or market risk, or where the transfer of beneficial interest or market risk is only between parties acting in concert or collusion. Certain practices such as crossing/pre-arranged trades could be considered accepted market practices and do not constitute market manipulation if undertaken according to the rules of the relevant trading venue. Improper matched orders are transactions where both buy and sell orders are entered at or nearly at the same time, with the same price and quantity by different but colluding parties. These constitute market manipulation unless they are legitimate trades carried out in conformity with trading platform rules.

text:
DOCUMENT: 1st Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Placing Orders with No Intention of Execution
ID: 31
CONTENT:
This involves entering orders, especially into electronic trading systems, which are higher/lower than the previous bid/offer of the market participant concerned. The intention is not to execute the order but to give a misleading impression that there is demand for or supply of the wholesale energy product at that price. The orders are then withdrawn from the market before execution. A variant involves placing a small order to move the bid/offer price of the wholesale energy product, being prepared for that order to be executed if it cannot be withdrawn in time.

DOCUMENT: 1st Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Price Positioning - Marking the Close
ID: 32
CONTENT:
Marking the close involves deliberately buying or selling wholesale energy products at the close of the market in an effort to alter the closing price of the wholesale energy product. This practice may take place on any individual trading day but is particularly associated with dates such as future/option expiry dates or quarterly/annual portfolio or index reference/valuation points.

text:
DOCUMENT: 1st Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Abusive Squeeze and Market Cornering
ID: 33
CONTENT:
Abusive squeeze, also known as 'market cornering', involves a party or parties with a significant influence over the supply of, or demand for, or delivery mechanisms for a wholesale energy product and/or the underlying product of a derivative contract exploiting a decisive position in order materially to distort the price at which others have to deliver, take delivery or defer delivery of the instrument/product in order to satisfy their obligations. The proper interaction of supply and demand can and often does lead to market tightness, but this is not of itself market manipulation. Having a significant influence over the supply of, demand for, or delivery mechanisms for a wholesale energy product by itself does not constitute market manipulation.

DOCUMENT: 1st Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Cross-Market Manipulation
ID: 34
CONTENT:
Cross-market manipulation involves trading on one market to improperly position the price of a wholesale energy product on a related market. This practice involves undertaking trading in one market with a view to improperly influencing the price of the same or a related wholesale energy product in another market. An example might be trading in the underlying product of a wholesale energy derivative to distort the price of the derivative contract. Transactions to take legitimate advantage of differences in prices of wholesale energy derivatives or underlying products as traded in different locations - 'arbitrage' - would not constitute manipulation.

text:
DOCUMENT: 1st Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Physical Withholding and Supply Manipulation
ID: 35
CONTENT:
Actions undertaken by persons that artificially cause prices to be at a level not justified by market forces of supply and demand, including actual availability of production, storage or transportation capacity, and demand constitute physical withholding. This includes the practice where a market participant decides not to offer on the market all the available production, storage or transportation capacity, without justification and with the intention to shift the market price to higher levels. Examples include not offering on the market, without justification, a power plant whose marginal cost is lower than the spot prices, or misusing infrastructure and transmission capacities that would result in abnormally high prices.

DOCUMENT: 1st Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Dissemination of False or Misleading Market Information
ID: 36
CONTENT:
Dissemination of false or misleading market information through media, including the internet, or by any other means (in some jurisdictions known as 'scalping') is done with the intention of moving the price of a wholesale energy product in a direction that is favourable to the position held or a transaction planned by the person disseminating the information.

text:
DOCUMENT: 1st Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Pump and Dump Scheme
ID: 37
CONTENT:
Pump and dump involves taking a long position in a wholesale energy product and then undertaking further buying activity and/or disseminating misleading positive information about the wholesale energy product with a view to increasing the price. Other market participants are misled by the resulting effect on price and are attracted into purchasing the wholesale energy product. The manipulator then sells out at the inflated price.

text:
DOCUMENT: 1st Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Circular Trading and Pre-Arranged Trading
ID: 38
CONTENT:
Circular trading is the process of executing a sell order with the knowledge that an offsetting buy order is being placed at the exact same time. The action is considered illegal because it excludes competition. Pre-arranged trading is the practice of two commodity dealers trading with each other at prices upon which they have agreed in advance. Pre-arranged trading is designed to exclude other dealers from the market, to gain a tax advantage, or both, and is therefore illegal. Certain more specific practices such as crossing/pre-arranged trades could be considered accepted market practices if undertaken according to the rules of the relevant trading venue.

SECTION: Dissemination of False and Misleading Information Without Transactions
ID: 39
CONTENT:
This type of market manipulation involves dissemination of false and misleading information without necessarily undertaking any accompanying transaction. This could include creating a misleading impression by failure properly to disclose a price sensitive piece of information which should be disclosed. For example, a market participant with information which would meet the Regulation's definition of 'inside information' fails properly to disclose that information with the result that the market is likely to be misled.

DOCUMENT: 1st Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Spreading False Information Through Media and Other Channels
ID: 40
CONTENT:
Spreading false/misleading information through the media involves behaviour such as posting information via internet or issuing a press release which contains false or misleading statements about a wholesale energy product which is admitted to trading on an organised market. The person spreading the information knows that it is false or misleading and is disseminating the information in order to create a false or misleading impression. Spreading false/misleading information through an officially recognised channel for disseminating information to users of an organised market is particularly serious as it is important that market participants are able to rely on information dissemination via such official channels. Other behaviour designed to spread false/misleading information would cover a course of conduct designed to give false and misleading impression through means other than the media, such as the movement of physical commodity stocks to create a misleading impression as to the supply or demand for a commodity.

text:
DOCUMENT: 1st Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Conclusions on Market Manipulation Examples
ID: 41
CONTENT:
The examples of various types of practices which could constitute market manipulation are inspired by European energy regulators' own experiences and the experiences in financial markets made by financial market authorities, with whom ACER and NRAs will closely cooperate in the application of REMIT. These examples can currently be taken as an indication for possible signals of market manipulation in wholesale energy markets according to REMIT. Market participants' behaviour must be coherent with their technical and economic constraints in a way to comply with competition law, especially concerning market power exercise. The Agency will constantly review its Guidance on market manipulation and publish a revised non-binding Guidance if considered appropriate.

DOCUMENT: 1st Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Duty to Establish Effective Arrangements and Procedures
ID: 43
CONTENT:
Article 15 of REMIT requires that 'any person professionally arranging transactions in wholesale energy products who reasonably suspects that a transaction might breach Articles 3 or 5 shall notify the NRA without further delay. Persons professionally arranging transactions in wholesale energy products shall establish and maintain effective arrangements and procedures to identify breaches of Articles 3 or 5.' The regulation and its implementing measures do not deal with the steps which the persons subject to this requirement need to take to identify such transactions. Those who are subject to the requirement clearly need to ensure that they comply with this obligation. The duty applies to any person professionally arranging transactions in wholesale energy products, including at least trading venues like energy exchanges and brokers. The Agency currently considers independent market surveillance departments in the case of energy exchanges and compliance officers in the case of brokers as best practices of effective arrangements to identify breaches of the prohibitions of market abuse.

SECTION: Market Surveillance and Compliance Mechanisms
ID: 44
CONTENT:
For market surveillance and compliance in the EU financial market legislation may serve as a guidance to establish and maintain such mechanisms. The notification regime laid down by REMIT requires that persons subject to it decide on a case-by-case basis where there are reasonable grounds for suspicion concerning the relevant transaction. The indications given are neither exhaustive (a particular transaction may be suspicious even if it matches none of the indications) nor determinative (a transaction may not necessarily be suspicious simply because it matches one or more of the indications).

ID: 45
CONTENT:
Examples of indications are only a starting point for consideration of whether a transaction is suspicious and are neither conclusive nor comprehensive. They are to be applied using judgement rather than necessarily being interpreted literally. It is recognised that transactions meeting signals may be legitimate and hence not give reasonable grounds for suspicion.

SECTION: Possible Signals of Insider Dealing
ID: 46
CONTENT:
The following events may be considered as signals of potential insider trading situations: a) significant trading by major market participants before the announcement of information having a significant price effect; b) transactions resulting in sudden and unusual changes in the volume of orders and prices before the announcement of information having a significant price effect.

DOCUMENT: 1st Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Possible Signals of Market Manipulation - False or Misleading Signals
ID: 47
CONTENT:
Non-exhaustive signals which should not necessarily be deemed in themselves to constitute market manipulation may be taken into account when transactions or orders to trade are examined by persons professionally arranging transactions related to false or misleading signals and to price securing: a) the extent to which orders to trade given or transactions undertaken represent a significant proportion of the daily volume of transactions in the relevant wholesale energy product on the trading venue concerned, in particular when these activities lead to a significant change in the price of the wholesale energy product; b) the extent to which orders to trade given or transactions undertaken by persons with a significant buying or selling position in a wholesale energy product lead to significant changes in the price of the wholesale energy product or a related wholesale energy product admitted to trading on a trading venue; c) whether transactions undertaken lead to no change in beneficial ownership of a wholesale energy product admitted to trading on a trading venue.

SECTION: Market Manipulation Signals - Position Reversals and Price Changes
ID: 48
CONTENT:
Additional signals for market manipulation examination: d) the extent to which orders to trade given or transactions undertaken include position reversals in a short period and represent a significant proportion of the daily volume of transactions in the relevant wholesale energy product on the trading venue concerned, and might be associated with significant changes in the price of a wholesale energy product admitted to trading on a trading venue; e) the extent to which orders to trade given or transactions undertaken are concentrated within a short time span in the trading session and lead to a price change which is subsequently reversed; f) the extent to which orders to trade given change the representation of the best bid or offer prices in a wholesale energy product admitted to trading on a trading venue, or more generally the representation of the order book available to market participants, and are removed before they are executed; g) the extent to which orders to trade are given or transactions are undertaken at or around a specific time when reference prices, settlement prices and valuations are calculated and lead to price changes which have an effect on such prices and valuations.

text:
DOCUMENT: 1st Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Method of Reporting Suspicious Transactions
ID: 50
CONTENT:
Any person professionally arranging transactions in wholesale energy products who reasonably suspects that a transaction might breach Article 3 or 5 of REMIT shall notify the competent NRA without further delay of all relevant information available. Where not all the relevant information is available at the time of notification, the notification shall include at least the reasons why the notifying persons suspect that the transaction might constitute insider dealing or market manipulation. All remaining information shall be provided to the competent authority as soon as it becomes available. Notification can be effected by mail, electronic mail, telecopy or telephone, provided that in the latter case, written confirmation is provided upon request by the competent authority.

text:
DOCUMENT: 1st Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Urgent Notification Procedures and Reporting Format
ID: 51
CONTENT:
Persons making suspicious transactions reports do not need to have all the required information before contacting the competent authority. If there is a need to alert the competent authority urgently, NRAs should receive notifications as soon as possible, even before all aspects of the transaction and all related information become known. This contact may take place by telephone if appropriate, giving the basic details and reasons for suspicion. The Agency recommends using a standard reporting format for suspicious transaction reporting. The format should include: Description of the transaction(s), Reasons for suspecting insider dealing/market manipulation, Identities of the market participant carrying out the transaction(s), Identities of any other market participant known to be involved, Further information which may be of significance, and Details of the person submitting the notification.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Preface by the Director on the 1st Edition
ID: 4
CONTENT:
Following its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union on 8 December 2011, Regulation (EU) No 1227/2011 on wholesale market integrity and transparency (REMIT) entered into force on 28 December 2011. Whilst the obligations for wholesale energy market participants to register with the competent National Regulatory Authority (NRA) and to provide the Agency for the Cooperation of Energy Regulators (the Agency) with records of transactions and information related to the capacity and use of energy facilities would only come into force after the adoption of implementing acts by the European Commission, the prohibitions of insider trading and market manipulation, the obligation to publish inside information and the obligations for persons professionally arranging transactions to establish and maintain effective arrangements and procedures to identify suspected breaches apply as of 28 December 2011. According to Article 16(1) of REMIT, the Agency shall aim to ensure that NRAs carry out their tasks under REMIT in a coordinated and consistent way.

ID: 5
CONTENT:
The Agency shall publish non-binding Guidance on the application of the definitions set out in Article 2 of REMIT, as appropriate. The entry into force of REMIT and of the aforementioned prohibitions and obligations was considered an appropriate moment to publish the First Edition of such Guidance. The Guidance is updated in later editions on the basis of the experience gained by the Agency and NRAs in the implementation of REMIT, including through feedback from energy market participants and other stakeholders. The 1st edition of ACER Guidance on the application of REMIT definitions was published on 21 December 2011, one week before the entry into force of REMIT, focusing on providing guidance to NRAs in priority areas. The 1st edition was well received by stakeholders. Less than a year later, the 2nd edition was published, taking into account the experience gained so far, including through feedback from NRAs, energy market participants and other stakeholders. In this 2nd edition, the Guidance was updated on the application of the market abuse definitions and extended to the scope of REMIT in relation to EU financial market legislation, the application of definitions of wholesale energy market, wholesale energy products and market participant, the application of the obligation to disclose inside information and the application and implementation of the prohibitions against market abuse.

ID: 8
CONTENT:

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Scope of the Regulation
ID: 12
CONTENT:
According to Article 1(2) of REMIT, the Regulation applies to trading in wholesale energy products. Articles 3 and 5 of REMIT shall not apply to wholesale energy products which are financial instruments subject to Article 9 of Directive 2003/6/EC. REMIT is without prejudice to Directives 2003/6/EC and 2004/39/EC and European competition law. Article 1(2) requires defining a borderline between market abuse prohibitions of REMIT Articles 3 and 5 versus the Market Abuse Directive (MAD). However, Article 4(1) of REMIT on disclosure of inside information applies regardless of whether the wholesale energy product is a financial instrument.

DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Financial Instruments and Market Abuse Directive Application
ID: 13
CONTENT:
According to Article 9(1) of MAD, the Directive applies to any financial instrument admitted to trading on a regulated market in at least one Member State, or for which admission has been requested, irrespective of whether transactions actually take place on that market. Article 9(2) of MAD extends application to financial instruments not admitted to trading but whose value depends on admitted financial instruments. The list of financial instruments subject to MAD includes derivatives on commodities and instruments admitted to trading on regulated markets. Any wholesale energy product which is a financial instrument but not admitted to trading on a regulated market in a Member State would be covered by REMIT market abuse prohibitions instead of MAD.

SECTION: Wholesale Energy Products Definition
ID: 16
CONTENT:
Article 2(4) of REMIT defines wholesale energy products as contracts and derivatives, irrespective of where and how they are traded: (a) contracts for supply of electricity or natural gas where delivery is in the Union; (b) derivatives relating to electricity or natural gas produced, traded or delivered in the Union; (c) contracts relating to transportation of electricity or natural gas in the Union; (d) derivatives relating to transportation of electricity or natural gas in the Union. Contracts for supply and distribution of electricity or natural gas for use of final customers are not wholesale energy products.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Wholesale Energy Products - Definition and Scope
ID: 18
CONTENT:
Distribution of electricity or natural gas to final customers with a consumption capacity greater than the threshold set out in the second paragraph of point (5) shall be treated as wholesale energy products. Article 2(5) of REMIT clarifies the notion of 'consumption capacity' relevant for the understanding of the notion of 'wholesale energy products': 'consumption capacity' means the consumption of a final customer of either electricity or natural gas at full use of that customer's production capacity. It comprises all consumption by that customer as a single economic entity, in so far as consumption takes place on markets with interrelated wholesale prices. For the purposes of this definition, consumption at individual plants under the control of a single economic entity that have a consumption capacity of less than 600 GWh per year shall not be taken into account in so far as those plants do not exert a joint influence on wholesale energy market prices due to their being located in different relevant geographical markets.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Contracts and Derivatives as Wholesale Energy Products
ID: 19
CONTENT:
In view of the definition of wholesale energy products in Article 2(4) of REMIT, the Agency considers contracts for the supply or transportation of electricity and gas traded intraday, withinday, day-ahead, two-days-ahead, weekend, long-term or any other time period generally accepted in the market as contracts for the supply or transportation of electricity or natural gas. Derivatives are understood as financial instruments as set out in points (4) to (10) of Section C of Annex I to Directive 2004/39/EC as implemented in Articles 38 and 39 of Regulation (EC) No 1287/2006. Conversely, the Agency considers contracts for green certificates and emission allowances not to be wholesale energy products as they do not fulfil the requirements set out in Article 2(4) of REMIT. The Agency is aware that these contracts can have a significant price effect on wholesale energy markets. According to Article 10 of REMIT, emission allowances or derivatives relating to emission allowances collected by trade repositories or competent authorities overseeing trading in emission allowances or derivatives thereof shall be provided to the Agency together with access to records of transactions in such allowances and derivatives. As the definition of wholesale energy products applies to contracts and derivatives 'irrespective of how and where they are traded', the Agency considers that intragroup transactions, i.e. over-the-counter (OTC) contracts entered into with another counterparty which is part of the same group, are considered to be wholesale energy products under REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Wholesale Energy Market - Definition and Components
ID: 20
CONTENT:
Article 2(6) of REMIT defines a wholesale energy market as follows: 'wholesale energy market' means any market within the Union on which wholesale energy products are traded. According to Recital 5 of REMIT, wholesale energy markets encompass both commodity markets and derivative markets, which are of vital importance to the energy and financial markets, and price formation in both sectors is interlinked. They include, inter alia, regulated markets, multilateral trading facilities and over-the-counter (OTC) transactions and bilateral contracts, direct or through brokers. The Agency's understanding is that the definition of wholesale energy markets furthermore includes, among others, but not limited to: Balancing markets for the trading of electricity or natural gas with delivery in the Union; Intraday or withinday markets for the trading of electricity or natural gas with delivery in the Union; Day-ahead or two-day-ahead markets for the trading of electricity or natural gas with delivery in the Union, including weekend products; Physical markets for the trading of electricity or natural gas with delivery in the Union, including markets for physical forward contracts and non-standardised long-term contracts; Markets for the transportation capacities of electricity or natural gas in the Union; Derivatives markets relating to electricity or natural gas produced, traded or delivered in the Union, including financial OTC markets; Derivatives markets relating to the transportation of electricity or natural gas in the Union. In future, also generation capacity markets (CRM) may have to be considered.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Market Participant - Definition and Obligations
ID: 21
CONTENT:
Article 2(7) of REMIT defines a market participant as follows: 'market participant' means any person, including transmission system operators, who enters into transactions, including the placing of orders to trade, in one or more wholesale energy markets. The notion of a market participant is closely linked with the understanding of the notions of wholesale energy market and wholesale energy products. The understanding of the notion of market participant is crucial for several reasons. Firstly, the obligation to disclose inside information according to Article 4(1) of REMIT lies with the market participant. Secondly, according to Article 8(1) of REMIT, being a market participant entails the obligation to provide the Agency (i) with a record of wholesale energy market transactions, including orders to trade, by the market participant itself or through a person or authority listed in points (b) to (f) of Article 8(4) of REMIT and (ii) with the information described in Article 8(5) of REMIT. Lastly, pursuant to Article 9(1) of REMIT, market participants have to register with the competent NRA if entering into transactions which are required to be reported to the Agency in accordance with Article 8(1) of REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Categories of Market Participants
ID: 22
CONTENT:
In the light of the Agency's understanding of the notions of wholesale energy market and wholesale energy products, the Agency currently considers at least the following persons to be market participants under REMIT if entering into transactions, including orders to trade, in one or more wholesale energy markets: Energy trading companies in the meaning of 'electricity undertaking' pursuant to Article 2(35) of Directive 2009/72/EC carrying out at least one of the following functions: transportation, supply, or purchase of electricity, and in the meaning of 'natural gas undertaking' pursuant to Article 2(1) of Directive 2009/73/EC carrying out at least one of the following functions: transportation, supply or purchase of natural gas, including LNG; Producers of electricity or natural gas in the meaning of Article 2(2) of Directive 2009/72/EC and Article 2(1) of Directive 2009/73/EC, including producers supplying their production to their in-house trading unit or energy trading company; Shippers of natural gas; Wholesale customers in the meaning of Article 2(8) of Directive 2009/72/EC and Article 2(29) of Directive 2009/73/EC; Final customers in the meaning of Article 2(9) of Directive 2009/72/EC and Article 2(27) of Directive 2009/73/EC, unless only entering into contracts for the supply and distribution of electricity or natural gas for their own full use of consumption capacity of less than 600 GWh; Transmission system operators (TSOs) in the meaning of Article 2(4) of Directive 2009/72/EC and Directive 2009/73/EC; Storage system operators (SSOs) in the meaning of Article 2(10) of Directive 2009/73/EC; LNG system operators (LSOs) in the meaning of Article 2(12) of Directive 2009/73/EC, and Investment firms in the meaning of Article 4(1) No 1 of Directive 2004/39/EC.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Storage and LNG System Operators - Special Considerations
ID: 23
CONTENT:
The crucial criterion for the assessment of whether a company is a market participant is the entering into transactions, including the placing of orders to trade, in wholesale energy markets. For instance, SSOs and LSOs are explicitly mentioned as market participants in Article 3(4)(b) of REMIT and are therefore considered as market participants if entering into transactions in one or more wholesale energy market. LSOs may sell contracts which eventually lead to the feed in or extraction of gas from the gas network. In several markets, some SSOs conclude contracts for the supply of gas in cases where storage facilities experience operational problems, but despite the malfunction, seek to provide customers with gas and therefore acquire volumes over the spot market. As a result of this and for the purposes of REMIT, these LSOs and SSOs are market participants and are required to publish inside information according to Article 4(1) of REMIT. Information related to the capacity and use of facilities for storage and the use of LNG facilities is considered inside information according to Article 4(1) of REMIT and considered to be reported to the Agency according to Article 8(5) of REMIT. SSOs and LSOs seem to be best placed to fulfill this disclosure obligation and data reporting requirement under REMIT. Accordingly, the Agency considers it as best practice if SSOs and LSOs, even if not entering into transactions in wholesale energy products, facilitate publication of information in relation to Article 4(1) of REMIT on behalf of the potentially multiple market participants involved. The system operator is typically best placed to publish relevant REMIT related information and by doing so can avoid duplicate, and potentially misleading publications by individual market participants involved. Market participants should however ensure they have backup arrangements for publication to cover situations where the system operator is not able to publish, for instance due to technical reasons, or where the system operator's publication of information is not deemed to have met the requirements for publication of information under Article 4(1) of REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Application of REMIT to Non-EU and Non-EEA Market Participants
ID: 24
CONTENT:
The Agency also considers it necessary to give further guidance on the application of the notion of market participant on market participants from non-EU and non-EEA countries. According to Article 2(6) of REMIT, a market participant is any person who enters into transactions in one or more wholesale energy markets. This applies irrespective of the location of the person. Accordingly, also persons from non-EU and non-EEA countries are covered by REMIT provided that they enter into transactions in wholesale energy markets. Article 9(1) of REMIT confirms this understanding that REMIT also applies to market participants from non-EU and non-EEA countries as it requires market participants not established or resident in the Union entering into transactions which are required to be reported to the Agency in accordance with Article 8(1) of REMIT, to register in a Member State in which they are active. In the light of the above, the Agency considers that also non-EU and non-EEA market participants are covered by the notion of market participant according to Article 2(7) of REMIT if entering into transactions, including the placing of orders to trade, in one or more wholesale energy markets. Accordingly, the obligations to register pursuant to Article 9(1) of REMIT with the competent NRA and to report data to the Agency according to Article 8(1) and (5) of REMIT also applies to such non-EU and non-EEA market participants. The same holds for the prohibitions of market abuse pursuant to Articles 3 and 5 of REMIT.

DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: REMIT Information Definition and Criteria
ID: 26
CONTENT:
Article 2(1), second subparagraph, of REMIT clarifies what is meant by the term 'information' as follows: (a) information which is required to be made public in accordance with Regulations (EC) No 714/2009 and (EC) No 715/2009, including guidelines and network codes adopted pursuant to those Regulations; (b) information relating to the capacity and use of facilities for production, storage, consumption or transmission of electricity or natural gas or related to the capacity and use of LNG facilities, including planned or unplanned unavailability of these facilities; (c) information which is required to be disclosed in accordance with legal or regulatory provisions at Union or national level, market rules, and contracts or customs on the relevant wholesale energy market, insofar as this information is likely to have a significant effect on the prices of wholesale energy products; and (d) other information that a reasonable market participant would be likely to use as part of the basis of its decision to enter into a transaction relating to, or to issue an order to trade in, a wholesale energy product.

SECTION: Inside Information Qualification Requirements
ID: 27
CONTENT:
In order to consider an information an inside information, it still has to fulfil all four criteria of Article 2(1), first subparagraph, of REMIT: that the information must be of a precise nature, that it has not been made public, that it relates, directly or indirectly, to one or more wholesale energy products and that, if made public, it would be likely to significantly affect the prices of those wholesale energy products. The Agency considers that it is possible to identify separately the factors which should be taken into account in respect of each criterion.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Transparency Information versus Inside Information
ID: 28
CONTENT:
The concept of 'transparency information' contains all data that shall be published under the transparency obligation of Regulations (EC) No 714/2009 and (EC) No 715/2009, including applicable guidelines and network codes. The concept of 'inside information' comprises on the one hand only those transparency information that is likely to have a significant effect on the prices of wholesale energy products, but on the other hand goes even beyond and also includes other information that a reasonable market participant would be likely to use as part of the basis of its decision to enter into a transaction relating to, or to issue an order to trade in, a wholesale energy product, insofar as this information is likely to have a significant effect on the prices of wholesale energy products. Transparency information is periodic, structured data subject to Regulations (EC) No 714/2009 and (EC) No 715/2009. Inside information should be considered as an ad hoc, structured data that is likely to have a significant effect on price that has not been disclosed to the market.

SECTION: Scope of Inside Information - Facility Capacity and Use
ID: 29
CONTENT:
Inside information may relate to any item of information within the scope of applicable regulations as well as the following further information insofar as this information is likely to have a significant effect on the prices of wholesale energy products: Information relating to the capacity and use of facilities for production of electricity or natural gas, including planned and unplanned unavailability of these facilities; Information relating to the capacity and use of facilities for storage of electricity or natural gas, including planned and unplanned availability of these facilities; Information relating to the capacity and use of facilities for consumption of electricity or natural gas, including planned and unplanned unavailability of these facilities; Information relating to the capacity and use of facilities for transmission, including planned or unplanned unavailability of these facilities; Information relating to the capacity and use of LNG facilities, including planned and unplanned unavailability of these facilities.

DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Scope of Inside Information - Legal, Regulatory, and Market Requirements
ID: 30
CONTENT:
Inside information may also include: Information required to be issued in accordance with legal or regulatory provisions at Union or National level; Information required to be issued in accordance with Market Rules; Information required to be issued in accordance with Contracts; Information required to be issued in accordance with Customs on the market; and other information that a reasonable market participant would be likely to use as part of the basis of its decision to enter into a transaction relating to, or to issue an order to trade in, a wholesale energy product. The interpretation of 'inside information' is likely to be subject to interpretation of national and European Courts and has to take into account rulings on the definition of inside information under MAD insofar as the same concepts are applied under this Directive and under REMIT.

DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Precise Nature of Information
ID: 31
CONTENT:
Article 2(1), third subparagraph, of REMIT provides indications as to what is meant by the term 'information of precise nature': Information shall be deemed to be of a precise nature if it indicates a set of circumstances which exists or may reasonably be expected to come into existence, or an event which has occurred or may reasonably be expected to do so, and if it is specific enough to enable a conclusion to be drawn as to the possible effect of that set of circumstances or event on the prices of wholesale energy products. The precise nature of the information is to be assessed by the holder of the information on a case-by-case basis and depends on what the information is and on the surrounding context.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Trading Plans and Strategies Exclusion
ID: 32
CONTENT:
According to Recital 12 of REMIT, information regarding the market participant's own plans and strategies for trading should not be considered as inside information. The Agency currently considers 'trading plans' as a systematic method for screening and evaluating wholesale energy products, determining the amount of risk that is or should be taken, and formulating short and long-term investment objectives. A successful trading plan will also involve details like the type of trading system to be used. Most plans require the use of various types of technical analysis tools. The Agency furthermore considers 'trading strategies' as a set of objective rules designating the conditions that must be met for trade entries and exits to occur. A trading strategy includes specifications for trade entries, including trade filters and triggers, as well as rules for trade exits, money management, timeframes, order types, etc.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Made Public - Broad Trading Public Access
ID: 33
CONTENT:
Inside information is deemed to be public knowledge if such information has been made available to the broad trading public, i.e. an unspecified number of individuals. In this regard it is irrelevant who made the inside information public. No distinction is made as to whether the inside information were made public by the market participant or by any other party. It is sufficient, but also required, that inside information is made available simultaneously to the broad trading public, ensuring equal access to the information since any interested market participant may apprise themselves of the inside information (a concept referred to as 'sectoral publicity'). This can be the case, for example, if a generally accessible electronic system for the dissemination of information is used, but does not require publication in the media.

DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Made Public - Energy Exchange and News Board Limitations
ID: 34
CONTENT:
Publishing inside information within an energy exchange information service or news board available only to selected participants does not satisfy the requirement of informing the broad trading public. In this context the Agency has considered real-time power data services, i.e. companies measuring real-time production at different power plants and selling these data to subscribers of the service. The Agency deems that the information provided through such services is considered to be publicly available as soon as the information is published by the provider. The Agency has not found any indication that these services are not available to everyone who wishes to subscribe to them.

DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Made Public - Real-Time Services and Partial Information
ID: 35
CONTENT:
A market participant responsible for disclosing the information may be holding inside information even though part of the information is published through a real-time service. Any information such as the cause of the incident, the duration etc. which are not published by the provider of real-time services could still to be considered as inside information (if that information is or subsequently becomes known to the market participant). Therefore market participants should not only rely on such service providers to publish inside information on their behalf.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Significant Price Effect - Likelihood Assessment
ID: 36
CONTENT:
Information is deemed to constitute inside information only if the circumstances on which the information is based would, if it became publicly known, likely have significant effect on the prices of a wholesale energy product. The Agency understands the criterion of significant price effect to narrow the wide notion of information down to that information which is crucial enough in order to have a potential to significantly affect prices. According to Article 2(1) of REMIT, the likelihood to significantly affect the prices of wholesale energy products is sufficient in order for the information to be qualified as inside information. Hence, no actual price effect is required.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Significant Price Effect - Assessment Methodology
ID: 37
CONTENT:
The concept of likelihood requires an assessment of the extent to which such circumstances would affect the price of a wholesale energy product if they were made public. Such an assessment has to take into consideration the anticipated impact of the information in light of the related market participant's activity, as well as the market situation, including specificities of the market (size of the market, balance of demand and supply, steepness of the relevant offer curve - correlated with demand but also with already existing production limitations, information on supply variation already published, time of day - e.g. weekday/weekend, office hours/out of office hours, etc.) and any other market variables likely to affect the related wholesale energy product in the given circumstances. Ex-post information may be used to check the presumption that the information has a significant price effect, but should not be used to take action against someone who drew reasonable conclusions from such presumption.

SECTION: Significant Price Effect - Useful Indicators
ID: 38
CONTENT:
The Agency currently considers that the following should be taken into consideration as useful indicators of whether information is likely to have a significant price effect: the type of information is the same as information which has, in the past, had a significant effect on prices; pre-existing analysts research reports, price reporter publications and opinions indicate that the type of information in question has effects on prices; the market participant itself has already treated similar events as inside information; another reasonable market participant has already treated similar events as inside information.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Inside Information Indicators and REMIT Examples
ID: 39
CONTENT:
Factors indicating inside information should not be treated as definitive in determining whether information will necessarily have a significant price effect. REMIT provides examples of inside information in its Recitals 12 and 15. The use or attempted use of inside information to trade on one's own account or on behalf of a third party is clearly prohibited. Use of inside information can consist in trading in wholesale energy products by persons who know, or ought to know, that the information they possess is inside information. Information regarding a market participant's own plans and strategies for trading should not be considered as inside information. Information required to be made public under Regulation (EC) No 714/2009 or Regulation (EC) No 715/2009, including guidelines and network codes, may serve as the basis for market participants' decisions and could constitute inside information until made public if it is price-sensitive.

DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Journalist Disclosure of Inside Information
ID: 40
CONTENT:
The disclosure of inside information in relation to a wholesale energy product by journalists acting in their professional capacity should be assessed taking into account the rules governing their profession and the rules governing freedom of the press. However, this exception does not apply when those persons derive, directly or indirectly, an advantage or profits from the dissemination of the information, or when disclosure is made with the intention of misleading the market as to the supply of, demand for, or price of wholesale energy products.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Inside Information in Wholesale Electricity Markets
ID: 41
CONTENT:
Regulation (EC) No 714/2009, including guidelines and network codes, places obligations on TSOs to provide information on transmission infrastructure and its use, generation, load, balancing, and wholesale market aspects. Market participants must provide TSOs with relevant data for publication. Information on network infrastructure includes capacity allocation, congestion management procedures, and operational and planning security standards. Published information includes data on available transmission capacity, capacity used, aggregated commercial and physical flows, and planned and unplanned outages of generation units larger than 100 MW. Forecast demand and generation information, as well as realized values, must also be published. Examples of inside information for wholesale electricity products include any planned outage, limitation, expansion or dismantling of capacity of one generation unit, consumption or transmission facility that equals or exceeds 100 MW, including changes of such plans, and any unplanned outage or failure of capacity that equals or exceeds 100 MW for one generation unit, consumption or transmission facility, including updates on such outages or failures.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Inside Information in Wholesale Gas Markets
ID: 42
CONTENT:
Regulation (EC) No 715/2009 stipulates transparency requirements for market participants, including requirements for LNG and storage facilities according to Article 19. Legally-binding transparency requirements are most detailed for transmission systems, with basic transparency requirements for LNG and storage facilities and entry points according to Chapter 3 of Annex 1 of Regulation (EC) No 715/2009 and ERGEG Guidelines for Good Practice. Examples of inside information for wholesale gas products include any information relevant to the capacity and use of facilities for production, storage, consumption, or transmission of natural gas, including planned or unplanned unavailability of these facilities, and any information related to the capacity and use of LNG facilities, including planned or unplanned unavailability.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Gas Market Thresholds and National Regulation
ID: 43
CONTENT:
Since gas markets differ in size, structure and liquidity, it is not currently possible to define one single European threshold for inside information that would be of practical value. There are no thresholds in the transparency rules either. For this reason, National Regulatory Authorities (NRAs), after proper market consultation, may define an indicative threshold for the relevant gas market in accordance with the Accepted Market Practices regime. The threshold should be made available through the ACER website. By collating threshold data, the Agency will provide market participants active in more than one Member State with an overview of thresholds Europe-wide. The nationally set threshold can be revised by the relevant NRA to account for possible developments, considering feedback from market participants. This approach should apply until transparency guidelines according to Regulation (EC) No 715/2009 stipulate a threshold at European level.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Conclusions on Inside Information Definition
ID: 44
CONTENT:
In view of limited experiences with the application of inside information definition in wholesale energy markets, the notion of 'inside information' should currently be primarily understood in relation to information required to be made public under Regulations (EC) No 714/2009 and (EC) No 715/2009, including guidelines and network codes, and information required to be disclosed under other legal or regulatory provisions at Union or national level, insofar as this information is likely to have a significant effect on wholesale energy product prices. Experience will show which other information is likely to have a significant price effect. Respect of transparency requirements is currently essential to avoid breaches of inside information rules. Further guidance will be provided as more experience on REMIT application is gained. The definition of inside information will evolve over time, and adoption of Commission guidelines on fundamental data transparency may alter the understanding of inside information and applicable disclosure mechanisms. The Agency will constantly review its guidance and publish revised versions as appropriate.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Introduction to Market Manipulation Definition
ID: 45
CONTENT:
This chapter provides NRAs with examples of market activities that would fulfill the definition of market manipulation stipulated in Article 2(2) and (3) of REMIT. The guidance and accompanying examples are intended to help NRAs develop a common understanding of what constitutes market manipulation. The guidance and examples could facilitate the identification of relevant variables, diagnostic flags, or signals of market manipulation that could be monitored by competent authorities and market participants to detect or avoid engaging in market manipulation. The examples of types of practice are deliberately described in non-legal technical terms, and the descriptions are not intended to affect the scope of interpretation of REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: REMIT Definition of Market Manipulation Elements
ID: 46
CONTENT:
Article 2(2) of REMIT distinguishes four elements of market manipulation: (1) market manipulation through false or misleading transactions, (2) price positioning, (3) transactions involving fictitious devices or deception, and (4) dissemination of false and misleading information. These include entering into any transaction or issuing any order to trade in wholesale energy products which gives, or is likely to give, false or misleading signals as to the supply of, demand for, or price of wholesale energy products; secures or attempts to secure, by a person or persons acting in collaboration, the price of one or several wholesale energy products at an artificial level, unless the person establishes that their reasons are legitimate and the transaction conforms to accepted market practices; or employs or attempts to employ a fictitious device or any other form of deception or contrivance which gives, or is likely to give, false or misleading signals regarding supply, demand, or price. Additionally, disseminating information through media, including the internet, or by any other means, which gives, or is likely to give, false or misleading signals as to the supply of wholesale energy products constitutes market manipulation.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Market Manipulation Definition under REMIT
ID: 47
CONTENT:
Market manipulation includes dissemination of rumours and false or misleading news regarding wholesale energy products, where the disseminating person knew or ought to have known the information was false or misleading. When information is disseminated for journalism or artistic expression, assessment takes into account freedom of press and expression rules, unless: (i) those persons derive directly or indirectly an advantage or profits from dissemination; or (ii) disclosure is made with intention to mislead the market as to supply, demand, or price of wholesale energy products.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Attempted Market Manipulation under REMIT Article 2(3)
ID: 48
CONTENT:
Attempted market manipulation includes: (a) entering into transactions, issuing orders to trade, or taking actions relating to wholesale energy products with intention to: (i) give false or misleading signals as to supply, demand, or price; (ii) secure prices at artificial levels, unless reasons are legitimate and conform to accepted market practices; or (iii) employ fictitious devices or deception giving false signals; or (b) disseminating information through media or other means with intention of giving false or misleading signals. The 'acceptable market practice' argument can only be used for price positioning categories, not other categories.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: REMIT Examples of Market Manipulation - Recitals 13 and 14
ID: 49
CONTENT:
Manipulation involves actions that artificially cause prices not justified by market forces of supply and demand, including actual availability of production, storage or transportation capacity. Forms include: placing and withdrawal of false orders; spreading false or misleading information through media or internet; deliberately providing false information to price assessment undertakings; and deliberately misrepresenting availability of electricity generation, natural gas, or transmission capacity. Effects may occur across borders, between electricity and gas markets, and across financial and commodity markets including emission allowances. Examples include securing decisive positions over supply or demand with price-fixing effects, and offering or buying/selling products to mislead market participants based on reference prices.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: False and Misleading Transactions - Wash Trades
ID: 50
CONTENT:
Wash trades involve arrangements for sale or purchase of wholesale energy products where there is no change in beneficial interests or market risk, or where transfer occurs only between colluding parties. Certain specific practices like crossing or pre-arranged trades may be considered accepted market practices and thus not constitute manipulation, provided they are undertaken according to relevant trading venue rules. Conduct in conformity with trading venue rules is generally sufficient to promote market integrity.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: False and Misleading Transactions - Improper Matched Orders and Phantom Orders
ID: 51
CONTENT:
Improper matched orders are transactions where both buy and sell orders are entered at or nearly the same time, with same price and quantity by different colluding parties. These constitute market manipulation unless they are legitimate trades in conformity with trading platform rules. Placing orders with no intention of executing them involves entering orders higher or lower than previous bid/offer to give misleading impression of demand or supply, then withdrawing before execution. A variant places small orders to move bid/offer prices while being prepared for execution if withdrawal fails.

DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Price Positioning - Marking the Close
ID: 52
CONTENT:
Marking the close involves deliberately buying or selling wholesale energy products at market close to alter closing prices. This may occur on any trading day but is particularly associated with future/option expiry dates or quarterly/annual portfolio or index reference/valuation points.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Price Positioning - Abusive Squeeze and Market Cornering
ID: 53
CONTENT:
Abusive squeeze involves a party or parties with significant influence over supply, demand, or delivery mechanisms for wholesale energy products exploiting a decisive position to materially distort prices at which others must deliver, take delivery, or defer delivery to satisfy obligations. Proper supply and demand interaction can lead to market tightness without constituting manipulation. Having significant influence over supply, demand, or delivery mechanisms by itself does not constitute market manipulation.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Price Positioning - Cross-Market Manipulation and Physical Withholding
ID: 54
CONTENT:
Cross-market manipulation involves trading on one market to improperly position prices on related markets, such as trading underlying products of derivatives to distort derivative contract prices. Legitimate arbitrage transactions exploiting price differences across locations do not constitute manipulation. Physical withholding occurs when market participants decide not to offer available production, storage or transportation capacity without justification, intending to shift prices higher, such as not offering power plants with marginal costs below spot prices or misusing infrastructure to create abnormally high prices.

DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Fictitious Devices and Deception - False Information Dissemination
ID: 55
CONTENT:
Dissemination of false or misleading market information through media, internet, or other means (known as 'scalping' in some jurisdictions) is done with intention to move wholesale energy product prices in directions favourable to positions held or transactions planned by the disseminating person.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Fictitious Devices and Deception - Pump and Dump, Circular Trading, Pre-arranged Trading
ID: 56
CONTENT:
Pump and dump involves taking long positions in wholesale energy products, undertaking further buying activity and/or disseminating misleading positive information to increase prices, then selling at inflated prices after misleading other market participants. Circular trading executes sell orders with knowledge that offsetting buy orders are placed simultaneously, excluding competition and constituting illegal conduct. Pre-arranged trading involves commodity dealers trading at pre-agreed prices designed to exclude other dealers or gain tax advantages, making it illegal. Certain crossing or pre-arranged trades may be accepted market practices if undertaken according to trading venue rules.

SECTION: Dissemination of False and Misleading Information Without Transactions
ID: 57
CONTENT:
This market manipulation type involves disseminating false and misleading information without necessarily undertaking accompanying transactions. It includes creating misleading impressions by failing to properly disclose price-sensitive information that should be disclosed, such as when market participants with inside information fail to properly disclose it as defined by Regulation.
