text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Market Manipulation: False and Misleading Information
ID: 58
CONTENT:
Spreading false or misleading information through media involves posting information via internet or issuing press releases containing false or misleading statements about wholesale energy products admitted to trading on organized markets. The person spreading the information knows or ought to have known that it is false or misleading and is disseminating it to create a false or misleading impression. Spreading false or misleading information through officially recognized channels for disseminating information to market users is particularly serious as market participants must be able to rely on such official channels. Other behavior designed to spread false or misleading information covers courses of conduct designed to give false impressions through means other than media, such as moving physical commodity stocks to create misleading impressions about supply or demand for commodities or deliverables into commodity futures contracts.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Market Manipulation: Conclusions and Agency Guidance
ID: 59
CONTENT:
Examples of practices constituting market manipulation are inspired by NRAs' experiences and financial market authorities' experiences, with whom the Agency and NRAs will closely cooperate in implementing REMIT. These examples serve as indications for possible signals of market manipulation in wholesale energy markets according to REMIT until more experience is gained. Market participants' behavior must be coherent with their technical and economic constraints to comply with competition law, especially concerning market power exercise. The Agency will constantly review its Guidance on market manipulation and publish revised non-binding Guidance if considered appropriate. Cooperation between the Agency, NRAs, and competition authorities is essential in this respect.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Inside Information Disclosure Obligation: Overview
ID: 60
CONTENT:
Article 4(1) of REMIT obliges market participants to publicly disclose in an effective and timely manner inside information they possess in respect of business or facilities which the market participant, its parent undertaking, or related undertaking owns or controls, or for whose operational matters that market participant or undertaking is responsible, either in whole or in part. The disclosure obligation lies with the market participant according to Article 2(7) of REMIT and relates to inside information of parent undertakings or related undertakings. The obligation extends to inside information regarding business or facilities which market participants or undertakings control or for whose operational matters they are responsible, either in whole or in part.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Inside Information Disclosure: Extended Obligations and Confidentiality Exceptions
ID: 61
CONTENT:
Article 4(3) of REMIT extends the disclosure obligation to persons employed by or acting on behalf of market participants who receive inside information in the normal course of their employment, profession, or duties. Such market participants or persons must ensure simultaneous, complete, and effective disclosure of that information. However, this obligation does not apply if the person receiving the information has a duty of confidentiality, regardless of whether such duty derives from law, regulation, articles of association, or contracts. This exception limitation means that no such exception applies to market participants in relation to parent undertakings or related undertakings according to Article 4(1) of REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Effective Public Disclosure: Platforms and Mechanisms
ID: 62
CONTENT:
Inside information should be disclosed in a manner ensuring it is capable of being disseminated to as wide a public as possible. The Agency considers disclosure through platforms as the most effective mechanism. For effective and timely disclosure, the Agency currently recommends a dual approach: First, if platforms for disclosing inside information exist, operated by Transmission System Operators (TSOs) such as RTE-UFE transparency initiative or energy exchanges like Nord Pool Spot and EEX Transparency platform, in accordance with Regulations (EC) No 714/2009 and (EC) No 715/2009, market participants with inside information should use such disclosure mechanisms unless otherwise specified. Publication through such platforms constitutes simultaneous, complete, and effective public disclosure under Article 4(4) of REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Inside Information Disclosure: Website Publication as Fallback
ID: 63
CONTENT:
If adequate transparency platforms do not yet exist or simultaneously to publication through a platform, market participants may be allowed, at least for an interim period and unless otherwise specified, to publish inside information on their own website. However, such disclosure must enhance transparency across the EU and not distort information dissemination. Information must be disclosed free of charge, in a nondiscriminatory, user-friendly, and quantifiable manner. Information should be published in the official language(s) of the relevant Member State and in English or in English only. Simultaneous publication on a market participant's website is not necessary if a transparency platform is used which discloses inside information in a timely manner, decreasing organizational burden on market participants.

ID: 64
CONTENT:
Regardless of whether information is published on a transparency platform or market participant's website, publications should contain: the caption 'Publication according to Article 4(1) of REMIT / UMM – Urgent Market Message'; a subject heading summarizing main content; the name and contact information of the market participant; if applicable, the name and location of the respective asset; if applicable, the balancing area or market area concerned; the time and date of the relevant occurrence, including estimated duration of outages; the time and date of publication; if applicable, reasons for unavailability of generation units, consumption units, or parts of electricity or gas grids; if applicable, a history of prior publications regarding the same event. Each publication should be as short as reasonably possible and usually not exceed 10 to 20 lines, excluding statements by company executives, advertisements, or irrelevant information.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Inside Information Disclosure: Prognosis and Disclaimer Requirements
ID: 65
CONTENT:
The Agency discourages the use of disclaimers in inside information publications. If disclaimers are used, they should be clearly separated from the main body. If publication requires a prognosis regarding duration of outages or similar matters, the Agency understands such prognosis contains an element of uncertainty. Market participants fulfill publication requirements if the prognosis is based on all available data and prepared with reasonable effort. If a prognosis changes over time, the publication must be updated accordingly. Disclosure of inside information in an incomplete or incorrect manner would be considered non-effective disclosure and thus a breach of Article 4(1) of REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: IT Standards for Inside Information Disclosure: Regulated Information Service Requirements
ID: 66
CONTENT:
The following IT standards are considered effective for disclosing inside information through company websites or transparency platforms. Platforms must fulfill Regulated Information Service (RIS) requirements: have adequate policies and arrangements to make public inside information as close to real time as technically possible on reasonable commercial basis; efficiently and consistently disseminate inside information ensuring fast access on nondiscriminatory basis in formats facilitating consolidation with similar data from other sources; ensure high availability consistent with market expectations; operate and maintain effective administrative arrangements preventing conflicts of interests with market participants; have sound security mechanisms guaranteeing security of information transfer means, minimizing data corruption risk and unauthorized access, and preventing information leakage before publication.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: IT Standards for Inside Information Disclosure: Resources, Reporting, and Data Retention
ID: 67
CONTENT:
Platforms must maintain adequate resources and foresee backup facilities to avoid temporary technical problems and define emergency procedures describing what market participants shall do if the platform application is out of order. Platforms must be able to report inside information received from market participants for disclosure to the Agency and NRAs as non-aggregated and individual data once REMIT implementing acts apply. Platforms must keep historic inside information available for at least 2 years. Market participants disclosing inside information on their own website as fallback or simultaneously to platform disclosure must make information available through web feeds in formats facilitating consolidation with similar data from other sources. Social media shall only be used as additional sources, not replacing website publications.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Transparency Platform Disclosure and Technical Issues
ID: 69
CONTENT:
While market participants are responsible for the disclosure of inside information, the Agency understands that they do not have influence on the operation of transparency platforms. Therefore, the Agency believes that market participants are not responsible for temporary technical problems of such platforms fulfilling the above-mentioned RIS requirements. If the information was transmitted to the transparency platform in time, the market participant should therefore not be charged for having breached the obligation to disclose inside information. If technical problems persist, however, market participants have to use other platforms or their own website instead. Although delayed disclosure of inside information due to technical problems of transparency platforms does not imply a breach of the disclosure obligation, the market participant is not allowed to trade based on that information as long as it is not available to the market. The Agency regards the enclosed Urgent Market Message role models for the disclosure of inside information as best practice examples for the effective disclosure of inside information according to Article 4(1) of REMIT through platforms.

DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Timely Public Disclosure Requirements
ID: 70
CONTENT:
As regards the timely disclosure of inside information, the Agency currently considers that: if the inside information has to be published in accordance with Regulations (EC) No 714/2009 and (EC) No 715/2009, including guidelines and network codes adopted pursuant to those Regulations, the delay in publishing under these rules and regulations, including in aggregated form, is considered simultaneous, complete and effective public disclosure (Article 4(4) of REMIT). However, it has to be stressed that even if Article 4(4) of REMIT considers the publication of inside information, including in aggregated form, in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 714/2009 or (EC) No 715/2009, or guidelines and network codes adopted pursuant to those Regulations, to constitute simultaneous, complete and effective public disclosure, it does not necessarily constitute disclosure in a timely manner and the inside information has to be published, in any case, before the prohibition of insider trading ceases to apply.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Disclosure Timeframes for Non-Regulated Information
ID: 71
CONTENT:
If the inside information does not have to be made public in accordance with Regulations (EC) No 714/2009 and (EC) No 715/2009, including guidelines and network codes adopted pursuant to those Regulations, the Agency currently considers that there is no reason for applying a different reasonable timeframe for the disclosure of information. Such information must therefore normally be published within one hour if not otherwise specified in applicable rules and regulations. But in any case the inside information has to be published before the prohibition of insider trading ceases to apply. The Agency considers that market participants should develop a clear compliance plan towards real time or close to real time disclosure of inside information, beyond compliance with existing Third Package transparency obligations.

SECTION: Exemptions and Reporting Requirements for Inside Information
ID: 72
CONTENT:
Article 3(4)(b) and Article 4(2) of REMIT provide for exemptions from the obligation to timely publish inside information and from the prohibition to trade on this information before it is published in a number of specified cases. In all these cases, however, the relevant information should be reported to the Agency and the relevant NRA without delay. In order to assist those market participants who are subject to the obligation to report information according to Article 3(4)(b) and Article 4(2) of REMIT, the Agency has developed a standard notification format, based on the experience in financial markets, and recommends its adoption by all NRAs. The Agency foresees to collect the notifications required by Article 3(4)(b) and Article 4(2) of REMIT mainly through an electronic format, especially when there are data standards relating to this information (like for information to be published in accordance with Regulations (EC) No 714/2009 and (EC) 715/2009). The relevant electronic format is published on the Agency's website.

ID: 74
CONTENT:
The market abuse prohibitions of REMIT are based on the Market Abuse Directive, but tailored to the gas and electricity markets. Market abuse means insider dealing and market manipulation, which have become explicitly prohibited with the entry into force of REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Seven Types of Market Abuse Behavior
ID: 75
CONTENT:
The following seven types of behaviour may amount to market abuse, the first three of which constitute insider trading, the last four constitute market manipulation, including attempted market manipulation: 1. Insider trading – when an insider trades, or tries to trade, in wholesale energy products on the basis of inside information relating to that wholesale energy product, Article 3(1)(a) of REMIT. 2. Improper disclosure of inside information – where an insider improperly discloses inside information to another person, unless such disclosure is made in the normal course of the exercise of their employment, profession or duties, Article 3(1)(b) of REMIT. 3. Recommending on the basis of inside information – where an insider is recommending or inducing, on the basis of inside information, another person to acquire or dispose of wholesale energy products to which that information relates, Article 3(1)(c) of REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Application of Insider Trading Prohibition and Definition of Insiders
ID: 78
CONTENT:
Whilst the prohibition of market manipulation applies to any engagement in, or attempt to engage in, market manipulation on wholesale energy markets by any person, the application of the prohibition of insider trading is limited to the following persons who possess inside information in relation to a wholesale energy products ("insider"): 1. members of the administrative, management or supervisory bodies of an undertaking; 2. persons with holdings in the capital of an undertaking; 3. persons with access to the information through the exercise of their employment, profession or duties; 4. persons who have acquired such information through criminal activity; 5. persons who know, or ought to know, that it is inside information. Article 3(5) of REMIT clarifies that where the person who possesses inside information in relation to a wholesale energy product is a legal person, the prohibitions laid down in Article 3(1) of REMIT shall also apply to the natural persons who take part in the decision to carry out the transaction for the account of the legal person concerned.

SECTION: Attempted Insider Dealing and Prohibition Scope
ID: 79
CONTENT:
The prohibition of insider dealing also contains elements of attempted behaviour. Article 3(1)(a) of REMIT not only prohibits from using inside information by acquiring or disposing of wholesale energy products to which that information relates but also prohibits from using inside information by trying to acquire or dispose of wholesale energy products to which that information relates.

SECTION: Exemptions from Insider Trading Prohibition - TSO Operations
ID: 80
CONTENT:
Paragraphs 3 and 4 of Article 3 of REMIT stipulate exemptions from the prohibition of insider trading. However, it should be stressed that the exemptions may only apply for the prohibition of insider trading and are without prejudice of the obligation to publish inside information according to Article 4(1) of REMIT. Article 3(3) of REMIT stipulates: Points (a) and (c) of paragraph 1 of this Article shall not apply to transmission system operators when purchasing electricity or natural gas in order to ensure the safe and secure operation of the system in accordance with their obligations under points (d) and (e) of Article 12 of Directive 2009/72/EC or points (a) and (c) of Article 13(1) of Directive 2009/73/EC.

SECTION: Exemptions from Insider Trading Prohibition - Obligations and Physical Loss
ID: 81
CONTENT:
Article 3(4) of REMIT stipulates exemptions: (a) transactions conducted in the discharge of an obligation that has become due to acquire or dispose of wholesale energy products where that obligation results from an agreement concluded, or an order to trade placed, before the person concerned came into possession of inside information; (b) transactions entered into by electricity and natural gas producers, operators of natural gas storage facilities or operators of LNG import facilities the sole purpose of which is to cover the immediate physical loss resulting from unplanned outages, where not to do so would result in the market participant not being able to meet existing contractual obligations or where such action is undertaken in agreement with the transmission system operator(s) concerned in order to ensure safe and secure operation of the system. In such a situation, the relevant information relating to the transactions shall be reported to the Agency and the national regulatory authority. This reporting obligation is without prejudice to the obligation set out in Article 4(1).

ID: 82
CONTENT:
Article 3(4)(c) of REMIT stipulates: market participants acting under national emergency rules, where national authorities have intervened in order to secure the supply of electricity or natural gas and market mechanisms have been suspended in a Member State or parts thereof. In this case the authority competent for emergency planning shall ensure publication in accordance with Article 4. The Agency understands that the exemption of Article 3(3) of REMIT does not apply to point (b) of paragraph 1 of this Article. Therefore, TSOs when purchasing electricity or natural gas in order to ensure the safe and secure operation of the system in accordance with their above-mentioned obligations under Directives 2009/72/EC and 2009/73/EC shall be prohibited from disclosing that information to any other person unless such disclosure is made in the normal course of the exercise of their employment, profession or duties.

SECTION: Insider Trading Exemptions and Market Participant Obligations
ID: 85
CONTENT:
Since the exemption for insider trading also applies to orders to trade placed before the person concerned came into possession of inside information, the Agency considers that the market participant is obliged to refrain from any amendment or selective withdrawal of the order placed ('hands-off approach') in order to comply with the prohibition of insider trading. Concerning the exemption in Article 3(4)(b) of REMIT, the Agency considers that, since the exemption is limited in scope to the market participants mentioned therein, any unplanned outage under the exemption of Article 3(4)(b) may only relate to production, storage or LNG import facilities. It furthermore considers that the exemption may only be applied for unplanned events, i.e. an event which is not ex-ante known by the primary owner of the data, that any physical loss needs to be caused immediately and solely through the unplanned event and that any transaction going beyond the immediate physical loss may not benefit from the exemption.

SECTION: Exemption Application in Unplanned Outage Circumstances
ID: 86
CONTENT:
The exemption may only be applied by the aforementioned market participants in the aforementioned circumstances in the following two instances: Where the sole purpose of the transactions entered into is to cover the immediate physical loss resulting from unplanned outages, where not to do so would result in the market participant not being able to meet existing contractual obligations or Where such action is undertaken in agreement with the TSO(s) concerned in order to ensure safe and secure operation of the system. Regarding the first alternative, the Agency considers that the contractual obligations referred to must exist ex-ante of the immediate physical loss resulting from unplanned outages. The existing contractual obligations must relate to the relevant period of the unplanned event. The Agency considers a market participant 'not being able' to meet such existing contractual obligations in particular if the market participant has no other own assets available to cover the loss.

The Agency considers a market participant 'not being able' to meet such existing contractual obligations in particular if the market participant has no other own assets available to cover the loss.

SECTION: Emergency Planning and Delayed Disclosure Requirements
ID: 87
CONTENT:
With regard to the exemption of Article 3(4)(c) of REMIT, the Agency considers that it will normally coincide with the exemption of Article 4(2) of REMIT and that in such case the authority competent for emergency planning shall ensure publication in accordance with Article 4(1) of REMIT. In case a market participant not only aims at applying the exemptions from the prohibition of insider trading according to Article 3(3) and (4) of REMIT, but also the exemption of Article 4(2) of REMIT concerning the delayed disclosure of inside information, the Agency and the relevant NRA(s) must be notified accordingly. According to Article 4(2) of REMIT, the market participant concerned shall without delay provide that information, together with a justification for the delay of the public disclosure, to the Agency and the relevant NRA having regard to Article 8(5) of REMIT, if the conditions of Article 4(2) of REMIT are met. Notification forms for delayed disclosure of inside information are available at the Agency's website.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Application of the Prohibition of Market Manipulation
ID: 88
CONTENT:
REMIT does not only prohibit market manipulation, but also applies the concept of attempted market manipulation. Proving market manipulation would require a regulator to demonstrate that either a manipulative order was placed or a manipulative transaction was executed. However, there are situations where a person takes steps towards a manipulative behaviour and there is clear evidence of an intention to manipulate the market but either an order is not placed, or a transaction is not executed. The Regulation expressly prohibits attempts at market manipulation. This prohibition will enhance market integrity.

ID: 89
CONTENT:

Moreover, they are to be applied using judgement rather than necessarily being interpreted literally. SECTION: Possible Signals of Insider Dealing
ID: 90
CONTENT:
The following events may be considered as signals of potential insider trading situations: a) significant trading by major market participants before the announcement of information having a significant price effect; b) transactions resulting in sudden and unusual changes in the volume of orders and prices before the announcement of information having a significant price effect.

DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Possible Signals of Market Manipulation - False or Misleading Signals
ID: 91
CONTENT:
The following non-exhaustive list of signals, which should not necessarily be deemed in themselves sufficient to determine market manipulation, may be taken into account when transactions or orders to trade are examined by persons professionally arranging transactions related to false or misleading signals and to price securing: a) the extent to which orders to trade given or transactions undertaken represent a significant proportion of the daily volume of transactions in the relevant wholesale energy product on the trading venue concerned, in particular when these activities lead to a significant change in the price of the wholesale energy product; b) the extent to which orders to trade given or transactions undertaken by persons with a significant buying or selling position in a wholesale energy product lead to significant changes in the price of the wholesale energy product or a related wholesale energy product admitted to trading on a trading venue; c) whether transactions undertaken lead to no change in beneficial ownership of a wholesale energy product admitted to trading on a trading venue.

SECTION: Market Manipulation Signals - Deception and Contrivance
ID: 94
CONTENT:

DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Method of Reporting Suspicious Transactions
ID: 95
CONTENT:
Any person professionally arranging transactions in wholesale energy products who reasonably suspects that a transaction might breach Article 3 or 5 of REMIT shall notify the competent NRA without further delay of all relevant information available. Where not all the relevant information is available at the time of notification, the notification shall include at least the reasons why the notifying persons suspect that the transaction might constitute insider dealing or market manipulation. All remaining information shall be provided to the competent authority as soon as it becomes available. Notification to the competent authority can be effected by mail, electronic mail, telecopy or telephone, provided that in the latter case, written confirmation is provided upon request by the competent authority.

SECTION: Standard Reporting Format and NRA Recommendations
ID: 96
CONTENT:
The Agency considers that it would assist those subject to the obligation to report suspicious transactions if there were a standard reporting format for doing so. The Agency, based on the experiences in financial markets, therefore recommends using the format published on the Agency's website and urges NRAs to adopt it for suspicious transaction reporting to NRAs, the notification of which has to be forwarded to the Agency without delay pursuant to Article 16(2) of REMIT.

SECTION: Obligations of Persons Professionally Arranging Transactions
ID: 97
CONTENT:
Persons making suspicious transactions reports do not need to have all the required information before contacting the competent authority. If the case is one for which (the persons subject to the reporting obligation consider that) there is a need to alert the competent authority urgently, then the Agency would expect that NRAs receive notifications as soon as possible, even before all aspects of the transaction and all related information become known. This contact may take place by telephone if appropriate, giving the basic details and reasons for suspicion. The other information can be supplied subsequently.

DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Duty to Establish Effective Arrangements and Procedures
ID: 98
CONTENT:
Article 15 of REMIT requires that 'any person professionally arranging transactions in wholesale energy products who reasonably suspects that a transaction might breach Articles 3 or 5 shall notify the NRA without further delay. Persons professionally arranging transactions in wholesale energy products shall establish and maintain effective arrangements and procedures to identify breaches of Articles 3 or 5. The regulation and its implementing measures do not deal with the steps which the persons subject to this requirement need to take to identify such transactions. Those who are subject to the requirement clearly need to ensure that they comply with this obligation.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Guidance on Effective Arrangements and Applicable Persons
ID: 99
CONTENT:
The following guidance draws on experiences in financial markets as to what might constitute effective arrangements to identify breaches of the prohibitions of market abuse and signals of a suspicious transaction. The duty to establish and maintain effective arrangements and procedures to identify breaches of Articles 3 or 5 of REMIT is on any person professionally arranging transactions in wholesale energy products. These include at least trading venues like energy exchanges and brokers. Concerning gas hubs, the Agency considers that normally the TSO operates the gas hub, but it might be the case that gas hubs operate separately from the TSO. At gas hubs transfer of title (ownership) takes places, which can be considered a transaction. Thus the person owning the gas hub can be considered as a person professionally arranging transactions.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Market Surveillance and Transaction Notification Under REMIT
ID: 100
CONTENT:
Arranging transactions according to REMIT Article 15 requires consideration of data depth available to hubs, which varies on a hub-by-hub basis. Certain hubs may be unable to conduct surveillance (for example, hubs receiving highly aggregated data without price details), with market monitoring conducted elsewhere such as at an Exchange. TSOs or persons acting on their behalf may be regarded as persons professionally arranging transactions insofar as they are arranging balancing markets. The Agency considers independent market surveillance departments in energy exchanges and compliance officers in brokers as best practices for effective arrangements to identify breaches of market abuse prohibitions. Applicable rules for market surveillance and compliance in EU financial market legislation may serve as guidance to establish and maintain such mechanisms. The notification regime laid down by REMIT requires that persons subject to it decide on a case-by-case basis where there are reasonable grounds for suspicion concerning the relevant transaction. Indications provided are neither exhaustive nor determinative—a particular transaction may be suspicious even if it matches none of the indications, and a transaction may not necessarily be suspicious simply because it matches one or more indications.

DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Application of Prohibitions of Market Abuse and Interim Enforcement Powers
ID: 101
CONTENT:
According to Article 13(1) of REMIT, NRAs shall ensure that the prohibitions set out in Articles 3 and 5 and the obligation set out in Article 4 are applied. In the interim phase until data collection according to Article 8 applies and investigatory and enforcement powers are implemented at national level according to Articles 13(2) and penalties according to Article 18 apply, NRAs should make use of their existing powers, particularly those conferred through national implementation of the Third Energy Package. This ensures that market integrity and transparency of wholesale energy markets are aimed at with REMIT's entry into force.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Accepted Market Practices (AMPs) Regime - Definition and Scope
ID: 102
CONTENT:
According to Recital 27 of REMIT, the Agency's guidance addresses accepted market practices. Article 2(2)(a)(ii) and (3)(a)(ii) of REMIT stipulate that accepted market practices, such as those applying in financial services defined by Article 1(5) of Directive 2003/6/EC on insider dealing and market manipulation, could be a legitimate way for market participants to secure a favourable price for a wholesale energy product. Accepted market practices are defined as practices reasonably expected in one or more financial markets and accepted by the competent authority in accordance with Commission guidelines. Under Directive 2003/6/EC, the concept may apply either in relation to market manipulation or concerning information users of commodity derivatives markets would expect to be made public.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: AMPs Under REMIT - Agency Conclusions and Distinctions
ID: 103
CONTENT:
The Agency concludes that AMPs accepted by competent authorities according to Directive 2003/6/EC may apply under REMIT, but AMPs under REMIT are not limited to these practices. New AMPs may be established under REMIT, particularly concerning wholesale energy commodity markets. The Agency distinguishes between practices and activities carried out in wholesale energy markets. 'Activities' cover different types of operations or strategies such as arbitrage, hedging, and short selling. 'Market practices' cover the way these activities are handled and executed. Activities are considered too broad to qualify for AMP status. An activity such as hedging could be undertaken in different ways; if carried out without constituting market manipulation, AMP status does not arise. If an activity would constitute market manipulation, a competent authority would be unlikely to accept it as an AMP. Giving an activity blanket AMP status would be neither meaningful nor desirable.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Specific Practices and AMP Status - Crossing, Bidding, and Marketplace Rules
ID: 104
CONTENT:
The Agency agrees with financial market authorities on whether certain specific practices, such as crossing/pre-arranged trades or gross bidding, should be given accepted market practice status, subject to the condition that these practices be undertaken according to the rules of the relevant organised marketplace. In most such cases, conduct conforming to organised marketplace rules would be sufficient to promote market integrity, and the question of giving the practice AMP status would not arise. The decision whether a process constitutes an AMP is a matter of national or regional specificities. AMPs are primarily the responsibility of individual NRAs, so a practice one competent authority considers an AMP may not be viewed as such by another. However, each NRA has a duty to consult nationally and with other relevant NRAs, and to coordinate with the Agency prior to disclosing accepted market practices. The Agency must coordinate and publish AMPs on its website in standard ACER format with links to national legal text after recognition and requisite consultation processes.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Factors for Assessing Market Practices in Wholesale Energy Markets
ID: 105
CONTENT:
Competent authorities should consider the following non-exhaustive factors when assessing particular practices in wholesale energy markets: The level of transparency of the relevant market practice to the whole market—transparency by market participants is crucial; the less transparent a practice is, the more likely it is not to be accepted. However, practices on non-regulated markets might be less transparent than similar practices on regulated markets and should not themselves be considered unacceptable. The need to safeguard market forces and proper interplay of supply and demand—practices inhibiting supply and demand interaction by limiting opportunities for other participants to respond create higher risks for market integrity and are less likely to be accepted. The degree to which the practice impacts market liquidity and efficiency—practices enhancing liquidity and efficiency are more likely to be accepted than those reducing them. The degree to which the practice takes into account the trading mechanism and enables market participants to react properly and timely to new market situations. The risk inherent in the practice for integrity of directly or indirectly related markets, whether regulated or not, in relevant wholesale energy products within the Union.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Additional Assessment Factors and Overriding Principles for AMPs
ID: 106
CONTENT:
Additional factors for assessing market practices include: the outcome of any investigation by competent authorities, particularly whether the practice breached rules or regulations designed to prevent market abuse or codes of conduct on the market in question or related markets within the Union; the structural characteristics of the relevant market including whether it is regulated, the types of wholesale energy products traded, and the type of market participants. Overriding principles to be observed by competent authorities to ensure accepted market practices do not undermine market integrity while fostering innovation and dynamic development of wholesale energy markets include: new or emerging accepted market practices should not be assumed unacceptable simply because not previously accepted; practising fairness and efficiency by market participants is required to avoid prejudice to normal market activity and integrity. Competent authorities should analyse the impact of relevant market practices before they are carried out.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Application of AMPs Regime and Inside Information Disclosure
ID: 107
CONTENT:
The Agency currently considers the application of the AMPs regime only in relation to information users of wholesale energy markets would expect to be made public concerning wholesale energy products for the following incidents, possibly in coordination with competent national financial market authorities: Disclosure of inside information through regional or national inside information platforms fulfilling RIS requirements if nominated by competent NRA(s) following public consultation and notified to the Agency—NRAs should aim at regional platforms agreed with relevant NRAs for relevant markets. Disclosure of inside information in aggregated/anonymised way to comply with competition law and notified to the Agency if considered necessary at national level and agreed upon by the national NRA with the national competition authority. Definition of national/regional thresholds for inside information disclosure in relevant wholesale gas markets following market participant consultation and accepted by competent NRA(s) and notified to the Agency.

text:
DOCUMENT: 2nd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Compliance Regime for Market Participants Under REMIT
ID: 108
CONTENT:
The Agency is of the opinion that market participants should develop a clear compliance regime towards real time or close to real time disclosure of inside information and further REMIT requirements, beyond compliance with existing Third Package transparency obligations. NRAs should consider the following best practice example of such compliance regime for market participants, taking into account the market participant's size and trading capacity: Compliance culture—creation of corporate culture to comply with REMIT requirements. Compliance objectives—compliance with REMIT requirements, namely registration, disclosure and reporting obligations and market abuse prohibitions. Compliance organisation—definition of roles and responsibilities in internal organisation, including responsibilities for REMIT requirements (centralised vs. decentralised), internal vs. external reporting lines, internal vs. external interfaces, and provision of human and technical (IT Systems) resources. Compliance risks—identification and assessment of concrete compliance risks. Compliance programme—identification of concrete actions to define compliant/noncompliant behaviour. Communication—communication of rules and regulations to all relevant parties.

metadata.title: Compliance Regime for Market Participants Under REMIT
metadata.original_text: The Agency is of the opinion that market participants should develop a clear compliance regime towards real time or close to real time disclosure of inside information and further REMIT requirements, beyond compliance with existing Third Package transparency obligations. NRAs should consider the following best practice example of such compliance regime for market participants, taking into account the market participant's size and trading capacity: Compliance culture—creation of corporate culture to comply with REMIT requirements. Compliance objectives—compliance with REMIT requirements, namely registration, disclosure and reporting obligations and market abuse prohibitions. Compliance organisation—definition of roles and responsibilities in internal organisation, including responsibilities for REMIT requirements (centralised vs. decentralised), internal vs. external reporting lines, internal vs. external interfaces, and provision of human and technical (IT Systems) resources. Compliance risks—identification and assessment of concrete compliance risks. Compliance programme—identification of concrete actions to define compliant/noncompliant behaviour. Communication—communication of rules and regulations to all relevant parties.

SECTION: Penalty Regimes Under REMIT Article 18
ID: 110
CONTENT:
When Member States establish penalty rules for REMIT infringements under Article 18 of the Regulation, NRAs should develop penalties covering all potential breaches. These include: market abuse prohibitions under Articles 3 and 5; failure to notify relevant information to the Agency and competent NRA per Article 3(4)(b); non-disclosure of inside information per Article 4(1); failure to notify delayed disclosure of inside information per Article 4(2); failure to provide transaction records including trade orders per Article 8(1); failure to register with the competent NRA per Article 8(1); and violations of obligations by persons professionally arranging transactions under Article 15.

CONTENT:
One of the Agency's tasks under REMIT is to ensure that National Regulatory Authorities (NRAs) carry out their tasks under this Regulation in a consistent and coordinated way. CONTENT:

text:
DOCUMENT: 3rd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Scope of REMIT Regulation and Application to Financial Instruments
ID: 18
CONTENT:
According to Article 1(2) of REMIT, the Regulation applies to trading in wholesale energy products, whilst Articles 3 and 5 of this Regulation shall not apply to wholesale energy products which are financial instruments and to which Article 9 of Directive 2003/6/EC applies. Article 1(2) of REMIT stipulates that the Regulation is without prejudice to Directives 2003/6/EC and 2004/39/EC, as well as to the application of European competition law to the practices covered by REMIT. Article 1(2) of REMIT therefore requires the definition of a borderline between the application of the market abuse prohibitions of Articles 3 and 5 of REMIT and of the market abuse prohibitions of Directive 2003/6/EC (Market Abuse Directive - MAD). However, Article 1(2) of REMIT does not affect the disclosure of inside information according to Article 4(1) of REMIT, which applies regardless of whether the wholesale energy product is a financial instrument or not.

According to Article 9(1) of MAD, the Directive applies to any financial instrument admitted to trading on a regulated market in at least one Member State, or for which a request for admission to trading on such a market has been made, irrespective of whether or not the transaction itself actually takes place on that market. According to Article 9(2) of MAD, Articles 2, 3 and 4 of MAD shall also apply to any financial instrument not admitted to trading on a regulated market in a Member State, but whose value depends on a financial instrument as referred to in Article 9(1) of MAD. Article 6(1) to (3) of MAD shall therefore not apply to issuers who have not requested the admission of their financial instruments to trading on a regulated market in a Member State or whose request has not been approved.

SECTION: Financial Instruments Subject to MAD and Regulated Market Definition
ID: 20
CONTENT:
The list of financial instruments subject to MAD provisions as specified in Article 1(3) of MAD includes derivatives on commodities and any other instrument admitted to trading on a regulated market in a Member State or for which a request for admission to trading on such a market has been made. Article 4(1), No 14, of Directive 2004/39/EC (Markets in Financial Instruments Directive – MiFID) defines regulated market as a multilateral system operated and/or managed by a market operator, which brings together or facilitates the bringing together of multiple third party buying and selling interests in financial instruments in the system and in accordance with its nondiscretionary rules in a way that results in a contract, in respect of the financial instruments admitted to trading under its rules and/or systems, and which is authorised and functions regularly and in accordance with the provisions of Title III of MiFID.

SECTION: REMIT Coverage of Wholesale Energy Products Not Admitted to Regulated Markets
ID: 21
CONTENT:
Any wholesale energy product which is a financial instrument, including those listed in Section C of Annex I of MiFID, but which is not admitted to trading on a regulated market in a Member State and for which a request for admission to trading on such a market has not been made would be covered by market abuse prohibitions of REMIT. In particular, a derivative on energy only admitted to trading at Multilateral Trading Facilities according to Article 4(1) No 15 of MiFID is not covered by the market abuse prohibitions of MAD, but by the market abuse prohibitions of REMIT. This understanding applies until the scope of the financial instruments under MAD is extended and aligned with the MiFID scope as currently considered in the review of these directives. The Guidance will then be reviewed accordingly.

SECTION: Wholesale Energy Products - Definition and Scope
ID: 24
CONTENT:
Article 2(4) of REMIT defines wholesale energy products as the following contracts and derivatives, irrespective of where and how they are traded: (a) contracts for the supply of electricity or natural gas where delivery is in the Union; (b) derivatives relating to electricity or natural gas produced, traded or delivered in the Union; (c) contracts relating to the transportation of electricity or natural gas in the Union; (d) derivatives relating to the transportation of electricity or natural gas in the Union.

DOCUMENT: 3rd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Wholesale Energy Products - Final Customers Exception
ID: 25
CONTENT:
Contracts for the supply and distribution of electricity or natural gas for the use of final customers are not wholesale energy products. However, contracts for the supply and distribution of electricity or natural gas to final customers with a consumption capacity greater than the threshold set out in the second paragraph of point (5) shall be treated as wholesale energy products. For the purposes of REMIT, the definition of final customer draws on the relevant definition in Directives 2009/72/EC and 2009/73/EC. These directives define a final customer as meaning 'a customer purchasing electricity or natural gas for his own use'.

SECTION: Consumption Capacity Definition and Calculation
ID: 26
CONTENT:
Article 2(5) of REMIT clarifies the notion of 'consumption capacity' relevant for the understanding of the notion of 'wholesale energy products': 'consumption capacity' means the consumption of a final customer of either electricity or natural gas at full use of that customer's production capacity. It comprises all consumption by that customer as a single economic entity, in so far as consumption takes place on markets with interrelated wholesale prices. For the purposes of this definition, consumption at individual plants under the control of a single economic entity that have a consumption capacity of less than 600 GWh per year shall not be taken into account in so far as those plants do not exert a joint influence on wholesale energy market prices due to their being located in different relevant geographical markets.

text:
DOCUMENT: 3rd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Agency Understanding of Consumption Capacity at Full Use
ID: 27
CONTENT:
The Agency understands 'consumption [...] at full use of that customer's production capacity' to mean the maximum amount of energy (electricity or natural gas) that a final customer could consume in a year, i.e. if the customer were to run its consumption assets fully at all times throughout this year. It is this consumption capacity that market participants should consider whenever assessing whether the consumption capacity threshold of 600 GWh is exceeded. The consumption capacity comprises all consumption by that customer, i.e. of electricity or natural gas, as a single economic entity, in so far as consumption takes place on markets with interrelated wholesale prices.

text:
DOCUMENT: 3rd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Separate Calculation of Electricity and Natural Gas Consumption
ID: 28
CONTENT:
It is the Agency's understanding that final customers should calculate their consumption capacity of electricity and natural gas separately from each other, and not cumulate them, whenever assessing whether the threshold of 600 GWh is exceeded. Within a single economic entity, consumption at individual plants below the threshold of 600 GWh are not taken into account in so far as those plants do not exert a joint influence on wholesale energy market prices due to their being located in different relevant geographical markets. However, individual plants that each has a consumption capacity below the threshold of 600 GWh, but that are located in the same geographical market, shall be taken into account whenever assessing whether the threshold of 600 GWh is exceeded.

DOCUMENT: 3rd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Single Economic Entity - Definition and Assessment Criteria
ID: 29
CONTENT:
As for the notion of 'single economic entity', guidance can be obtained from international practices of competition law and especially from the precedents of the European Court of Justice. Under the competition rules, the unified conduct on the market of two or more companies takes precedence over the formal legal structure of those companies. Therefore, the relevant question is not whether two given companies are separate legal persons, but rather whether they behave together as a single unit in the market. The following elements may be taken into consideration when assessing whether two or more companies form a single economic entity: Decision making powers, procedures and sharing of liability between the relevant companies; Ownership (e.g. majority shareholding); Ownership structure of the relevant companies; and Participating interests or influence over the relevant companies.

DOCUMENT: 3rd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Interrelated Wholesale Prices and Union-Wide Consumption Capacity
ID: 30
CONTENT:
As regards the understanding of 'markets with interrelated wholesale prices', the Agency considers that wholesale energy markets are increasingly interlinked across the Union. There is already a high degree of interrelation of wholesale electricity and natural gas prices across the Union and there is an expectation of increased interrelation as the development of a single European energy market continues to progress. Having this in mind, the Agency considers it prudent for market participants to take into account the consumption capacity of all their plants across the Union when assessing whether the consumption capacity threshold of 600 GWh is exceeded.

SECTION: Wholesale Energy Products - Time Periods and Derivatives
ID: 31
CONTENT:
In view of the definition of wholesale energy products in Article 2(4) of REMIT, the Agency considers contracts for the supply or transportation of electricity and natural gas traded intraday, within-day, day-ahead, two-day-ahead, week-end, long-term or any other time period generally accepted in the market as contracts for the supply or transportation of electricity or natural gas. Derivatives are understood as financial instruments as set out in points (4) to (10) of Section C of Annex I to Directive 2004/39/EC, as implemented in Articles 38 and 39 of Regulation (EC) No 1287/2006.

SECTION: Exclusions from Wholesale Energy Products
ID: 32
CONTENT:
The Agency considers contracts for green certificates and emission allowances not to be wholesale energy products, as they do not fulfil the requirements set out in Article 2(4) of REMIT. The Agency is aware that these contracts can have a significant price effect on wholesale energy markets. According to Article 10 of REMIT, trade repositories or competent authorities responsible for overseeing and collecting information on trading in emission allowances or derivatives thereof shall provide the Agency with access to records of transactions in such allowances and derivatives.

SECTION: Wholesale Energy Market - Definition
ID: 34
CONTENT:
Article 2(6) of REMIT defines a wholesale energy market as follows: 'wholesale energy market' means any market within the Union on which wholesale energy products are traded. According to Recital 5 of REMIT, wholesale energy markets encompass both commodity markets and derivative markets, which are of vital importance to the energy and financial markets, as price formation in both sectors is interlinked. They include, inter alia, regulated markets, multilateral trading facilities and over-the-counter (OTC) transactions and bilateral contracts, traded directly or through brokers.

DOCUMENT: 3rd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Market Participant - Regulatory Obligations
ID: 38
CONTENT:
The understanding of the notion of market participant is crucial for several reasons. Firstly, the obligation to disclose inside information according to Article 4(1) of REMIT lies with the market participant. Secondly, according to Article 8(1) of REMIT, being a market participant entails the obligation to provide the Agency (i) with a record of wholesale energy market transactions, including orders to trade, by the market participant itself or through a person or authority listed in points (b) to (f) of Article 8(4) of REMIT and (ii) with the information described in Article 8(5) of REMIT (fundamental data). Lastly, pursuant to Article 9(1) of REMIT, market participants have to register with the competent NRA if entering into transactions which are required to be reported to the Agency in accordance with Article 8(1) of REMIT.

DOCUMENT: 3rd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Market Participants Definition and REMIT Coverage
ID: 42
CONTENT:
A market participant is any person who enters into transactions in one or more wholesale energy markets, including the placing of orders to trade. This definition applies irrespective of the location of the person. SSOs (Storage System Operators) and LSOs (LNG System Operators) are explicitly mentioned as market participants in Article 3(4)(b) of REMIT. LSOs may sell contracts which eventually lead to the feed in or extraction of gas from the gas network. In several markets, some SSOs conclude contracts for the supply of gas in cases where storage facilities experience operational problems. As a result, these LSOs and SSOs are market participants and are required to publish inside information according to Article 4(1) of REMIT.

DOCUMENT: 3rd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Information Disclosure and Reporting Obligations for SSOs and LSOs
ID: 43
CONTENT:
Information related to the capacity and use of facilities for storage and the use of LNG facilities is required to be reported to the Agency according to Article 8(5) of REMIT. SSOs and LSOs are best placed to fulfill this disclosure obligation and data reporting requirement. The Agency considers it best practice if SSOs and LSOs, even if not entering into transactions in wholesale energy products, facilitate publication of information in relation to Article 4(1) of REMIT on behalf of the potentially multiple market participants involved. The system operator is typically best placed to publish relevant REMIT related information and by doing so can avoid duplicate and potentially misleading publications by individual market participants involved. Market participants however remain responsible for publication and should have appropriate back-up arrangements in place in case the system operator is not able to publish due to technical reasons or where the system operator's publication does not meet the requirements for publication under Article 4(1) of REMIT.

SECTION: Application of REMIT for Non-EU and Non-EEA Market Participants
ID: 44
CONTENT:
According to Article 2(7) of REMIT, a market participant is any person who enters into transactions in one or more wholesale energy markets, regardless of location. Persons from non-EU and non-EEA countries are covered by REMIT provided that they enter into transactions in wholesale energy markets. Article 9(1) of REMIT confirms this understanding by requiring market participants not established or resident in the Union entering into transactions which are required to be reported to the Agency to register in a Member State in which they are active. Non-EU and non-EEA market participants are covered by the notion of market participant according to Article 2(7) of REMIT if entering into transactions in one or more wholesale energy markets. Accordingly, the obligations to register pursuant to Article 9(1) of REMIT with the competent NRA and to report data to the Agency according to Article 8(1) and (5) of REMIT also apply to such non-EU and non-EEA market participants, as do the prohibitions of market abuse pursuant to Articles 3 and 5 of REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 3rd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Registration of Market Participants - Introduction and Overview
ID: 45
CONTENT:
Chapter 4 illustrates the Agency's current understanding of the application of Article 9 of REMIT and provides guidance to NRAs concerning the registration process and their role in this process, in order to facilitate the harmonisation of practices across the Union. Accurate information in the national registers and the European register of market participants is a prerequisite for efficient and effective market monitoring. According to Article 9(1) of REMIT, market participants entering into transactions which are required to be reported to the Agency in accordance with Article 8(1) shall register with the national regulatory authority.

text:
DOCUMENT: 3rd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Market Participants Obliged to Register
ID: 46
CONTENT:
According to Article 9(1) of REMIT, the obligation to register as a market participant only applies to those market participants entering into transactions which are required to be reported to the Agency in accordance with Article 8(1). The requirement to register under REMIT applies to any person, legal or natural, that enters into transactions which are required to be reported. All market participants entering into transactions which are required to be reported to the Agency in accordance with Article 8(1) must register, even if a parent, subsidiary or other related undertaking is already registered or is registering. Provided they are not separate legal persons, branches of a market participant do not need to register as separate market participants. A market participant may allow a third party to submit registration information on their behalf, in which case the relevant NRA may require the third party to provide evidence of such permission.

text:
DOCUMENT: 3rd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Registration Information Requirements
ID: 47
CONTENT:
Article 9(3) of REMIT requires the Agency, in cooperation with NRAs, to determine and publish the format in which NRAs should transmit registration information on market participants to the Agency. On 26 June 2012, the Agency adopted a Decision determining the registration format to be used for the establishment of the European register of market participants. The registration format consists of 5 sections: Section 1 - Data related to the market participant; Section 2 - Data related to the natural persons linked to the market participant; Section 3 - Data related to the ultimate controller or beneficiary of the market participant; Section 4 - Data related to the corporate structure of the market participant; Section 5 - Data related to the delegated parties for reporting on behalf of the market participant. All market participants entering into transactions which are required to be reported to the Agency in accordance with Article 8(1) are required to provide this information.

text:
DOCUMENT: 3rd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Establishment of National Registers
ID: 48
CONTENT:
According to Article 9(2) of REMIT, not later than 3 months after the date on which the Commission adopts the implementing acts set out in Article 8(2), national regulatory authorities shall establish national registers of market participants. Each NRA shall establish a registration system by which market participants can provide registration information to that NRA no later than 3 months after the adoption of the implementing acts. NRAs can open the registration process to market participants earlier than this if they wish. NRAs are free to use whatever system they deem most appropriate for their market. The Agency is developing a system to be used to establish the European register of market participants, which will also be available to NRAs as a means of registering market participants in their own Member State. NRAs should ensure that market participants are provided with information on how to register. The Agency will make available a Registration User Manual (RUM) to NRAs to provide guidance on how the fields in the registration format should be populated. On the basis of the RUM, NRAs may provide guidance to market participants on how to register. The manual will be updated periodically based on feedback from NRAs.

text:
DOCUMENT: 3rd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: NRA Registration Requirements and Establishment Criteria
ID: 49
CONTENT:
According to Article 9(1) of REMIT, market participants entering into transactions which are required to be reported to the Agency shall register with the national regulatory authority in the Member State in which they are established or resident, or, if they are not established or resident in the Union, in a Member State in which they are active. According to settled case law of the Court of Justice of the European Union, a legal or natural person can be established in more than one Member State. The legal or natural person is established in the Member State(s) in which it pursues a professional activity on a stable and continuous basis. If a market participant is established in more than one Member State, the Agency would normally expect market participants to register in the Member State in which they have their primary establishment. For market participants not established or resident in the Union, such market participants may choose in which Member State to register, as long as they are active in that Member State.

text:
DOCUMENT: 3rd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Registration Submission Deadlines and Reporting Obligations
ID: 50
CONTENT:
According to Article 9(4) of REMIT, market participants shall submit the registration form to the NRA prior to entering into a transaction which is required to be reported to the Agency in accordance with Article 8(1). Market participants must submit all Sections of the registration form (Sections 1 to 5) before entering into any transaction which is required to be reported to the Agency. In line with Article 12(2) of the Implementing Regulation No 1348/2014, the reporting obligation will apply to market participants from 7 October 2015 and from 7 April 2016, according to the type of data to be reported to the Agency. For market participants entering into transactions on an Organized Market Place (OMP), the registration obligation takes effect at the latest prior to 7 October 2015. For all other market participants, the registration obligation takes effect at the latest prior to 7 April 2016 or prior to the first day they enter into transactions which are required to be reported to the Agency. Any person who enters into a transaction which is required to be reported to the Agency from 7 October 2015 or 7 April 2016 without having submitted the registration form to the relevant NRA is in breach of Article 9 of REMIT.

SECTION: Registration Form Updates and Timeline
ID: 53
CONTENT:
Market participants registered before 17 March 2015 must update their registration form in Section 4 at the latest by 17 June 2015. Section 4 contains data related to corporate structure of the market participant. Market participants are required to fill Section 4 with data available at the European register, including all data on related undertakings which are registered market participants. If a related undertaking registers after the initial deadline, the market participant must update Section 4 accordingly once the related undertaking's registration is published. Additionally, market participants have an obligation to promptly update any other information provided in their registration form at any time once that change takes effect, as defined in Article 9(5) of REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 3rd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Example 1: Market Participant A - Pre-Publication Registration
ID: 54
CONTENT:
Market Participant A registered before 17 March 2015 and completed Sections 1, 2, 3 and 5 of the registration form before submission. Section 4 was not filled at the time of first submission because the European register was first published on 17 March 2015. After 17 March 2015, MP A has three months (until 17 June 2015) to fill Section 4 with data on all related undertakings which are registered market participants. If a related undertaking MP B registers after 17 June 2015, MP A must update Section 4 accordingly once MP B's registration is published. MP A must also promptly update any other information in its registration form, such as updating Section 5 if it chooses a new Registered Reporting Mechanism (RRM).

DOCUMENT: 3rd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Example 2: Market Participant C - Post-Publication Registration
ID: 55
CONTENT:
Market Participant C registered after 17 March 2015 and is obliged to complete all Sections (1 to 5) of the registration form with updated data at the time of submission. In Section 4, MP C must include all its related undertakings which are registered market participants, including those published in the European register at the time of form submission. If a related undertaking MP D registers at a later stage, MP C must promptly update its registration form once MP D's registration is published. MP C must also promptly update any other information in its registration form once changes take effect, as defined in Article 9(5) of REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 3rd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Issuance of the ACER Code
ID: 56
CONTENT:
Each market participant registered under REMIT will be issued with a unique identifier called the ACER code, as required by Article 9(2) of REMIT. The ACER code enables market participants to report data under Article 8 of REMIT and is necessary for providing information relating to Section 4 of the registration format. According to Article 9(4) of REMIT, market participants must submit the registration form prior to entering into transactions required to be reported to the Agency. The ACER code is issued upon transmission of information from national registers to the Agency in accordance with ACER Decision No 01/12. National Regulatory Authorities (NRAs) should promptly transmit registration information to the Agency once submitted by the market participant, after which the Agency immediately issues the ACER code. NRAs must ensure market participants receive the ACER code in a timely manner, before transactions are required to be reported to the Agency.

text:
DOCUMENT: 3rd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: ACER Code Issuance Timeline and Registration System
ID: 57
CONTENT:
The registration system provides automatic checks to prevent incomplete registration forms from being submitted. For market participants registering before the Agency first publishes the European register, the ACER code is issued upon submission of first phase information (Sections 1, 2, 3 and 5) to the relevant NRA. However, receipt of an ACER code does not confirm completion of the registration process; market participants must still provide Section 4 information. For market participants registering after the Agency first publishes the European register, the ACER code is issued upon submission of all sections (1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) to the relevant NRA. According to ACER Decision No 01/2012, NRAs shall provide the Agency with information in electronic format through a secure channel using CSV or XML formats.

text:
DOCUMENT: 3rd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Requirement to Keep Registration Information Up to Date
ID: 58
CONTENT:
According to Article 9(5) of REMIT, market participants must communicate promptly to the national regulatory authority any change which has taken place regarding information provided in the registration form. Registration is not a one-off event but an ongoing requirement. Market participants must update their registration form with any changes in accordance with Article 9(5) of REMIT. If mandatory registration information changes are not communicated promptly, the registration is considered incomplete. Market participants with outdated registration forms may be in breach of Article 9 of REMIT. Although market participants bear responsibility for updating information, it is best practice for NRAs to set up regular reminders (e.g., annually) asking market participants to verify that submitted information remains correct and up to date.

text:
DOCUMENT: 3rd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: The Role of NRAs in the Registration Process
ID: 59
CONTENT:
Registration of market participants under REMIT is primarily a national process, with NRAs obliged to undertake three key roles. First, NRAs act as a source of support for market participants seeking to register. The Agency provides a Registration User Manual (RUM) to NRAs for supporting market participants, though ultimate responsibility for successful registration lies with market participants. Second, NRAs transmit information from their national registers to the Agency in accordance with ACER Decision No 01/2012, promptly transmitting registration information once submitted by the market participant. Third, NRAs ensure accuracy of registration information by establishing and maintaining registers of market participants. Accurate information in national and European registers is prerequisite for an efficient market monitoring system. NRAs should have systems to check registration information for omissions and errors, with detected errors promptly notified to the Agency.

text:
DOCUMENT: 3rd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Registration System Accuracy and ACER Code Issuance
ID: 60
CONTENT:
The registration system provides automatic checks to prevent incomplete registration forms from being submitted. Market participants are allowed to trade without breaching Article 9 as soon as they submit complete registration forms to the relevant NRA, regardless of whether an ACER code has been issued. The Agency aims to issue the ACER code immediately upon receipt of registration information from the NRA. However, the Agency also aims to ensure high accuracy in the European register of market participants and may delay publication of information while conducting additional checks. It is important to note that through the registration process, NRAs do not issue authorization or licenses to trade. Completion of registration does not constitute a 'know-your-customer' check or 'fit-and-proper' assessment of the market participant.

text:
DOCUMENT: 3rd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Registration Process Steps for Pre-Publication Registrants
ID: 61
CONTENT:
For market participants starting registration before the Agency publishes the European register, the registration process includes the following steps: (1) Before entering into reportable transactions, the market participant submits a registration form to the relevant NRA providing information for Sections 1, 2, 3 and 5 of ACER Decision No 01/2012. NRAs should encourage advance registration. Market participants are responsible for providing correct and complete information. (2) The NRA promptly transmits information to the Agency. (3) Immediately following transmission, the Agency issues a unique ACER code to the market participant and relevant NRA. (4) The Agency establishes a European register based on information provided by NRAs and publishes a list of market participants. (5) The market participant completes the second phase by submitting Section 4 information within 3 months of the first European register publication.

text:
DOCUMENT: 3rd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Registration Requirements for Post-Publication Registrants and Final Guidance
ID: 62
CONTENT:
Any market participant registering after the Agency first publishes the European list of market participants must provide all relevant information (Sections 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5) during initial registration. Market participants must transmit the registration form to the NRA prior to entering into transactions required to be reported to the Agency in accordance with Article 8(1) of REMIT. A clear and consistent message must be given to market participants: registration under REMIT does not constitute any kind of authorization or license to trade and is without prejudice to obligations to comply with applicable trading and balancing rules. The Agency will announce early guidance regarding these requirements.

text:
DOCUMENT: 3rd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: REMIT Inside Information Definition and Framework
ID: 63
CONTENT:
This Chapter covers what the Agency currently considers to constitute 'inside information' as defined by Article 2(1) of REMIT. Article 2(1) of REMIT defines 'inside information' as: information of a precise nature, which has not been made public, which relates, directly or indirectly, to one or more wholesale energy products and which, if it were made public, would be likely to significantly affect the prices of those wholesale energy products. The criteria on information of a precise nature and on significant price effect are very much linked to each other and are therefore to be considered together. The examples of types of practice set out in this document are deliberately described in non-legal technical terms and it is emphasised that the descriptions are not intended to affect the scope of interpretation of REMIT.

SECTION: Definition of Information Under REMIT Article 2(1)
ID: 64
CONTENT:
Article 2(1), second subparagraph, of REMIT clarifies what is meant by the term 'information' as follows: (a) information which is required to be made public in accordance with Regulations (EC) No 714/2009 and (EC) No 715/2009, including guidelines and network codes adopted pursuant to those Regulations; (b) information relating to the capacity and use of facilities for production, storage, consumption or transmission of electricity or natural gas or related to the capacity and use of LNG facilities, including planned or unplanned unavailability of these facilities; (c) information which is required to be disclosed in accordance with legal or regulatory provisions at Union or national level, market rules, and contracts or customs on the relevant wholesale energy market, insofar as this information is likely to have a significant effect on the prices of wholesale energy products; and (d) other information that a reasonable market participant would be likely to use as part of the basis of its decision to enter into a transaction relating to, or to issue an order to trade in, a wholesale energy product.

SECTION: Inside Information Criteria and Requirements
ID: 65
CONTENT:
In order to consider information as inside information, it still has to fulfil all four criteria of Article 2(1), first subparagraph, of REMIT: the information must be of a precise nature, that it has not been made public, that it relates, directly or indirectly, to one or more wholesale energy products and that, if made public, it would be likely to significantly affect the prices of those wholesale energy products. The concept of 'transparency information' refers to all data that shall be published under the transparency obligation of Regulation (EC) No 714/2009 and (EC) No 715/2009, including applicable guidelines and network codes adopted pursuant to those Regulations. This includes information referred to in the Commission Regulation (EU) No 543/2013, which amends the guidelines annexed to Regulation (EC) No 714/2009.

DOCUMENT: 3rd Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Transparency Information versus Inside Information
ID: 66
CONTENT:
Transparency information is cited in Article 2(1)(a) of REMIT as a type of information that may constitute inside information. The concept of 'inside information' comprises, on the one hand, the transparency information that is likely to have a significant effect on the prices of wholesale energy products, but, on the other hand, goes further and also includes other information that a reasonable market participant would be likely to use as part of the basis of its decision to enter into a transaction relating to, or to issue an order to trade in, a wholesale energy product, insofar as this information is likely to have a significant effect on the prices of wholesale energy products. Transparency information is normally periodic, structured data subject to Regulations (EC) No 714/2009 and (EC) No 715/2009. Inside information should normally be considered as an ad hoc, structured data that is likely to have a significant effect on price that has not been disclosed to the market.
