text:
DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Conclusions on Market Manipulation Practices
ID: 92
CONTENT:
The examples of various types of practices which could constitute market manipulation are inspired by the NRAs' own experiences and the experiences in financial markets made by financial market authorities, with whom the Agency and NRAs will closely cooperate in the implementation of REMIT. These examples can currently be taken as an indication for possible signals of market manipulation in wholesale energy markets according to REMIT. These considerations apply until more experience is gained about market manipulation in wholesale energy markets. Market participants' behaviour must be coherent with their technical and economic constraints in a way to comply with competition law, especially concerning market power exercise. The cooperation of the Agency and NRAs with the competition authorities, as foreseen by REMIT, must be understood in this respect.

SECTION: Article 4(1) REMIT: Market Participant Disclosure Obligations
ID: 94
CONTENT:
According to Article 4(1) of REMIT, Market participants shall publicly disclose in an effective and timely manner inside information which they possess in respect of business or facilities which the market participant concerned, or its parent undertaking or related undertaking, owns or controls or for whose operational matters that market participant or undertaking is responsible, either in whole or in part. Such disclosure shall include information relevant to the capacity and use of facilities for production, storage, consumption or transmission of electricity or natural gas or related to the capacity and use of LNG facilities, including planned or unplanned unavailability of these facilities.

SECTION: Scope of Disclosure Obligation and Related Undertakings
ID: 95
CONTENT:
The obligation to disclose inside information lies with the market participant according to Article 4(1) of REMIT. The disclosure obligation relates not only to inside information in respect of the market participant's own business or facilities, but also to inside information of the market participant's parent undertaking or related undertaking. In addition, the disclosure obligation is not only related to inside information in respect of business or facilities which the market participant or the respective undertakings own or control, but also in respect of business or facilities for whose operational matters the market participant or respective undertaking is responsible, either in whole or in part.

SECTION: Limitations on Disclosure Obligation and Third-Party Information
ID: 96
CONTENT:
The obligation to disclose inside information does not apply to a person or a market participant who possesses inside information in respect of another market participant's business or facilities, in so far as that owner of this inside information is not a parent or related undertaking. Notwithstanding this, persons holding information in such circumstances will need to consider their compliance with Article 3 and in particular whether they hold such information as one of the persons listed in Article 3(2). In relation to this, the Agency encourages persons holding such information to promptly inform the relevant market participant(s) in order to promote effective and timely compliance with Article 4(1) of REMIT.

SECTION: Article 4(3) REMIT: Disclosure by Employees and Representatives
ID: 97
CONTENT:
Article 4(3) of REMIT extends the disclosure obligation of Article 4(1) of REMIT to a person employed by, or acting on behalf of, a market participant when that person discloses inside information to any other person in the normal course of the exercise of their employment, profession or duties as referred to in Article 3(1)(b) of REMIT. In such a case, that market participant or person shall ensure simultaneous, complete and effective disclosure of that information. However, the disclosure obligation of Article 4(3) of REMIT does not apply if the person receiving the information has a duty of confidentiality, regardless of whether such duty derives from law, regulation, articles of association or contracts.

DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Disclosure Mechanisms and Inside Information Platforms
ID: 98
CONTENT:
The transparency of the wholesale energy markets requires the disclosure of inside information in a manner that enables the dissemination of information to as wide a public as possible, granting easy and equal access to all users of this information. The Agency believes that, in order to achieve effective disclosure according to Article 4 of REMIT, the information shall be disclosed using a platform for the disclosure of inside information (Inside Information Platform or IIP), i.e. an electronic system for the delivery of information which allows multiple market participants to share information with the wide public and complies with the minimum quality requirements listed in Chapter 7.2.2.

DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Rationale for Inside Information Platforms as Default Mechanism
ID: 99
CONTENT:
Using Inside Information Platforms as the default disclosure mechanism is supported by the fact that: (a) This disclosure mechanism is indicated by a combined reading of Article 4(1) and Article 4(4) of REMIT. According to Article 4(4) of REMIT the publication of inside information, including in aggregated form, in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 714/2009 or (EC) No 715/2009, or guidelines and network codes adopted pursuant to those Regulations, constitutes simultaneous, complete and effective public disclosure. The transparency rules under these regulations stipulate a publication of transparency information on central information transparency platforms. Therefore, the disclosure by Inside Information Platforms would then foster a consistent understanding of effective disclosure according to Article 4(1) of REMIT and Article 4(4) of REMIT.

SECTION: Convergence with Financial Market Standards and Complexity Reduction
ID: 100
CONTENT:
This disclosure mechanism promotes convergence with technical standards established under financial market legislation in this regard, in particular those established under Article 17 of MAR, as further specified in Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2016/1055 laying down implementing standards with regards to the technical means for appropriate public disclosure of inside information. The reduction in the number of publication channels leads to a significant reduction in complexity and effort for market participants to access and use information that is published according to Article 4 of REMIT.

CONTENT:

ID: 102
CONTENT:

SECTION: Additional Publication Channels and Information Consistency
ID: 103
CONTENT:
A simultaneous publication on the market participant's website or through social media may be used as an additional source for publication. However, it cannot replace the disclosure on Inside Information Platforms. In case additional means for publication are used, e.g. a market participant's website, the market participant must ensure that the published information is identical to the one published on the Inside Information Platform. The publication of inside information on platforms facilitates access to information for all market participants and promotes the overall transparency of the market. Moreover, this solution decreases overall the technical and organisational burden for market participants.

SECTION: Emission Allowance Market Participants and Market Abuse Regulation Compliance
ID: 105
CONTENT:
According to Article 2(2) of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2016/1055, emission allowance market participants required to disclose inside information in accordance with Article 4 of REMIT may use the technical means established for the purpose of disclosing inside information under REMIT for the disclosure of inside information under Article 17(2) of Regulation (EU) No 596/2014 (Market Abuse Regulation), provided the inside information required to be disclosed has substantially the same content and the technical means used for the disclosure ensure that the inside information is communicated to the relevant media. The Agency believes that REMIT inside information disclosure through platforms will allow market participants to meet these requirements, provided that the inside information platform fulfils the requirements of the Market Abuse Regulation as well as the Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2016/1055.

SECTION: Minimum Quality Requirements for Inside Information Platforms - Part 1
ID: 106
CONTENT:
The following minimum requirements shall be fulfilled by the Inside Information Platform in order to ensure an effective disclosure of inside information: inside information shall be disclosed to as wide a public as possible on a nondiscriminatory basis and shall be accessible free of charge, simultaneously throughout the affected energy market(s); electronic means shall be used to ensure that the completeness, integrity and confidentiality of the information provided by the market participants is maintained during its transmission, reception, storage and processing to the platform; inside information shall be made publicly available in a way that must have the ability to actively distribute the information with the goal to reach the public at large and specific for the disclosure of inside information, allowing easy and fast access by the public.

CONTENT:
The platform shall facilitate active distribution of inside information by means of web feeds in a way that enables the Agency to collect and market participants to process these data efficiently, in line with the Guidance on the implementation of web feeds and the REMIT MoP published on the REMIT Portal; the filtering of information, including historical information, by relevant data categories should be possible in order to promote its efficient use, including in a downloadable format; historical inside information, including any edited information, shall be kept available for the public for a period of at least 5 years after the termination of the corresponding event(s); any history of prior publications regarding the same event shall be easily accessible and a functionality should be provided linking the previous publications to the new publication(s) in a comprehensible and easy-to-use manner.

ID: 111
CONTENT:
Without prejudice to Article 1(2) of REMIT, publication of inside information should be as concise, specific, precise and complete as reasonably possible to allow correct understanding of underlying events that might affect wholesale energy product prices. Inside information should be disclosed in a format that enhances transparency and ensures a Union-wide level playing field. Each publication under Article 4(1) of REMIT in the form of Urgent Market Message (UMM) should include the information set described in ANNEX VII of the REMIT MoP, as applicable. All fields and allowed values listed in ANNEX VII should be supported by the platform.

SECTION: Content Standards and Disclaimer Guidelines
ID: 112
CONTENT:
Each publication should not include statements by company executives, advertisements, or irrelevant information. The Agency discourages the use of disclaimers. If disclaimers are used, they should be clearly separated from the main body. Publications requiring a prognosis, such as regarding outage duration, should be based on all available data and prepared with reasonable effort. If a prognosis changes over time, the publication should be updated accordingly as soon as new information is available. Incomplete or incorrect disclosure of inside information would be considered non-effective disclosure and breach of Article 4(1) of REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Timely Disclosure of Inside Information
ID: 113
CONTENT:
If inside information must be published according to Regulations (EC) No 714/2009 and (EC) No 715/2009, including guidelines and network codes, and Commission Regulation (EU) No 543/2013, publishing according to these rules is considered simultaneous, complete and effective public disclosure under Article 4(4) of REMIT. However, this does not necessarily constitute timely disclosure. Inside information must be published before trading in wholesale energy products to which that information relates or recommending another person to trade. If inside information does not require publication under those Regulations, the Agency considers no different reasonable timeframe should apply. Such information should normally be published as soon as possible, but at the latest within one hour if not otherwise specified. Market participants should develop a clear compliance plan towards real time or close to real time disclosure beyond existing Third Package transparency obligations.

DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Delayed Disclosure of Inside Information
ID: 114
CONTENT:
According to Article 4(2) of REMIT, a market participant may exceptionally delay public disclosure of inside information under its own responsibility so as not to prejudice its legitimate interests, provided such omission is not likely to mislead the public, the market participant can ensure confidentiality, and does not make trading decisions based on that information. The market participant must without delay provide that information with justification for the delay to the Agency and relevant national regulatory authority per Article 8(5). The decision to delay is for market participants to make, not for the Agency or NRAs to preapprove. Market participants must ensure delays are not likely to mislead the public, do not make trading decisions on that information, and information remains confidential. Application of Article 4(2) cannot coincide with Article 3(4)(b) of REMIT. As soon as legitimate interests cease, the market participant must disclose the inside information in accordance with Article 4(1).

metadata.title: Delayed Disclosure of Inside Information
metadata.original_text: According to Article 4(2) of REMIT, a market participant may exceptionally delay public disclosure of inside information under its own responsibility so as not to prejudice its legitimate interests, provided such omission is not likely to mislead the public, the market participant can ensure confidentiality, and does not make trading decisions based on that information. The market participant must without delay provide that information with justification for the delay to the Agency and relevant national regulatory authority per Article 8(5). The decision to delay is for market participants to make, not for the Agency or NRAs to preapprove. Market participants must ensure delays are not likely to mislead the public, do not make trading decisions on that information, and information remains confidential. Application of Article 4(2) cannot coincide with Article 3(4)(b) of REMIT. As soon as legitimate interests cease, the market participant must disclose the inside information in accordance with Article 4(1).

SECTION: Exemption for Critical Infrastructure Protection
ID: 116
CONTENT:
According to Article 4(7) of REMIT, Articles 4(1) and 4(2) are without prejudice to the right of market participants to delay disclosure of sensitive information relating to protection of critical infrastructure as provided in point (d) of Article 2 of Council Directive 2008/114/EC of 8 December 2008. Article 4(7) is only relevant to 'critical infrastructure' as defined in Article 2(a) of Council Directive 2008/114/EC, meaning an asset, system or part thereof located in Member States essential for maintenance of vital societal functions, health, safety, security, economic or social well-being of people, whose disruption or destruction would have significant impact in a Member State.

SECTION: Sensitive Critical Infrastructure Protection Information
ID: 117
CONTENT:
If a market participant holds inside information about critical infrastructure it owns, controls, or is responsible for operational matters, and that information constitutes 'sensitive critical infrastructure protection related information' as defined in Article 2(d) of Council Directive 2008/114/EC (facts about critical infrastructure which if disclosed could be used to plan disruption or destruction), then the market participant can delay publication of inside information. However, market participants are not allowed to use this exemption for all inside information relating to critical infrastructure. If inside information does not constitute 'sensitive critical infrastructure protection related information', the obligation to publish remains.

SECTION: Market Abuse Prohibitions Overview
ID: 118
CONTENT:
Chapter 8 provides guidance to NRAs on application of market abuse prohibitions and indications of transactions involving inside information or market manipulation as defined in Article 2(1) to (3) of REMIT. Market abuse prohibitions of REMIT are based on those in MAD but tailored to gas and electricity markets. Market abuse means insider dealing and market manipulation, which became explicitly prohibited with REMIT's entry into force.

text:
DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Types of Market Abuse Behavior
ID: 119
CONTENT:
Seven types of behaviour may amount to market abuse: the first three constitute insider trading, the last four constitute market manipulation including attempted market manipulation. (1) Insider trading - when an insider trades or tries to trade in wholesale energy products based on inside information relating to that product under Article 3(1)(a) of REMIT. Market participants holding inside information must refrain from amendment or selective withdrawal of placed orders ('hands-off approach'). (2) Improper disclosure of inside information - where an insider improperly discloses inside information to another person, unless disclosure is made in normal course of employment, profession or duties under Article 3(1)(b) of REMIT. (3) Recommending on basis of inside information - where an insider recommends or induces another person to acquire or dispose of wholesale energy products based on inside information under Article 3(1)(c) of REMIT.

DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Market Manipulation Types
ID: 120
CONTENT:
Four types of behaviour constitute market manipulation: (4) False/misleading transactions - trading or placing orders to trade which gives or is likely to give false or misleading signals as to supply, demand, or price of wholesale energy products under Article 2(2)(a)(i) and (3)(a)(i) of REMIT. (5) Price positioning - trading or placing orders to trade which secures or attempts to secure, by a person or persons acting in collaboration, the price of one or several wholesale energy products at an artificial level, unless the person who entered into the transaction or issued the order establishes that reasons are legitimate and the transaction or order conforms to accepted market practices.

SECTION: Market Manipulation Prohibitions - Fictitious Devices and False Information
ID: 121
CONTENT:
Transactions involving fictitious devices/deception - trading, or placing orders to trade, which employs fictitious devices or any other form of deception or contrivance (Article 2(2)(a)(iii) and (3)(a)(iii) of REMIT). Dissemination of false and misleading information - giving out information that conveys a false or misleading impression about a wholesale energy product where the person doing this knows or ought to have known the information to be false or misleading (Article 2(2)(b) and (3)(b) of REMIT).

text:
DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Application of Insider Trading Prohibition - Eligible Persons
ID: 122
CONTENT:
The prohibition of insider trading applies to persons who possess inside information in relation to wholesale energy products ('insider'): members of the administrative, management or supervisory bodies of an undertaking; persons with holdings in the capital of an undertaking; persons with access to the information through the exercise of their employment, profession or duties; persons who have acquired such information through criminal activity; and persons who know, or ought to know, that it is inside information. Article 3(5) of REMIT clarifies that where the person who possesses inside information is a legal person, the prohibitions shall also apply to the natural persons who take part in the decision to carry out the transaction for the account of the legal person concerned.

SECTION: Insider Trading Prohibition - Attempted Behavior
ID: 123
CONTENT:
The prohibition of insider dealing contains elements of attempted behaviour. Article 3(1)(a) of REMIT not only prohibits the use of inside information by acquiring or disposing of wholesale energy products to which that information relates, but also prohibits the use of inside information by trying to acquire or dispose of wholesale energy products to which that information relates.

SECTION: Exemptions from Insider Trading Prohibition - Overview
ID: 124
CONTENT:
Paragraphs 3 and 4 of Article 3 of REMIT stipulate exemptions from the prohibition of insider trading. The exemptions may only apply to the prohibition of insider trading and are without prejudice of the obligation to publish inside information according to Article 4(1) of REMIT. This guidance is intended to provide NRAs with consistent understanding on the circumstances in which these exemptions may be applied.

SECTION: TSO Exemption for System Operation
ID: 125
CONTENT:
Article 3(3) of REMIT provides that transmission system operators are exempt from insider trading prohibitions when purchasing electricity or natural gas to ensure safe and secure operation of the system in accordance with their obligations under Directive 2009/72/EC or Directive 2009/73/EC. However, this exemption does not apply to the prohibition on disclosing inside information. TSOs remain prohibited from disclosing inside information to any other person unless such disclosure is made in the normal course of the exercise of their employment, profession or duties.

DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Market Participants with TSO-Like Duties
ID: 126
CONTENT:
The Agency acknowledges that market models of some Member States provide for specific tasks for certain market participants similar to those of TSOs regarding responsibility to ensure safe and secure operation of the system. These market participants hold information which can constitute insider information and carry out transactions in the name and on behalf of other market participants. While there is an explicit exemption for TSOs, national particularities cannot be subsumed under the REMIT exemption. Any such particularity needs to be assessed by competent national authorities on a case-by-case basis.

SECTION: Exemption for Pre-Existing Obligations
ID: 127
CONTENT:
According to Article 3(4)(a) of REMIT, the prohibitions of insider trading shall not apply to transactions conducted in the discharge of an obligation that has become due to acquire or dispose of wholesale energy products where that obligation results from an agreement concluded, or an order to trade placed, before the person concerned came into possession of inside information. The Agency considers that market participants are obliged to refrain from any amendment or selective withdrawal of the order placed ('hands-off approach') in order to comply with the prohibition of insider trading.

SECTION: Exemption for Covering Physical Loss from Unplanned Outages
ID: 128
CONTENT:
Article 3(4)(b) of REMIT exempts transactions entered into by electricity and natural gas producers, operators of natural gas storage facilities or operators of LNG import facilities where the sole purpose is to cover the immediate physical loss resulting from unplanned outages. This applies where not doing so would result in the market participant not being able to meet existing contractual obligations or where such action is undertaken in agreement with the transmission system operator(s) to ensure safe and secure operation. Relevant information relating to such transactions shall be reported to the Agency and the national regulatory authority.

text:
DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Scope and Conditions of Unplanned Outage Exemption
ID: 129
CONTENT:
The Agency considers that the exemption in Article 3(4)(b) is limited in scope to the market participants mentioned therein. Any unplanned outage may only relate to production, storage or LNG import facilities. The exemption may only be applied for unplanned outages, i.e. outages which are not ex ante known by the primary owner of the data. Physical loss must be caused immediately and solely by that unplanned outage. Market participants can only use this exemption to enter into transactions to cover the immediate physical loss. Any further trading beyond covering immediate physical loss does not fall under the scope of this exemption.

SECTION: Two Instances for Applying Unplanned Outage Exemption
ID: 130
CONTENT:
The exemption in Article 3(4)(b) of REMIT may only be applied in two instances: where not doing so would result in the market participant not being able to meet existing contractual obligations; or where such action is undertaken in agreement with the TSO(s) concerned to ensure safe and secure operation of the system. Regarding the first instance, contractual obligations must exist ex ante of the immediate physical loss and must relate to the relevant period of the unplanned outage. A market participant is considered 'not being able' to meet obligations only if it has no other own assets available and the physical loss cannot be covered through existing frameworks such as intraday/within day or balancing markets.

ID: 131
CONTENT:
The application of exemption in Article 3(4)(b) cannot coincide with the application of Article 4(2) concerning delayed disclosure of inside information, as Article 4(2) requires that the market participant does not make decisions based upon the relevant inside information. If a market participant applies the exemption, relevant information relating to the transactions shall be reported to the Agency and to the NRA as soon as possible, according to the market participant's best capacity. The Agency has developed a standard notification format and recommends its adoption by all NRAs.

SECTION: Timeframe and Duration of Unplanned Outage Exemption
ID: 132
CONTENT:
The Agency considers the timeframe allowed under the exemption in Article 3(4)(b) valid for as long as a causal link between the outage and the amount to be covered under the strict exemptions is in place. Therefore, the exemption may only be applied for the duration of the market participant not being able to meet existing contractual obligations or where such action is undertaken in agreement with the transmission system operator(s) to ensure safe and secure operation of the system.

SECTION: Emergency Rules Exemption
ID: 133
CONTENT:
Article 3(4)(c) of REMIT provides an exemption for market participants acting under national emergency rules, where national authorities have intervened to secure the supply of electricity or natural gas and market mechanisms have been suspended in a Member State or parts thereof. In this case, the authority competent for emergency planning shall ensure publication in accordance with Article 4. The Agency considers that this exemption will normally coincide with the exemption of Article 4(2) of REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Market Manipulation Prohibition - Attempted Behavior
ID: 134
CONTENT:
REMIT does not only prohibit market manipulation, but also applies the concept of attempted market manipulation. Proving market manipulation would require a regulator to demonstrate that either a manipulative order was placed or a manipulative transaction was executed. However, there are situations where a person takes steps towards manipulative behaviour and there is clear evidence of an intention to manipulate the market, but either an order is not placed or a transaction is not executed. The Regulation expressly prohibits such attempted market manipulation.

SECTION: Market Manipulation Prohibition and Breach Indicators
ID: 135
CONTENT:
Attempts at market manipulation are prohibited to enhance market integrity. Indications of potential REMIT breaches include signals that should be regarded as starting points when considering whether a transaction gives rise to possible breaches. These signals are neither conclusive nor comprehensive and should be applied using judgment rather than literal interpretation. Transactions corresponding to listed signals may be legitimate and do not necessarily give reasonable grounds for suspicion.

SECTION: Possible Signals of Insider Dealing
ID: 136
CONTENT:
The following events may be considered as signals of potential insider trading situations: (a) significant trading by major market participants before the announcement of information, having a significant price effect; (b) transactions resulting in sudden and unusual changes in the volume of orders and prices, before the announcement of information, having a significant price effect.

DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Possible Signals of Market Manipulation - False or Misleading Signals and Price Securing
ID: 137
CONTENT:
Non-exhaustive signals for examining transactions or orders related to false or misleading signals and price securing include: (a) the extent to which orders represent a significant proportion of daily volume in the relevant wholesale energy product, particularly when leading to significant price changes; (b) the extent to which orders by persons with significant buying or selling positions lead to significant price changes in the wholesale energy product or related products; (c) whether transactions lead to no change in beneficial ownership; (d) the extent to which orders include position reversals in short periods representing significant daily volume proportions and might be associated with significant price changes; (e) the extent to which orders are concentrated within short time spans leading to price changes subsequently reversed; (f) the extent to which orders change the representation of best bid or offer prices or the order book and are removed before execution; (g) the extent to which orders are given at or around specific times when reference prices, settlement prices and valuations are calculated and lead to price changes affecting such prices; (h) the extent to which persistent execution of trades that would be uneconomic and counterintuitive on a stand-alone basis trigger manipulation by deliberately lowering or increasing market price, enabling a market participant to profit through separate trading activity via a larger connected accrued position.

DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Application of Obligations of Persons Professionally Arranging Transactions (PPATs) - Introduction
ID: 139
CONTENT:
This chapter provides guidance to NRAs concerning supervision of obligations imposed on persons professionally arranging transactions (PPATs) by Article 15 of REMIT. According to Article 15, any person professionally arranging transactions in wholesale energy products who reasonably suspects that a transaction might breach Article 3 or 5 shall notify the national regulatory authority without further delay. PPATs shall establish and maintain effective arrangements and procedures to identify breaches of Article 3 or 5. An important number of trades in wholesale energy markets are intermediated by PPATs. Through their role as intermediates, PPATs have exclusive knowledge of the market and their clients, positioning them well to monitor trading activities and identify potential REMIT breaches. REMIT imposes explicit responsibility on PPATs to monitor and contribute to the integrity, transparency and proper functioning of European wholesale energy markets.

SECTION: Delimitation of the Concept of PPAT
ID: 140
CONTENT:
Apart from Article 15 of REMIT, Article 8(4)(d) of REMIT and Article 2(4) of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 1348/2014 include references linked to the concept of PPAT. Article 8(4)(d) provides an overview of entities that could be considered as PPATs: organised markets, trade-matching systems or other persons professionally arranging transactions. Therefore, organised market places and trade-matching systems fall under the definition of PPATs, and any other entities engaged in similar activities must be included in the concept.

text:
DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Relationship Between PPAT, Organised Market Places and Trade-Matching Systems
ID: 141
CONTENT:
The concepts of 'organised market place' or 'organised market' are defined in Article 2(4) of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 1348/2014 as: (a) A multilateral system which brings together or facilitates the bringing together of multiple third party buying and selling interests in wholesale energy products in a way that results in a contract; (b) any other system or facility in which multiple third-party buying and selling interests in wholesale energy products are able to interact in a way that results in a contract. These include electricity and gas exchanges, brokers and other persons professionally arranging transactions, and trading venues as defined in Article 4 of Directive 2014/65/EU. As the concept of other PPATs is not explicitly defined, the existence of different elements should be assessed on a case-by-case basis to clarify which entities fall under the PPAT definition and are subject to Article 15 obligations.

text:
DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Criteria for PPAT Classification - Person, Professionally, and Arranging Transactions
ID: 142
CONTENT:
For an entity to be considered a PPAT, it must fulfill three cumulative criteria: (1) Person: means either natural or legal person; (2) Professionally: engaged in a specified activity as part of one's normal and regular paid occupation; (3) Arranging transactions: an activity that aims to enable or assist third parties (buyer or seller) in a way that directly brings about a particular wholesale energy transaction, or provide a facility that facilitates the entering into transactions by third parties in wholesale energy products. Simply providing the means by which parties to a transaction are able to communicate with each other is excluded from the PPAT concept. If a person makes arrangements that go beyond providing the means of communication and adds value to what is provided, it will lose this benefit and shall be recognized as a PPAT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Further Considerations for PPAT Definition
ID: 143
CONTENT:
The main characteristic of a PPAT is its intermediary role (whether acting as a principal or as an agent), i.e., arranging transactions in wholesale energy products. Its legal form, ownership, the type of market it operates, the type of wholesale energy product and the number of parties it represents are not relevant elements in determining whether an entity is a PPAT. REMIT places different obligations on PPATs and market participants, making it necessary to establish in each case whether the person concerned is acting as a PPAT or as a market participant. Whereas a market participant enters into transactions involving a wholesale energy product, a PPAT arranges the transaction. The same entity may qualify as a PPAT in one transaction and as a market participant in another, or be both in the same transaction. The arranging activity can comprise the whole trade lifecycle or be restricted to one or more parts of it. Some transactions may involve several PPATs and others may not involve any PPAT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Examples of PPAT Application - Energy Exchanges and Brokers
ID: 144
CONTENT:
Selected entities were assessed against PPAT characteristics to identify whether they fulfill classification criteria. Energy Exchanges meet all three cumulative criteria: they are persons, act professionally, and arrange transactions by bringing about transactions through introducing buyers/sellers or providing a facility that facilitates entering into transactions by third parties, allowing placement of orders, matching orders and executing transactions. Broker platforms/Brokers similarly meet all three criteria through the same mechanisms of bringing about transactions by introducing buyers/sellers or providing facilities that facilitate transaction entry, allowing placement of orders, matching orders and executing transactions.

text:
DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Market Participants and Transaction Facilitation
ID: 145
CONTENT:
Secondary capacity allocation platforms, TSOs (or persons acting on their behalf) organising gas trades, energy balancing, capacity trading, and Sleeves (arranging) all facilitate transactions by bringing about transactions through introducing buyer/seller or providing a facility that facilitates the entering into transactions by third parties. These entities allow placement of orders, match orders and execute transactions. Sleeves (arranging) offer a service to act as an intermediary to sell or purchase commodities on behalf of other market participants that do not have an agreement to trade with each other. Sleeves (not arranging) enter into transactions to allow the sale or purchase of commodities between other market participants without trading on behalf of those participants. Communication facilities only provide a generic facility not specifically designed for the entering into transactions by third parties.

text:
DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Article 15(1) REMIT: Notification Obligation for Potential Breaches
ID: 146
CONTENT:
According to Article 15(1) of REMIT: Any person professionally arranging transactions in wholesale energy products who reasonably suspects that a transaction might breach Article 3 or 5 shall notify the national regulatory authority without further delay. This obligation specifies what, whom, when and how to notify potential breaches. The assumption of a reasonable suspicion lies within the responsibility of the PPAT (Person Professionally Arranging Transactions). Although the obligation to notify relates to Articles 3 and 5 of REMIT, PPATs when performing their monitoring duties might become aware of a potential breach of another REMIT provision. In such cases, as a good cooperation practice, PPATs are invited to transmit all available information to the relevant NRA(s) through adequate communication channels.

text:
DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: What to Notify: Content Requirements for Suspicious Transaction Reports
ID: 147
CONTENT:
The notification of a potential REMIT breach should be clear and accurate to enable the NRA(s) to understand the basic facts and should contain as much information as possible for assessment. When reporting a potential breach of Article 3 or 5, PPATs should provide information on the identity of market participant(s), timing of the potential breach, market(s) concerned and details on related transaction(s)/order(s)/behaviour(s). A Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) should contain: (1) type of market abuse (insider trading and/or market manipulation) and identification of subcategory; (2) details of notifying party including identification, position, contact details, notification date and time; (3) description of potential breach including order(s)/transaction(s)/behaviour(s) with product(s) involved, delivery location, delivery date, timestamps, load type, contract ID(s), transaction ID(s), and description of inside information or potential inside information for Article 3 breaches.

text:
DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: STR Content Requirements: Persons Involved and Reasons for Suspicion
ID: 148
CONTENT:
A Suspicious Transaction Report should include: (4) reasons for suspecting that the order(s)/transaction(s)/behaviour(s) might constitute insider trading or market manipulation; (5) identification of persons involved in the potential breach including name, organisation, position and contact details, as well as identification of any other person(s) associated with the potential breach; (6) identification of notified parties including relevant NRA(s) to be notified and identification of other entities that were notified; (7) further information of significance including analysis of behaviour, spreadsheet analysing relevant transaction(s)/order(s)/behaviour(s), copy of communications with market participant or other entities, any action already undertaken by the PPAT, estimation of impact on market prices, estimation of benefit from potential breach, Member State(s) affected with supporting evidence, and any other information the PPAT considers relevant.

text:
DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Whom to Notify: NRA Selection Criteria
ID: 149
CONTENT:
According to Article 15(1) of REMIT, PPATs should notify at least the following NRA(s): The NRA(s) in the Member State(s) of the delivery of the wholesale energy product(s); and The NRA in the Member State in which the Market Participant involved in the potential breach has registered in the Centralised European Register of Energy Market Participants (CEREMP). If a single NRA meets both criteria, only that NRA should be notified. Otherwise all NRAs that meet at least one criterion should be notified. Where a PPAT notifies more than one NRA, it should inform each NRA of the other NRAs being notified. If the PPAT has already notified at least the NRA(s) fulfilling the criteria based on available evidence at notification time, the PPAT should not be held responsible for not notifying other NRAs identified afterward. However, where national law requires notification to another NRA, the PPAT should notify this NRA in addition to those mentioned above.

DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Financial Instruments and Parallel Notification Requirements
ID: 150
CONTENT:
Article 1(2) of REMIT refers that Articles 3 and 5 shall not apply to wholesale energy products which are financial instruments and to which Article 9 of MAD (Market Abuse Directive) applies. However, if a potential breach involves wholesale energy products that are also financial instruments according to Article 9 of MAD, the PPAT should notify the NRA(s) identified above in parallel with the relevant financial authorities to promote cooperation between different investigatory authorities.

text:
DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: When to Notify: Timeliness and Four-Week Recommendation
ID: 151
CONTENT:
Article 15 of REMIT provides that persons who reasonably suspect a transaction might breach Article 3 or 5 shall notify the national regulatory authority without further delay. The notion of 'without further delay' is linked to the existence of a reasonable suspicion of a potential breach. The PPAT shall notify the NRA(s) after preliminary analysis of an anomalous event and as soon as it has reasonable grounds to suspect a potential REMIT breach. Timeliness is crucial for collecting evidence. PPATs shall notify the NRA(s) as soon as possible once they have reasonable grounds to suspect a REMIT breach, and should usually do so no later than four weeks from the occurrence of the anomalous event. This recommendation means PPATs should perform market surveillance routinely, detect anomalous events, collect evidence and conduct necessary analysis within four weeks to assess whether reasonable grounds exist and produce a good quality STR.

text:
DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Notification Timing: Complex Cases and Delayed Breaches
ID: 152
CONTENT:
Should an anomalous event be of particular complexity, or should the PPAT be unable for other objective reasons to conclude on the existence of reasonable grounds of suspicion within the four-week timeframe, the PPAT should proceed with its analysis and notify the NRA(s) as soon as it has reasonable grounds to suspect a REMIT breach. The practice of delaying STR submission to incorporate further STRs cannot be reconciled with the obligation to act without further delay when sufficient evidence has been gathered. Arrangements and procedures shall entail the possibility to notify a potential breach which occurred in the past, where reasonable grounds of suspicion have arisen in light of subsequent events or information. In such cases, the PPAT should explain the delay between occurrence and notification according to specific circumstances if requested by the NRA. PPATs should also transmit any relevant additional information they become aware of after the original notification is submitted.

text:
DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: How to Notify: Secure Communication Channels and Notification Platform
ID: 153
CONTENT:
PPATs shall use secure communication channels to notify the NRA(s). The Agency has established on its website a secure 'Notification Platform' for the notification of Suspicious Transaction Reports by PPATs (available at: https://www.acer-remit.eu/np/home). The Notification Platform enables PPATs to fulfil their notification obligations, allowing them to directly notify, simultaneously and in a standardised manner, one or several of the 28 NRAs together with the Agency. To ensure legal certainty, the notifying PPAT receives an immediate confirmation of its notification. PPATs may also choose to notify using secure communication channels that NRAs may have put at their disposal. NRAs should publish on their website the communication channel that PPATs should use to notify potential breaches. Any contact through means other than secure communication channels does not replace the submission of an STR.

text:
DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: REMIT Article 15 Responsibilities and Market Surveillance Overview
ID: 155
CONTENT:
Article 15 of REMIT sets out the responsibility of a PPAT not only to notify whenever it has reasonable grounds to suspect a potential breach, but also to proactively monitor the wholesale energy markets in which it is involved. PPATs vary in size and organisational characteristics, and operate different markets (e.g. electricity, gas, spot, futures, capacity, etc.), so there is no one-size-fits-all governance or organisational arrangement. The effectiveness of the market surveillance activity of a PPAT, and its level of internal and external independence and integrity, depend on the organisational arrangements and procedures in place. While some recommendations concern basic requirements applicable to all PPATs, the way to implement the recommended measures shall take into consideration the specificities of each PPAT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Minimum Organisational and Procedural Arrangements for PPATs
ID: 156
CONTENT:
The Agency defines minimum organisational and procedural arrangements that NRAs should expect PPATs to put in place. In establishing a governance model, the PPAT has to take into account the conflicts of interest at individual and corporate level. Individual conflicts of interest may arise when a market surveillance team member has close contacts with market participants who trade on its platform. The market surveillance team member might be inclined not to internally report an anomalous event or notify a potential breach to the NRA(s) for a number of reasons, including to avoid damaging its relationships and future career prospects with the market participants. Corporate conflicts may arise when a market surveillance team member wants to report an anomalous event/notify a potential breach regarding a market participant, while the management team does not want to, for commercial or other reasons.

text:
DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Identifying and Managing Conflicts of Interest in Market Surveillance
ID: 157
CONTENT:
In order to identify and to prevent or manage conflicts of interest, it is important to consider all the steps to be undertaken by the PPAT, from detecting an anomalous event to finally notifying a potential breach to the NRA(s). Appropriate governance models, based on the assessment of the potential sources of risk within the PPAT, could mitigate risks by addressing how market surveillance teams are structured, how they report to the management team (internal reporting) and how they notify STRs to NRAs (external reporting). The existence and the nature of corporate conflicts is affected, among other things, by the structure of control, the governance model, as well as the nature of the business activity performed by the PPAT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Market Monitoring Unit (MMU) Governance Model
ID: 158
CONTENT:
In this governance model the market surveillance team operates independently from the other parts of the PPAT. The MMU is only accountable towards an Independent Body, not involved in the daily management of the PPAT (e.g. Exchange Council, Supervisory Board) that is responsible for the supervision of the effective execution of the unit activities. Differences may exist in the structure, duties and composition of the Independent Body (for example, members may be external to the PPAT or at least some of them, including NRA representatives). As the market surveillance team operates as a segregated unit from the other PPAT activities and does not report to the management team, the conflicts of interest at corporate level can in theory be more effectively mitigated. The composition and the duties of the Independent Body are of utmost importance in this model to ensure that the mitigation of these risks is effective and that the confidentiality of the market surveillance activities is secured. The governance structure should include clear rules on the nomination of the members of the Independent Body, as well as on its duties, to adequately mitigate the individual potential conflicts of interest.

text:
DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Market Monitoring Department (MMD) Governance Model
ID: 159
CONTENT:
In this governance model, the market surveillance team operates as any other department within the organisation, reporting to a Director who may be member of the Management Team. Some consideration should be given to the reporting lines to prevent conflicts of interests. The market surveillance team should not report to a Director whose objectives or performance are evaluated based on commercial achievements rather than on the fulfilment of the mission of the market surveillance function. Appropriate arrangements, based on the nature and assessment of the PPAT's conflicts of interests, should be in place to manage the flow of confidential information (also at the Management Team level). Appropriate processes that enable the auditing of the reporting from the Market Monitoring Department to the Management Team should be in place to mitigate potential conflicts of interest. The independent body or an auditing body can take responsibilities for the supervision of these communications. The appointment of a compliance officer could also be envisaged.

DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Market Monitoring Committee (MMC) Governance Model
ID: 160
CONTENT:
In this governance model, the market surveillance team consists of a number of experts, working in different parts of the PPAT. The MMC is accountable towards the Management Team as a whole or to a designated Director. Appropriate arrangements should be in place to mitigate potential conflicts of interest and to ensure the confidentiality of the data as it might flow through different parts of the organisation. The members of the MMC should not have their objectives or performance evaluated based on commercial achievements but rather on the fulfilment of the mission of the market surveillance function. Also, the members of the MMC should not simultaneously work for the teams in the PPAT with commercial responsibilities. Due consideration should be given to the reporting lines of the market surveillance team. Appropriate processes that enable the auditing of the reporting from the MMC to the Management Team should be in place to mitigate potential conflicts of interest. The independent body or an auditing body can take responsibilities for the supervision of these flows of information. The appointment of a compliance officer could also be envisaged.

SECTION: Organisational Setup Dimensions for Market Surveillance
ID: 161
CONTENT:
Proper organisation of the market surveillance activity is essential for its ability to detect market abuse. This involves at least five dimensions: adequacy of resources; human resources policy; appropriate amount of human resources dedicated to market surveillance (referred to as market surveillance team); communication with other units and confidentiality. For each dimension the PPAT should be able to justify why its organisational setup is best suited for the tasks of the market surveillance team. The market surveillance activity requires availability of some fundamental resources, which include human resources, analytical tools and data/information. The appropriate amount of resources dedicated to the market surveillance activity is dependent on the size of the PPAT. The adequacy of these resources, both in terms of quantity and quality, is fundamental in order to ensure effectiveness and true independence of market surveillance.

DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Resources and Analysis Requirements for Market Surveillance
ID: 162
CONTENT:
The human resources, analytical tools and data/information should be adequate to perform real-time and ex post analyses on anomalous events which are deemed relevant for the markets the PPAT operates. For example, markets with low transactions volumes might be better suited for manual supervision, but markets with high transactions volumes could benefit from automated systems. There should always be an element of human analysis in the detection of potential REMIT breaches as the most effective form of surveillance will likely be a mix of both automated and human forms.

SECTION: Human Resources Policy for Market Surveillance Staff
ID: 163
CONTENT:
Various internal and external factors, such as potential conflicts of interest at individual level, have the potential to influence the work of the market surveillance team. In order to ensure an adequate level of quality, consistency and effectiveness of the market surveillance team work, there should be a human resource policy with specific requirements for the market surveillance staff that can contribute to establish and safeguard the independence and integrity of the team. That policy can include the principles for the management of conflicts of interest (including the list of interests that need to be declared). As part of the specific requirements for the market surveillance staff, the human resource policy should develop specific incentives which are based on the accomplishment of the market surveillance function and not correlated to financial/commercial achievements.

SECTION: Dedicated Market Surveillance Team and Segregation Measures
ID: 164
CONTENT:
The specificities of the market surveillance function require the identification of a dedicated team. The market surveillance team will be specifically assigned to the monitoring activities, endowed with the relevant skills and able to devote the required time and operate in a timely manner. Implementation of appropriate segregation measures (e.g., Chinese walls) is critical in the creation of a dedicated market surveillance team in order to ensure the integrity and confidentiality of the information assessed.

SECTION: Delegation and Outsourcing of Market Surveillance Functions
ID: 165
CONTENT:
PPATs belonging to a group of companies should be able to delegate their monitoring functions to another entity within the same group. In addition, PPATs should be able to outsource a part of their monitoring activity, including the analysis of orders and transactions, alerts generation for the detection of anomalous events, as well as the identification of potential breaches of Articles 3 and 5 of REMIT. However, PPATs should: retain the expertise and resources necessary for evaluating the quality of the services provided and the organisational adequacy of the providers, and for supervising the outsourced services effectively and managing the risks associated on an ongoing basis; have direct access to the relevant information related to the outsourced service; define in a written agreement their rights and obligations and those of the providers. The outsourcing agreement should allow PPATs to terminate it. In any case, PPATs shall ensure that the delegated entity complies with the organisational and procedural arrangements described in this Guidance. PPATs will remain fully responsible for the obligations stated in Article 15 and should submit themselves any STR to the competent NRA(s). Furthermore, PPATs should still be able to conduct any complementary analysis.

CONTENT:

SECTION: Clear Definition of Market Surveillance Function
ID: 168
CONTENT:
A clear definition of the market surveillance function is essential to maintain trust and effectiveness. The market surveillance team should have a clear written function and be trusted by PPAT management, employees, and members/customers. Without this clarity and trust, the team cannot adequately investigate anomalous events or notify potential REMIT breaches. The mission should be broader than individual team tasks and affect all PPAT employees. The PPAT should ensure employees outside the market surveillance team are aware of the function's mission to prevent compliance gaps.

SECTION: Procedural Arrangements Overview
ID: 169
CONTENT:
Procedural arrangements are key to ensuring PPAT fulfills its Article 15 REMIT obligations. These include market monitoring strategy, human resources policies, communications, and traceability procedures. All procedural arrangements should be documented, including changes and updates. Documentation on PPAT compliance with these arrangements should also be maintained for at least five years.

DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Market Monitoring Strategy Requirements
ID: 170
CONTENT:
PPATs must have a documented market monitoring strategy designed based on risk assessment to identify potential breaches of Articles 3 or 5 of REMIT. The strategy shall define thresholds for investigating alerts and include processes to identify potential breaches. It should prescribe actions for the monitoring team to assess anomalous events. The risk assessment must identify different types of market abuse that may constitute breaches and graduate them based on expected risk of occurrence. The strategy must be revised regularly, particularly when evidence shows it is not comprehensive or when market changes occur. PPATs should be able to explain to the NRA how they manage generated alerts and why their automation level is appropriate.

SECTION: Human Resources Policies and Conflict of Interest Management
ID: 171
CONTENT:
Conflicts of interest can affect the integrity and focus of the market surveillance team. The PPAT's human resources policies should safeguard the independence and integrity of market surveillance team members and other affected departments, with focus on conflicts of interest throughout the organization. Relevant employees should declare potential interests in wholesale energy markets, including shareholdings or family relationships. Basic background checks covering fraud and criminal records should be conducted at employment commencement. Due diligence should be applied when employing market surveillance staff. Consideration should be given to potential psychological harassment of the team by trading-related persons. Appropriate training on handling harassment situations and safeguards should be in place.

SECTION: Training and Development for Market Surveillance Teams
ID: 172
CONTENT:
Members of the market surveillance team should receive appropriate training and guidance on REMIT and practical considerations for Article 15 application. Training should be delivered regularly according to a training map and updated in line with Agency and NRA guidance. Training should not be restricted to market surveillance team members but offered across the organization where appropriate. Records of training attendance and completion should be kept, and training effectiveness should be assessed by the PPAT.

DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Communication Procedures and Protocols
ID: 173
CONTENT:
Internal policies should cover data and information use by the market surveillance team and allow members to access information helping explain anomalous events. The team should be able to request information from market participants regarding anomalous events. Communication with persons involved in potential REMIT breaches should be carefully considered to avoid tipping off suspects. The team should have and follow a policy for approaching members/customers, with all communications noted or recorded. Once an STR is submitted to an NRA, the team should not contact the member/customer unless agreed with the NRA and should never disclose that an STR was submitted. In exceptional circumstances, contact may be necessary to enforce sanctions, but NRA engagement from the start is important. For cross-market manipulation cases, internal policies should detail procedures for inter-PPAT communications with clear guidelines on what can be discussed and all contacts recorded.

SECTION: Traceability and Record-Keeping Requirements
ID: 174
CONTENT:
All work by the market surveillance team should be recorded in a dedicated case management system, shared folder, or traceable email records for at least five years. A clear written policy on monitoring procedures should detail processes for investigating anomalous events. The full decision-making process from initial alert to STR submission should be traceable with key decision points recorded. All transactions, orders, and behaviors relating to anomalous events should be stored for a defined period. NRAs may place further retention requirements on PPATs. Information documenting analysis of anomalous events and reasons for STR submission decisions should be maintained for at least five years and provided to NRAs upon request. All processes and decisions should be recorded. PPATs should conduct internal audits or hire external auditors to review processes at least annually.

SECTION: NRA Compliance Advocacy and Enforcement
ID: 175
CONTENT:
Within their investigatory and sanctioning powers, NRAs shall enforce PPAT compliance with Article 15. NRAs may issue Systems and Controls Questionnaires relating to Article 15 processes and conduct visits to assess surveillance and monitoring processes. NRAs may run STR Supervision Forums focusing on best-practice sharing. Each NRA has discretion on conducting visits, issuing questionnaires, or holding forums, with adequate notice given to PPATs. NRAs can implement peer reviews on STR quality and benchmark PPAT performance against references to improve Article 15 compliance.

According to Article 13(1) of REMIT, NRAs shall ensure that prohibitions in Articles 3 and 5 and obligations in Article 4 are applied. DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Accepted Market Practices (AMPs) - Definition and Framework
ID: 178
CONTENT:
According to Recital 27 of REMIT, the Agency's guidance should address the issue of accepted market practices (AMPs). Article 2(2)(a)(ii) and (3)(a)(ii) of REMIT provide that AMPs such as those applying in the financial services area, which are currently defined by Article 1(5) of MAD and which may be adapted if that Directive is amended, could be a legitimate way for market participants to secure a favourable price for a wholesale energy product. According to Article 1(5) of MAD, 'AMPs' mean practices that are reasonably expected in one or more financial markets and are accepted by the competent authority in accordance with guidelines adopted by the Commission in accordance with the procedure laid down in Article 17(2) of the same Directive.

text:
DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: AMPs Application under MAD and REMIT
ID: 179
CONTENT:
Under MAD, the concept of AMPs may either apply in relation to market manipulation according to Article 1(2) of that Directive, or in relation to the information which users of commodity derivatives markets would expect to be made public concerning commodity derivatives according to Article 1(1) of the same Directive. The Agency concludes that AMPs accepted by competent authorities according to MAD may also apply under REMIT, but AMPs under REMIT are not limited to these AMPs. Accordingly, new AMPs may be established under REMIT, in particular concerning wholesale energy commodity markets.

text:
DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Distinction between Activities and Market Practices
ID: 180
CONTENT:
In the same way as financial market authorities have consistently made a distinction between practices and activities, the Agency will distinguish between practices and activities carried out in wholesale energy markets. 'Activities' would cover different types of operations or strategies that may be undertaken such as arbitrage, hedging and short selling. 'Market practices' would cover the way these activities are handled and executed in the market. 'Activities' are considered too broad to qualify for the status of AMPs. An 'activity' such as hedging could be undertaken in different ways. If the activity is carried out in a way which does not constitute market manipulation, then the question of giving it accepted market practice status does not arise. On the other hand, if the 'activity' is carried out in a way which would constitute market manipulation, it is unlikely that a competent authority would be prepared to accept it as an AMP.

DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Specific Practices and Organised Market Place Rules
ID: 181
CONTENT:
The Agency agrees with financial market authorities on their considerations of the issue of whether certain more specific practices, such as crossing/pre-arranged trades or gross bidding, should be given accepted market practice status, subject to the condition that these practices should be undertaken according to the rules of the relevant organised market place applicable to their conduct. As in most of such cases, conduct of the practice in conformity with the rules of the organised market place would be sufficient in itself to promote market integrity and therefore the question of giving the practice accepted market practice status would not arise.

text:
DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: National and Regional Specificities of AMPs
ID: 182
CONTENT:
The decision on whether a process constitutes an AMP is a matter of national or regional specificities. AMPs, therefore, are primarily the responsibility of individual NRAs and so a practice which one competent authority considers is an AMP may not be viewed as such by another. However, each NRA has a duty to consult, both nationally and with other relevant NRAs, and to coordinate with the Agency prior to disclosing any market practices that they have accepted. There is also an obligation on the Agency to coordinate and publish the AMPs on its website. These will be published in a standard ACER format and a link provided to the national legal text once they have been recognised and have undergone the requisite national and European consultation process.

DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Factors for Assessing Market Practices
ID: 183
CONTENT:
The following non-exhaustive list of factors shall be taken into account by competent authorities when assessing particular practices in wholesale energy markets: The level of transparency of the relevant market practice to the whole market - Transparency of market practices by market participants is crucial for considering whether a particular market practice can be accepted by competent authorities. The less transparent a practice is, the more likely it is not to be accepted. However, practices on non-regulated markets might for structural reasons be less transparent than similar practices on regulated markets. Such practices should not be in themselves considered as unacceptable by competent authorities. The need to safeguard the operation of market forces and the proper interplay of the forces of supply and demand - Market practices inhibiting the interaction of supply and demand by limiting the opportunities for other market participants to respond to transactions can create higher risks for market integrity and are, therefore, less likely to be accepted by competent authorities.

text:
DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Additional Assessment Factors for Market Practices
ID: 184
CONTENT:
The degree to which the relevant market practice has an impact on market liquidity and efficiency - Market practices which enhance liquidity and efficiency are more likely to be accepted than those reducing them. The degree to which the relevant practice takes into account the trading mechanism of the relevant market and enables market participants to react properly and in a timely manner to the new market situation created by that practice. The risk inherent in the relevant practice for the integrity of, directly or indirectly, related markets, whether regulated or not, in the relevant wholesale energy product within the whole Union. The outcome of any investigation of the relevant market practice by any competent authority, in particular whether the relevant market practice breached rules or regulations designed to prevent market abuse, or codes of conduct, be it on the market in question or on directly or indirectly related markets within the Union. The structural characteristics of the relevant market including whether it is regulated or not, the types of wholesale energy products traded and the type of market participants.

metadata.title: Additional Assessment Factors for Market Practices
metadata.original_text: The degree to which the relevant market practice has an impact on market liquidity and efficiency - Market practices which enhance liquidity and efficiency are more likely to be accepted than those reducing them. The degree to which the relevant practice takes into account the trading mechanism of the relevant market and enables market participants to react properly and in a timely manner to the new market situation created by that practice. The risk inherent in the relevant practice for the integrity of, directly or indirectly, related markets, whether regulated or not, in the relevant wholesale energy product within the whole Union. The outcome of any investigation of the relevant market practice by any competent authority, in particular whether the relevant market practice breached rules or regulations designed to prevent market abuse, or codes of conduct, be it on the market in question or on directly or indirectly related markets within the Union. SECTION: Overriding Principles for AMPs
ID: 185
CONTENT:
Overriding principles to be observed by competent authorities to ensure that AMPs do not undermine market integrity, while fostering innovation and the continued dynamic development of wholesale energy markets, includes: new or emerging AMPs should not be assumed to be unacceptable by the competent authority simply because they have not been previously accepted by it; practising fairness and efficiency by market participants is required in order not to create prejudice to normal market activity and market integrity. Competent authorities should analyse the impact of the relevant market practice when assessing whether such practice constitutes an AMP.

SECTION: AMPs Application to Information Disclosure
ID: 186
CONTENT:
The Agency currently considers the application of the AMPs regime primarily in relation to the information which users of wholesale energy markets would expect to be made public concerning wholesale energy products for the following incidents and possibly in coordination with the competent national financial market authority: Disclosure of inside information through regional or national inside information platforms fulfilling the minimum quality requirements listed by the Agency in Chapter 7.2.2 of this Guidance, if nominated by the competent NRA(s) following a public consultation and notified to the Agency. NRAs should aim at regional platforms agreed on with relevant NRAs for relevant markets. Disclosure of inside information in an aggregated/anonymised way in order to comply with competition law and notified to the Agency if considered necessary at national level and agreed upon by the national NRA with the national competition authority and notified to the Agency.

ID: 187
CONTENT:

NRAs should consider the following best practice example of such compliance regime for market participants, but taking into account the market participant's size and trading capacity: Compliance culture - the creation of a corporate culture to comply with REMIT requirements. Compliance objectives - the compliance with REMIT requirements, namely the registration, disclosure and reporting obligations and the market abuse prohibitions.

SECTION: Penalty Regimes under REMIT
ID: 190
CONTENT:
According to Article 18 of REMIT, Member States should have laid down the rules on penalties applicable to infringements of REMIT by 29 June 2013. In order to ensure an effective implementation of REMIT, the Agency considers it important that penalties are put in place for all potential infringements of REMIT, which may consist of breaches of the market abuse prohibitions of Articles 3 and 5 of the Regulation, but also of breaches of the obligation to notify the relevant information to the Agency and the competent NRA in situations according to Article 3(4)(b) of the Regulation.

SECTION: Document Overview and Agency Introduction
ID: 0
CONTENT:
Guidance on the application of Regulation (EU) No 1227/2011 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 25 October 2011 on wholesale energy market integrity and transparency 4th Edition 17-June-2016. The Agency for the Cooperation of Energy Regulators (the Agency) is the European Union body created by the Third Energy Package to achieve the Internal Energy Market (IEM). The Agency was officially launched in March 2011 and has its seat in Ljubljana, Slovenia. As an independent European body which fosters cooperation among European energy regulators, the Agency ensures that market integration and the harmonisation of regulatory frameworks are achieved in accordance with the EU's energy policy objectives.

text:
DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Agency Mission and REMIT Responsibilities
ID: 1
CONTENT:
The overall mission of the Agency, as stated in its founding Regulation, is to complement and coordinate the work of national energy regulators at EU level, and to work towards the completion of a single EU energy market for electricity and natural gas. The Agency's missions and tasks are defined by the Directives and Regulations of the Third Energy Package, especially Regulation (EC) No 713/2009 establishing the Agency. In 2011, the Agency received additional tasks under Regulation (EU) No 1227/2011 on wholesale energy market integrity and transparency (REMIT). According to REMIT, the Agency is responsible for monitoring wholesale energy markets to detect market abuse.

CONTENT:
The monitoring of wholesale energy markets by the Agency shall be based on the timely collection of data relating to the transactions executed and the orders placed on wholesale energy markets in the European Union (trading data), as well as on fundamental data, that is, data relating to the operational conditions of the energy systems in both the electricity and gas sectors. DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Focus of 4th Edition on Article 15 REMIT
ID: 8
CONTENT:
Taking into account the experience gained so far, including the feedback received from NRAs, market participants and other stakeholders, the Agency now considers necessary to update the Guidance and publish a 4th edition. In this 4th edition, strong emphasis is put on Article 15 of REMIT. The Agency intends to provide more detailed guidance to NRAs concerning the supervision of the obligations imposed on persons professionally arranging transactions by Article 15 of REMIT, taking into account the important number of trades in the wholesale energy markets that they intermediate. This edition defines the Agency's understanding of the notion of persons professionally arranging transactions and provides guidance to NRAs on how to monitor the compliance of these persons with the obligations to (i) notify potential REMIT breaches and (ii) establish and maintain effective arrangements and procedures to identify such potential breaches.

SECTION: Purpose and Scope of Non-Binding Guidance
ID: 10
CONTENT:
The non-binding Guidance on the application of REMIT provided in this document is directed to National Regulatory Authorities (NRAs) to ensure the required coordination and consistency in their monitoring activities under REMIT. It is deliberately drafted in non-legal terms and made public for transparency purposes only. The non-binding Guidance is updated from time to time to reflect the changing market conditions and the experience gained by the Agency and NRAs in the implementation of REMIT, including through the feedback of market participants and other stakeholders. This Guidance is without prejudice to Directive 2003/6/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 28 January 2003 (market abuse) and Directive 2004/39/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 21 April 2004 on markets in financial instruments applying to wholesale energy products which are financial instruments, as well as to the application of European competition law to the practices covered by REMIT.

DOCUMENT: 4th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Scope of REMIT Regulation
ID: 14
CONTENT:
According to Article 1(2) of REMIT, the Regulation applies to trading in wholesale energy products. However, Articles 3 and 5 of REMIT shall not apply to wholesale energy products which are financial instruments and to which Article 9 of Directive 2003/6/EC (market abuse - MAD) applies. REMIT is without prejudice to MAD and Directive 2004/39/EC (MiFID), as well as to the application of European competition law. Article 1(2) of REMIT requires definition of a borderline between market abuse prohibitions of Articles 3 and 5 of REMIT and market abuse prohibitions of MAD.
