SECTION: Registration User Manual and NRA Guidance
ID: 42
CONTENT:
NRAs should ensure that market participants are provided with information on how to register. For this purpose, and for the purpose of ensuring accuracy in the European register of market participants established by the Agency in accordance with Article 9(3) of REMIT, the Agency will make available a Registration User Manual (RUM) to NRAs. The RUM will provide guidance on how the fields in the registration format should be populated. On the basis of the RUM, NRAs may provide guidance to market participants on how to register. The manual will be updated periodically, on the basis of the feedback from NRAs.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: NRA Selection for Market Participant Registration
ID: 43
CONTENT:
According to Article 9(1) of REMIT, Market participants entering into transactions which are required to be reported to the Agency in accordance with Article 8(1) shall register with the national regulatory authority in the Member State in which they are established or resident, or, if they are not established or resident in the Union, in a Member State in which they are active. According to settled case law of the Court of Justice of the European Union, a legal or natural person can be established in more than one Member State. The legal or natural person is established in the Member State(s) in which it pursues a professional activity on a stable and continuous basis. If a market participant is established in more than one Member State, the Agency would normally expect market participants to register in the Member State in which they have their primary establishment. For market participants not established or resident in the Union, it is the Agency's understanding that such market participants may choose in which Member State to register, as long as they are active in that Member State.

DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Registration Submission Deadlines
ID: 44
CONTENT:
According to Article 9(4) of REMIT, Market participants shall submit the registration form to the NRA prior to entering into a transaction which is required to be reported to the Agency in accordance with Article 8(1). Thus, market participants must submit all the Sections of the registration form (Sections 1 to 5) before entering into any transaction which is required to be reported to the Agency. In line with Article 12(2) of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 1348/2014, the reporting obligation will apply to market participants from 7 October 2015 and from 7 April 2016, according to the type of data to be reported to the Agency. For market participants entering into transactions on an organised market place (OMP), the registration obligation takes effect, at the latest, prior to 7 October 2015. For all other market participants, the registration obligation takes effect, at the latest, prior to 7 April 2016, or prior to the first day they enter into transactions which are required to be reported to the Agency.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Example 1: Market Participant A Registered Before 17 March 2015
ID: 48
CONTENT:
Market participant A registered before 17 March 2015 and completed Sections 1, 2, 3 and 5 of the registration form before submission. Section 4 was not filled at first submission since the European register was first published on 17 March 2015. After 17 March 2015, MP A has three months (until 17 June 2015) to fill Section 4 with data available at the European register, including all related undertakings registered as MPs. If related undertaking MP B registers after 17 June 2015, MP A must update Section 4 accordingly once MP B's registration is published. MP A must also promptly update any other information in its registration form per Article 9(5) of REMIT when changes take effect, such as selecting a new Registered Reporting Mechanism (RRM) requiring Section 5 update.

SECTION: Issuance of the ACER Code
ID: 50
CONTENT:
As required by Article 9(2) of REMIT, each registered market participant receives a unique identifier called the 'ACER code', enabling them to report data under Article 8 of REMIT. Market participants need the list of ACER codes to provide information for Section 4 of the registration form regarding corporate structure. According to Article 9(4) of REMIT, market participants must submit the registration form prior to entering into transactions required to be reported to the Agency per Article 8(1) of REMIT. The ACER code is issued upon transmission of information from national registers to the Agency for the first time, per Agency Decision No 01/12.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: ACER Code Issuance Process and Timing
ID: 51
CONTENT:
According to Article 2 of Agency Decision No 01/12, NRAs should promptly transmit registration information to the Agency once submitted by the market participant, after which the Agency immediately issues the ACER code. NRAs must ensure market participants receive the ACER code timely, before transactions are required to be reported to the Agency per Article 8(1) of REMIT. This enables market participants to fulfill reporting obligations and supports efficient Agency data collection. The registration system provides automatic checks preventing incomplete registration forms from being submitted. For participants registering before the Agency first publishes the European register, the ACER code is issued upon submission of initial phase information (Sections 1, 2, 3 and 5). However, such participants should not consider ACER code receipt as confirmation of completed registration; they must still provide Section 4 information as described in Chapter 4.6.

This enables market participants to fulfill reporting obligations and supports efficient Agency data collection. The registration system provides automatic checks preventing incomplete registration forms from being submitted. For participants registering before the Agency first publishes the European register, the ACER code is issued upon submission of initial phase information (Sections 1, 2, 3 and 5). However, such participants should not consider ACER code receipt as confirmation of completed registration; they must still provide Section 4 information as described in Chapter 4.6.

DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Requirement to Keep Registration Information Up to Date
ID: 53
CONTENT:
According to Article 9(5) of REMIT, market participants must communicate promptly to the national regulatory authority any change regarding information provided in the registration form. Registration is not a one-off event but an ongoing requirement. REMIT requires market participants to register with an NRA prior to entering into a transaction and to update their registration form with any changes per Article 9(5). If mandatory registration information changes are not communicated promptly, the registration is considered incomplete. Market participants with outdated registration forms may breach Article 9 of REMIT. Although market participants bear responsibility for updating information, the Agency considers it best practice for NRAs to set up regular reminders (e.g., annually) asking market participants to verify submitted information remains correct and current.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: The Role of NRAs in the Registration Process
ID: 54
CONTENT:
Market participants must register at the national level, not directly with the Agency, making registration a national process. NRAs undertake three roles during registration. First, they act as support sources for market participants seeking to register. The Agency provides a Registration User Manual (RUM) to NRAs for supporting market participants, though ultimate registration responsibility lies with market participants. Second, NRAs transmit national register information to the Agency. Per Article 2 of Agency Decision No 01/2012, NRAs should promptly transmit registration information once submitted by market participants, after which the Agency immediately issues the ACER code. Third, NRAs ensure registration information accuracy. Per Article 9(2) of REMIT, NRAs establish and maintain market participant registers. Accurate national and European register information is prerequisite for efficient market monitoring. The Agency considers it best practice for NRAs to have systems checking registration information to identify omissions and errors, with detected errors promptly notified to the Agency.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Registration Accuracy and ACER Code Issuance Timing
ID: 55
CONTENT:
The Agency's registration system provides automatic checks preventing incomplete registration form submission. Market participants may trade without breaching Article 9 once they submit complete registration forms to the relevant NRA, regardless of ACER code issuance. The Agency aims to issue the ACER code immediately upon receiving registration information from the NRA while ensuring high accuracy in the European register. The Agency may delay publishing information transmitted by NRAs while conducting additional registration information checks. Importantly, through registration, NRAs do not issue trading authorization or licenses. Registration completion does not constitute a 'know-your-customer' check or 'fit-and-proper' assessment.

SECTION: Registration Process Steps for Pre-Publication Registrants
ID: 56
CONTENT:
For market participants starting registration before the Agency first publishes the European register list, the registration process includes: (1) Before entering into reportable transactions per Article 8(1) of REMIT, the market participant submits a registration form to the relevant NRA providing information for Sections 1, 2, 3 and 5 of Agency Decision No 01/2012. NRAs should encourage advance registration for smooth processes, with market participants responsible for providing correct, complete information. (2) The NRA promptly transmits national register information to the Agency. (3) Immediately following NRA-to-Agency transmission, the Agency issues a unique identifier (ACER code) and informs the market participant and relevant NRA. (4) The Agency establishes a European register based on NRA-provided information, publishing a market participant list.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Market Participant Registration Process and Requirements
ID: 57
CONTENT:
The market participant completes the second phase of the registration process by submitting information relevant to Section 4 of the registration format. The deadline for the submission of this information is 3 months after the Agency publishes for the first time the European register of market participants. Any market participant that is registering after the Agency for the first time publishes the European list of market participants must provide all relevant information, i.e. information relevant to Sections 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5, during its initial registration. Market participants must transmit the registration form to the NRA prior to entering into a transaction which is required to be reported to the Agency in accordance with Article 8(1) of REMIT. It is however important that a clear and consistent message is given to market participants regarding registration under REMIT: the registration of market participants does not constitute any kind of authorisation or license to trade, and is without prejudice to obligations to comply with the applicable trading and balancing rules. The Agency will announce early in advance when it intends to publish for the first time the European register of market participants.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Application of the Definition of Inside Information - Introduction
ID: 58
CONTENT:
This chapter covers what the Agency currently considers 'inside information' under REMIT. Qualifying a specific fact as 'inside information' under REMIT requires a two-step approach. Firstly, it must be determined whether there is an item of information (according to at least one of (a) to (d) criteria defined in Article 2(1), second subparagraph, of REMIT). Secondly, it must be ascertained whether it fulfils the four cumulative conditions established in Article 2(1), first subparagraph, of REMIT (i.e., it is precise, not public, related to one or more wholesale energy products, and likely to significantly affect prices). The remainder of this chapter is structured along the two-step approach by providing guidance on what the Agency considers 'information' under REMIT and on the definition of 'inside information', including the application of the four cumulative conditions that qualify information as 'inside information'.

DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: The Concept of Information Under REMIT - Regulatory Framework
ID: 59
CONTENT:
Article 2(1), second subparagraph, of REMIT specifies the meaning of the term 'information' as follows: (a) information which is required to be made public in accordance with Regulations (EC) No 714/2009 and (EC) No 715/2009, including guidelines and network codes adopted pursuant to those Regulations; (b) information relating to the capacity and use of facilities for production, storage, consumption or transmission of electricity or natural gas or related to the capacity and use of LNG facilities, including planned or unplanned unavailability of these facilities; (c) information which is required to be disclosed in accordance with legal or regulatory provisions at Union or national level, market rules, and contracts or customs on the relevant wholesale energy market, insofar as this information is likely to have a significant effect on the prices of wholesale energy products; and (d) other information that a reasonable market participant would be likely to use as part of the basis of its decision to enter into a transaction relating to, or to issue an order to trade in, a wholesale energy product.

DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Information Requirements Under EU Regulations and Facility Capacity
ID: 60
CONTENT:
Article 2(1)(a) of REMIT states that all information which is required to be disclosed under Regulations (EC) No 2019/943 and (EC) No 715/2009 establishing the conditions for access to the network for cross-border exchanges in electricity and access to natural gas transmission networks (including applicable guidelines and network codes adopted pursuant to those Regulations) is also considered 'information' under REMIT. The concept of 'information' under REMIT also encompasses information related to all planned or unplanned changes in the capacity or output of any size at a facility for production, storage, consumption or transmission of natural gas or electricity (Article 2(1)(b) of REMIT). This specifically holds true for any fact related to: the capacity and use of facilities for production of electricity or natural gas, including planned and unplanned unavailability of these facilities; the capacity and use of facilities for storage of electricity or natural gas, including planned and unplanned availability of these facilities; the capacity and use of facilities for consumption of electricity or natural gas, including planned and unplanned unavailability of these facilities; the capacity and use of facilities for transmission, including planned or unplanned unavailability of these facilities; and the capacity and use of LNG facilities, including planned and unplanned unavailability of these facilities.

DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Disclosure Requirements and Transparency Information
ID: 61
CONTENT:
Article 2(1)(c) of REMIT explains that the concept of 'information' under REMIT also covers facts that are required to be disclosed in accordance with: legal or regulatory provisions at national level; legal or regulatory provisions at the European Union level; market rules; contracts; and the customs on the market. In that respect, it is important to highlight the regulatory provisions at the European Union level included in Regulation (EC) 543/2013 on the submission and publication of data in electricity markets (usually referred to as 'transparency information'). It establishes a multitude of different obligations to publish facts that would also constitute 'information' according to Article 2(1)(c) of REMIT. Finally, Article 2(1)(d) of REMIT establishes that any other information that a reasonable market participant would be likely to use as part of the basis of its decision to enter into a transaction relating to a wholesale energy product, or their decision to issue an order to trade in a wholesale energy product, should be considered 'information' under REMIT.

DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: The Reasonable Market Participant Test
ID: 62
CONTENT:
The Agency recommends that NRAs use the 'reasonable market participant test' to help determine whether a given fact qualifies as 'information' under REMIT, but only when such facts is not already covered by Articles 2(1)(a), (b) and (c) of REMIT. It is the Agency's understanding that the concept of the 'reasonable market participant' may encompass different profiles of market participants (e.g. beginner, average, informed, professional market participant) with different trading strategies (e.g. portfolio optimisation, arbitrage, speculative) covering short-term and/or long-term products. The concept of 'reasonability' is rather related to the use of cognitive elements by the market participant in its trading decisions (at least partially). By contrast, a market participant that makes trading decisions based on non-cognitive elements, such as instinct or mood, should not be considered reasonable. To qualify a fact as information under REMIT, it is enough that at least one of these profiles is likely to use the fact as part of the basis of their decision to enter into a transaction relating to a wholesale energy product, or their decision to issue an order to trade in a wholesale energy product.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Application of the Reasonable Market Participant Test - Indicators
ID: 63
CONTENT:
When using the 'reasonable market participant test', the NRAs may take into consideration, as indicators, that: the concept of 'would be likely to use' should be distinguished from the concept of 'would like to use' – the test is not about whether there is a wish on the part of the reasonable market participant to use some type of information. Rather, the test is used to assess whether it is reasonable for a market participant to have a legitimate expectation that such information is available. Therefore, the concept of 'would be likely to use' should be interpreted based on what can be reasonably expected to be published (for example, the fact that a market participant would like to use its competitors' trading plans for its own trading strategy does not mean that these plans are 'information' under REMIT, as they are not information that 'can reasonably be expected to be published' and that would likely be used by a reasonable market participant). The fact that a market participant used comparable facts (for example, at a different moment in time) as the basis for its trading decisions, could be considered a proxy to further assess with an ad hoc analysis if the fact is information that would be likely to be used by a 'reasonable market participant'.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: The Definition of Inside Information - Four Cumulative Conditions
ID: 64
CONTENT:
Pursuant to Article 2(1), second subparagraph, of REMIT, information qualifies as 'inside information' if it fulfils the four cumulative conditions included in Article 2(1), first subparagraph, of REMIT i.e., 'Inside information' means information of a precise nature, which has not been made public, which relates, directly or indirectly, to one or more wholesale energy products and which, if it were made public, would be likely to significantly affect the prices of those wholesale energy products. The application of each of these four conditions will be further explained in subsequent chapters. It is the responsibility of market participants to ascertain whether the information they hold potentially constitutes 'inside information' according to the above-mentioned four cumulative conditions, and therefore, needs to be made public according to Article 4(1) of REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Internal Compliance Rules for Market Participants
ID: 65
CONTENT:
In order to have an appropriate framework for the assessment of information, it is recommended that market participants have clear internal compliance rules that are adapted to their activities and to the specificities of the information, they use and have access to. The best practices for internal compliance rules may include: a framework for the assessment of whether the facts at hand can be qualified as inside information. This may include, for example, measures on how to identify inside information, appropriately tested thresholds, etc.; an adequate workflow of information compliant with the presence of inside information. This may include, for example, a mapping of the flow of information, measures on how to handle inside information, etc.; and a lists of insiders and/or mechanisms in place to identify insiders. The internal compliance rules should be consistent with a market participant's organisational structure and trading strategy.

SECTION: Examples of Information Under REMIT - TSO Transfer Capacity
ID: 66
CONTENT:
Information on the TSO's available transfer capacity: The estimates of TSOs A and B of the available transfer capacity for each day and the available transfer capacity already reserved in the electricity interconnector between bidding zones C and D. text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Definition and Assessment of Precise Nature Information
ID: 70
CONTENT:
Information shall be deemed to be of a precise nature if it indicates a set of circumstances which exists or may reasonably be expected to come into existence, or an event which has occurred or may reasonably be expected to do so, and if it is specific enough to enable a conclusion to be drawn as to the possible effect of that set of circumstances or event on the prices of wholesale energy products. The precise nature of the information is to be assessed by the information holder on a case-by-case basis and depends on what the information is, as well as on the surrounding context. In that assessment, the holder of the information may, among other things, take into consideration: (i) that there is a realistic prospect that a fact will occur; (ii) that the estimation of the potential price effect of information disclosure is irrelevant for the assessment of the precise nature; and (iii) that intermediate steps in a lengthy process may be precise information.

DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Realistic Prospect as a Criterion for Precise Information
ID: 71
CONTENT:
It is enough that there is a realistic prospect that the fact will occur to make the information related to that event precise. Information is precise as long as there is a realistic prospect that the circumstances or events it refers to will come into existence or occur, considering all the factors existing at the time of the assessment. The assessment should consider whether there is a realistic prospect that the circumstances or events will materialize, based on all available evidence and context at the time of evaluation.

metadata.title: Realistic Prospect as a Criterion for Precise Information
metadata.original_text: It is enough that there is a realistic prospect that the fact will occur to make the information related to that event precise. Information is precise as long as there is a realistic prospect that the circumstances or events it refers to will come into existence or occur, considering all the factors existing at the time of the assessment. The assessment should consider whether there is a realistic prospect that the circumstances or events will materialize, based on all available evidence and context at the time of evaluation.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Example 1: Information on Strikes Affecting Generation Units
ID: 72
CONTENT:
Information on strikes provided to the market participant impacting workers relevant for the normal operation of a generation unit can be seen as having a realistic prospect of happening due to, for example, the existence of historical records of this information resulting in effective strikes impacting the production of this unit. Therefore, it can be considered that there is a realistic prospect of a strike happening, considering all the factors existing at the time of the assessment. This information on strikes would then qualify as precise information, despite the fact that the strike can still be cancelled and/or that there may be some uncertainty about the overall duration of the strike or other elements. Any further developments of the situation (cancellation of the strike, update on the dates of the strike, scope of workers affected etc.) may make the prospect of the strike less realistic. However, as long as they occur after the market participant assessed whether the information was precise, they should not be taken into consideration by the NRA when assessing whether the information was precise at the time the market participant received the information. In any case, the market participant should provide updates to the public on the evolution of the information.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Example 2: Nuclear Safety Authority Security Tests Information
ID: 73
CONTENT:
Information or request by the nuclear safety authority to the market participant of possible security tests to be run at an electricity generation unit during the first half of the year can be seen as having a realistic prospect of happening due to, for example, the existence of previous information of the same type that resulted in effective security tests impacting the production and/or availability of the unit, episodes reflecting the planning of the nuclear safety authority, or previous expressions of concerns with the operation of the unit. Therefore, it can be considered that there is a realistic prospect of the security tests impacting the production and/or availability to happen considering all factors existing at the time of the assessment. It is to be noted that in some Member States there is an obligation deriving from the national legislation for the nuclear safety authority to publish this information on possible security tests.

DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Price Effect Estimation and Precise Nature Assessment
ID: 74
CONTENT:
The estimation of the potential price effect of information disclosure is irrelevant for the assessment of the precise nature of the information. However, the likelihood of a significant price effect should be assessed to determine if the information is inside information under REMIT. More specifically, in order for the information to have a precise nature, it is not necessary to be able to infer from that information, with a sufficient degree of probability, that, once it is made public, its potential effect on the prices of the relevant wholesale energy products in a particular direction. The calculation of the potential effect of the information on the prices of wholesale energy products is not an element to be taken into consideration in the assessment of the precise nature of the information.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Intermediate Steps in Lengthy Processes as Precise Information
ID: 75
CONTENT:
Intermediate steps in a lengthy process that are connected to bringing about future circumstances or events may be regarded as precise information. The knowledge of such steps could constitute an advantage that could undermine the spirit and objective protected by REMIT, which is to place market participants on an equal footing and enhance market integrity in terms of information symmetry. Intermediate steps connected to bringing about future circumstances or events shall be specific enough to enable conclusions to be drawn as to the likely effect of that set of circumstances or events on the prices of wholesale energy products.

DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Example 1: Commissioning of New Plants and Recommissioning of Mothballed Power Plants
ID: 76
CONTENT:
The process leading to the commissioning of new plants or recommissioning of mothballed power plants is a lengthy and complex process. Its major milestones (for example: management board approvals, regulatory approvals, licence granting, etc.) constitute intermediate steps in this process. Some facts generated by the intermediate steps leading to the commissioning or recommissioning of a power plant would qualify as precise information under REMIT, as they constitute a set of circumstances which exist or may reasonably be expected to come into existence and impact the realistic prospect of energy being produced from a certain point in time onwards. In order to decide whether these facts qualify as inside information, the three other criteria covered in sections 5.3.2 to 5.3.4 also need to be met.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Information That Has Not Been Made Public
ID: 77
CONTENT:
Inside information is information that has not been shared with the public and, as a consequence, creates information asymmetries between market participants. Effective disclosure to the public of market participants is the criterion that transforms non-public information into public information. Once the information becomes public, it enhances the integrity and transparency of the market, as envisaged by Recital 2 of REMIT. In general, information is deemed to be public knowledge if such information has been made, by any party, available to the public, i.e. to an unspecified number of market participants. In this regard, it is irrelevant who made the information public. No distinction is made as to whether the information was made public by a market participant or by any other party.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Requirements for Public Disclosure and Information Accessibility
ID: 78
CONTENT:
It is sufficient, but also required, that information is made available to the entire public of market participants simultaneously, ensuring equal access to the information, since any interested market participant may appraise the information. This can be the case, for example, if a generally accessible electronic system for the dissemination of information, that qualifies as an Inside Information Platform, is used. Publication by any party other than the market participant is a factor that has to be taken in account for the qualification of inside information only. When information is still qualified as inside information, the obligation to publish is on the market participant according to Article 4(1) of REMIT. Publishing information only to selected market participants, for example via an e-mail channel or news board which is available exclusively to exchange members, does not satisfy the requirement of informing the public.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Example 2: Planned Unavailability on Electricity Interconnector Due to Expansion Works
ID: 79
CONTENT:
The process leading to the expansion of capacity in an electricity interconnector is a lengthy and complex process. Its major milestones (for example: market participant's management board decisions, regulatory approvals, licence granting, decisions from the interconnector's operational centre to proceed with the unavailability) constitute intermediate steps. A management board decision (for example, on the unavailability on the existing interconnectors to allow the expansion of the existing infrastructure during a specific period), despite being an intermediate step that can still be subject to other approvals (for example by regulatory or operational centre), fulfils the criteria of precise nature under REMIT. Indeed, the management board decision to approve or disapprove a planned maintenance during a specific period is specific enough to enable a conclusion to be drawn as to the possible effect of that set of circumstances or events on the prices of wholesale energy products. In order to decide whether the management board decision can qualify as inside information, the three other criteria covered in sections 5.3.2 to 5.3.4 also need to be met.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Information Relating to Wholesale Energy Products
ID: 80
CONTENT:
The definition of 'inside information' in Article 2(1) of REMIT requires the relevant information to relate, directly or indirectly, to one or more wholesale energy products. 'Wholesale energy products' are defined under Article 2(4) of REMIT as: (a) contracts for the supply of electricity or natural gas where delivery is in the Union; (b) derivatives relating to electricity or natural gas produced, traded or delivered in the Union; (c) contracts relating to the transportation of electricity or natural gas in the Union; and (d) derivatives relating to the transportation of electricity or natural gas in the Union. Information that has a possible effect on the demand, supply and/or prices of a wholesale energy product, or on the expectations of the demand, supply and/or prices of a wholesale energy product, shall be considered as directly or indirectly related to the wholesale energy product.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Likelihood of Significant Price Effect on Wholesale Energy Products
ID: 81
CONTENT:
Information is deemed to constitute inside information only if, were it made public, it would be likely to have a significant effect on the prices of related wholesale energy product. Based on the condition of a significant price effect, the Agency narrowed the wide notion of information down to the information that is crucial enough to have the potential to significantly affect the prices of wholesale energy products, and therefore to information that is relevant for trading. It is important to note that the mere 'likelihood' of a significant price effect is enough to meet this condition and that no actual price effect is required. The assessment of the likelihood of price effect has to be performed by a market participant on a case-by-case basis. In this context, if the information is likely to have a significant effect on the prices of wholesale energy products, it is necessarily related to these products. Therefore, it is enough for the NRAs to assess the likelihood of a significant effect on the prices to establish whether the information relates to wholesale energy products.

DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Assessment Framework for Significant Price Effect
ID: 83
CONTENT:
Market participants should assess whether information is likely to have a significant price effect by considering the nature of the information and market specificities. Key factors include: market characteristics (size, timeframe, design, liquidity, participant types); event size; published information on supply/demand; transmission facility and network constraints; time of day; announcements on non-regular events; TSO system announcements; and other market variables (weather, CO2, fuel prices, geopolitical developments). Market participants should maintain systematic internal compliance frameworks reflecting these factors, adapted to their activities and information handling. Assessments must be performed ex ante before publication, allowing NRAs to use ex post information for verification without taking action against those who drew reasonable conclusions from available ex ante information.

DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: NRA Verification Methods for Price Effect Assessment
ID: 84
CONTENT:
NRAs can verify whether a market participant's assessment on likelihood of significant price effect is consistent with reasonable market participant expectations by checking: whether the information type has historically had significant price effects; whether pre-existing analyst reports, price publications, and opinions indicate the information type affects prices; whether the market participant itself previously treated similar events as inside information; whether another reasonable market participant treated similar events as inside information; or whether a reasonable market participant would likely use it in trading decisions.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Example 1: Unplanned Outage Status Update Assessment
ID: 85
CONTENT:
Market participant A operating a power plant discovers unplanned maintenance on a 100 MW generation unit will extend by 2 hours. With limited market liquidity, MP A assesses whether this information would significantly affect prices. Relevant factors: intraday market is open with two hourly and eight 15-minute products affected; limited order book depth means small fundamental changes may impact prices; event size is limited (100 MWh for two hours); no other outages announced; limited cross-border capacity; normal working hours; no additional announcements; no relevant wind forecast changes; day-ahead price provides baseline for intraday decisions. Assessment: MP A concludes a reasonable market participant would use this extension information in trading decisions, particularly for directly affected hourly and 15-minute products, making it likely to have significant price effect. This is consistent with MP A's previous decision to publish the initial outage.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Example 2: TSO Reserve Activation Request Assessment
ID: 86
CONTENT:
A TSO requests a balancing responsible party to activate a generation unit for 200 MWh due to potential system imbalance, 25 minutes before delivery time, while intraday market remains open. The TSO assesses whether this information would significantly affect prices. Relevant factors: intraday market is open with low bid-ask spread and relatively high market depth; event size is relevant given proximity to delivery period; no other outages announced; no cross-border transmission capacity available; information issued very close to delivery period; no additional announcements; no relevant market variable changes. Assessment: TSO concludes that activation of balancing bids provides valuable information on system imbalance direction, and a reasonable market participant would use this information in trading decisions, making it likely to have significant price effect on intraday products.

DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Information on Trading Plans and Strategies
ID: 87
CONTENT:
Information regarding a market participant's own trading plans and strategies should not be considered inside information under REMIT Recital 12. Trading plans are defined as systematic methods for evaluating supply, demand, or price of wholesale energy products, determining risk levels, and formulating short- and/or long-term investment targets guiding daily trading activity. Consequences of these targets in terms of energy needs and resulting trade orders are part of trading plans and not REMIT information. Trading strategies are sets of objective rules designating conditions for trade entries and exits, including order specifications with filters/triggers and exit rules. However, facts used to determine or change trading strategy details can constitute inside information, even if the strategy details themselves do not.

SECTION: Example: Order Details as Trading Strategy
ID: 88
CONTENT:
Market participant A submits an order with: Buy indicator; Initiator status; Flexible Hour order type (trades at any hour if price/volume matched); Fill and Float conditions (killed after matching, stays if unfilled); Active status; 1,500 MW minimum execution volume; 40.5 euro price limit; Good Till Cancelled duration. Assessment: This order detail is part of the market participant's trading strategy and does not qualify as inside information under REMIT.

SECTION: Market Manipulation Definition and Application
ID: 90
CONTENT:
This chapter provides NRAs with examples of market activities fulfilling the definition of market manipulation in Article 2(2) and (3) of REMIT. The guidance aims to help NRAs develop common understanding of market manipulation and identify relevant diagnostic variables or signals for detection by competent authorities and market participants. Examples are described in non-legal technical terms and are not intended to affect REMIT interpretation scope. Article 2(2) of REMIT distinguishes four different categories of market manipulation.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Market Manipulation Definition and Categories
ID: 91
CONTENT:
Market manipulation is defined through four main categories: (1) false/misleading transactions, (2) price positioning, (3) transactions involving fictitious devices/deception and (4) dissemination of false and misleading information. These involve entering into transactions or issuing orders to trade in wholesale energy products which give or are likely to give false or misleading signals as to supply, demand, or price; securing or attempting to secure the price of wholesale energy products at an artificial level unless legitimate reasons are established and the transaction conforms to accepted market practices; or employing fictitious devices or deception that gives false or misleading signals regarding supply, demand, or price of wholesale energy products.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Dissemination of False Information and Market Manipulation
ID: 92
CONTENT:
Disseminating information through media, including the internet, or by any other means which gives or is likely to give false or misleading signals as to supply, demand, or price of wholesale energy products constitutes market manipulation. This includes dissemination of rumours and false or misleading news, where the disseminating person knew or ought to have known that the information was false or misleading. However, information disseminated for journalism or artistic expression is assessed considering freedom of the press and expression rules, unless those persons derive advantage or profits from the dissemination or the disclosure is made with intention to mislead the market regarding supply, demand, or price of wholesale energy products.

DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Attempted Market Manipulation Under REMIT
ID: 93
CONTENT:
Article 2(3) of REMIT defines attempted market manipulation as entering into any transaction, issuing any order to trade or taking any other action relating to a wholesale energy product with the intention of: giving false or misleading signals as to supply, demand, or price; securing the price of wholesale energy products at an artificial level unless legitimate reasons are established and the transaction conforms to accepted market practices; or employing fictitious devices or deception. It also includes disseminating information through media or any other means with the intention of giving false or misleading signals as to supply, demand, or price. The 'acceptable market practice' argument can only be used for price positioning categories, not for other categories of market manipulation.

ID: 94
CONTENT:
According to REMIT Recitals 13 and 14, manipulation on wholesale energy markets involves actions that artificially cause prices to be at a level not justified by market forces of supply and demand, including actual availability of production, storage or transportation capacity. Forms include placing and withdrawal of false orders; spreading false or misleading information or rumours through media or internet; deliberately providing false information to undertakings providing price assessments or market reports; and deliberately making it appear that availability of electricity generation capacity, natural gas availability, or transmission capacity is other than actually technically available. Manipulation may occur across borders, between electricity and gas markets, and across financial and commodity markets including emission allowances markets.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Examples of Market Manipulation Conduct
ID: 95
CONTENT:
Examples of market manipulation include conduct by a person or persons acting in collaboration to secure a decisive position over supply of or demand for a wholesale energy product which has or could have the effect of fixing prices directly or indirectly or creating unfair trading conditions. This includes offering, buying or selling wholesale energy products with the purpose, intention or effect of misleading market participants acting on the basis of reference prices. However, accepted market practices such as those in financial services, currently defined by Article 1(5) of Directive 2003/6/EC, could be a legitimate way for market participants to secure a favourable price for a wholesale energy product.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Wash Trades and Improper Matched Orders
ID: 96
CONTENT:
Wash trades consist of entering into arrangements for sale or purchase of a wholesale energy product where there is no change in beneficial interests or market risk, or where beneficial interest or market risk is transferred between parties acting in concert or collusion. Improper matched orders are transactions where both buy and sell orders are entered at or nearly at the same time, with the same price and quantity by different but colluding parties. These transactions constitute market manipulation unless they are legitimate trades carried out in conformity with the rules of the relevant trading platform, such as crossing trades.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Layering and Spoofing Practices
ID: 97
CONTENT:
Layering consists of issuing multiple non-genuine orders to trade at different price levels (layers) on one side of the order book, in order to enter into one or multiple transactions on the other side of the order book. Spoofing consists of issuing a single large or multiple non-genuine orders at the same price level on one side of the order book, in order to enter into one or multiple transactions on the other side of the order book. Both practices are considered market manipulation techniques used to create misleading signals about supply, demand, or price.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Other Order-Based Behaviours and Marking the Close
ID: 98
CONTENT:
Other order-based behaviours involve issuing order(s) to trade, with or without an interest in their individual execution, which are likely to give misleading signals as to supply of, demand for, or price of wholesale energy products or likely to secure the price at an artificial level. Due to frequency and/or overall volume of orders, the behaviour results in transactions at terms generally more favourable to the market participant involved than would otherwise prevail. Marking the close involves deliberately buying or selling wholesale energy products at market close to alter the closing price, particularly associated with future/option expiry dates or quarterly/annual portfolio or index reference/valuation points.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Abusive Squeeze and Cross-Market Manipulation
ID: 99
CONTENT:
Abusive squeeze (market cornering) involves a party or parties with significant influence over supply of, demand for, or delivery mechanisms for a wholesale energy product exploiting a decisive position to materially distort the price at which others must deliver, take delivery or defer delivery to satisfy obligations. Proper supply and demand interaction leading to market tightness is not itself manipulation. Cross-market manipulation involves trading on one market to improperly position the price of a wholesale energy product on a related market, such as trading in underlying products to distort derivative contract prices. Legitimate arbitrage transactions would not constitute manipulation.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Manipulative Capacity Withholding
ID: 100
CONTENT:
Manipulative capacity withholding occurs when a market participant with relative ability to influence price or supply/demand interplay decides without justification not to offer or economically withhold available production, storage or transportation capacity on the market. This includes unduly limiting infrastructure or transmission capacities resulting in prices that likely do not reflect fair and competitive supply/demand interplay. Electricity generation capacity withholding refers to keeping available generation capacity from being competitively offered on wholesale electricity markets, even though offering it would lead to profitable transactions at prevailing market prices. It can occur via economic withholding or physical withholding by one or more market participants acting independently or in collaboration.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: REMIT Application to Capacity Withholding and Price Levels
ID: 101
CONTENT:
REMIT applies to electricity generation capacity withholding irrespective of whether competition law also applies. Electricity generation capacity withholding does not automatically amount to a breach of Article 5 of REMIT, requiring case-by-case analysis considering market circumstances and specificities. REMIT does not prohibit high prices provided they reflect fair and competitive interplay between supply and demand. A two-element concurrent approach can assess whether behaviour involving electricity generation capacity withholding amounts to a breach of Article 5 of REMIT regarding market manipulation.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Market Manipulation - Capacity Withholding and Transmission Capacity Hoarding
ID: 102
CONTENT:
To assess capacity withholding, two elements must be evaluated: (1) whether the market participant can influence the price or supply/demand interplay of a wholesale energy product through their behavior, and (2) whether the participant lacks legitimate technical, regulatory, or economic justification when not offering available generation capacity or offering it above marginal cost. In case of intent, any action involving capacity withholding can amount to market manipulation. Transmission capacity hoarding involves acquiring all or part of available transmission capacity without using it or without using it effectively.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Market Manipulation - Fictitious Devices and Deception
ID: 103
CONTENT:
Dissemination of false or misleading market information through media or other means (known as 'scalping' in some jurisdictions) is done with intention to move wholesale energy product prices favorably to the disseminator's position or planned transaction. Pump and dump involves taking a long position, undertaking buying activity and/or disseminating misleading positive information to increase prices, then selling at inflated prices. Circular trading executes sell orders with knowledge that offsetting buy orders are placed simultaneously, excluding competition. Pre-arranged trading involves two commodity dealers trading at pre-agreed prices to exclude other dealers or gain tax advantages. The Agency considers certain practices like crossing/pre-arranged trades as accepted market practices if undertaken according to trading venue rules.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Market Manipulation - Dissemination of False and Misleading Information
ID: 104
CONTENT:
This type of market manipulation involves disseminating false and misleading information without necessarily undertaking accompanying transactions. It includes creating misleading impressions by failing to properly disclose price-sensitive information that should be disclosed, such as 'inside information' under the Regulation. Spreading false/misleading information through media involves posting via internet or issuing press releases containing false statements about wholesale energy products admitted to trading on organized markets. The person spreading information knows or ought to know it is false or misleading. Other behavior designed to spread false/misleading information covers conduct giving false impressions through means other than media, such as moving physical commodity stocks to create misleading impressions about supply, demand, or deliverables into commodity futures contracts.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Market Manipulation - Conclusions and Regulatory Framework
ID: 105
CONTENT:
Examples of market manipulation practices are inspired by NRAs' experiences and financial market authorities' experiences, serving as indications of possible market manipulation signals in wholesale energy markets according to REMIT. Market participants' behavior must be coherent with their technical and economic constraints to comply with competition law, especially concerning market power exercise. The Agency and NRAs cooperate with competition authorities as foreseen by REMIT. The Agency will constantly review its guidance on market manipulation and publish revised non-binding guidance if appropriate.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Inside Information Disclosure Obligation - Introduction and Scope
ID: 106
CONTENT:
According to Article 4(1) of REMIT, market participants shall publicly disclose inside information in an effective and timely manner regarding business or facilities they own, control, or are responsible for operationally. Such disclosure includes information relevant to capacity and use of facilities for production, storage, consumption or transmission of electricity or natural gas, or related to LNG facilities, including planned or unplanned unavailability. The disclosure obligation applies to inside information of the market participant's parent or related undertakings. The obligation extends to business or facilities for which the market participant is responsible in whole or in part. However, the obligation does not apply to persons possessing inside information about another market participant's business unless they are a parent or related undertaking, though such persons should consider Article 3 compliance and promptly inform relevant market participants.

DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Inside Information Disclosure - Extended Obligations and Confidentiality
ID: 107
CONTENT:
Article 4(3) of REMIT extends the disclosure obligation to persons employed by or acting on behalf of a market participant when disclosing inside information to others in the normal course of employment, profession or duties. In such cases, the market participant or person must ensure simultaneous, complete and effective disclosure. However, this obligation does not apply if the information recipient has a duty of confidentiality, whether derived from law, regulation, articles of association or contracts.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Inside Information Disclosure Mechanisms and Platforms
ID: 108
CONTENT:
Effective disclosure of inside information requires dissemination enabling access to the widest possible public with easy and equal access for all users. The Agency believes inside information should be disclosed using an Inside Information Platform (IIP), an electronic system allowing multiple market participants to share information with the public while complying with minimum quality requirements. Using IIPs as the default mechanism is supported by: (1) combined reading of Article 4(1) and 4(4) of REMIT, where publication according to Regulation (EU) 2019/943 or (EC) No 715/2009 constitutes simultaneous, complete and effective disclosure; (2) convergence with financial market legislation technical standards, particularly Article 17 of MAR and Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2016/1055; (3) reduction in publication channels complexity and effort for market participants accessing and using published information.

A list of Inside Information Platforms available in Europe for disclosing inside information on wholesale energy markets is published on the Agency's REMIT Portal following assessment of IIPs' compliance with quality requirements, reporting requirements described in the REMIT Manual of Procedures on transaction data, fundamental data and inside information reporting (REMIT MoP), and Guidance on web feeds implementation. text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Inside Information Disclosure on Platforms and Simultaneous Public Disclosure
ID: 111
CONTENT:
Publication of inside information on Inside Information Platforms in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2019/943 or (EC) No 715/2009, including guidelines and network codes, and Commission Regulation (EU) No 543/2013, is considered simultaneous, complete and effective public disclosure under Article 4(4) REMIT, provided the published information concerns the same event(s) and has the same content and format conforming to minimum quality requirements. A simultaneous publication on the market participant's website or through social media may be used as an additional source but cannot replace disclosure on Inside Information Platforms. Market participants must ensure published information is identical across all platforms. Publication on platforms facilitates access for all market participants and promotes market transparency while decreasing technical and organisational burden. Market participants possessing inside information must promptly provide and regularly update information on publication places during registration per Article 9(5) of REMIT, with this information made publicly available through the European Register of Market Participants (CEREMP).

SECTION: MAR Compliance and Technical Means for Disclosure
ID: 112
CONTENT:
According to Article 2(2) of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2016/1055, emission allowance market participants required to disclose inside information under Article 4 of REMIT may use the same technical means for disclosing inside information under Article 17(2) of MAR, provided the inside information has substantially the same content and the technical means ensure communication to relevant media. The Agency believes REMIT inside information disclosure through platforms will allow market participants to meet MAR requirements, provided the inside information platform fulfils both MAR requirements and Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2016/1055.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Minimum Quality Requirements for Inside Information Platforms
ID: 113
CONTENT:
Inside Information Platforms must fulfil the following minimum requirements for effective disclosure: inside information shall be disclosed to as wide a public as possible on a nondiscriminatory basis and accessible free of charge, simultaneously throughout affected energy market(s); electronic means shall maintain completeness, integrity and confidentiality during transmission, reception, storage and processing; inside information shall be publicly available with active distribution capability to reach the public at large with easy and fast access; platforms shall facilitate active distribution via web feeds enabling the Agency to collect and market participants to process data efficiently, in line with Guidance on web feeds implementation and REMIT MoP published on the REMIT Portal; filtering of information by relevant data categories should be possible in downloadable format; historical inside information and edited information shall be kept available for at least 5 years after event termination; history of prior publications regarding the same event shall be easily accessible with functionality linking previous to new publications in comprehensible manner; effective redundancy, backup and fallback solutions with minimal publication delay and service unavailability shall be ensured; information should be published in official language(s) of relevant Member State and English or English only; effective administrative arrangements shall prevent conflicts of interest with market participants.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Market Participant Responsibility and Technical Problems
ID: 114
CONTENT:
While market participants are responsible for inside information disclosure, they do not have influence on platform operation. The Agency understands market participants are not responsible for temporary technical problems of platforms fulfilling minimum quality requirements. If information was transmitted to the platform in time and temporary technical problems occurred, the market participant should not be considered in breach of disclosure obligations. Market participants could consider backup solutions complying with the same minimum quality requirements, providing information on backup solutions during Article 9(5) REMIT registration. If technical problems persist, market participants should consider using other platforms to comply with disclosure obligations. Where disclosure is delayed, market participants must consider compliance with Article 3 prohibition prior to actual market disclosure.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Content Requirements and Format for Inside Information Publication
ID: 115
CONTENT:
Without prejudice to Article 1(2) of REMIT, inside information publication should be as concise and specific as reasonably possible, precise and complete enough to allow correct understanding of underlying events potentially affecting wholesale energy product prices. Inside information should be disclosed in format enhancing overall transparency and ensuring Union-wide level playing field for market participants. Each publication per Article 4(1) REMIT, in form of Urgent Market Message (UMM), should include information set described in tables (electricity, natural gas, and other event/information types) in ANNEX VII of REMIT MoP as applicable. Information must be provided according to explanatory rules in ANNEX VII of REMIT MoP. All fields and allowed values listed in ANNEX VII should be supported by the platform. Publications should not include company executive statements, advertisements or irrelevant information. The Agency discourages disclaimer use; if used, they should be clearly separated from main body. If publication requires prognosis regarding outage duration, such prognosis contains uncertainty elements. Market participants fulfil publication requirements if prognosis is based on available data and prepared with reasonable effort. If prognosis changes, publication should be updated accordingly as soon as new information is available.

SECTION: Incomplete or Incorrect Disclosure and Competition Law
ID: 116
CONTENT:
The obligation to disclose inside information is without prejudice to application of European Union competition law. The Agency's understanding is that disclosure of inside information in incomplete or incorrect manner would be considered non-effective disclosure and thus breach Article 4(1) of REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Timely Disclosure of Inside Information
ID: 117
CONTENT:
Regarding timely disclosure of inside information, the Agency currently considers: if inside information must be published per Regulation (EU) 2019/943 and (EC) No 715/2009, including guidelines and network codes, and Commission Regulation (EU) No 543/2013, publishing according to these regulations, including in aggregated form, is considered simultaneous, complete and effective public disclosure under Article 4(4) REMIT. However, even if Article 4(4) states publication constitutes simultaneous, complete and effective public disclosure, it does not necessarily constitute timely disclosure. Inside information must be published before trading in wholesale energy products to which information relates or recommending another person to trade in wholesale energy markets to which information relates. If inside information does not require publication per Regulation (EU) 2019/943, (EC) No 715/2009 and Commission Regulation (EU) No 543/2013, the Agency considers no reason exists for applying different reasonable timeframe than stated in above-mentioned Regulations. Such information should normally be published as soon as possible, but at latest within one hour if not otherwise specified in applicable rules and regulations. In any case, inside information must be published before trading in wholesale energy products to which information relates or recommending another person to trade. The Agency considers market participants should develop clear compliance plan towards real time or close to real time disclosure of inside information, beyond compliance with existing Third Package transparency obligations.

metadata.title: Timely Disclosure of Inside Information
metadata.original_text: Regarding timely disclosure of inside information, the Agency currently considers: if inside information must be published per Regulation (EU) 2019/943 and (EC) No 715/2009, including guidelines and network codes, and Commission Regulation (EU) No 543/2013, publishing according to these regulations, including in aggregated form, is considered simultaneous, complete and effective public disclosure under Article 4(4) REMIT. However, even if Article 4(4) states publication constitutes simultaneous, complete and effective public disclosure, it does not necessarily constitute timely disclosure. Inside information must be published before trading in wholesale energy products to which information relates or recommending another person to trade in wholesale energy markets to which information relates. If inside information does not require publication per Regulation (EU) 2019/943, (EC) No 715/2009 and Commission Regulation (EU) No 543/2013, the Agency considers no reason exists for applying different reasonable timeframe than stated in above-mentioned Regulations. Such information should normally be published as soon as possible, but at latest within one hour if not otherwise specified in applicable rules and regulations. In any case, inside information must be published before trading in wholesale energy products to which information relates or recommending another person to trade. The Agency considers market participants should develop clear compliance plan towards real time or close to real time disclosure of inside information, beyond compliance with existing Third Package transparency obligations.

DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Delayed Disclosure of Inside Information Under Article 4(2) REMIT
ID: 118
CONTENT:
According to Article 4(2) of REMIT, a market participant may exceptionally delay public disclosure of inside information under its own responsibility so as not to prejudice its legitimate interests, provided such omission is not likely to mislead the public and the market participant can ensure information confidentiality and does not make trading decisions based on that information. In such situation, the market participant shall without delay provide that information, together with justification for delay, to the Agency and relevant national regulatory authority per Article 8(5). The decision to exceptionally delay public disclosure is for market participants to make. It is not the Agency's or NRAs' role to pre-approve Article 4(2) application to specific circumstances. Where a market participant chooses to delay disclosure, it must ensure such delay is not likely to mislead the public, does not make trading decisions on that information, and information remains confidential. As Article 4(2) requires market participants do not make trading decisions based on inside information, this provision is critical to compliance.

SECTION: Article 4(2) Application and Disclosure Requirements
ID: 119
CONTENT:
Agency underlines that the application of Article 4(2) cannot coincide with the application of Article 3(4)(b) of REMIT. Whether a market participant rightly or falsely applied Article 4(2) can only be determined ex-post. As soon as the legitimate interests cease to exist, the market participant must disclose the inside information in accordance with Article 4(1). In order to assist those market participants who are subject to the obligation to report information on the delay of the public disclosure of inside information to the Agency and the NRA according to Article 4(2) of REMIT, the Agency has developed a standard notification format, based on the experience in financial markets, and recommends its adoption by all NRAs. The relevant electronic format is published on the Agency's website.

SECTION: Exemption in Article 4(7) - Critical Infrastructure Protection
ID: 120
CONTENT:
According to Article 4(7) of REMIT, Paragraphs 1 and 2 of Article 4 are without prejudice to the right of market participants to delay the disclosure of sensitive information relating to the protection of critical infrastructure as provided for in point (d) of Article 2 of Council Directive 2008/114/EC of 8 December 2008 on the identification and designation of European critical infrastructures and the assessment of the need to improve their protection, if it is classified in their country. Article 4(7) is only relevant to 'critical infrastructure' as defined in Article 2(a) of Council Directive 2008/114/EC, i.e. an asset, system or part thereof located in Member States which is essential for the maintenance of vital societal functions, health, safety, security, economic or social well-being of people, and the disruption or destruction of which would have a significant impact in a Member State as a result of the failure to maintain those functions.

SECTION: Sensitive Critical Infrastructure Protection Information and Disclosure Obligations
ID: 121
CONTENT:
If a market participant holds inside information about such a piece of critical infrastructure that it, or its parent undertaking or related undertaking owns or controls or for whose operational matters that market participant or undertaking is responsible and that information also constitutes 'sensitive critical infrastructure protection related information' as defined in Article 2(d) of Council Directive 2008/114/EC, i.e. facts about a critical infrastructure, which if disclosed could be used to plan and act with a view to causing disruption or destruction of critical infrastructure installations, then the market participant can delay the publication of inside information. However, it should be emphasised that market participants are not allowed to use this exemption for all inside information relating to critical infrastructure. If a market participant possesses inside information that does not constitute 'sensitive critical infrastructure protection related information', the obligation to publish this information remains.

SECTION: Market Abuse Prohibitions - Introduction and Overview
ID: 122
CONTENT:
This Chapter is intended to provide guidance to NRAs as to the application of the market abuse prohibitions and as to indications of transactions which may involve inside information or market manipulation as defined in Article 2(1) to (3) of REMIT. The market abuse prohibitions of REMIT are based on those in MAD, but tailored to the gas and electricity markets. Market abuse means insider dealing and market manipulation, which have become explicitly prohibited with the entry into force of REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Seven Types of Market Abuse Behaviour
ID: 123
CONTENT:
The following seven types of behaviour may amount to market abuse, the first three of which constitute insider trading, the last four constitute market manipulation, including attempted market manipulation: (1) Insider trading – when an insider trades, or tries to trade, in wholesale energy products on the basis of inside information relating to that wholesale energy product (Article 3(1)(a) of REMIT). The Agency considers that the market participant holding inside information is also obliged to refrain from any amendment or selective withdrawal of the order placed ('hands-off approach') in order to comply with the prohibition of insider trading. (2) Improper disclosure of inside information – where an insider improperly discloses inside information to another person, unless such disclosure is made in the normal course of the exercise of their employment, profession or duties (Article 3(1)(b) of REMIT). (3) Recommending on the basis of inside information – where an insider is recommending or inducing, on the basis of inside information, another person to acquire or dispose of wholesale energy products to which that information relates (Article 3(1)(c) of REMIT).

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Application of Insider Trading Prohibition - Persons and Scope
ID: 126
CONTENT:
Whilst the prohibition of market manipulation applies to any engagement in, or attempt to engage in, market manipulation on wholesale energy markets by any person, the application of the prohibition of insider trading is limited to the following persons who possess inside information in relation to a wholesale energy products ('insider'): (1) members of the administrative, management or supervisory bodies of an undertaking; (2) persons with holdings in the capital of an undertaking; (3) persons with access to the information through the exercise of their employment, profession or duties; (4) persons who have acquired such information through criminal activity; (5) persons who know, or ought to know, that it is inside information. Article 3(5) of REMIT clarifies that where the person who possesses inside information in relation to a wholesale energy product is a legal person, the prohibitions laid down in Article 3(1) of REMIT shall also apply to the natural persons who take part in the decision to carry out the transaction for the account of the legal person concerned. The prohibition of insider dealing also contains elements of attempted behaviour. Article 3(1)(a) of REMIT not only prohibits the use of inside information by acquiring or disposing of wholesale energy products to which that information relates, but also prohibits the use of inside information by trying to acquire or dispose of wholesale energy products to which that information relates.

SECTION: Exemptions from Insider Trading Prohibition - General Framework
ID: 127
CONTENT:
Paragraphs 3 and 4 of Article 3 of REMIT stipulate exemptions from the prohibition of insider trading. However, it should be stressed that the exemptions may only apply for the prohibition of insider trading and are without prejudice of the obligation to publish inside information according to Article 4(1) of REMIT, as specified in chapter 7 of this Guidance. This chapter is intended to provide guidance to NRAs concerning the use of these exemptions in order to ensure a consistent understanding on the circumstances in which these exemptions may be applied.

SECTION: TSO Exemption Under Article 3(3) of REMIT
ID: 128
CONTENT:
Article 3(3) of REMIT provides: Points (a) and (c) of paragraph 1 of this Article shall not apply to transmission system operators when purchasing electricity or natural gas in order to ensure the safe and secure operation of the system in accordance with their obligations under points (d) and (e) of Article 12 of Directive 2009/72/EC or points (a) and (c) of Article 13(1) of Directive 2009/73/EC. The Agency underlines that the exemption of Article 3(3) of REMIT does not apply to point (b) of paragraph 1 of this Article. Therefore, when purchasing electricity or natural gas in order to ensure the safe and secure operation of the system in accordance with their above-mentioned obligations under Directive 2009/72/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 July 2009 concerning common rules for the internal market in electricity and Directive 2009/73/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 July 2009 concerning common rules for the internal market in natural gas, TSOs shall be prohibited from disclosing inside information to any other person unless such disclosure is made in the normal course of the exercise of their employment, profession or duties.

DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: National Market Particularities and Case-by-Case Assessment
ID: 129
CONTENT:
The Agency is aware that the market models of some Member States provide for specific tasks for certain market participants, similar to those of TSOs as regards their responsibility to ensure the safe and secure operation of the system. As a result, these market participants hold information which, alone or in aggregate, can constitute insider information. In the exercise of the duties in connection with these specific tasks, those market participants carry out transactions in the name and on behalf of one or more other market participants. While there is an explicit exemption from the prohibition of insider trading in Article 3(3) of REMIT for TSOs as their duties are defined by EU law and are as such similar in all Member States, national particularities as described above cannot be subsumed under the exemption in REMIT. With respect to the possible differences in national market models and the legal design of principal-agent-relations in different Member States, the Agency is of the opinion that any such particularity needs to be assessed by the competent national authorities on a case-by-case basis.
