text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Application of REMIT for Non-EU and Non-EEA Market Participants
ID: 39
CONTENT:
The Agency also considers it necessary to give guidance on the application of the notion of market participant to market participants from non-EU and non-EEA countries. According to Article 2(7) of REMIT, a market participant is any person who enters into transactions in one or more wholesale energy markets. This applies irrespective of the location of the person. Accordingly, also persons from non-EU and non-EEA countries are covered by REMIT provided that they enter into transactions in wholesale energy markets. Article 9(1) of REMIT confirms this understanding that REMIT also applies to market participants from non-EU and non-EEA countries as it requires market participants not established or resident in the Union entering into transactions, which are required to be reported to the Agency in accordance with Article 8(1) of REMIT, to register in the Member State in which they are active.

Accordingly, also persons from non-EU and non-EEA countries are covered by REMIT provided that they enter into transactions in wholesale energy markets. CONTENT:

Accordingly, the obligations to register pursuant to Article 9(1) of REMIT with the competent NRA and to report data to the Agency according to Article 8(1) and (5) of REMIT also applies to such non-EU and non-EEA market participants. The same holds for the prohibitions of market abuse pursuant to Articles 3 and 5 of REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Introduction to Registration of Market Participants
ID: 41
CONTENT:
This Chapter illustrates the Agency's current understanding of the application of Article 9 of REMIT and is intended to provide guidance to NRAs concerning the registration process and their role in this process, in order to facilitate the harmonisation of practices across the Union. Accurate information in the national registers and the European register of market participants is a prerequisite for efficient and effective market monitoring.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Market Participants Obliged to Register
ID: 42
CONTENT:
According to Article 9(1) of REMIT, Market participants entering into transactions which are required to be reported to the Agency in accordance with Article 8(1) shall register with the national regulatory authority. According to Article 2(7) of REMIT, 'Market participant' means any person, including transmission system operators, who enters into transactions, including the placing of orders to trade, in one or more wholesale energy markets. The obligation to register as a market participant under Article 9(1) of REMIT only applies to those market participants entering into transactions which are required to be reported to the Agency in accordance with Article 8(1). The requirement to register under REMIT applies to any person, legal or natural, that enters into transactions which are required to be reported.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Registration Requirements for Related Entities and Third Parties
ID: 43
CONTENT:
It is important to note that all market participants entering into transactions, which are required to be reported to the Agency in accordance with Article 8(1), must register, even if a parent, subsidiary or other related undertaking is already registered or is registering. Provided they are not separate legal persons, branches of a market participant do not need to register as separate market participants. A market participant may allow a third party to submit registration information on their behalf. In such case, the relevant NRA may require the third party to provide evidence of such permission.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Registration Information Requirements
ID: 44
CONTENT:
Article 9(3) of REMIT requires the Agency, in cooperation with NRAs, to determine and publish, by 29 June 2012, the format in which NRAs should transmit registration information on market participants to the Agency. On 26 June 2012, the Agency adopted a Decision determining the registration format to be used for the establishment of the European register of market participants. The registration format consists of 5 sections: Section 1: Data related to the market participant; Section 2: Data related to the natural persons linked to the market participant; Section 3: Data related to the ultimate controller or beneficiary of the market participant; Section 4: Data related to the corporate structure of the market participant; Section 5: Data related to the delegated parties for reporting on behalf of the market participant. All market participants entering into transactions, which are required to be reported to the Agency in accordance with Article 8(1), are required to provide this information.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Establishment of National Registers
ID: 45
CONTENT:
According to Article 9(2) of REMIT: Not later than 3 months after the date on which the Commission adopts the implementing acts set out in Article 8(2), national regulatory authorities shall establish national registers of market participants. Thus, each NRA shall establish a registration system by which market participants can provide registration information to that NRA no later than 3 months after the adoption of the implementing acts. NRAs can, if they wish, open the registration process to market participants earlier than this. NRAs are free to use whatever system they deem most appropriate for their market.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: European Register and Registration User Manual
ID: 46
CONTENT:
The Agency is developing a system to be used to establish the European register of market participants. This system will also be available to NRAs as a means of registering market participants in their own Member State. NRAs should ensure that market participants are provided with information on how to register. For this purpose, and for the purpose of ensuring accuracy in the European register of market participants established by the Agency in accordance with Article 9(3) of REMIT, the Agency will make available a Registration User Manual (RUM) to NRAs. The RUM will provide guidance on how the fields in the registration format should be populated. On the basis of the RUM, NRAs may provide guidance to market participants on how to register. The manual will be updated periodically, on the basis of the feedback from NRAs.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Selection of Appropriate NRA for Registration
ID: 47
CONTENT:
According to Article 9(1): Market participants entering into transactions which are required to be reported to the Agency in accordance with Article 8(1) shall register with the national regulatory authority in the Member State in which they are established or resident, or, if they are not established or resident in the Union, in a Member State in which they are active. According to settled case law of the Court of Justice of the European Union, a legal or natural person can be established in more than one Member State. The legal or natural person is established in the Member State(s) in which it pursues a professional activity on a stable and continuous basis. If a market participant is established in more than one Member State, the Agency would normally expect market participants to register in the Member State in which they have their primary establishment. For market participants not established or resident in the Union, it is the Agency's understanding that such market participants may choose in which Member State to register, as long as they are active in that Member State.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Registration Submission Deadlines
ID: 48
CONTENT:
According to Article 9(4) of REMIT, Market participants (...) shall submit the registration form to the NRA prior to entering into a transaction which is required to be reported to the Agency in accordance with Article 8(1). Thus, market participants must submit all the Sections of the registration form (Sections 1 to 5) before entering into any transaction which is required to be reported to the Agency. In line with Article 12(2) of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 1348/2014, the reporting obligation will apply to market participants from 7 October 2015 and from 7 April 2016, according to the type of data to be reported to the Agency. For market participants entering into transactions on an organised market place (OMP), the registration obligation takes effect, at the latest, prior to 7 October 2015. For all other market participants, the registration obligation takes effect, at the latest, prior to 7 April 2016, or prior to the first day they enter into transactions which are required to be reported to the Agency.

SECTION: Section 4 Registration Form Completion Timeline
ID: 52
CONTENT:
Market participants who registered before 17 March 2015 were unable to complete Section 4 (data related to corporate structure) of the registration form at submission time. In accordance with Agency Decision No 01/2012, they must provide Section 4 information within 3 months from the first publication of the European register, updating their registration form by 17 June 2015 at the latest. This section requires information on all related undertakings that are registered market participants.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Example 1: Market Participant A Registered Before 17 March 2015
ID: 53
CONTENT:
Market participant A registered before 17 March 2015 and completed Sections 1, 2, 3, and 5 of the registration form at submission. Section 4 was not filled at initial submission since the European register was first published on 17 March 2015. After this date, MP A has three months (until 17 June 2015) to complete Section 4 with data on all related undertakings registered as market participants. If a related undertaking (MP B) registers after 17 June 2015, MP A must update Section 4 accordingly. MP A must also promptly update any other registration information when changes occur, such as selecting a new Registered Reporting Mechanism (RRM) in Section 5.

SECTION: Example 2: Market Participant C Registered After 17 March 2015
ID: 54
CONTENT:
If market participant C registers after 17 March 2015, it must complete all Sections (1 to 5) of the registration form with updated data at submission time. Section 4 must include all related undertakings that are registered market participants and published in the European register at the time of form submission. If a related undertaking (MP D) registers later, MP C must promptly update its registration form once MP D's registration is published. CONTENT:

SECTION: ACER Code Issuance Process and Timeline
ID: 56
CONTENT:
The ACER code is issued upon transmission of information from national registers to the Agency for the first time, in accordance with Agency Decision No 01/12. According to Article 2 of this Decision, NRAs should promptly transmit registration information to the Agency once submitted by the market participant, after which the Agency immediately issues the ACER code. NRAs must ensure market participants receive the ACER code in a timely manner and before transactions are required to be reported under Article 8(1) of REMIT. The registration system provides automatic checks to prevent incomplete registration forms from being submitted.

CONTENT:
According to Article 2 of Agency Decision No 01/2012, NRAs shall provide the Agency promptly with information from national registers in electronic format through a secure channel using either CSV or XML formats. text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Requirement to Keep Registration Information Up to Date
ID: 59
CONTENT:
According to Article 9(5) of REMIT, market participants must communicate promptly to the national regulatory authority any change regarding information provided in the registration form. Registration is not a one-off event but an ongoing requirement. Market participants must update their registration form with any changes in accordance with Article 9(5). If mandatory registration information changes are not communicated promptly, the registration is considered incomplete. Market participants with outdated registration forms may be in breach of Article 9 of REMIT. NRAs should set up regular reminders (e.g., annually) asking market participants to verify that submitted information remains correct and up to date.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: The Role of NRAs in the Registration Process
ID: 60
CONTENT:
Registration of market participants under REMIT is primarily a national process. NRAs undertake three key roles: First, they act as a source of support for market participants seeking to register, providing guidance using the Agency's Registration User Manual (RUM) when available. Second, they transmit information from national registers to the Agency promptly upon market participant submission, enabling immediate ACER code issuance. Third, they ensure accuracy of registration information by establishing and maintaining up-to-date registers of market participants as required by Article 9(2) of REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: NRA Responsibilities for Registration Accuracy and Checks
ID: 61
CONTENT:
Accurate information in national and European registers is essential for an efficient market monitoring system. NRAs should have systems in place to effectively check registration information provided by market participants to identify omissions and obvious errors. Any errors detected by NRAs should be promptly notified to the Agency. The Agency's registration system provides automatic checks to prevent incomplete registration forms from being submitted. NRAs do not issue authorization or licenses to trade through the registration process, nor does registration completion constitute a 'know-your-customer' check or 'fit-and-proper' assessment.

The Agency aims to issue the ACER code immediately upon receiving registration information from the NRA. However, the Agency may delay publication of information transmitted by NRAs while conducting additional accuracy checks on registration information submitted by market participants, ensuring a high level of accuracy in the European register.

text:

SECTION: Registration Process Steps for Early Registrants
ID: 63
CONTENT:
For market participants starting registration before the Agency first publishes the European register list, the process includes: (1) Before entering reportable transactions under Article 8(1) of REMIT, the market participant submits a registration form to the relevant NRA with information for Sections 1, 2, 3, and 5 of Agency Decision No 01/2012. NRAs should encourage advance registration for smooth processing. Market participants are responsible for providing correct and complete information. (2) The NRA promptly transmits national register information to the Agency. (3) Immediately following transmission, the Agency issues a unique ACER code and informs the market participant and relevant NRA. (4) The Agency establishes a European register based on NRA-provided information and publishes a market participant list. (5) The market participant completes the registration process.

SECTION: REMIT Registration Process and Requirements
ID: 64
CONTENT:
The second phase of the registration process requires submitting information relevant to Section 4 of the registration format. The deadline for submission is 3 months after the Agency publishes the European register of market participants for the first time. Any market participant registering after this publication must provide all relevant information from Sections 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 during initial registration. Market participants must transmit the registration form to the NRA prior to entering into a transaction required to be reported to the Agency in accordance with Article 8(1) of REMIT. Registration does not constitute authorization or license to trade and is without prejudice to obligations to comply with applicable trading and balancing rules. The Agency will announce in advance when it intends to publish the European register of market participants for the first time.

Registration does not constitute authorization or license to trade and is without prejudice to obligations to comply with applicable trading and balancing rules. The Agency will announce in advance when it intends to publish the European register of market participants for the first time.

DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Application of Inside Information Definition - Introduction
ID: 65
CONTENT:
This chapter covers what the Agency considers 'inside information' under REMIT. Qualifying a specific fact as 'inside information' requires a two-step approach. First, determine whether there is an item of information according to criteria (a) to (d) defined in Article 2(1), second subparagraph, of REMIT. Second, ascertain whether it fulfills four cumulative conditions established in Article 2(1), first subparagraph: it is precise, not public, related to one or more wholesale energy products, and likely to significantly affect prices. The chapter is structured along this two-step approach, providing guidance on what constitutes 'information' under REMIT and on the definition of 'inside information', including application of the four cumulative conditions.

DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: The Concept of Information Under REMIT
ID: 66
CONTENT:
Article 2(1), second subparagraph, of REMIT specifies 'information' as: (a) information required to be made public in accordance with Regulations (EC) No 714/2009 and (EC) No 715/2009, including guidelines and network codes; (b) information relating to capacity and use of facilities for production, storage, consumption or transmission of electricity or natural gas or related to LNG facilities, including planned or unplanned unavailability; (c) information required to be disclosed in accordance with legal or regulatory provisions at Union or national level, market rules, and contracts or customs on relevant wholesale energy markets, if likely to have significant effect on prices; and (d) other information that a reasonable market participant would likely use as basis for decision to enter into transaction relating to wholesale energy product or issue order to trade.

DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Information Requirements Under EU Regulations
ID: 67
CONTENT:
All information required to be disclosed under Regulations (EC) No 2019/943 and (EC) No 715/2009 establishing conditions for access to network for cross-border exchanges in electricity and access to natural gas transmission networks (including applicable guidelines and network codes) is considered 'information' under REMIT. The concept of 'information' encompasses information related to all planned or unplanned changes in capacity or output at facilities for production, storage, consumption or transmission of natural gas or electricity. This includes: capacity and use of production facilities including planned and unplanned unavailability; capacity and use of storage facilities including planned and unplanned availability; capacity and use of consumption facilities including planned and unplanned unavailability; capacity and use of transmission facilities including planned or unplanned unavailability; and capacity and use of LNG facilities including planned and unplanned unavailability.

DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Disclosure Requirements and Transparency Information
ID: 68
CONTENT:
The concept of 'information' under REMIT covers facts required to be disclosed in accordance with legal or regulatory provisions at national level, legal or regulatory provisions at European Union level, market rules, contracts, and customs on the market. Regulatory provisions at EU level included in Regulation (EC) 543/2013 on submission and publication of data in electricity markets (referred to as 'transparency information') establish multiple obligations to publish facts that constitute 'information' according to Article 2(1)(c) of REMIT. Article 2(1)(d) of REMIT establishes that any other information a reasonable market participant would likely use as basis for decision to enter into transaction relating to wholesale energy product, or decision to issue order to trade in wholesale energy product, should be considered 'information' under REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: The Reasonable Market Participant Test
ID: 69
CONTENT:
The Agency recommends that NRAs use the 'reasonable market participant test' to determine whether a given fact qualifies as 'information' under REMIT, but only when such facts are not already covered by Articles 2(1)(a), (b) and (c) of REMIT. The concept of 'reasonable market participant' may encompass different profiles (beginner, average, informed, professional) with different trading strategies (portfolio optimization, arbitrage, speculative) covering short-term and/or long-term products. The concept of 'reasonability' relates to use of cognitive elements by market participant in trading decisions. A market participant making decisions based on non-cognitive elements such as instinct or mood should not be considered reasonable. To qualify a fact as information, it is enough that at least one profile is likely to use the fact as basis for their decision to enter into transaction or issue order to trade.

DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Reasonable Market Participant Test - Indicators and Application
ID: 70
CONTENT:
When using the 'reasonable market participant test', NRAs may consider indicators that: the concept of 'would be likely to use' should be distinguished from 'would like to use' – the test assesses whether it is reasonable for market participant to have legitimate expectation that information is available, not whether there is wish to use it; the concept of 'would be likely to use' should be interpreted based on what can reasonably be expected to be published (for example, competitors' trading plans are not 'information' under REMIT as they are not information that 'can reasonably be expected to be published'); the fact that market participant used comparable facts at different moment in time as basis for trading decisions could be considered proxy to assess if fact is information likely to be used by 'reasonable market participant'.

DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Examples of Information Under REMIT
ID: 71
CONTENT:
Example 1 - Information on TSO's available transfer capacity: Estimates of TSOs A and B of available transfer capacity for each day and available transfer capacity already reserved in electricity interconnector between bidding zones C and D. Assessment: These facts are information under REMIT because they relate to information required to be disclosed in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 2019/943. According to Article 50(3), TSOs shall publish estimates of available transfer capacity for each day, indicating any available transfer capacity already reserved. Example 2 - Information on annual maintenance of generation units: Market participant A plans to perform annual maintenance on electricity generation unit XPTO with total capacity of 50 MW from 01/02/2025 to 01/04/2025. Assessment: This fact is information under REMIT as it constitutes information relating to capacity and use of facilities for production of electricity as specified in Article 2(1)(b) of REMIT.

DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Definition of Inside Information Under REMIT
ID: 72
CONTENT:
Pursuant to Article 2(1), second subparagraph, of REMIT, information qualifies as 'inside information' if it fulfills four cumulative conditions included in Article 2(1), first subparagraph: 'Inside information' means information of a precise nature, which has not been made public, which relates, directly or indirectly, to one or more wholesale energy products and which, if it were made public, would be likely to significantly affect prices of those wholesale energy products. It is responsibility of market participants to ascertain whether information they hold potentially constitutes 'inside information' according to these four cumulative conditions, and therefore needs to be made public according to Article 4(1) of REMIT.

DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Internal Compliance Rules for Market Participants
ID: 73
CONTENT:
Market participants should have clear internal compliance rules adapted to their activities and specificities of information they use and have access to. Best practices for internal compliance rules may include: a framework for assessment of whether facts can be qualified as inside information, including measures on how to identify inside information and appropriately tested thresholds; an adequate workflow of information compliant with presence of inside information, including mapping of information flow and measures on how to handle inside information; and lists of insiders and/or mechanisms in place to identify insiders. Internal compliance rules should be consistent with market participant's organizational structure and trading strategy.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Definition and Assessment of Precise Nature Information
ID: 76
CONTENT:
Information shall be deemed to be of a precise nature if it indicates a set of circumstances which exists or may reasonably be expected to come into existence, or an event which has occurred or may reasonably be expected to do so, and if it is specific enough to enable a conclusion to be drawn as to the possible effect of that set of circumstances or event on the prices of wholesale energy products. The precise nature of the information is to be assessed by the information holder on a case-by-case basis and depends on what the information is, as well as on the surrounding context. In that assessment, the holder of the information may, among other things, take into consideration: (i) that there is a realistic prospect that a fact will occur; (ii) that the estimation of the potential price effect of information disclosure is irrelevant for the assessment of the precise nature; and (iii) that intermediate steps in a lengthy process may be precise information.

DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Realistic Prospect Criterion for Precise Information
ID: 77
CONTENT:
It is enough that there is a realistic prospect that the fact will occur to make the information related to that event precise. Information is precise as long as there is a realistic prospect that the circumstances or events it refers to will come into existence or occur, considering all the factors existing at the time of the assessment. The assessment should not be affected by subsequent developments that occur after the market participant assessed whether the information was precise. However, the market participant should provide updates to the public on the evolution of the information.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Example 1: Information on Strikes Impacting Generation Units
ID: 78
CONTENT:
Information on strikes provided to the market participant impacting workers relevant for the normal operation of a generation unit can be seen as having a realistic prospect of happening due to, for example, the existence of historical records of this information resulting in effective strikes impacting the production of this unit. Therefore, it can be considered that there is a realistic prospect of a strike happening, considering all the factors existing at the time of the assessment. This information on strikes would then qualify as precise information, despite the fact that the strike can still be cancelled and/or that there may be some uncertainty about the overall duration of the strike or other elements. Any further developments of the situation (cancellation of the strike, update on the dates of the strike, scope of workers affected etc.) may make the prospect of the strike less realistic, but should not be taken into consideration by the NRA when assessing whether the information was precise at the time the market participant received the information.

DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Example 2: Nuclear Safety Authority Security Tests Information
ID: 79
CONTENT:
Information or request by the nuclear safety authority to the market participant of possible security tests to be run at an electricity generation unit during the first half of the year can be seen as having a realistic prospect of happening due to, for example, the existence of previous information of the same type that resulted in effective security tests impacting the production and/or availability of the unit, episodes reflecting the planning of the nuclear safety authority, or previous expressions of concerns with the operation of the unit. Therefore, it can be considered that there is a realistic prospect of the security tests impacting the production and/or availability to happen considering all factors existing at the time of the assessment. In some Member States there is an obligation deriving from the national legislation for the nuclear safety authority to publish this information on possible security tests.

DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Price Effect Estimation is Irrelevant to Precise Nature Assessment
ID: 80
CONTENT:
The calculation of the potential effect of the information on the prices of wholesale energy products is not an element to be taken into consideration in the assessment of the precise nature of the information. However, the likelihood of a significant price effect should be assessed to determine if the information is inside information under REMIT. More specifically, in order for the information to have a precise nature, it is not necessary to be able to infer from that information, with a sufficient degree of probability, that, once it is made public, its potential effect on the prices of the relevant wholesale energy products in a particular direction.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Intermediate Steps in Lengthy Processes as Precise Information
ID: 81
CONTENT:
Intermediate steps in a lengthy process that are connected to bringing about future circumstances or events may be regarded as precise information. The knowledge of such steps could constitute an advantage that could undermine the spirit and objective protected by REMIT, which is to place market participants on an equal footing and enhance market integrity in terms of information symmetry. Intermediate steps connected to bringing about future circumstances or events shall be specific enough to enable conclusions to be drawn as to the likely effect of that set of circumstances or events on the prices of wholesale energy products.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Example 1: Commissioning of New Plants and Recommissioning of Mothballed Power Plants
ID: 82
CONTENT:
The process leading to the commissioning of new plants or recommissioning of mothballed power plants is a lengthy and complex process. Its major milestones (for example: management board approvals, regulatory approvals, licence granting, etc.) constitute intermediate steps in this process. Some facts generated by the intermediate steps leading to the commissioning or recommissioning of a power plant would qualify as precise information under REMIT, as they constitute a set of circumstances which exist or may reasonably be expected to come into existence and impact the realistic prospect of energy being produced from a certain point in time onwards. In order to decide whether these facts qualify as inside information, the three other criteria covered in sections 5.3.2 to 5.3.4 also need to be met.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Information That Has Not Been Made Public
ID: 83
CONTENT:
Inside information is information that has not been shared with the public and, as a consequence, creates information asymmetries between market participants. Effective disclosure to the public of market participants is the criterion that transforms non-public information into public information. Once the information becomes public, it enhances the integrity and transparency of the market, as envisaged by Recital 2 of REMIT. In general, information is deemed to be public knowledge if such information has been made, by any party, available to the public, i.e. to an unspecified number of market participants. In this regard, it is irrelevant who made the information public. No distinction is made as to whether the information was made public by a market participant or by any other party.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Requirements for Public Information Disclosure
ID: 84
CONTENT:
It is sufficient, but also required, that information is made available to the entire public of market participants simultaneously, ensuring equal access to the information, since any interested market participant may appraise the information. This can be the case, for example, if a generally accessible electronic system for the dissemination of information, that qualifies as an Inside Information Platform, is used. Publishing information only to selected market participants, for example via an e-mail channel or news board which is available exclusively to exchange members, does not satisfy the requirement of informing the public. The Agency's understanding of effective and timely public disclosure of inside information is provided in Chapter 7 of this Guidance.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Example 2: Planned Unavailability on Electricity Interconnector Due to Expansion Works
ID: 85
CONTENT:
The process leading to the expansion of capacity in an electricity interconnector is a lengthy and complex process. Its major milestones (for example: market participant's management board decisions, regulatory approvals, licence granting, decisions from the interconnector's operational centre to proceed with the unavailability,...) constitute intermediate steps. A management board decision (for example, on the unavailability on the existing interconnectors to allow the expansion of the existing infrastructure during a specific period), despite being an intermediate step (that can still be subject to other approvals - for example by regulatory or operational centre), fulfils the criteria of precise nature under REMIT. Indeed, the management board decision to approve or disapprove a planned maintenance during a specific period is specific enough to enable a conclusion to be drawn as to the possible effect of that set of circumstances or events on the prices of wholesale energy products. In order to decide whether the management board decision can qualify as inside information, the three other criteria covered in sections 5.3.2 to 5.3.4 also need to be met.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Information Relating to Wholesale Energy Products
ID: 86
CONTENT:
The definition of 'inside information' in Article 2(1) of REMIT requires the relevant information to relate, directly or indirectly, to one or more wholesale energy products. 'Wholesale energy products' are defined under Article 2(4) of REMIT as: (a) contracts for the supply of electricity or natural gas where delivery is in the Union; (b) derivatives relating to electricity or natural gas produced, traded or delivered in the Union; (c) contracts relating to the transportation of electricity or natural gas in the Union; and (d) derivatives relating to the transportation of electricity or natural gas in the Union. Information that has a possible effect on the demand, supply and/or prices of a wholesale energy product, or on the expectations of the demand, supply and/or prices of a wholesale energy product, shall be considered as directly or indirectly related to the wholesale energy product.

metadata.original_text: The definition of 'inside information' in Article 2(1) of REMIT requires the relevant information to relate, directly or indirectly, to one or more wholesale energy products. 'Wholesale energy products' are defined under Article 2(4) of REMIT as: (a) contracts for the supply of electricity or natural gas where delivery is in the Union; (b) derivatives relating to electricity or natural gas produced, traded or delivered in the Union; (c) contracts relating to the transportation of electricity or natural gas in the Union; and (d) derivatives relating to the transportation of electricity or natural gas in the Union. Information that has a possible effect on the demand, supply and/or prices of a wholesale energy product, or on the expectations of the demand, supply and/or prices of a wholesale energy product, shall be considered as directly or indirectly related to the wholesale energy product.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Likelihood of Significant Price Effect on Wholesale Energy Products
ID: 87
CONTENT:
Information is deemed to constitute inside information only if, were it made public, it would be likely to have a significant effect on the prices of related wholesale energy product. Based on the condition of a significant price effect, the Agency narrowed the wide notion of information down to the information that is crucial enough to have the potential to significantly affect the prices of wholesale energy products, and therefore to information that is relevant for trading. It is important to note that the mere 'likelihood' of a significant price effect is enough to meet this condition and that no actual price effect is required. The assessment of the likelihood of price effect has to be performed by a market participant on a case-by-case basis. The market participant should take into consideration the anticipated effect of the information in light of the nature of the information, as well as the specificities of the market and the market situation at the time of the assessment.

DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Factors for Assessing Significant Price Effect of Information
ID: 89
CONTENT:
Market participants should consider multiple factors when assessing whether information is likely to have a significant price effect: characteristics of the market (size, timeframe, market design, liquidity, type of participants); the size of the event; already published information on supply or demand situation; availability and unavailability of transmission facilities, storage or network constraints; the time of day (weekday/weekend, office hours/out of office hours); existence of announcements on non-regular events (commissioning of new power plant, recommissioning of mothballed power plant, etc.); TSO announcements related to the system (imbalances, security of supply, technical constraints); and any other market variables likely to affect the price of the related wholesale energy product (weather conditions, CO2, fuel prices, news on political and geopolitical developments). Market participants are advised to have a systematic framework with clear internal compliance rules adapted to their activities and the specificities of the information they handle.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Ex Ante Assessment and NRA Verification Procedures
ID: 90
CONTENT:
The assessment of likelihood of price effect must be performed by market participants ex ante, before the information is published and used. NRAs can use ex post information to check the presumption but should take no action against persons who drew reasonable conclusions from ex ante information available to them. To evaluate whether a market participant's assessment is consistent with what would be expected from a reasonable market participant, NRAs could verify whether: the type of information is the same as information which has, in the past, had a significant effect on prices; pre-existing analysts research reports, price reporter publications and opinions indicate that the type of information in question has effects on prices; the market participant itself has already treated similar events as inside information; another reasonable market participant has already treated similar events as inside information; or a reasonable market participant would be likely to use it as part of its trading decisions.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Example 1: Update on Status of Unplanned Outage in Generation Unit
ID: 91
CONTENT:
Market participant A (MP A) operating a power plant realizes that its unplanned maintenance on a generation unit (100 MW unavailability) will have to be extended by 2 hours. The market liquidity is limited for the relevant wholesale electricity products. MP A must decide whether such information would likely have a significant price effect. Factors for ex-ante assessment include: market characteristics (intraday market open with two hourly products and eight 15-minute products directly affected; limited order depth); size of event (limited, only two additional hours for 100 MWh); information on supply or demand (ongoing outage with no other outages announced); other constraints (limited cross-border capacity); time of day (normal working hours); no additional announcements; and no relevant changes in wind forecasts. Assessment: Based on limited order book depth, absence of relevant cross-border transmission capacity, and the fact that the extension changes previously provided information, MP A can conclude that a reasonable market participant would likely use this information as part of trading decisions, and such information would likely have a significant price effect, particularly for hourly and 15-minute products directly linked to the extension.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Example 2: TSOs' Request to Activate Reserves
ID: 92
CONTENT:
In some EU Member States without specific national requirements for TSO to publish information on imbalances in real time, 25 minutes before delivery time, the TSO requests a balancing responsible party to activate a generation unit for 200 MWh for a specified period. The intraday market is still open. The TSO must decide whether such information would likely have a significant price effect. Factors for ex-ante assessment include: market characteristics (intraday market open with low bid-ask spread and relatively high market depth); size of event (relevant given proximity to delivery period); information on supply or demand (no other outages announced); other constraints (no cross-border transmission capacity); time of day (information issued very close to delivery period); no additional announcements; and no relevant changes. Assessment: Activation of balancing bids gives market participants valuable information regarding the direction of system imbalance. Based on these elements, the TSO can conclude that a reasonable market participant would likely use this information as part of trading decisions, and the information would likely have a significant price effect on intraday products.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Information on Trading Plans and Strategies
ID: 93
CONTENT:
Information regarding a market participant's own plans and strategies for trading should not be considered as inside information under REMIT Recital 12. Trading plans are defined as plans including a systematic method for evaluating supply, demand, or price of wholesale energy products, determining the amount of risk that is or should be taken, and/or formulating short- and/or long-term investment targets that may guide daily trading activity. The consequences of these targets, in terms of energy needs and resulting orders to trade, should be considered as part of trading plans and therefore not constituting information under REMIT. Trading strategies are defined as a set of objective rules designating the conditions that must be met for one or more trade entries and exits to occur, including specifications for order entries with filters and/or triggers, as well as rules for trade exits and order types. However, even if details of trading strategy do not qualify as inside information, the facts used to determine or change it can be inside information.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Trading Plans Passed to Authorized Persons and Broker Considerations
ID: 94
CONTENT:
NRAs should consider the particular case of trading plans and/or strategies passed on to persons authorized to execute orders on their behalf (for example, brokers). A client's order to trade sent to their broker is part of the client's own trading strategy and does not constitute information under REMIT, as far as the client is concerned. However, a broker receiving their client's order comes into possession of information on their client's trading plans. If deemed to be inside information, the broker will be expected not to trade on their own account on the basis of this information to be compliant with Article 3(1) of REMIT. The broker can legitimately execute their client's order but not use the knowledge of the client's order to trade on their own account, which would amount to behavior known as 'front running'.

DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Example 1: Details of Orders a Market Participant Intends to Submit
ID: 95
CONTENT:
Market participant A sends an order with the following details: Buy/Sell indicator: Buy order; Initiator/Aggressor: Initiator; Order type: Flexible Hour (a specific order that can trade at any hour provided that price and volume are matched); Order conditions: Fill and Float (an order which will be killed immediately after matching with any available volume on the order book; if not filled at all, it stays in the market); Order status: Active (the order has been activated by the system or participant and is visible in the active order book); Minimum execution volume: 1,500 MW; Price limit: 40.5 euro; Order duration: Good Till Cancelled (an order which persists until the user cancels the order or it reaches the system maximum duration). Assessment: This fact is part of the trading strategy of the market participant and therefore does not qualify as inside information under REMIT.

DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Example 2: Decisions on Changes in Risk Optimisation Strategy
ID: 96
CONTENT:
Market participant A makes a decision to change its portfolio optimization strategy, i.e., how to source its supply needs. Such decision will change its strategy of how much electricity is: purchased through standardized electricity products on the electricity exchange versus through bilateral contracts; and purchased in different timeframes (e.g., percentage of weekly, monthly, yearly products). Assessment: Decision on changes in the risk optimization strategy of a market participant is usually part of its trading plan and therefore does not qualify as inside information under REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Application of the Definition of Market Manipulation - Introduction
ID: 97
CONTENT:
This chapter is aimed at providing NRAs with examples of the types of market activities which, in the view of the Agency, would fulfill the definition of market manipulation provided in Article 2(2) and (3) of REMIT. The guidance and accompanying examples are intended to help NRAs develop a common understanding of what constitutes market manipulation. The guidance and examples could also facilitate the identification of relevant variables (diagnostic flags or signals) for detecting market manipulation.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: REMIT Market Manipulation Definition and Categories
ID: 98
CONTENT:
Article 2(2) of REMIT distinguishes four different categories of market manipulation: (1) false/misleading transactions, (2) price positioning, (3) transactions involving fictitious devices/deception and (4) dissemination of false and misleading information. Market manipulation includes entering into any transaction or issuing any order to trade in wholesale energy products which gives, or is likely to give, false or misleading signals as to the supply of, demand for, or price of wholesale energy products; secures or attempts to secure the price of one or several wholesale energy products at an artificial level, unless the person establishes that his reasons are legitimate and conform to accepted market practices; or employs a fictitious device or any other form of deception which gives false or misleading signals regarding supply, demand, or price of wholesale energy products.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: REMIT Dissemination of False Information
ID: 99
CONTENT:
Market manipulation includes disseminating information through the media, including the internet, or by any other means, which gives, or is likely to give, false or misleading signals as to the supply of, demand for, or price of wholesale energy products, including the dissemination of rumours and false or misleading news, where the disseminating person knew, or ought to have known, that the information was false or misleading. When information is disseminated for the purposes of journalism or artistic expression, such dissemination shall be assessed taking into account the rules governing the freedom of the press and freedom of expression in other media, unless those persons derive, directly or indirectly, an advantage or profits from the dissemination, or the disclosure is made with the intention of misleading the market.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Attempted Market Manipulation Under REMIT
ID: 100
CONTENT:
Article 2(3) of REMIT defines attempted market manipulation as entering into any transaction, issuing any order to trade or taking any other action relating to a wholesale energy product with the intention of giving false or misleading signals as to the supply of, demand for, or price of wholesale energy products; securing the price of one or several wholesale energy products at an artificial level, unless the person establishes that his reasons are legitimate and conform to accepted market practices; or employing a fictitious device or any other form of deception which gives false or misleading signals. It also includes disseminating information through the media, including the internet, or by any other means with the intention of giving false or misleading signals as to supply, demand, or price of wholesale energy products. The 'acceptable market practice' argument can only be used in respect to price positioning categories.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: REMIT Examples of Market Manipulation from Recitals
ID: 101
CONTENT:
Manipulation on wholesale energy markets involves actions undertaken by persons that artificially cause prices to be at a level not justified by market forces of supply and demand, including actual availability of production, storage or transportation capacity. Forms include placing and withdrawal of false orders; spreading of false or misleading information or rumours through media, including the internet; deliberately providing false information to undertakings which provide price assessments or market reports; and deliberately making it appear that the availability of electricity generation capacity, natural gas availability, or transmission capacity is other than the capacity which is actually technically available. Manipulation and its effects may occur across borders, between electricity and gas markets and across financial and commodity markets, including emission allowances markets.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Market Manipulation Examples: Securing Positions and Misleading Conduct
ID: 102
CONTENT:
Examples of market manipulation and attempts to manipulate the market include conduct by a person, or persons acting in collaboration, to secure a decisive position over the supply of, or demand for, a wholesale energy product which has, or could have, the effect of fixing, directly or indirectly, prices or creating other unfair trading conditions; and the offering, buying or selling of wholesale energy products with the purpose, intention or effect of misleading market participants acting on the basis of reference prices. However, accepted market practices such as those applying in the financial services area, which are currently defined by Article 1(5) of Directive 2003/6/EC, could be a legitimate way for market participants to secure a favourable price for a wholesale energy product.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Wash Trades and Improper Matched Orders
ID: 103
CONTENT:
Wash trades consist of entering into arrangements for the sale or purchase of a wholesale energy product, where there is no change in beneficial interests or market risk, or where beneficial interest or market risk is transferred between parties who are acting in concert or collusion. Improper matched orders are transactions where both buy and sell orders are entered at or nearly at the same time, with the same price and quantity by different but colluding parties. These transactions constitute market manipulation unless they are legitimate trades carried out in conformity with the rules of the relevant trading platform, such as crossing trades.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Layering and Spoofing Market Manipulation Practices
ID: 104
CONTENT:
Layering behaviour consists of issuing multiple non-genuine orders to trade at different price levels (layers) on one side of the order book, in order to enter into one or multiple transactions on the other side of the order book. Spoofing behaviour consists of issuing a single large or multiple non-genuine orders at the same price level on one side of the order book, in order to enter into one or multiple transactions on the other side of the order book. Both practices are designed to create misleading signals about supply, demand, or price.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Other Order-Based Behaviours and Marking the Close
ID: 105
CONTENT:
Other order-based behaviours involve issuing order(s) to trade, with or without an interest in their individual execution, which are likely to give misleading signals as to the supply of or demand or price for wholesale energy products or likely to secure the price at an artificial level. Due to the frequency and/or overall volume of the order(s) to trade, the behaviour results in entering into transactions at overall terms and conditions that are generally more favourable, directly or indirectly, to the market participant involved than those that would have otherwise prevailed. Marking the close involves deliberately buying or selling wholesale energy products at the close of the market in an effort to alter the closing price, particularly associated with dates such as future/option expiry dates or quarterly/annual portfolio or index reference/valuation points.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Abusive Squeeze and Cross-Market Manipulation
ID: 106
CONTENT:
Abusive squeeze (also known as 'market cornering') involves a party or parties with a significant influence over the supply of, or demand for, or delivery mechanisms for a wholesale energy product and/or the underlying product of a derivative contract exploiting a decisive position in order to materially distort the price at which others have to deliver, take delivery or defer delivery. The proper interaction of supply and demand can lead to market tightness, but this is not of itself market manipulation. Cross-market-manipulation involves trading on one market to improperly position the price of a wholesale energy product on a related market, such as trading in the underlying product of a wholesale energy derivative to distort the derivative contract price. Arbitrage transactions to take legitimate advantage of price differences would not constitute manipulation.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Manipulative Capacity Withholding
ID: 107
CONTENT:
Actions undertaken by persons that artificially cause prices to be at a level not justified by market forces of supply and demand constitute market manipulation. Manipulative capacity withholding occurs when a market participant with the relative ability to influence the price or the interplay of supply and demand of a wholesale energy product decides, without justification, not to offer or to economically withhold the available production, storage or transportation capacity on the market. This includes the unduly limiting of infrastructure or transmission capacities, resulting in prices that likely do not reflect the fair and competitive interplay of supply and demand. Electricity generation capacity withholding refers to the practice of keeping available generation capacity from being competitively offered on the wholesale electricity market, even though offering it competitively would lead to profitable transactions at prevailing market prices.

metadata.title: Manipulative Capacity Withholding
metadata.original_text: Actions undertaken by persons that artificially cause prices to be at a level not justified by market forces of supply and demand constitute market manipulation. Manipulative capacity withholding occurs when a market participant with the relative ability to influence the price or the interplay of supply and demand of a wholesale energy product decides, without justification, not to offer or to economically withhold the available production, storage or transportation capacity on the market. This includes the unduly limiting of infrastructure or transmission capacities, resulting in prices that likely do not reflect the fair and competitive interplay of supply and demand. Electricity generation capacity withholding refers to the practice of keeping available generation capacity from being competitively offered on the wholesale electricity market, even though offering it competitively would lead to profitable transactions at prevailing market prices.

SECTION: Economic and Physical Withholding
ID: 108
CONTENT:
Electricity generation capacity withholding can occur in two ways: via economic withholding or physical withholding. Electricity generation capacity withholding may be performed by one or more market participants, acting independently or in collaboration. REMIT applies to electricity generation capacity withholding irrespective of whether competition law also applies.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Capacity Withholding and Article 5 REMIT Breach Assessment
ID: 110
CONTENT:
Capacity withholding does not automatically amount to a breach of Article 5 of REMIT. A case-by-case analysis that takes into account the circumstances and specificities of the market is therefore needed. REMIT does not prohibit prices to be high, provided that they reflect a fair and competitive interplay between supply and demand.

The following approach, based on two concurrent elements, can assess whether a behaviour involving electricity generation capacity withholding amounts to a breach of Article 5 of REMIT in view of the market manipulation criteria as defined in Article 2(2) of REMIT. The first element to assess is whether the market participant concerned is able, in the case-specific circumstances, to influence the price or the interplay of supply and demand of a wholesale energy product by engaging in such behaviour. The second element to assess is whether the market participant has no legitimate technical, regulatory and/or economic justification for its behaviour when it does not offer its available generation capacity or has offered it above marginal cost. In case of intent, any action involving capacity withholding, even beyond the issuing of orders to trade or the entering into transactions, can amount to an attempt to manipulate the market.

ID: 111
CONTENT:
Transmission capacity hoarding is a practice that involves the acquisition of all or part of the available transmission capacity without using it or without using it effectively.

ID: 112
CONTENT:
Dissemination of false or misleading market information through media, including the internet, or by any other means (in some jurisdictions this is known as 'scalping') is done with the intention of moving the price of a wholesale energy product in a direction that is favourable to the position held or a transaction planned by the person disseminating the information.

SECTION: Pump and Dump Market Manipulation
ID: 113
CONTENT:
Pump and dump is a practice that involves taking a long position in a wholesale energy product and then undertaking further buying activity and/or disseminating misleading positive information about the wholesale energy product with a view to increasing the price of the wholesale energy product. Other market participants are misled by the resulting effect on price and are attracted into purchasing the wholesale energy product. The manipulator then sells out at the inflated price.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Circular Trading and Pre-arranged Trading
ID: 114
CONTENT:
Circular trading is the process of executing a sell order with the knowledge that an offsetting buy order is being placed at the exact same time. The action is considered illegal because it excludes competition.

Pre-arranged trading is the practice of two commodity dealers trading with each other at prices upon which they have agreed in advance. Pre-arranged trading is designed to exclude other dealers from the market, to gain a tax advantage, or both. As a result, pre-arranged trading is illegal.

The Agency considers that certain more specific practices, such as crossing/pre-arranged trades, could be considered accepted market practices, and thus do not constitute market manipulation, provided that they are undertaken according to the rules of the relevant trading venue applicable to their conduct. But in most of such cases, conduct of the practice in conformity with the rules of the trading venue would be sufficient in itself to promote market integrity and therefore the question of giving the practice accepted market practice status does not arise.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Dissemination of False and Misleading Information Without Transactions
ID: 115
CONTENT:
Market manipulation can involve dissemination of false and misleading information without necessarily undertaking any accompanying transaction. This could include creating a misleading impression by failing to properly disclose a price sensitive piece of information which should be disclosed. For example, a market participant with information which would meet the Regulation's definition of 'inside information' fails to properly disclose that information with the result that the market is likely to be misled.

Spreading false/misleading information through the media involves behaviour such as posting information via internet or issuing a press release which contains false or misleading statements about a wholesale energy product which is admitted to trading on an organised market. The person spreading the information knows or ought to have known that it is false or misleading and is disseminating the information in order to create a false or misleading impression. Spreading false/misleading information through an officially recognised channel for disseminating information to users of an organised market is particularly serious as it is important that market participants are able to rely on information dissemination via such official channels.

ID: 116
CONTENT:
Other behaviour designed to spread false/misleading information would cover a course of conduct designed to give a false and misleading impression through means other than the media. An example might be the movement of physical commodity stocks to create a misleading impression as to the supply or demand for a commodity or the deliverable into a commodity futures contract.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Market Manipulation Conclusions and Guidance
ID: 117
CONTENT:
The aforementioned examples of the various types of practices which could constitute market manipulation are inspired by the NRAs' own experiences and the experiences in financial markets made by financial market authorities, with whom the Agency and NRAs will closely cooperate in the implementation of REMIT. The examples can therefore currently be taken as an indication for possible signals of market manipulation in wholesale energy markets according to REMIT. These considerations apply until more experience is gained about market manipulation in wholesale energy markets.

More generally, the Agency considers that market participants' behaviour must be coherent with their technical and economic constraints in a way to comply with competition law, especially concerning market power exercise. The cooperation of the Agency and NRAs with the competition authorities, as foreseen by REMIT, must be understood in this respect. The Agency will constantly review its guidance on market manipulation and publish a revised non-binding guidance if considered appropriate.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Introduction to Inside Information Disclosure Obligations
ID: 118
CONTENT:
This chapter covers the Agency's current understanding of the application of the obligation to disclose inside information in accordance with Article 4 of REMIT. This chapter, as lastly amended, should be fully complied with after a transition period which will be communicated by the Agency.

According to Article 4(1) of REMIT, Market participants shall publicly disclose in an effective and timely manner inside information which they possess in respect of business or facilities which the market participant concerned, or its parent undertaking or related undertaking, owns or controls or for whose operational matters that market participant or undertaking is responsible, either in whole or in part. Such disclosure shall include information relevant to the capacity and use of facilities for production, storage, consumption or transmission of electricity or natural gas or related to the capacity and use of LNG facilities, including planned or unplanned unavailability of these facilities.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Scope and Application of Inside Information Disclosure Obligation
ID: 119
CONTENT:
The obligation to disclose inside information lies with the market participant according to Article 4(1) of REMIT. The disclosure obligation relates not only to inside information in respect of the market participant's own business or facilities, but also to inside information of the market participant's parent undertaking or related undertaking. In addition, the disclosure obligation is not only related to inside information in respect of business or facilities which the market participant or the respective undertakings own(s) or control(s), but also in respect of business or facilities for whose operational matters the market participant or respective undertaking is responsible, either in whole or in part.

The obligation to disclose inside information does not apply to a person or a market participant who possesses inside information in respect of another market participant's business or facilities, in so far as that owner of this inside information is not a parent or related undertaking. Notwithstanding this, persons holding information in such circumstances will need to consider their compliance with Article 3 and in particular whether they hold such information as one of the persons listed in Article 3(2). In relation to this, the Agency encourages persons holding such information to promptly inform the relevant market participant(s) in order to promote effective and timely compliance with Article 4(1) of REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Extended Disclosure Obligation for Employees and Representatives
ID: 120
CONTENT:
Article 4(3) of REMIT extends the disclosure obligation of Article 4(1) of REMIT to a person employed by, or acting on behalf of, a market participant when that person discloses inside information to any other person in the normal course of the exercise of their employment, profession or duties as referred to in Article 3(1)(b) of REMIT. In such a case, that market participant or person shall ensure simultaneous, complete and effective disclosure of that information.

However, the disclosure obligation of Article 4(3) of REMIT does not apply if the person receiving the information has a duty of confidentiality, regardless of whether such duty derives from law, regulation, articles of association or contracts.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Inside Information Platform Disclosure Mechanisms
ID: 121
CONTENT:
The transparency of the wholesale energy markets requires the disclosure of inside information in a manner that enables the dissemination of information to as wide a public as possible, granting easy and equal access to all users of this information. The Agency believes that, in order to achieve effective disclosure according to Article 4 of REMIT, the information shall be disclosed using a platform for the disclosure of inside information (Inside Information Platform or IIP), i.e. an electronic system for the delivery of information which allows multiple market participants to share information with the wide public and complies with the minimum quality requirements listed in Chapter 7.2.2.

Using Inside Information Platforms as the default disclosure mechanism is supported by the fact that this disclosure mechanism is indicated by a combined reading of Article 4(1) and Article 4(4) of REMIT. According to Article 4(4) of REMIT the publication of inside information, including in aggregated form, in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2019/943 or (EC) No 715/2009, or guidelines and network codes adopted pursuant to those Regulations, constitutes simultaneous, complete and effective public disclosure. The transparency rules under these regulations stipulate a publication of transparency information on central information transparency platforms. Therefore, the disclosure by Inside Information Platforms would then foster a consistent understanding of effective disclosure according to Article 4(1) of REMIT and Article 4(4) of REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Inside Information Platform Standards and Benefits
ID: 122
CONTENT:
This disclosure mechanism promotes convergence with technical standards established under financial market legislation in this regard, in particular those established under Article 17 of MAR, as further specified in Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2016/1055 laying down implementing standards with regards to the technical means for appropriate public disclosure of inside information.

The reduction in the number of publication channels leads to a significant reduction in complexity and effort for market participants to access and use information that is published according to Article 4 of REMIT. In order to facilitate the compliance with the disclosure obligation, a list of Inside Information Platforms available in Europe for the disclosure of inside information on wholesale energy markets is maintained.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Inside Information Platforms and REMIT Compliance
ID: 123
CONTENT:
Inside Information Platforms (IIPs) are listed on the Agency's REMIT Portal following assessment of compliance with quality requirements in Chapter 7.2.2, reporting requirements described in the REMIT Manual of Procedures (REMIT MoP), and Guidance on web feeds implementation. IIPs must apply to be listed and will be approved if they meet requirements. Publication of inside information in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2019/943, (EC) No 715/2009, and Commission Regulation (EU) No 543/2013 is considered simultaneous, complete and effective public disclosure under Article 4(4) REMIT, provided the published information concerns the same event(s), has identical content and format, and conforms to minimum quality requirements. Market participants may use their websites or social media as additional publication sources, but these cannot replace disclosure on Inside Information Platforms. When additional means are used, published information must be identical to that on the Inside Information Platform.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Benefits and Registration Requirements for Inside Information Disclosure
ID: 124
CONTENT:
Publication of inside information on platforms facilitates access for all market participants and promotes market transparency while decreasing technical and organizational burden. In the registration process under Article 9(5) of REMIT, market participants possessing inside information must promptly provide and regularly update information on the place of publication. This information is made publicly available by the Agency as part of the European Register of Market Participants (CEREMP). According to Article 2(2) of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2016/1055, emission allowance market participants may use technical means established for REMIT inside information disclosure for disclosure under Article 17(2) of MAR, provided the inside information has substantially the same content and technical means ensure communication to relevant media. The Agency believes REMIT inside information disclosure through platforms will allow market participants to meet these requirements if the platform fulfils both REMIT and MAR requirements.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Minimum Quality Requirements for Inside Information Platforms
ID: 125
CONTENT:
Inside Information Platforms must fulfill the following minimum requirements for effective disclosure: (1) Inside information shall be disclosed to as wide a public as possible on a nondiscriminatory basis and be accessible free of charge, simultaneously throughout affected energy market(s); (2) Electronic means shall maintain completeness, integrity and confidentiality during transmission, reception, storage and processing; (3) Inside information shall be publicly available with active distribution capability to reach the public at large, allowing easy and fast access; (4) The platform shall facilitate active distribution via web feeds enabling the Agency to collect and market participants to process data efficiently, in line with Guidance on web feeds and REMIT MoP; (5) Filtering of information by relevant data categories should be possible in downloadable format; (6) Historical inside information, including edited information, shall be kept available for at least 5 years after event termination; (7) History of prior publications regarding the same event shall be easily accessible with functionality linking previous to new publications in comprehensible manner.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Platform Technical Requirements and Administrative Arrangements
ID: 126
CONTENT:
Inside Information Platforms must ensure: (1) Effective redundancy, backup and/or fallback solutions with minimal publication delay and service unavailability; (2) Information published in official language(s) of relevant Member State and English, or English only; (3) Effective administrative arrangements to prevent conflicts of interest with market participants. While market participants are responsible for inside information disclosure, the Agency recognizes they lack influence over platform operations. Therefore, market participants are not responsible for temporary technical problems of platforms meeting minimum quality requirements. If information was transmitted in time and temporary technical problems occurred, the market participant should not be considered in breach. Market participants could use backup solutions complying with the same minimum quality requirements, providing information on backup solutions during registration under Article 9(5) of REMIT. If technical problems persist, market participants should use other platforms to comply with disclosure obligations.

text:
DOCUMENT: 5th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Content Requirements and Format Standards for Inside Information
ID: 127
CONTENT:
Publication of inside information should be as concise, specific, precise and complete as reasonably possible to allow correct understanding of underlying events that might affect wholesale energy product prices. Inside information should be disclosed in format enhancing overall transparency and ensuring Union-wide level playing field. Each publication under Article 4(1) of REMIT as Urgent Market Message (UMM) should include the information set described in tables in ANNEX VII of REMIT MoP (one for electricity, one for natural gas, one for other events/information), as applicable. Information must be provided according to explanatory rules in ANNEX VII of REMIT MoP. All fields and allowed values in ANNEX VII must be supported by the platform. Publications should not include company executive statements, advertisements or irrelevant information. The Agency discourages disclaimers; if used, they should be clearly separated from main body. Incomplete or incorrect disclosure is considered non-effective and breaches Article 4(1) of REMIT.
