text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Inside Information Definition and Concept
ID: 21
CONTENT:
Inside information under REMIT is defined as information of a precise nature that has not been made public, relates to wholesale energy product(s), and is likely to have a significant price effect on wholesale energy products. The concept of 'information' under REMIT encompasses data and facts that could influence market prices. Information must be precise in nature, meaning it must be specific and not vague or general. The information must not have been made public, ensuring it remains non-public at the time of consideration. Information on trading plans and strategies may also constitute inside information if it meets the other criteria of the definition.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Disclosure of Inside Information Requirements
ID: 22
CONTENT:
Inside information must be disclosed in an effective manner through appropriate disclosure mechanisms that meet minimum quality requirements. Disclosure must occur in a timely manner to ensure market participants have access to the information when needed. The obligation to disclose inside information is subject to certain conditions and exemptions. Delayed disclosure of inside information may be permitted under specific circumstances. Article 4(7) of REMIT provides an exemption from the disclosure obligation under certain conditions, allowing for delayed disclosure in specific situations where immediate disclosure could prejudice legitimate interests.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Insider Trading Prohibition and Definition
ID: 23
CONTENT:
Insider trading is prohibited under REMIT and is defined as engaging in trading activities using inside information, disclosing inside information to others, or recommending or inducing trading on the basis of inside information. Insider trading by using inside information involves executing transactions based on non-public information that is likely to affect market prices. Insider trading by disclosing inside information involves sharing such information with others who may then trade on it. Insider trading by recommending or inducing trading involves encouraging others to trade based on inside information. The prohibition applies to all persons who possess inside information and engage in these activities.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Insider Trading Indicators and Exemptions
ID: 24
CONTENT:
Possible signals of insider trading include unusual trading patterns, timing of trades relative to information disclosure, and trading volumes that deviate from normal activity. Types of practices that may indicate insider trading include front-running, layering, and spoofing. The scope of the insider trading provision covers all market participants and persons with access to inside information. Exemptions under Article 3(3) of REMIT apply to certain activities conducted in the ordinary course of business. Exemptions under Article 3(4) of REMIT provide relief for specific circumstances where insider trading prohibitions do not apply, such as certain trading activities by market makers and liquidity providers acting in their professional capacity.

SECTION: Market Manipulation and Attempted Market Manipulation
ID: 25
CONTENT:
Market manipulation and attempted market manipulation are prohibited under REMIT. Market manipulation is defined as engaging in conduct that gives, is likely to give, or attempts to give false or misleading signals regarding the supply, demand, or price of wholesale energy products. Attempted market manipulation involves conduct that seeks to secure or is likely to secure the price of wholesale energy products at an artificial level. These prohibitions protect the integrity of wholesale energy markets by preventing deceptive and manipulative trading practices that distort fair price formation.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Introduction to REMIT Guidance - 6.1st Edition
ID: 29
CONTENT:
This document contains the 6.1st edition of the non-binding Guidance on the application of REMIT, as amended by Regulation 2024/1106 ('REMIT revision'), directed at NRAs, pursuant to Article 16(1) of Regulation (EU) No 1227/2011 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 25 October 2011 on wholesale energy market integrity and transparency (REMIT). It provides guidance regarding the scope of REMIT, including definitions of 'wholesale energy products', 'wholesale energy market' and 'market participant'; the concept of 'inside information'; the obligation to disclose inside information; the prohibition of insider trading; the prohibition of market manipulation; the obligation on notification of algorithmic trading and direct electronic access; registration of market participants; obligations of persons professionally arranging or executing transactions; and best practices on compliance and penalty regimes.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: REMIT Scope - Introduction and Objectives
ID: 31
CONTENT:
Regulation (EU) No 1227/2011 on wholesale energy market integrity and transparency (REMIT) established a sector-specific framework for the monitoring of wholesale energy markets, with the objective of detecting and deterring insider trading and market manipulation. REMIT was originally seen by the legislators as a 'basic tailor-made market abuse framework in the energy sector legislation for all electricity and gas products not covered by the Market Abuse Directive' (the predecessor of MAR and CS MAD). The scope of REMIT was specifically designed to accommodate the operational complexity of physical energy markets and specificities of the energy sector (electricity and natural gas) and to appropriately complement the market abuse legislation covering the financial sector.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: REMIT Scope - Evolution and Hydrogen Inclusion
ID: 32
CONTENT:
The REMIT revision updated the scope of the original REMIT Regulation, adapting it to the evolving market circumstances. In addition, Article 83 of the recast Gas Regulation amended REMIT directly to include hydrogen in certain Articles where the term 'electricity or natural gas' is mentioned. This chapter intends to provide guidance to the NRAs on the scope of REMIT, including the enlarged scope introduced by the REMIT revision, by presenting the Agency's understanding of the notions of wholesale energy products ('WEP') and wholesale energy markets ('WEM') as defined by Article 2 of REMIT. Subchapter 2.2 identifies the products and markets that fall in the general scope of REMIT; Subchapter 2.3 provides guidance on the geographical scope of REMIT application; Subchapter 2.4 specifies the type of natural or legal persons that can fall into the scope of REMIT; and Subchapter 2.5 explains the interactions between REMIT and the financial legislation as laid down in Article 1(2) of REMIT.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Wholesale Energy Products (WEP) - Definition and Scope
ID: 33
CONTENT:
Article 1(2) of REMIT establishes that REMIT applies to wholesale energy products. The concept of WEPs is further defined in Article 2(4) of REMIT as follows: 'Wholesale energy products means the following contracts and derivatives, irrespective of where and how they are traded: (a) contracts for the supply of electricity, hydrogen or natural gas, including LNG, where delivery is in the Union; (b) contracts for the supply of electricity which may result in delivery in the Union as a result of single day-ahead and intraday coupling; (c) derivatives relating to electricity, hydrogen or natural gas produced, traded or delivered in the Union; (d) derivatives relating to electricity which may result in delivery in the Union as a result of single day-ahead and intraday coupling; (e) contracts relating to the transportation of electricity, hydrogen or natural gas in the Union; (f) derivatives relating to the transportation of electricity, hydrogen or natural gas in the Union; (g) contracts relating to the storage of electricity, hydrogen or natural gas in the Union; (h) derivatives relating to the storage of electricity, hydrogen or natural gas in the Union'.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Wholesale Energy Products - Final Customer Exemption and Threshold
ID: 34
CONTENT:
In addition to wholesale energy products, Article 2(4), second subparagraph, adds that: 'Contracts for the supply and distribution of electricity, hydrogen or natural gas for the use of final customers are not wholesale energy products. However, contracts for the supply and distribution of electricity, hydrogen or natural gas to final customers with a consumption capacity greater than [600 GWh] shall be treated as wholesale energy products.' In view of the definition of wholesale energy products in Article 2(4) of REMIT, the Agency considers contracts for the supply, transportation or storage of electricity, hydrogen and natural gas traded in balancing markets, intraday, within-day, day-ahead, two-day-ahead, week-end, week, monthly, quarterly, yearly, long-term or during any other time period generally accepted in the market as contracts for the supply, transportation or storage of electricity, hydrogen or natural gas.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Wholesale Energy Products and Financial Instruments under REMIT
ID: 35
CONTENT:
Wholesale energy products which are derivatives can be financial instruments as well if they fall under points (5), (6), (7) or (10) of Annex I Section C of MiFID II. The definition of wholesale energy product applies to contracts and derivatives irrespective of how and where they are traded, covering contracts and derivatives that are arranged or executed by persons professionally arranging or executing transactions (PPAETs). This includes contracts traded bilaterally or over the counter (OTC), as well as intra-group transactions where contracts are entered into with another counterparty that is part of the same group. Contracts for the supply of electricity and any derivative related to electricity resulting from generation capacity markets, capacity remuneration mechanisms, and flexibility markets where applicable, shall be considered wholesale energy products according to REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Electricity Contracts from Coupled Markets and Natural Gas Supply
ID: 36
CONTENT:
Concerning contracts and derivatives for the supply of electricity which may result in delivery in the Union as a result of single day-ahead and intraday coupling, all contracts derived from coupled markets fall within the scope of the definition, as an order placed in such a market has the potential for delivery in the Union. The coupled markets function in a way that orders to trade placed by a market participant on a market located outside of the EU may result in a contract for the supply of electricity with delivery in the Union, due to the market coupling. Concerning contracts for the supply of natural gas, pursuant to Article 2(28) of Directive (EU) 2024/1788 (Recast Gas Directive) 2009/73/EC, 'supply' means the sale, including resale, of natural gas, including liquefied natural gas (LNG), or hydrogen in the form of liquid organic hydrogen carriers or liquid hydrogen to customers. Contracts for the supply of LNG, or hydrogen in the form of liquid organic hydrogen carriers or liquid hydrogen with delivery in the European Union are wholesale energy contracts pursuant to Article 2(4)(a) of REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Storage and Biogas Contracts under REMIT
ID: 37
CONTENT:
Regarding contracts or derivatives relating to the storage of electricity, hydrogen or natural gas in the Union, 'storage' means energy storage and energy from a storage facility, including a hydrogen storage facility, as respectively defined in Article 2 points (59) and (60) of Directive 2019/944, and in Article 2 point (5) of the Recast Gas Directive. Pursuant to the Recast Gas Directive, the rules established for natural gas, including LNG and hydrogen, shall also apply in a non-discriminatory way to biogas and gas from biomass or other types of gas, in so far as such gases can technically and safely be injected into, and transported through, the natural gas system. If biogas can technically and safely be injected into, and transported through, the natural gas system, it will meet all criteria to be treated as natural gas and REMIT will apply for the biogas and the renewable gas supply/transportation/storage contracts.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Green Certificates, Emission Allowances, and Final Customer Contracts
ID: 38
CONTENT:
Regarding contracts for green certificates and emission allowances, they are not wholesale energy products, as they do not fulfil the requirements set out in Article 2(4) of REMIT. Contracts for the supply and distribution of electricity, hydrogen or natural gas for the use of final customers are not wholesale energy products either. However, if these contracts involve final customers with a consumption capacity greater than 600 GWh per year, these contracts will fall within the scope of REMIT wholesale energy products.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Final Customers with Consumption Capacity Greater than 600 GWh/year
ID: 39
CONTENT:
For the purposes of REMIT, the definition of 'final customer' draws on the relevant definition in the Directive (EU) 2019/944, and the Recast Gas Directive concerning common rules for the internal market in natural gas. These Directives define a final customer as a customer purchasing electricity or natural gas or hydrogen for his own use. Article 2(5) of REMIT clarifies the notion of 'consumption capacity': 'Consumption capacity' means the consumption of a final customer of either electricity, hydrogen or natural gas at full use of that customer's production capacity. It comprises all consumption by that customer as a single economic entity, in so far as consumption takes place on markets with interrelated wholesale prices. For the purposes of this definition, consumption at individual plants under the control of a single economic entity that have a consumption capacity of less than 600 GWh per year shall not be taken into account in so far as those plants do not exert a joint influence on wholesale energy market prices due to their being located in different relevant geographical markets.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Understanding Consumption Capacity and Full Use of Production Capacity
ID: 40
CONTENT:
The Agency understands 'consumption [...] at full use of that customer's production capacity' to mean the maximum amount of energy (electricity, hydrogen or natural gas) that a final customer could consume in a year, i.e. if the customer was to run their consumption assets fully at all times throughout the year (technical capability to consume). It is this consumption capacity that final consumers should consider whenever assessing whether the consumption capacity threshold of 600 GWh is exceeded. The consumption capacity comprises all consumption of electricity, hydrogen or natural gas by that customer as a single economic entity, in so far as consumption takes place on markets with interrelated wholesale prices. Final customers should calculate their consumption capacity of electricity, hydrogen and natural gas separately from each other, and not cumulate them, whenever assessing whether the threshold of 600 GWh is exceeded.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Individual Plants and Single Economic Entity Assessment
ID: 41
CONTENT:
Within a single economic entity, consumption at individual plants below the threshold of 600 GWh is not taken into account, in so far as those plants do not exert a joint influence on wholesale energy market prices due to them being located in different relevant geographical markets. However, individual plants that each have a consumption capacity below the threshold of 600 GWh but that are located in the same geographical market shall be taken into account whenever assessing whether the threshold of 600 GWh is exceeded. As for the notion of 'single economic entity', guidance can be obtained from international practices of competition law and especially from the precedents of the Court of Justice of the European Union. Under the competition rules, the unified conduct on the market of two or more companies takes precedence over the formal legal structure of those companies. Therefore, the relevant question is not whether two given companies are separate legal persons, but rather whether they behave together as a single unit in the market.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Elements for Assessing Single Economic Entity Status
ID: 42
CONTENT:
The following elements may be taken into consideration when assessing whether two or more companies form a single economic entity: decision making powers, procedures and sharing of liability between the relevant companies; ownership (e.g. majority shareholding); ownership structure of the relevant companies; and participating interests or influence over the relevant companies. As regards the understanding of 'markets with interrelated wholesale prices', wholesale energy markets are increasingly interlinked across the Union. There is already a high degree of interrelation of wholesale electricity and natural gas prices across the Union, and interrelation is expected to increase with the introduction of hydrogen and as the development of a single European energy market continues to progress. Market participants should take into account the consumption capacity of all their plants across the Union when assessing whether the consumption capacity threshold of 600 GWh is exceeded.

SECTION: Products In Scope of REMIT - Supply and Transportation Contracts
ID: 43
CONTENT:
Contracts for the supply of electricity, hydrogen or natural gas with delivery in the EU are in scope of REMIT, including: balancing, intraday, within-day, day-ahead, two-day-ahead, week-end, week, monthly, quarterly, yearly and long-term or any other time period generally accepted in the market as contracts for the supply of electricity, hydrogen or natural gas. Contracts for the supply of electricity which may result in delivery in the Union as a result of single day-ahead and intraday coupling are in scope. Transportation contracts in the Union of electricity, hydrogen or natural gas traded in balancing, intraday, within-day, day-ahead, two-day-ahead, week-end, week, monthly, quarterly, yearly and long-term or any other time period generally accepted in the market are in scope. Gas or hydrogen transport capacity contracts in the Union related to upstream pipeline networks are in scope.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Products In Scope of REMIT - Capacity Rights and Storage
ID: 44
CONTENT:
Contracts relating to the transportation of electricity, hydrogen or natural gas including at least one location or bidding zone in the Union concluded as a result of a primary explicit capacity allocation by or on behalf of the TSO, specifying physical or financial capacity rights or obligations (PTRs/FTRs) are in scope of REMIT. Contracts relating to the transportation of electricity, hydrogen or natural gas including at least one location or bidding zone in the Union concluded between market participants on secondary markets, specifying physical or financial capacity rights or obligations (PTRs/FTRs), including resale and transfer of such contracts are in scope. Contracts relating to the storage of electricity, hydrogen or natural gas in the Union are in scope. text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Wholesale Energy Markets Definition and Scope
ID: 48
CONTENT:
Wholesale energy markets are defined as any market within the Union on which wholesale energy products are traded. According to REMIT Recital 5, these markets encompass both commodity markets and derivative markets, which are of vital importance to the energy and financial markets, as price formation in both is interlinked. They include regulated markets, multilateral trading facilities, organised trading facilities, OTC transactions, and bilateral contracts traded directly or through brokers.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Types of Markets Included in REMIT Scope
ID: 49
CONTENT:
The definition of wholesale energy markets includes: balancing markets for electricity, hydrogen or natural gas with EU delivery; redispatching and countertrading mechanisms; intraday or within-day markets; coupled markets for day-ahead and intraday trading; day-ahead or two-day-ahead markets including week-end products; physical markets for forward contracts and non-standardised long-term contracts; markets for transportation capacities; derivatives markets relating to electricity, hydrogen or natural gas; generation capacity markets and capacity remuneration mechanisms; and local flexibility markets for electricity, all in so far as wholesale energy products are traded there.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Geographical Scope of REMIT
ID: 50
CONTENT:
The geographical scope of REMIT is solely determined by the geographical delimitation of wholesale energy products and not by the location of trading persons or trading venues. Although the scope is anchored in concepts of delivery, production, trading, transportation in the EU, non-EU persons are also covered by REMIT provided they enter into transactions in wholesale energy products. Non-EU persons entering into reportable transactions must designate a representative in a Member State where they are active and register with the competent NRA. The prohibitions of market abuse and obligations to publish inside information apply irrespective of the location of the person involved in a potential breach.

SECTION: Place of Trading and Geographical Limitations
ID: 51
CONTENT:
REMIT does not define any geographical limitation regarding the place of trading. Provided that a wholesale energy product meets the definition under Article 2(4) of REMIT, it is irrelevant where such a product is traded. Even if traded outside the EU, it will still qualify as a wholesale energy product if it meets the definition and therefore falls under the scope of REMIT.

SECTION: Six Criteria for Geographical Delimitation
ID: 52
CONTENT:
Depending on the contract typology, six criteria for geographical delimitation are relevant: 'Delivered in the EU' for supply contracts; 'May be delivered in the EU' for supply contracts and related derivatives; 'Produced, traded or delivered in the EU' for derivatives; 'Relating to transportation in the EU' for transportation-related products; 'Relating to storage in the EU' for storage-related products; and consumption in the EU for supply and distribution contracts to final customers with consumption greater than 600 GWh/year.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Delivered in the Union - Supply Contracts
ID: 53
CONTENT:
For contracts for the supply of electricity, hydrogen or natural gas under Article 2(4)(a) of REMIT, the key element is that a delivery point must be in the EU. Contracts for supply produced in the EU but delivered outside its borders will not be within REMIT scope. Similarly, contracts produced and delivered outside the EU are excluded. However, contracts produced outside the EU but delivered within EU borders fall under REMIT scope. For LNG supply contracts, any delivery or offloading at LNG facilities in the EU, including flanges connecting vessels to terminals, qualifies as 'delivery in the EU' as long as delivery occurs in the EU.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: May be Delivered in the EU - Coupled Markets
ID: 54
CONTENT:
For contracts for electricity supply that may result in delivery in the union through single day-ahead and intraday coupling, the key element is that coupled markets must include at least one Member State to which potential delivery can occur. Within coupled systems, orders from market participants in one country can be matched by orders from participants in other coupled countries. The fact that bids and offers are placed on the same platform with potential to be matched is sufficient for the product to be considered as having potential delivery in the EU. All bids and offers placed within coupled markets must be reported to the Agency as part of organised marketplace reporting.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Produced, Traded or Delivered in the EU - Derivatives
ID: 55
CONTENT:
For derivative contracts relating to electricity, hydrogen or natural gas, Article 2(4)(b) of REMIT establishes they must relate to electricity, hydrogen or natural gas produced, traded or delivered in the EU. This geographical scope extends beyond Article 2(4)(a) requirements and includes derivative contracts relating to electricity, hydrogen or natural gas produced or traded in the EU, irrespective of whether delivery occurs in the EU. If the underlying contract is not produced, traded or delivered in the EU, the derivative contract will not qualify as a wholesale energy product and falls outside REMIT scope. A derivative contract traded in the EU relating to electricity for delivery outside the EU qualifies as a wholesale energy product if its underlying contract is also traded in the EU.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Transportation Contracts - Geographical Scope Requirements
ID: 57
CONTENT:
Concerning transportation contracts under Article 2(4)(c) of REMIT, it is required that they relate to the transportation of electricity, hydrogen or natural gas in the EU. The same geographical scope applies for derivative contracts under 2(4)(d) of REMIT, as they must relate to the transportation of electricity, hydrogen or natural gas in the EU. The concept of 'transportation of electricity, hydrogen or natural gas' in the EU shall be interpreted by NRAs as including at least one bidding zone/delivery point located inside the EU: all transportation of electricity, hydrogen or natural gas (including LNG) between bidding zones or specific delivery points that are (totally or partially) geographically located in the EU territory; all transportation of electricity, hydrogen or natural gas (including LNG) from a bidding zone or point that is geographically located outside of the EU to a bidding zone or delivery point located (totally or partially) inside the EU; and all transportation of electricity, hydrogen or natural gas (including LNG) from a bidding zone or delivery point that is geographically located inside of the EU (totally or partially) to a bidding zone or delivery point located outside the EU.

SECTION: Example: Gas Transportation Contract for Delivery at EU Border
ID: 59
CONTENT:
Situation: A market participant bought yearly firm transportation capacity of natural gas so that it can import natural gas from Norway into the EU (the contract stipulates that the entry point is in a Norwegian location and the delivery point is at a receiving terminal in Germany). Assessment: This contract is a wholesale energy product pursuant to Article 2(4)(c) of REMIT, as it fulfils all relevant criteria: It is a contract for the transportation of natural gas – this contract involves the transportation of natural gas from Norway to Germany. It is related to transportation in the EU – the delivery point of the natural gas to be transported is in Germany (as Germany is an EU Member State while Norway is not).

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Supply and Distribution Contracts - Consumption in the EU
ID: 62
CONTENT:
In line with Article 2(5) of REMIT, contracts for the supply and distribution to final customers with a consumption greater than 600 GWh/year shall be treated as wholesale energy products. Therefore, the geographical scope of contracts under Article 2(4)(a) of REMIT is also applicable to the contracts for the supply and distribution of electricity, hydrogen or natural gas to final customers with a consumption greater than 600 GWh/year. As the electricity, hydrogen or natural gas delivered under the contract for the supply and distribution to final customers is required to be delivered in the EU, the final customer's consumption must also be located inside the EU. Contracts for the supply and distribution of electricity or natural gas to final customers whose consumption is located outside the EU are not within the geographical scope of REMIT.

SECTION: Legal and Natural Persons in Scope - Overview
ID: 63
CONTENT:
This subchapter identifies the type of natural or legal persons that can fall within the scope of REMIT for different provisions. In general terms, it can be stated that any person (legal or natural) can fall within the overall scope of REMIT and not only market participants (the concept of 'market participant' is explained in the box at the end of this subchapter). That being said, it is important to note that not all REMIT prohibitions or obligations apply to the same array of persons. Some provisions have a broader scope while others a more restricted one.

SECTION: Personal Scope of REMIT Prohibitions and Obligations
ID: 64
CONTENT:
This subchapter sets out the personal scope of the prohibitions and obligations defined in REMIT towards legal and natural persons for which NRAs are responsible for investigating and/or enforcing: (i) prohibition of insider trading under Article 3(1) of REMIT; (ii) obligation to publish inside information under Article 4(1) of REMIT; (iii) prohibition of market manipulation under Article 5 of REMIT; (iv) obligation to notify and to have effective systems and risk controls for the use of algorithmic trading and direct electronic access under Article 5a of REMIT; (v) obligation to report LNG data under Article 7c of REMIT; (vi) obligation to report REMIT data under Article 8 of REMIT; (vii) obligation to register under Article 9(1) of REMIT; and (viii) obligations to notify and to maintain effective arrangements, systems and procedures to identify market abuse by persons professionally arranging or executing transactions under Article 15 of REMIT.

SECTION: Prohibition of Insider Trading - Persons Covered
ID: 65
CONTENT:
The prohibition of insider trading under Article 3(1) of REMIT only applies to the limited number of persons listed in Article 3(2) of REMIT: members of the administrative, management or supervisory bodies of an undertaking; natural or legal persons with holdings in the capital of an undertaking; natural or legal persons with access to the information through the exercise of their employment, profession or duties; natural or legal persons who have acquired such information through criminal activity; natural or legal persons who know, or ought to know, that it is inside information. More detailed information on the personal scope of the prohibition of insider trading can be found in Subchapter 5.4.

SECTION: Obligation to Publish Inside Information - Personal Scope
ID: 66
CONTENT:
The obligation to publish inside information under Article 4(1) of REMIT applies to market participants who possess inside information in respect of business or facilities which the market participant concerned, or its parent undertaking or related undertaking, owns or controls or for whose operational matters that market participant or undertaking is responsible, either in whole or in part. Market participants who possess inside information in respect of business or facilities of other market participants are not covered by the personal scope of obligation to publish inside information of Article 4(1) of REMIT. However, in relation to such inside information, they still need to comply with the prohibition of insider trading. More detailed information on the personal scope of the obligation to publish inside information can be found in Subchapter 4.1.

SECTION: Market Manipulation - Persons Covered
ID: 67
CONTENT:
The prohibition of market manipulation or attempted market manipulation applies to any person, or persons acting in collaboration. Article 2(8) of REMIT lays down that person means any natural or legal person. Therefore, the prohibition of market manipulation (and attempted market manipulation) under Article 5 of REMIT applies to any natural or legal person and represents the widest personal scope of REMIT application. More information on the personal scope of the prohibition of market manipulation is provided in Subchapter 6.4.1.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Algorithmic Trading and Direct Electronic Access - Notification Obligations
ID: 68
CONTENT:
The obligation to notify the use of algorithmic trading applies to market participants who engage in algorithmic trading. They shall notify this engagement to the NRA of the Member State where they are registered pursuant to Article 9(1) of REMIT, and to the Agency. Doing so via the Agency's CEREMP system will enable the market participants to notify both the relevant NRA and the Agency concomitantly. Please note that market participants registered in Italy, Romania and Slovenia will have to notify the relevant NRA directly, and by doing so they will be considered to have notified also the Agency.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Direct Electronic Access - Provider and Client Obligations
ID: 69
CONTENT:
The obligation to notify if a market participant provides direct electronic access (DEA) to an organised market place applies to a market participant that allows another person to use its trading code so that person may electronically transmit and place orders to trade relating to a wholesale energy product directly to the organised market place. The direct electronic access provider shall notify this engagement to the NRA of the Member State where it is registered pursuant to Article 9(1) of REMIT and to the Agency. metadata.title: Direct Electronic Access - Provider and Client Obligations
metadata.original_text: The obligation to notify if a market participant provides direct electronic access (DEA) to an organised market place applies to a market participant that allows another person to use its trading code so that person may electronically transmit and place orders to trade relating to a wholesale energy product directly to the organised market place. SECTION: Definition and Concept of Market Participant
ID: 74
CONTENT:
Article 2(7) of REMIT defines a market participant as: "Market participant means any person, including transmission system operators, distribution system operators, storage system operators and LNG system operators, who enters into transactions, including the placing of orders to trade, in one or more wholesale energy markets." The understanding of the notion of market participant is crucial for several reasons. Firstly, the obligation to disclose inside information according to Article 4(1) of REMIT lies with the market participant. Secondly, according to Article 8(1) of REMIT, market participants have the obligation to provide the Agency with a record of wholesale energy market transactions, including orders to trade, executed by the market participant itself or through a person or authority listed in points (b) to (f) of Article 8(4) of REMIT, and with the information described in Article 8(5) of REMIT (fundamental data). Lastly, pursuant to Article 9(1) of REMIT, market participants have to register with the competent NRA if entering into transactions which are required to be reported to the Agency in accordance with Article 8(1) of REMIT, as well as designate a representative in such Member State in case the market participant is established or resident in a 3rd country.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Interaction between REMIT and Financial Legislation
ID: 77
CONTENT:
There is a comprehensive regulatory framework at EU level for the identification, investigation and enforcement of market abuse in the EU energy markets (natural gas, electricity, and hydrogen). REMIT creates a tailored-made market abuse framework for the trading of wholesale energy products (WEPs). The Market Abuse Regulation (MAR) provides a regulatory framework on market abuse involving financial instruments, which in some cases are also WEPs. Considering that some WEPs are also financial instruments, there is a partial overlap between REMIT and MAR for some potential market abuse cases and the obligation to publish inside information (Article 3, 4, 5 of REMIT and Articles 14, 15 and 17 of MAR). Since some inside information and market manipulation behaviours may concern multiple types of products, including WEPs that are both financial instruments and non-financial instruments, it is paramount to identify which products fall under what category. Such exercise will allow to determine whether only REMIT applies, or whether MAR also applies concurrently, and what type of cooperation obligations the different entities involved may have.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Cooperation Principles between REMIT and MAR
ID: 78
CONTENT:
The REMIT and MAR market abuse legal frameworks have been designed to ensure an appropriate level of cooperation between the different responsible authorities. Article 1(3) of REMIT, Article 25(3) of MAR and Article 10(2) of the Commission Implementing Regulation 2020/1406 establish the fundamental, high-level principles in relation to the generic cooperation and coordination provisions. Article 1(2) of REMIT provides that REMIT is without prejudice to MAR, MiFIR, EMIR and MiFID II, as well as to the application of EU competition law to the practices covered by REMIT. More detailed information on the interaction between REMIT and EU competition law relating to market manipulation can be found in Subchapter 6.4.2.

SECTION: Financial Instruments Under MiFID II and REMIT Application
ID: 82
CONTENT:
A quarterly future product that is not a financial instrument falls outside the scope of Articles 14 and 15 of MAR. Instead, only the prohibitions of insider trading and market manipulation under Articles 3 and 5 of REMIT are fully applicable to transactions in this product. The determination of whether a product qualifies as a financial instrument depends on its characteristics, including whether it has an underlying asset, how its final settlement price is determined, and whether it involves physical or cash settlement.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Example: WEP Not a Financial Instrument - 2024 Yearly Gas Forward
ID: 83
CONTENT:
Broker X reported a suspicious A-B-A wash trade involving a product called '2024 yearly gas forward' for physical delivery in Market Area A. The product characteristics include: no underlying asset, final settlement price based on agreed price at transaction time, and mandatory physical settlement with no cash settlement option. The seller must physically deliver 5 MW of gas into Market Area A on each delivery day of 2024, and the buyer must take delivery. Counterparty risk is managed by the parties themselves with no margining service. This physically settled forward contract is equivalent to a spot product with deferred delivery and is not an electricity or natural gas derivative. As a contract for supply of natural gas in the EU, it qualifies as a wholesale energy product under Article 2(4)(a) of REMIT. Therefore, only Articles 3 and 5 of REMIT apply, while Articles 14 and 15 of MAR do not apply.

SECTION: Example: WEP That Is a Financial Instrument - Market Area A Power Base Year Future
ID: 84
CONTENT:
Potential insider trading was identified on a regulated market involving the product 'Market Area A Power Base Year Future' for 2024. Product characteristics include: underlying is the day-ahead electricity price of Market Area A; final settlement price is based on an index corresponding to the mean value of all auction prices of hourly day-ahead contracts for Market Area A Base load delivery; and fulfillment involves delivery or acceptance of 1 MW electricity into Market Area A during each delivery day of 2024 with cash settlement instead of physical delivery. The seller (buyer) must settle in cash on execution day the difference between agreed price and final settlement price. The organised marketplace manages counterparty risk through initial and maintenance margins. This product is a derivative since its final settlement price depends on the underlying day-ahead electricity price. As a cash-settled derivative traded on a regulated market, it is a financial instrument under Annex I Section C of MiFID II and falls within MAR scope. Both Articles 3 and 5 of REMIT and Articles 14 and 15 of MAR apply to this product.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Application of Inside Information Definition Under REMIT - Introduction
ID: 86
CONTENT:
Qualifying a specific fact as 'inside information' under REMIT requires a two-step approach. First, determine whether there is a piece of information according to at least one of criteria (a) to (d) defined in Article 2(1), second subparagraph of REMIT. Second, ascertain whether it fulfills four cumulative conditions established in Article 2(1), first subparagraph of REMIT: it must be precise, not public, related to one or more wholesale energy products, and likely to significantly affect prices. This chapter provides guidance on what constitutes 'information' under REMIT and the definition of 'inside information' including application of the four cumulative conditions.

SECTION: The Concept of Information Under REMIT - Regulatory Requirements
ID: 87
CONTENT:
Article 2(1), second subparagraph of REMIT defines 'information' as: (a) information required to be made public under Regulations (EU) 2019/943 and (EC) No 715/2009, including guidelines and network codes; (b) information relating to capacity and use of facilities for production, storage, consumption or transmission of electricity, hydrogen or natural gas, or related to LNG facilities, including planned or unplanned unavailability; (c) information required to be disclosed under legal or regulatory provisions at Union or national level, market rules, contracts or customs on the relevant wholesale energy market, if likely to significantly affect wholesale energy product prices; (ca) information conveyed by a market participant or persons acting on their behalf to a service provider relating to pending orders in wholesale energy products, of precise nature and relating directly or indirectly to wholesale energy products; and (d) other information a reasonable market participant would likely use as basis for deciding to enter into a transaction or issue an order in a wholesale energy product.

SECTION: Capacity and Facility Information Under REMIT Article 2(1)(b)
ID: 89
CONTENT:
The concept of 'information' under REMIT encompasses information related to all planned or unplanned changes in capacity or output at any facility for production, storage, consumption or transmission of natural gas, hydrogen or electricity. This includes: capacity and use of production facilities including planned and unplanned unavailability; capacity and use of storage facilities including planned and unplanned availability; capacity and use of consumption facilities including planned and unplanned unavailability; capacity and use of transmission facilities including planned or unplanned unavailability; and capacity and use of LNG facilities including planned and unplanned unavailability.

SECTION: Disclosure Requirements Under REMIT Article 2(1)(c)
ID: 90
CONTENT:
The concept of 'information' under REMIT covers facts required to be disclosed in accordance with legal or regulatory provisions at national level, legal or regulatory provisions at European Union level, market rules, contracts, and customs on the market. Notably, Regulation (EC) 543/2013 on submission and publication of data in electricity markets establishes multiple obligations to publish facts that constitute 'information' according to Article 2(1)(c) of REMIT. These transparency information requirements are integral to REMIT's information definition.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: REMIT Information Definition and Reasonable Market Participant Test
ID: 92
CONTENT:
Article 2(1)(d) of REMIT establishes that any other information that a reasonable market participant would be likely to use as part of the basis of its decision to enter into a transaction relating to a wholesale energy product, or its decision to issue an order to trade in a wholesale energy product, should be considered 'information' under REMIT. The Agency recommends that NRAs use the 'reasonable market participant test' to help determine whether a given fact qualifies as 'information' under REMIT, but only when such facts is not already covered by Articles 2(1)(a), (b),(c) and (ca) of REMIT. The concept of the 'reasonable market participant' may encompass different profiles of market participants (e.g. beginner, average, informed, professional market participant) with different trading strategies (e.g. portfolio optimisation, arbitrage, speculative) covering short-term and/or long-term products. The concept of 'reasonability' is rather related to the use of cognitive elements by the market participant in its trading decisions (at least partially). By contrast, a market participant that makes trading decisions based on non-cognitive elements, such as instinct or mood, should not be considered reasonable.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Reasonable Market Participant Test - Key Indicators
ID: 93
CONTENT:
To qualify a fact as information under REMIT, it is enough that at least one of these profiles is likely to use the fact as part of the basis of their decision to enter into a transaction relating to a wholesale energy product, or their decision to issue an order to trade in a wholesale energy product. When using the 'reasonable market participant test', the NRAs may take into consideration, as indicators, that: the concept of 'would be likely to use' should be distinguished from the concept of 'would like to use' – the test is not about whether there is a wish on the part of the reasonable market participant to use some type of information. Rather, the test is used to assess whether it is reasonable for a market participant to have a legitimate expectation that such information is available. The concept of 'would be likely to use' should be interpreted based on what can be reasonably expected to be published (for example, the fact that a market participant would like to use its competitors' trading plans for its own trading strategy does not mean that these plans are 'information' under REMIT, as they are not information that 'can reasonably be expected to be published' and that would likely be used by a reasonable market participant). The fact that a market participant used comparable facts (for example, at a different moment in time) as the basis for its trading decisions, could be considered a proxy to further assess with an ad hoc analysis if the fact is information that would be likely to be used by a 'reasonable market participant'.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Examples of Information Under REMIT - TSO Transfer Capacity and Generation Maintenance
ID: 94
CONTENT:
Example 1 - Information on the TSO's available transfer capacity: The estimates of TSOs A and B of the available transfer capacity for each day and the available transfer capacity already reserved in the electricity interconnector between bidding zones C and D. Assessment: These facts are information under REMIT because as specified in Article 2(1)(a) of REMIT, they relate to information required to be disclosed in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 2019/943. According to Article 50(3) thereof, TSOs shall publish estimates of available transfer capacity for each day, indicating any available transfer capacity already reserved. Example 2 - Information on the annual maintenance of generation units: Market participant A plans to perform annual maintenance on its electricity generation unit XPTO, with a total capacity of 50 MW from 01/02/2025 to 01/04/2025. Assessment: This fact is information under REMIT as it constitutes information relating to the capacity and use of facilities for the production of electricity as specified in Article 2(1)(b) of REMIT. The fact that the unavailable capacity is below the 100 MW threshold included in Regulation (EC) No 543/2013 is relevant for the assessment of whether it constitutes information under Article 2(1)(c) of REMIT but not under Articles 2(1)(a), (b), (ca) and (d) of REMIT.

SECTION: Definition of Inside Information Under REMIT
ID: 95
CONTENT:
Pursuant to Article 2(1), second subparagraph of REMIT, information qualifies as 'inside information' if it fulfils the four cumulative conditions included in Article 2(1), first subparagraph, of REMIT: 'Inside information' means information of a precise nature, which has not been made public, which relates, directly or indirectly, to one or more wholesale energy products and which, if it were made public, would be likely to significantly affect the prices of those wholesale energy products. It is the responsibility of market participants to ascertain whether the information they hold a) potentially constitutes 'inside information' according to the above-mentioned four cumulative conditions, and, b) therefore, needs to be made public according to Article 4(1) of REMIT. In order to have an appropriate framework for the assessment of information, it is recommended that market participants have clear internal compliance rules that are adapted to their activities and to the specificities of the information they use and have access to.

SECTION: Internal Compliance Rules for Market Participants
ID: 96
CONTENT:
The best practices for internal compliance rules may include: a framework for the assessment of whether the facts at hand can be qualified as inside information. This may include, for example, measures on how to identify inside information, appropriately tested thresholds, etc.; an adequate workflow of information compliant with the presence of inside information. This may include, for example, a mapping of the flow of information, measures on how to handle inside information, etc.; and a list of insiders and/or mechanisms in place to identify insiders. The internal compliance rules should be consistent with a market participant's organisational structure and trading strategies.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Information of a Precise Nature - Definition and Assessment
ID: 97
CONTENT:
Article 2(1), third subparagraph of REMIT describes what is meant by the term information of a 'precise nature' as follows: 'Information shall be considered to be of a precise nature if it indicates a set of circumstances which exists or may reasonably be expected to come into existence, or an event which has occurred or may reasonably be expected to occur, and if it is specific enough to enable a conclusion to be drawn as to the possible effect of that set of circumstances or event on the prices of wholesale energy products. Information may be considered to be of a precise nature if it relates to a protracted process that is intended to bring about, or that results in, particular circumstances or a particular event, including future circumstances or future events, and also if it relates to the intermediate steps of that process which are connected with bringing about or resulting in those future circumstances or future events. An intermediate step in a protracted process shall be considered to be inside information if it, by itself, satisfies the criteria of inside information.' The precise nature of the information is to be assessed by the information holder on a case-by-case basis and depends on what the information is, as well as on the surrounding context.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Assessment Considerations for Precise Nature of Information
ID: 98
CONTENT:
In assessing the precise nature of information, the holder of the information may, among other things, take into consideration: (i) that there is a realistic prospect that a fact will occur; (ii) that the estimation of the potential price effect of information disclosure is irrelevant for the assessment of the precise nature; and (iii) that intermediate steps in a protracted processes may be precise information. Information is precise as long as there is a realistic prospect that the circumstances or events it refers to will come into existence/occur, considering all the factors existing at the time of the assessment. The calculation of the potential effect of the information on the prices of wholesale energy products is not an element to be taken into consideration in the assessment of the precise nature of the information. However, the likelihood of a significant price effect should be assessed to determine if the information is inside information under REMIT. In order for the information to have a precise nature, it is not necessary to be able to infer from that information, with a sufficient degree of probability, that, once it is made public, its potential effect on the prices of the relevant wholesale energy products in a particular direction.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Examples of Realistic Prospect - Strikes and Nuclear Safety Tests
ID: 99
CONTENT:
Example 1 - Information on strikes impacting workers relevant for the normal operation of a generation unit: Such information on strikes can be seen as having a realistic prospect of happening due to, for example, the existence of historical records of this information resulting in effective strikes impacting the production of this unit. Therefore, it can be considered that there is a realistic prospect of a strike happening, considering all the factors existing at the time of the assessment. This information on strikes would then qualify as precise information. This is despite the fact that the strike can still be cancelled and/or that there may be some uncertainty about the overall duration of the strike or other elements. Any further developments of the situation (cancellation of the strike, update on the dates of the strike, scope of workers affected etc.) may make the prospect of the strike less realistic. However, as long as they occur after the market participant assessed whether the information was precise, they should not be taken into consideration by the NRA when assessing whether the information was precise at the time the market participant received the information. In any case, the market participant should provide updates to the public on the evolution of the information. Example 2 - Information/request by the nuclear safety authority regarding possible security tests: Such information can be seen as having a realistic prospect of happening due to, for example, the existence of previous information of the same type that resulted in effective security tests impacting the production and/or availability of the unit, episodes reflecting the planning of the nuclear safety authority, or previous expressions of concerns with the operation of the unit. Therefore, it can be considered that there is a realistic prospect of the security tests impacting the production and/or availability to happen considering all factors existing at the time of the assessment.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Commissioning of New Plants and Recommissioning of Mothballed Power Plants
ID: 102
CONTENT:
The process leading to the commissioning of new plants or recommissioning of mothballed power plants is a protracted and complex process. Its major milestones (for example: management board approvals, regulatory approvals, licence granting, etc.) constitute intermediate steps in this process. Some facts generated by the intermediate steps leading to the commissioning or recommissioning of a power plant would qualify as precise information under REMIT, as they constitute a set of circumstances which exist or may reasonably be expected to come into existence and impact the realistic prospect of energy being produced from a certain point in time onwards. In order to decide whether these facts qualify as inside information, the three other criteria covered in Subchapters 3.3.2 to 3.3.4 also need to be met.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Planned Unavailability on Electricity Interconnector Due to Expansion Works
ID: 103
CONTENT:
The process leading to the expansion of capacity in an electricity interconnector is a protracted and complex process. Its major milestones (for example: market participant's management board decisions, regulatory approvals, licence granting, decisions from the interconnector's operational centre to proceed with the unavailability) constitute intermediate steps. A management board decision (for example, on the unavailability on the existing interconnectors to allow the expansion of the existing infrastructure during a specific period), despite being an intermediate step (that can still be subject to other approvals - for example by regulatory or operational centre), fulfils the criteria of precise nature under REMIT. The management board decision to approve or disapprove a planned maintenance during a specific period is specific enough to enable a conclusion to be drawn as to the possible effect of that set of circumstances or events on the prices of wholesale energy products. In order to decide whether the management board decision can qualify as inside information, the three other criteria covered in Subchapters 3.3.2 to 3.3.4 also need to be met.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Information That Has Not Been Made Public
ID: 104
CONTENT:
Inside information is information that has not been shared with the public and, as a consequence, creates information asymmetries between market participants. Effective disclosure to the public of market participants is the criterion that transforms non-public information into public information. Once the information becomes public, it enhances the integrity and transparency of the market, as envisaged by Recital 2 of REMIT. In general, information is deemed to be public knowledge if such information has been made, by any party, available to the public, i.e. to an unspecified number of market participants. In this regard, it is irrelevant who made the information public. No distinction is made as to whether the information was made public by a market participant or by any other party.

SECTION: Public Disclosure Requirements and Inside Information Platforms
ID: 105
CONTENT:
It is sufficient, but also required, that information is made available to the entire public of market participants simultaneously, ensuring equal access to the information, since any interested market participant may appraise the information. This can be the case, for example, if a generally accessible electronic system for the dissemination of information, that qualifies as an Inside Information Platform is used (see Chapter 4 for more details). Publishing information only to selected market participants, for example via an email channel or news board which is available exclusively to exchange members, does not satisfy the requirement of informing the public. The Agency's understanding of effective and timely public disclosure of inside information is provided in Chapter 4 of this Guidance.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Information Relating to Wholesale Energy Products
ID: 106
CONTENT:
The definition of 'inside information' in Article 2(1) of REMIT requires the relevant information to relate, directly or indirectly, to one or more wholesale energy products. 'Wholesale energy products' are defined under Article 2(4) of REMIT and further explained under Subchapter 2.2 of this Guidance. The penultimate paragraph of Article 2(1) of REMIT stipulates that information that has a possible effect on the demand, supply and/or prices of a wholesale energy product, or on the expectations of the demand, supply and/or prices of a wholesale energy product, shall be considered as directly or indirectly related to the wholesale energy product. If the information is likely to have a significant effect on the prices of wholesale energy products, it is necessarily related to these products. Therefore, it is enough for the NRAs to assess the likelihood of a significant effect on the prices to establish whether the information relates to wholesale energy products.

Therefore, it is enough for the NRAs to assess the likelihood of a significant effect on the prices to establish whether the information relates to wholesale energy products.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Likelihood of Significant Price Effect on Wholesale Energy Products
ID: 107
CONTENT:
Information is deemed to constitute inside information only if, were it made public, it would be likely to have a significant effect on the prices of related wholesale energy product. Based on the condition of a significant price effect, the Agency narrowed the wide notion of information down to the information that is crucial enough to have the potential to significantly affect the prices of wholesale energy products, and therefore to information that is relevant for trading. It is important to note that if the information would be likely to have a significant price effect, that effect is enough to meet this condition and that no actual price effect is required.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Case-by-Case Assessment of Price Effect Likelihood
ID: 108
CONTENT:
The assessment of the likelihood of price effect has to be performed by a market participant on a case-by-case basis. The market participant should take into consideration the anticipated effect of the information in light of the nature of the information, as well as the specificities of the market and the market situation at the time of the assessment. Factors typically relevant for this assessment include: the characteristics of the market (size, timeframe, market design, liquidity, type of participants etc.); the size of the event; the already published information on supply or demand situation; availability and unavailability of transmission facilities, storage or network constraints; the time of day (e.g. weekday/weekend, office hours/out of office hours); the existence of announcements on non-regular events (for example, the commissioning of new power plant, the recommissioning of mothballed power plant, etc.); TSO announcements related to the system (imbalances, security of supply, technical constrains etc.); and any other market variables likely to affect the price of the related wholesale energy product in the given circumstances (e.g. weather conditions, CO2, fuel prices, news on political and geopolitical developments etc.).

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Systematic Framework for Price Effect Assessment and Ex Ante Evaluation
ID: 109
CONTENT:
Market participants are advised to have a systematic framework for the assessment of whether particular information is likely to have a significant price effect, i.e. clear internal compliance rules that reflect the non-exhaustive list of factors and are adapted both to their activities and to the specificities of the information they handle. As the assessment of the likelihood of the price effect has to be performed by the market participant ex ante, i.e. before the information is published and used by the market participant, NRAs can use ex post information to check the presumption but should take no action against persons who drew reasonable conclusions from ex ante information available to them. The last subparagraph of Article 2(1) of REMIT stipulates that 'information which, if it were made public, would be likely to significantly affect the prices of the wholesale energy products means information that a reasonable market participant would be likely to use as part of the basis of his or her decision concerning trading with wholesale energy products.'

SECTION: Verification of Reasonable Market Participant Assessment
ID: 110
CONTENT:
In order to evaluate whether a market participant's assessment on the likelihood of some information having a significant price effect is consistent with what would be expected from a reasonable market participant, the NRAs could verify whether: the type of information is the same as information which has, in the past, had a significant effect on prices; pre-existing analysts research reports, price reporter publications and opinions indicate that the type of information in question has effects on prices; the market participant itself has already treated similar events as inside information; another reasonable market participant has already treated similar events as inside information; or a reasonable market participant would be likely to use it as part of its trading decisions.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Example: Update on Status of Unplanned Outage in Generation Unit
ID: 111
CONTENT:
Market participant A (MP A) operating a power plant realises that its unplanned maintenance (previously disclosed) on a generation unit (100 MW unavailability) will have to be extended by 2 hours. The market liquidity is limited for the relevant wholesale electricity products. MP A needs to decide whether such information would be likely to have a significant price effect. In order to make its decision, MP A should consider whether a reasonable market participant would be likely to use this information as part of the basis of its trading decision. For the ex-ante assessment, MP A should consider: Characteristics of the market - The intraday market is open. Two hourly products and eight 15-minute products are directly affected by the extension of the outage. The order depth during the last hour was limited and therefore small changes on fundamentals may have an impact. Size of the event - The size of the event is limited. Only two additional hours affected for 100 MWh. Information on supply or demand situation already published - This unplanned outage is ongoing and there are no other outages announced. Other constraints - Cross-border capacity is limited at this point in time in the only existing border with another bidding zone. Time of day - Normal working hours. Existence of announcements on non-regular events or TSO events - No additional announcements. Any other market variables - No relevant changes in wind forecasts.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: TSOs' Request to Activate Reserves - Assessment Framework
ID: 114
CONTENT:
In some EU Member States without specific national requirements for TSO to publish information on imbalances in real time due to potential system imbalance, 25 minutes before delivery time, the TSO requests a balancing responsible party to activate a generation unit for 200 MWh for a specified period. At this point, the intraday market is still open. The TSO needs to decide whether such information would be likely to have a significant price effect. A reasonable market participant would be likely to use this information as part of the basis of its trading decision. Factors to consider include: characteristics of the market (intraday market open, low bid-ask spread, relatively high market depth), size of the event (relevant given proximity to delivery period), information on supply or demand already published (no other outages announced), other constraints (cross-border transmission capacity inexistent), time of day (issued very close to delivery period), existence of announcements on non-regular events, and any other market variables (no relevant changes). Activation of balancing bids gives market participants valuable information regarding direction of system imbalance, and the TSO can conclude that information on imbalances would be likely to have significant price effect on intraday products.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Information on Trading Plans and Strategies - Definition and Scope
ID: 115
CONTENT:
Information regarding a market participant's own plans and strategies for trading should not be considered as inside information according to Recital 12 of REMIT. Trading plans are defined as plans including a systematic method for evaluating supply, demand, or price of wholesale energy products, determining amount of risk that is or should be taken, and/or formulating short- and/or long-term investment targets that may guide daily trading activity. Consequences of these short- and/or long-term investment targets, in terms of energy needs and resulting orders to trade, should be considered as part of trading plans and therefore not constituting information under REMIT. Trading strategies are defined as a set of objective rules designating conditions that must be met for one or more trade entries and exits to occur, including specifications for order entries with filters and/or triggers, as well as rules for trade exits and order types. However, even if details of trading strategy do not qualify as inside information under REMIT, the facts used to determine or change it can be inside information.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Examples of Facts Not Constituting Inside Information - Order Details
ID: 116
CONTENT:
Details of orders that a market participant intends to submit during the trading day do not constitute inside information. Example: Market participant A sends an order with the following details: Buy order, Initiator, Flexible Hour order type (specific order that can trade at any hour provided price and volume are matched), Fill and Float order conditions (order killed immediately after matching with available volume; if not filled, stays in market), Active status (order activated by system or participant and visible in active order book), Minimum execution volume of 1,500 MW, Price limit of 40.5 euro, Good Till Cancelled order duration (persists until user cancels or reaches system maximum duration). This fact is part of the trading strategy of the market participant and therefore does not qualify as inside information under REMIT.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Examples of Facts Not Constituting Inside Information - Risk Optimisation Strategy Changes
ID: 117
CONTENT:
Decisions on changes in risk optimisation strategy of a market participant do not constitute inside information. Example: Market participant A makes decision to change its portfolio optimisation strategy, i.e., how to source its supply needs. Such decision will change its strategy of how much electricity is purchased through standardized electricity products on electricity exchange versus through bilateral contracts, and purchased in different timeframes (e.g., percentage of weekly, monthly, yearly products). Decision on changes in risk optimisation strategy of a market participant is usually part of its trading plan and therefore does not qualify as inside information under REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Obligation to Disclose Inside Information - Introduction and Scope
ID: 118
CONTENT:
According to Article 4(1) subparagraph 1 of REMIT, market participants shall publicly disclose in an effective and timely manner inside information which they possess in respect of business or facilities which the market participant concerned, or its parent undertaking or related undertaking, owns or controls or for whose operational matters that market participant or undertaking is responsible, either in whole or in part. Such disclosure shall include information relevant to capacity and use of facilities for production, storage, consumption or transmission of electricity, hydrogen or natural gas or related to capacity and use of LNG facilities, including planned or unplanned unavailability of these facilities. The obligation to disclose inside information lies with the market participant according to Article 4(1) of REMIT. The disclosure obligation relates not only to inside information in respect of market participant's own business or facilities, but also to inside information of market participant's parent undertaking or related undertaking. Disclosure obligation is not only related to inside information in respect of business or facilities which market participant or respective undertakings own or control, but also in respect of business or facilities for whose operational matters market participant or respective undertaking is responsible, either in whole or in part.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Disclosure Obligation - Scope and Related Undertakings
ID: 119
CONTENT:
The obligation to disclose inside information does not apply to a person or market participant who possesses inside information in respect of another market participant's business or facilities, in so far as that owner of this inside information is not a parent or related undertaking. Notwithstanding this, persons holding information in such circumstances will need to consider their compliance with Article 3 and in particular whether they hold such information as one of the persons listed in Article 3(2). The Agency encourages persons holding such information to promptly inform relevant market participant(s) in order to promote effective and timely compliance with Article 4(1) of REMIT. Article 4(3) of REMIT extends disclosure obligation of Article 4(1) to a person employed by, or acting on behalf of, a market participant when that person discloses inside information to any other person in normal course of exercise of their employment, profession or duties as referred to in Article 3(1)(b) of REMIT. In such case, that market participant or person shall ensure simultaneous, complete and effective disclosure of that information. However, disclosure obligation of Article 4(3) does not apply if person receiving information has duty of confidentiality, regardless of whether such duty derives from law, regulation, articles of association or contracts.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Disclosure Mechanisms and Inside Information Platforms
ID: 120
CONTENT:
Transparency of wholesale energy markets requires disclosure of inside information in manner that enables dissemination of information to as wide a public as possible, granting easy and equal access to all users of this information. According to Article 4(1) subparagraph 2 of REMIT, market participants shall disclose inside information through IIPs (Inside Information Platforms). IIPs shall ensure that inside information is made public in manner which enables prompt access to that information, including through website or clear application programming interface, and complete, correct and timely assessment of that information by public. An Inside Information Platform or IIP is defined as a person authorised pursuant to REMIT to provide service of operating platform for disclosure of inside information and for reporting of disclosed inside information to the Agency on behalf of market participants. To achieve effective disclosure, IIPs shall ensure inside information is made public in manner enabling prompt access, including through website or clear application programming interface, and complete, correct and timely assessment by public.

SECTION: IIP Authorization, Supervision and Compliance Requirements
ID: 121
CONTENT:
The Agency's process for authorisation and supervision of IIPs established in Article 4a of REMIT will be covered by delegated act issued by Commission. In order to facilitate compliance with disclosure obligation, list of Inside Information Platforms available in Europe for disclosure of inside information on wholesale energy markets is published on Agency's REMIT Portal, following assessment of IIPs' compliance with quality requirements listed in Subchapter 4.2.2, requirements for reporting of inside information to Agency described in REMIT Manual of Procedures on transaction data, fundamental data and inside information reporting (REMIT MoP) and Guidance on implementation of web feeds.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Platform Listing and Inside Information Disclosure Requirements
ID: 122
CONTENT:
Platforms should apply to be listed by the Agency and will be listed if they comply with the requirements. From 2025, the Agency will be operating a platform serving as a sector-specific electronic access point for inside information disclosed pursuant to Article 4(1) of REMIT. Regarding the publication of inside information, including in aggregated form, in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2019/943 or (EC) No 715/2009, and with guidelines and network codes adopted pursuant to those Regulations, and Commission Regulation (EU) No 543/2013, this shall constitute effective disclosure, provided that the published information concerns the same event(s) and has the same content and format and conforms to the minimum quality requirements as the information required to be disclosed according to Article 4(1) of REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Publication Methods and Market Transparency
ID: 123
CONTENT:
A simultaneous publication on the market participant's website or through social media may be used as an additional source for publication. However, it cannot replace the disclosure on Inside Information Platforms. In case additional means for publication are used, the market participant must ensure that the published information is identical to the one published on the Inside Information Platform. The publication of inside information on IIPs facilitates access to information for all market participants and promotes the overall transparency of the market. Moreover, this solution decreases overall the technical and organisational burden for market participants. In the registration process according to Article 9(5) of REMIT, market participants possessing inside information are required to promptly provide and regularly update information on the place of publication of inside information. This information is made publicly available by the Agency as part of the European Register of Market Participants (CEREMP).
