text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Staff Protection and Training Requirements
ID: 366
CONTENT:
Consideration should be given to potential psychological harassment of the market surveillance team by persons involved in trading-related activities, such as brokers or traders within the PPAT. A broker or trader within the PPAT could be investigated for a potential breach of REMIT and that broker or trader could then harass the market surveillance team member during the investigation. Appropriate training should be given to the market surveillance team on how to handle potential psychological harassment situations and safeguards should be in place to manage this. Members of the market surveillance team should be given appropriate training and guidance on REMIT and the practical considerations for the application of Article 15. Training should be delivered regularly according to the training map and should be updated in line with any guidance offered by the Agency and NRAs. Training on REMIT should not be restricted to the members of the market surveillance team and should be offered across the organisation where appropriate. A record of training attendance or completion should be kept and the effectiveness of training shall be assessed by the PPAT. It constitutes good practice that surveillance staff is not relieved from their duties without the prior consent of the responsible NRA or exchange supervisory authority.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Communication Procedures and Information Access
ID: 367
CONTENT:
Internal policies should cover the use of data and information by the market surveillance team and should allow its members to access any information or data which may help to explain the suspicious event under investigation. The market surveillance team should also be able to request information from the market participant in relation to a suspicious event. Communication between the market surveillance team and anyone involved in a suspicious event/potential breach of REMIT should be carefully considered in order to avoid tipping off the company or person under suspicion. The market surveillance team should have and follow a policy setting the process for approaching members/customers and all communication in relation to a suspicious event/potential breach should be noted or recorded on file.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: STOR Submission and Contact Protocols
ID: 368
CONTENT:
As a general rule, once a STOR has been submitted to ACER and the relevant NRA(s), the market surveillance team should not make contact with the member/customer in relation to that incident unless agreed with the responsible NRA(s) and ACER. Furthermore, under no circumstance should the market surveillance team make the member/customer aware that a STOR has been submitted to ACER. In exceptional circumstances it may be necessary for the market surveillance team or senior management at the PPAT to contact the member/customer reported in a STOR and they may enforce a sanction such as suspension of trading. By its nature, this form of contact may tip the member/customer off that an investigation is being conducted, but it may be necessary in order to avoid further harm to the market. If this is to happen, engagement with the relevant NRA and ACER from the start is important.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Cross-Market Communication and Escalation Procedures
ID: 369
CONTENT:
In circumstances where contacts between market surveillance teams of different PPATs are envisaged, for example in potential cases of cross-market manipulation, internal policies should detail procedures accordingly. Guidelines relating to what can be discussed between market surveillance teams should be clearly defined in the internal policies and all contact and decisions should be recorded so that if a STOR is raised, the relevant NRA is aware of the work that has already been carried out and if it is not this can be justified. The communication policy in place should detail how staff members outside of the market surveillance function identify and/or escalate suspicions of market abuse.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Traceability and Record Keeping Requirements
ID: 370
CONTENT:
All work carried out by the market surveillance team should be recorded whether in a dedicated case management system, a shared folder or in traceable email records, for a period of at least five years. It is advisable to have a clear written policy on surveillance procedures which details the processes that the market surveillance team should follow when looking into a suspicious event. The full PPATs' decision-making process related to the qualification of a suspicious event as a potential breach (from the initial alert to the STOR being raised) should be traceable and key decision points should be recorded. All transaction(s)/order(s)/behaviour(s), including related updates to them, particularly relating to a suspicious event/potential breach should be stored by the PPAT for a defined amount of time. The relevant NRA may place further retention requirements on the PPAT where appropriate.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Documentation and Audit Requirements
ID: 371
CONTENT:
NRAs should request PPATs to maintain for a period of at least five years the information documenting the analysis carried out with regard to a suspicious event/potential breach which have been examined and the reasons as to whether or not submitting a STR. This information shall be provided to the NRA upon request. All processes and decisions made by the market surveillance team should also be recorded. The PPAT should conduct internal audits or hire an external auditor to review their processes at least on a regular annual basis and in certain circumstances an NRA may wish to conduct a visit or audit.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Compliance Advocacy and Enforcement
ID: 372
CONTENT:
Within the limits of their investigatory and/or sanctioning powers, ACER and the relevant NRAs shall enforce PPAETs compliance with Article 15. Based on their competencies, ACER and NRAs may choose to issue 'Systems and Controls Questionnaires' relating to the PPAET's Article 15 processes, amongst other. They may also conduct visits to the PPAET's market surveillance and monitoring teams to assess their surveillance and monitoring processes in practice. This will help ACER and NRAs understand the processes that STORs have gone through to consider their next steps. ACER and NRAs may also choose to run STOR Supervision Fora, focussing on best-practice sharing between the PPAETs. It is at the discretion of ACER and NRAs whether to conduct visits, issue questionnaires or hold fora relating to REMIT Article 15 processes. Adequate notice should be given to the PPAET ahead of any such activities.

SECTION: REMIT Compliance and Penalty Regimes Overview
ID: 373
CONTENT:
This chapter provides some considerations from the Agency on best practices that market participants could implement to ensure their compliance with REMIT and the Agency's current understanding on the enforcement of the different REMIT obligations and prohibitions through national penalty regimes under Article 18 of REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Market Participant Compliance Regime
ID: 374
CONTENT:
The Agency is of the opinion that market participants should develop a clear compliance regime towards real time or close to real time disclosure of inside information and towards the other obligations and prohibitions of REMIT. NRAs should consider the following best practice examples of such compliance regime for market participants, taking into account the market participant's size and trading capacity: Compliance culture - the creation of a corporate culture to comply with REMIT requirements; Compliance objectives - the compliance with REMIT requirements, namely the registration, disclosure and reporting obligations.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Compliance Organisation and Risk Management
ID: 375
CONTENT:
Compliance organisation involves defining roles and responsibilities in the internal organisation, including responsibilities for REMIT requirements (centralised vs. decentralised), internal vs. external reporting lines, internal vs. external interfaces, and provision of resources (human and technical IT Systems resources). Compliance risks require identification and assessment of concrete compliance risks. A compliance programme must identify concrete actions to define compliant and non-compliant behaviour. Communication of rules and regulations includes internal communication and training concepts to raise employee awareness, external communication and reporting to the Agency and NRAs, and reporting processes for internal compliance reports, infringements, and status of current processes. Monitoring improvements involve internal controls, audits, reporting lines for monitoring results, and documentation of processes and actions.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Penalty Regimes Under REMIT Article 18
ID: 376
CONTENT:
Article 18(1) of REMIT stipulates that Member States shall lay down rules on penalties applicable to REMIT infringements and take all necessary measures to ensure implementation. Penalties must be effective, dissuasive, and proportional. Member States must notify these provisions in detail to the Commission and Agency, and notify them without delay of any subsequent amendments. The Agency considers it important that penalties are in place for all potential REMIT infringements, including breaches of market abuse prohibitions (Articles 3 and 5), failure to notify relevant information to the Agency and competent NRA (Article 3(4)(b)), failure to disclose inside information (Article 4(1)), failure to notify delayed disclosure of inside information (Article 4(2)), failure to submit daily LNG market data (Article 7c(1)), failure to provide wholesale energy market transaction records (Article 8(1)), failure to register with competent NRA (Article 9(1)), and obligations of PPAETs (Article 15).

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Administrative Fines and Measures Framework
ID: 377
CONTENT:
Article 18(3) of REMIT requires Member States to ensure national regulatory authorities have power to impose administrative fines and other administrative measures for breaches, including: (a) requiring the breach to be brought to an end; (b) ordering disgorgement of profits gained or losses avoided due to breaches insofar as they can be determined; (c) issuing public warnings or notices; (d) imposing periodic penalty payments; and (e) imposing administrative fines. Article 18 differentiates between 'administrative fines' (Article 18(3)(e)) and 'other administrative measures' (Article 18(3)(a)-(d)). Articles 18(4) and 18(5) differentiate between penalties for natural persons and legal persons, setting minimum levels for maximum administrative fine thresholds.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Administrative Fines for Natural Persons
ID: 378
CONTENT:
Article 18(4) of REMIT establishes minimum levels for maximum administrative fines for natural persons: (a) for breaches of Articles 3 and 5, at least EUR 5,000,000; (b) for breaches of Articles 4 and 15, at least EUR 1,000,000; (c) for breaches of Articles 8 and 9, at least EUR 500,000. The amount of administrative fine shall not exceed 20% of the yearly income in the preceding calendar year of the natural person concerned. Where the natural person has directly or indirectly benefited financially from the breach, the amount of the administrative fine shall be at least equal to that benefit. Member States can set maximum thresholds at or above these minimum levels in their national law, and NRAs can impose fines up to the maximum amount provided under their national threshold, provided it does not exceed the 20% yearly income cap.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Natural Persons Penalty Example
ID: 379
CONTENT:
Example: Market Participant A (MP A), a natural person, breached Articles 3, 4 and 15 of REMIT and directly benefitted financially by EUR 10,000. The NRA could impose separate administrative fines for each infringement: For Article 3 breach, the maximum fine should be at least EUR 5,000,000 (Member State can set higher, e.g., EUR 8,000,000), not exceeding 20% of MP A's yearly income. For Article 4 breach, the maximum fine should be at least EUR 1,000,000 (Member State can set higher, e.g., EUR 2,000,000), not exceeding 20% of yearly income. For Article 15 breach, the maximum fine should be at least EUR 1,000,000 (Member State can set higher, e.g., EUR 2,000,000), not exceeding 20% of yearly income. Additionally, the NRA could order disgorgement of EUR 10,000 in profits gained. The 20% cap applies to each infringement separately, and each fine must be at least equal to the EUR 10,000 benefit received.

ID: 380
CONTENT:
Article 18(5) of REMIT establishes minimum levels for maximum administrative fines for legal persons: (a) for breaches of Articles 3 and 5, at least 15% of total annual turnover in the preceding business year; (b) for breaches of Articles 4 and 15, at least 2% of total annual turnover in the preceding business year; (c) for breaches of Articles 8 and 9, at least 1% of total annual turnover in the preceding business year. The amount of administrative fine shall not exceed 20% of total annual turnover in the preceding business year of the legal person concerned. Where the legal person has directly or indirectly benefited financially from the breach, the amount of the administrative fine shall be at least equal to that benefit.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Legal Persons Penalty Example
ID: 381
CONTENT:
Example: Market Participant B (MP B), a legal person, breached Article 8 of REMIT, and it was not possible to determine whether MP B directly or indirectly financially benefitted from the breach. For the Article 8 breach, Article 18(5)(c) provides that the maximum administrative fine should be at least 1% of total annual turnover in the preceding business year. The Member State can set a maximum threshold of minimum 1% or higher (e.g., 7%), provided it does not exceed 20%. The NRA could impose a fine on MP B up to the maximum amount provided under its national threshold (e.g., 7% of total annual turnover in the preceding business year), ensuring the administrative fine does not exceed 20% of MP B's total annual turnover.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT updated.pdf
SECTION: Considerations for Determining Penalties
ID: 382
CONTENT:
Article 18(7) of REMIT provides that when determining the type and level of administrative fines and other administrative measures, national regulatory authorities must take into account all relevant circumstances, including: (a) the gravity and duration of the infringement; (b) the degree of responsibility of the person responsible for the infringement; (c) the financial strength of the person responsible, as indicated by total annual turnover of a legal person or yearly income of a natural person; (d) the importance of profits gained or losses avoided by the person responsible, insofar as they can be determined; (e) the level of cooperation of the person responsible with the competent authority, without prejudice to ensuring disgorgement of profits gained or losses avoided; (f) previous infringements by the person responsible; (g) measures taken by the person responsible to prevent repetition; and (h) the duplication of criminal and administrative proceedings and fines for the same infringement.

SECTION: Disclosure of Penalties and NRA Cooperation
ID: 383
CONTENT:
Article 18(6) of REMIT empowers NRAs with discretion to disclose measures or penalties imposed for infringements. Article 18(8) of REMIT indicates that national regulatory authorities shall cooperate closely to ensure that the exercise of their supervisory and investigative powers, and the administrative fines they impose, and other administrative measures they take, are effective and appropriate under this Regulation. They shall coordinate their actions in accordance with Article 16(2) to avoid duplication and overlaps when exercising supervisory and investigative powers and when imposing administrative fines in respect of cross-border cases.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: ACER's Role and Mandate under REMIT
ID: 1
CONTENT:
The European Union Agency for the Cooperation of Energy Regulators (ACER) is the EU agency created by the Third Energy Package to achieve the Internal Energy Market (IEM). According to REMIT (Regulation (EU) No 1227/2011 on wholesale energy market integrity and transparency), ACER is responsible for monitoring wholesale energy markets to detect market abuse. National Regulatory Authorities (NRAs) are in charge of investigating suspicious cases of market abuse and enforcing REMIT within their national legal framework.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Purpose and Scope of ACER Guidance
ID: 2
CONTENT:
Article 16(1) of REMIT provides that ACER shall publish non-binding guidance on the application of definitions set out in Article 2 of REMIT. ACER aims to ensure that NRAs carry out their tasks under REMIT in a coordinated and consistent way. The non-binding Guidance provided in this document is aimed at helping NRAs ensure required coordination and consistency in their activities under REMIT. It is deliberately drafted in non-legal terms and made public for transparency purposes only. The Guidance is updated as needed to reflect changing market conditions and experience gained by ACER and NRAs in implementing and applying REMIT, including feedback from market participants and stakeholders.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: REMIT Overview and Guidance Evolution
ID: 12
CONTENT:
REMIT (Regulation on wholesale energy market integrity and transparency) plays a major role as the guarantee of well-functioning, transparent and trustworthy EU wholesale electricity and gas markets. The application of REMIT in a consistent and coordinated way across Europe represents a major challenge for the Agency. The issuance of Guidance on the application of REMIT pursuant to Article 16(1) of REMIT to the National Regulatory Authorities (NRAs) constitutes a key instrument used by the Agency to overcome it. Over the last 10 years, five editions of the Guidance have been published (as well as several updates and three Guidance Notes on topical issues).

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: ACER Guidance Editions 1-3: Core Definitions and Market Participant Registration
ID: 13
CONTENT:
The 1st edition of ACER Guidance on the application of REMIT, published on 21 December 2011, focused on the areas which the Agency considered as priorities following the entry into force of REMIT, including the application of the definition of inside information and possible signals of insider trading and market manipulation. The 2nd edition, published on 28 September 2012 and updated for the last time on 22 April 2013, developed the understanding on the application of the definitions of wholesale energy market, wholesale energy products and market participant, the application of the obligation to disclose inside information and of the market abuse prohibitions. The 3rd edition, published on 29 October 2013 and updated for the last time on 3 June 2015, provided guidance to NRAs by elaborating on their role in the registration of market participants. It also provided further clarifications concerning the definitions of wholesale energy products and inside information, and concerning the obligation to publish inside information.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: ACER Guidance Editions 4-5 and 6th Edition Revamp
ID: 14
CONTENT:
In the 4th edition, published on 17 June 2016 and updated for the last time on 15 October 2019, the Agency provided more detailed guidance to NRAs concerning the supervision of the obligations imposed on persons professionally arranging transactions by Article 15 of REMIT. In the 5th edition, published on 8 April 2020 and updated for the last time on 11 May 2021, the Agency provided more detailed guidance on the definitions of information and inside information under REMIT. On the 10th anniversary of the first publication, and taking into account the expected market developments resulting from the implementation of the European Green Deal, as well as the experience gained so far, including the feedback received from NRAs, market participants and other stakeholders, the Agency considers it necessary to structurally revamp its ACER Guidance with the publication of a 6th edition. In this new edition, the Agency has made significant changes to the document: its structure was fully revisited to make it more intuitive, and additional content was provided on the scope of REMIT and on the core prohibitions of insider trading and market manipulation.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: REMIT Scope: Introduction and Products/Markets
ID: 16
CONTENT:
The scope of REMIT encompasses wholesale energy products and wholesale energy markets. Wholesale energy products (WEP) and wholesale energy markets (WEM) are defined within the regulation. The geographical scope of REMIT includes: products delivered in the Union for supply contracts under Article 2(4)(a) of REMIT; derivatives produced, traded or delivered in the EU under Article 2(4)(b) of REMIT; transportation contracts transported in the EU under Article 2(4)(c) and derivative contracts under Article 2(4)(d) of REMIT; and contracts for the supply and distribution to final customers with a consumption greater than 600 GWh/year in the EU.

The regulation also addresses the interaction between REMIT and the financial legislation, establishing how REMIT provisions coordinate with other regulatory frameworks governing financial markets and energy trading activities.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Definition of Inside Information Under REMIT
ID: 18
CONTENT:
Inside information under REMIT is defined as information of a precise nature that has not been made public, relates to wholesale energy product(s), and is likely to have a significant price effect on wholesale energy products. The concept of 'information' under REMIT encompasses various types of data relevant to energy markets. Inside information also includes information on trading plans and strategies that could materially affect market prices. Information must meet all criteria to be classified as inside information under REMIT.

SECTION: Obligation to Disclose Inside Information
ID: 19
CONTENT:
Market participants are obligated to disclose inside information in an effective manner through appropriate disclosure mechanisms that meet minimum quality requirements for effective disclosure. Inside information must be disclosed in a timely manner. Delayed disclosure of inside information is permitted under specific circumstances outlined in the regulation. Article 4(7) of REMIT provides an exemption to the disclosure obligation under certain conditions.

SECTION: Prohibition of Insider Trading: Definition and Scope
ID: 20
CONTENT:
Insider trading is prohibited under REMIT and includes three forms: insider trading by using inside information, insider trading by disclosing inside information, and insider trading by recommending or inducing trading on the basis of inside information. The prohibition applies to persons who possess inside information and engage in trading activities or communications based on that information. Indicators of insider trading include possible signals and various types of practices that suggest market abuse.

CONTENT:

These exemptions apply to specific circumstances where trading or disclosures occur for legitimate purposes and do not constitute market abuse. The scope of the insider trading provision is limited to persons falling within the definition of market participants and those with access to inside information.

SECTION: Market Manipulation and Attempted Market Manipulation Prohibitions
ID: 22
CONTENT:
Market manipulation and attempted market manipulation are prohibited under REMIT. These prohibitions cover four main categories: giving, being likely to give or attempting to give false or misleading signals; securing the price at an artificial level; employing a fictitious device, deception or contrivance; and disseminating false or misleading information. Indicators of market manipulation include possible signals and various types of practices that suggest abusive behavior in wholesale energy markets.

SECTION: Registration of Market Participants
ID: 24
CONTENT:
Market participants are obliged to register with the appropriate National Regulatory Authority (NRA). Market participants are required to provide specific information during registration. National registers are established by each NRA to maintain registration information. Market participants must register with the NRA in their jurisdiction. Registration submissions have specific deadlines that must be met. Upon successful registration, market participants receive an ACER code. Market participants are required to keep their registration information up to date.

CONTENT:

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: REMIT Scope and Objectives
ID: 27
CONTENT:
Regulation (EU) No 1227/2011 on wholesale energy market integrity and transparency (REMIT) establishes a sector-specific framework for the monitoring of wholesale energy markets, with the objective of detecting and deterring insider trading and market manipulation. REMIT was originally seen by legislators as a 'basic tailor-made market abuse framework in the energy sector legislation for all electricity and gas products not covered by the Market Abuse Directive' (the predecessor of MAR and CS MAD). The scope of REMIT was specifically designed to accommodate the operational complexity of physical energy markets and specificities of the energy sector (electricity and natural gas) and to appropriately complement the market abuse legislation covering the financial sector.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Definition of Wholesale Energy Products (WEP)
ID: 29
CONTENT:
Article 2(4) of REMIT defines 'Wholesale energy products' as the following contracts and derivatives, irrespective of where and how they are traded: (a) contracts for the supply of electricity or natural gas where delivery is in the Union; (b) derivatives relating to electricity or natural gas produced, traded or delivered in the Union; (c) contracts relating to the transportation of electricity or natural gas in the Union; (d) derivatives relating to the transportation of electricity or natural gas in the Union. Contracts for the supply and distribution of electricity or natural gas for the use of final customers are not wholesale energy products. However, contracts for the supply and distribution of electricity or natural gas to final customers with a consumption capacity greater than 600 GWh shall be treated as wholesale energy products.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Scope of Wholesale Energy Products - Time Periods and Trading Methods
ID: 30
CONTENT:
The Agency considers contracts for the supply or transportation of electricity and natural gas traded intraday, within-day, day-ahead, two-day-ahead, week-end, week, monthly, quarterly, yearly, long-term or during any other time period generally accepted in the market as contracts for the supply or transportation of electricity or natural gas to be wholesale energy products. Wholesale energy products which are derivatives can be financial instruments as well if they fall under points (5), (6), (7) or (10) of Annex I Section C of MiFID II. As the definition of wholesale energy product applies to contracts and derivatives 'irrespective of how and where they are traded', this definition covers contracts and derivatives that are intermediated by persons personally arranging transactions (PPATs) but also that are traded bilaterally and/or over the counter (OTC). Intra-group transactions, i.e. contracts entered into with another counterparty which is part of the same group, are considered to be wholesale energy products under REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Wholesale Energy Products - Electricity Generation and Natural Gas
ID: 31
CONTENT:
Contracts for the supply of electricity and any derivative related to electricity resulting from generation capacity markets, capacity remuneration mechanisms, and flexibility markets where applicable, shall be considered wholesale energy markets according to REMIT. Concerning contracts for the supply of natural gas, pursuant to Article 2(7) of Directive 2009/73/EC, 'supply' means the sale, including resale, of natural gas, including liquefied natural gas ('LNG'), to customers. Accordingly, contracts for the supply of LNG with delivery in the European Union ('EU') are wholesale energy contracts pursuant to Article 2(4)(a) of REMIT. Pursuant to Article 1(2) of Directive 2009/73/EC, the rules established for natural gas, including LNG, shall also apply in a non-discriminatory way to biogas and gas from biomass or other types of gas, in so far as such gases can technically and safely be injected into, and transported through, the natural gas system.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Biogas, Renewable Gas, and Excluded Products
ID: 32
CONTENT:
If biogas can technically and safely be injected into, and transported through, the natural gas system, (i) it will meet all criteria to be treated as natural gas and (ii) REMIT will apply for the biogas and the renewable gas supply/transportation contracts. Regarding contracts for green certificates and emission allowances, it is the Agency's understanding that they are not wholesale energy products, as they do not fulfil the requirements set out in Article 2(4) of REMIT. Contracts for the supply and distribution of electricity or natural gas for the use of final customers are not wholesale energy products either. However, if these contracts involve final customers with a consumption capacity greater than 600 GWh, these contracts will fall within the scope of REMIT wholesale energy products.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Definition of Final Customer and Consumption Capacity
ID: 35
CONTENT:
Internal market in natural gas is defined by Directives that define a final customer as 'a customer purchasing electricity or natural gas for his own use'. Article 2(5) of REMIT clarifies 'consumption capacity' as the consumption of a final customer of either electricity or natural gas at full use of that customer's production capacity. It comprises all consumption by that customer as a single economic entity, in so far as consumption takes place on markets with interrelated wholesale prices. For plants under the control of a single economic entity with consumption capacity less than 600 GWh per year, consumption shall not be taken into account if those plants do not exert a joint influence on wholesale energy market prices due to being located in different relevant geographical markets.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Agency Understanding of Consumption Capacity Assessment
ID: 36
CONTENT:
The Agency understands 'consumption at full use of that customer's production capacity' to mean the maximum amount of energy (electricity or natural gas) that a final customer could consume in a year if running consumption assets fully at all times throughout the year (technical capability to consume). Final consumers should calculate their consumption capacity of electricity and natural gas separately from each other, and not cumulate them, whenever assessing whether the threshold of 600 GWh is exceeded. Within a single economic entity, consumption at individual plants below 600 GWh is not taken into account if those plants do not exert joint influence on wholesale energy market prices due to being located in different relevant geographical markets. However, individual plants each with consumption capacity below 600 GWh but located in the same geographical market shall be taken into account when assessing whether the threshold is exceeded.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Single Economic Entity Definition and Assessment Criteria
ID: 37
CONTENT:
The notion of 'single economic entity' can be understood through international practices of competition law and precedents of the Court of Justice of the European Union. Under competition rules, unified conduct on the market of two or more companies takes precedence over their formal legal structure. The relevant question is not whether two companies are separate legal persons, but whether they behave together as a single unit in the market. Elements to consider when assessing whether two or more companies form a single economic entity include: decision making powers, procedures and sharing of liability between relevant companies; ownership (e.g. majority shareholding); ownership structure of the relevant companies; and participating interests or influence over the relevant companies.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Markets with Interrelated Wholesale Prices
ID: 38
CONTENT:
The Agency considers that wholesale energy markets are increasingly interlinked across the Union. There is already a high degree of interrelation of wholesale electricity and natural gas prices across the Union, and interrelation is expected to increase as development of a single European energy market continues to progress. The Agency considers it prudent for market participants to take into account the consumption capacity of all their plants across the Union when assessing whether the consumption capacity threshold of 600 GWh is exceeded.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Products In Scope of REMIT - Supply and Transportation Contracts
ID: 39
CONTENT:
Contracts for the supply of electricity or natural gas with delivery in the EU are in scope of REMIT, including balancing, intraday, within-day, day-ahead, two-day-ahead, weekend, week, monthly, quarterly, yearly and long-term or any other time period generally accepted in the market. Transportation contracts in the Union of electricity or natural gas traded with these same time periods are also in scope. Gas transport capacity contracts in the Union related to upstream pipeline networks fall within REMIT scope. Contracts relating to transportation of electricity or natural gas including at least one location or bidding zone in the Union concluded as a result of primary explicit capacity allocation by or on behalf of the TSO, specifying physical or financial capacity rights or obligations (PTRs/FTRs) are in scope. Contracts relating to transportation concluded between market participants on secondary markets, specifying physical or financial capacity rights or obligations (PTRs/FTRs), including resale and transfer of such contracts, are also in scope.

metadata.title: Products In Scope of REMIT - Supply and Transportation Contracts
metadata.original_text: Contracts for the supply of electricity or natural gas with delivery in the EU are in scope of REMIT, including balancing, intraday, within-day, day-ahead, two-day-ahead, weekend, week, monthly, quarterly, yearly and long-term or any other time period generally accepted in the market. Transportation contracts in the Union of electricity or natural gas traded with these same time periods are also in scope. Gas transport capacity contracts in the Union related to upstream pipeline networks fall within REMIT scope. Contracts relating to transportation of electricity or natural gas including at least one location or bidding zone in the Union concluded as a result of primary explicit capacity allocation by or on behalf of the TSO, specifying physical or financial capacity rights or obligations (PTRs/FTRs) are in scope. Contracts relating to transportation concluded between market participants on secondary markets, specifying physical or financial capacity rights or obligations (PTRs/FTRs), including resale and transfer of such contracts, are also in scope.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Products In Scope of REMIT - Derivatives, Intra-group Transactions, and Demand Response
ID: 40
CONTENT:
Derivatives relating to electricity or natural gas produced, traded or delivered in the Union are in scope of REMIT. Derivatives of transportation contracts of electricity or natural gas in the Union are in scope. Intra-group transactions of electricity and natural gas for delivery in the Union are in scope. Contracts for the provision of demand response services or flexibility in the Union are in scope. Contracts for the supply of electricity and any derivative related to electricity traded in generation capacity markets and through capacity remuneration mechanisms in the Union are in scope. Contracts for the supply of electricity or natural gas for the use of final customer with a consumption capacity greater than 600 GWh/year in the Union are in scope. Contracts for green certificates and emission allowances are NOT in scope. Production of electricity or gas by a production unit which is consumed within the same production facility is NOT in scope.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Wholesale Energy Markets Definition and Components
ID: 41
CONTENT:
Article 2(6) of REMIT defines 'Wholesale energy market' as any market within the Union on which wholesale energy products are traded. According to Recital 5 of REMIT, wholesale energy markets encompass both commodity markets and derivative markets, which are of vital importance to the energy and financial markets, as price formation in both is interlinked. They include regulated markets, multilateral trading facilities, organised trading facilities, OTC transactions and bilateral contracts, traded directly or through brokers. The Agency's understanding of wholesale energy markets includes: balancing markets for trading of electricity or natural gas with delivery in the EU; redispatching and countertrading mechanisms where wholesale energy products are traded; intraday or within-day markets for trading of electricity or natural gas with delivery in the EU; day-ahead or two-day-ahead markets for trading of electricity or natural gas with delivery in the EU, including week-end products; physical markets for trading of electricity or natural gas with delivery in the EU, including markets for physical forward contracts and non-standardised long-term contracts; markets for transportation capacities of electricity or natural gas in the EU; derivatives markets relating to electricity or natural gas produced, traded or delivered in the Union, including financial OTC markets; derivatives markets relating to transportation of electricity or natural gas in the EU; generation capacity markets and capacity remuneration mechanisms where wholesale energy products are traded; local flexibility markets for electricity where wholesale energy products are traded.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Geographical Scope of REMIT - General Principles
ID: 42
CONTENT:
The geographical scope of REMIT is solely determined by the geographical delimitation of the concept of wholesale energy products defined under Article 2(4) of REMIT and not by the geographical location of the legal or natural person trading these products or by the place of trading. Although the geographical scope of wholesale energy products is anchored in the concepts of delivered, produced, traded, transported and/or facilities located in the EU, non-EU persons are also covered by REMIT provided that they enter into transactions in wholesale energy products. Article 9(1) of REMIT requires persons not established or resident in the EU entering into transactions required to be reported to the Agency in accordance with Article 8(1) of REMIT to register in the EU Member State in which they are active. The obligations to register with the competent NRA pursuant to Article 9(1) and to report data to the Agency according to Article 8(1) and (5) of REMIT also apply to such non-EU persons. The same holds for the prohibitions of market abuse pursuant to Articles 3 and 5 of REMIT, and the prohibitions of insider trading also apply to non-EU persons.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Geographical Scope - Place of Trading and Delimitation Criteria
ID: 43
CONTENT:
REMIT does not define any geographical limitation regarding the place of trading. Provided that the wholesale energy product meets the definition of wholesale energy products under Article 2(4) of REMIT, it is irrelevant where such a product is traded. Even if traded outside the EU, it will still qualify as a wholesale energy product and therefore fall under the scope of REMIT. Pursuant to Article 2(4) of REMIT, depending on the typology of contract, four criteria for geographical delimitation of the scope of REMIT are relevant: 'Delivered in the EU', for wholesale energy products defined under Article 2(4)(a); 'Produced, traded or delivered in the EU', for wholesale energy products defined under Article 2(4)(b); 'Relating to transportation in the EU', for wholesale energy products defined under Articles 2(4)(c) and 2(4)(d); and consumption in the EU, for contracts for the supply and distribution to final customers with consumption greater than 600 GWh/year.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Delivered in the Union - Supply Contracts Geographical Scope
ID: 44
CONTENT:
Concerning contracts for the supply of electricity or natural gas under Article 2(4)(a) of REMIT, the key element of the geographical scope is that a delivery point of such electricity or natural gas must be in the EU. As a consequence, contracts for the supply of electricity or natural gas produced/generated in the EU but delivered outside of its borders will not be within the scope of REMIT, as they do not fulfil the criteria included in the definition of wholesale energy products under Article 2(4)(a) of REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: REMIT Scope: Electricity and Natural Gas Supply Contracts
ID: 45
CONTENT:
Contracts for the supply of electricity or natural gas produced/generated and delivered outside of the EU fall outside REMIT scope. However, contracts for the supply of electricity or natural gas produced/generated outside the EU but delivered within the EU borders are under the scope of REMIT. Supply means the sale, including resale of natural gas, including liquefied natural gas (LNG), to customers. The form of the contract (bilateral, OTC, etc.) is irrelevant for the qualification as a wholesale energy product.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Example: LNG Supply Contract with EU Delivery
ID: 46
CONTENT:
Situation: Bilateral over-the-counter contract for the delivery of LNG at the OLT offshore LNG terminal of Toscana (Italy). Assessment: This contract is a wholesale energy product pursuant to Article 2(4)(a) of REMIT. The LNG is delivered in EU territorial waters (Italian territorial waters - EU member state). It is not relevant whether delivery occurs at an offshore or onshore facility. Any delivery or offloading of LNG in any LNG facility (including flanges connecting the LNG vessel to the LNG terminal) qualifies as 'delivery in the EU' as long as the delivery takes place in the EU. Reload-contracts at a regasification terminal or vessel where LNG delivery is not in the EU will not qualify as 'delivery in the EU' and therefore will not qualify as a wholesale energy product under Article 2(4)(a) of REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Derivative Contracts: Produced, Traded or Delivered in the EU
ID: 47
CONTENT:
For derivative contracts relating to electricity or natural gas under Article 2(4)(b) of REMIT, they must relate to electricity or natural gas produced, traded or delivered in the EU. The geographical scope extends beyond Article 2(4)(a) of REMIT (delivered in the EU) to also include derivative contracts relating to electricity or natural gas produced or traded in the EU. Such contracts are wholesale energy products irrespective of whether the related electricity or natural gas is delivered in the EU. If the underlying electricity or gas is not produced, traded or delivered in the EU, such a derivative contract will not qualify as a wholesale energy product and falls outside REMIT scope.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Example: Derivative Contract Traded in EU with Non-EU Delivery
ID: 48
CONTENT:
Situation: A market participant trades on a platform based in Germany a derivative contract with an underlying electricity spot contract for delivery in the United Kingdom. That spot contract is also traded on that EU platform. Assessment: This contract is a wholesale energy product pursuant to Article 2(4)(b) of REMIT as it fulfils all relevant criteria: It is a 'derivative' - the contract qualifies as a derivative of the electricity spot contract. It is related to 'electricity' 'traded in the Union' - the derivative contract relates to the electricity spot contract traded at an organised marketplace located in the EU (Germany). Note: This contract is not reportable to the Agency under REMIT as per the first sentence of Article 3(1)(a) of Implementing Regulation.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Transportation Contracts: Transported in the EU
ID: 49
CONTENT:
Concerning transportation contracts under Article 2(4)(c) of REMIT, they must relate to the transportation of electricity or natural gas in the EU. The same geographical scope applies for derivative contracts under Article 2(4)(d) of REMIT, as they must relate to the transportation of electricity or natural gas in the EU. The concept of 'transportation of electricity or natural gas' in the EU shall be interpreted by NRAs as including at least one bidding zone/delivery point located inside the EU.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Transportation Scope: Bidding Zones and Delivery Points
ID: 50
CONTENT:
Transportation contracts within REMIT scope include: all transportation of electricity or natural gas (including LNG) between bidding zones or specific delivery points that are (totally or partially) geographically located in the EU territory; all transportation of electricity or natural gas (including LNG) from a bidding zone or point geographically located outside of the EU to a bidding zone or delivery point located (totally or partially) inside the EU; and all transportation of electricity or natural gas (including LNG) from a bidding zone or delivery point geographically located inside of the EU (totally or partially) to a bidding zone or delivery point located outside the EU. Contracts or derivatives related to transportation of electricity or natural gas (including LNG biogas and renewable gases) involving transportation between bidding zones or points totally located outside of the EU are outside REMIT geographical scope.

metadata.title: Transportation Scope: Bidding Zones and Delivery Points

Contracts or derivatives related to transportation of electricity or natural gas (including LNG biogas and renewable gases) involving transportation between bidding zones or points totally located outside of the EU are outside REMIT geographical scope.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Example: Gas Transportation Contract at EU Border
ID: 51
CONTENT:
Situation: A market participant bought yearly firm transportation capacity of natural gas to import natural gas from Russia into the EU. The contract stipulates that the entry point is in a Russian location and the delivery point is at the border between Ukraine and Slovakia. Assessment: This contract is a wholesale energy product pursuant to Article 2(4)(c) of REMIT. It involves the transportation of natural gas from Russia to Slovakia. The delivery point of the natural gas to be transported is the border between Slovakia and Ukraine that is partially located in the EU (as Slovakia is the EU Member State while Ukraine is not).

The delivery point of the natural gas to be transported is the border between Slovakia and Ukraine that is partially located in the EU (as Slovakia is the EU Member State while Ukraine is not).

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Supply and Distribution to Final Customers: Consumption in the EU
ID: 52
CONTENT:
In line with Article 2(5) of REMIT, contracts for the supply and distribution to final customers with a consumption greater than 600 GWh/year shall be treated as wholesale energy products. The geographical scope of contracts for supply under Article 2(4)(a) of REMIT (delivery in the EU) is also applicable for contracts for supply and distribution of electricity or natural gas to final customers with consumption greater than 600 GWh/year. The electricity or natural gas delivered under such contracts must be delivered in the EU, and the final customer's consumption must be located inside the EU. Contracts for supply and distribution to final customers whose consumption is located outside the EU are not within REMIT geographical scope.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Legal and Natural Persons in Scope of REMIT
ID: 53
CONTENT:
Any person (legal or natural) can fall within the overall scope of REMIT, not only market participants. However, not all REMIT prohibitions or obligations apply to the same array of persons. Some provisions have a broader scope while others are more restricted. The personal scope of REMIT provisions varies for: (i) prohibition of insider trading under Article 3(1); (ii) obligation to publish inside information under Article 4(1); (iii) prohibition of market manipulation under Article 5; (iv) obligation to report REMIT data under Article 8; (v) obligation to register under Article 9(1); and (vi) obligations to notify and identify market abuse by persons professionally arranging transactions under Article 15.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Prohibition of Insider Trading: Personal Scope
ID: 54
CONTENT:
The prohibition of insider trading under Article 3(1) of REMIT only applies to limited persons listed in Article 3(2) of REMIT: members of the administrative, management or supervisory bodies of an undertaking; natural or legal persons with holdings in the capital of an undertaking; natural or legal persons with access to information through the exercise of their employment, profession or duties; natural or legal persons who have acquired such information through criminal activity; and natural or legal persons who know, or ought to know, that it is inside information.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Obligation to Publish Inside Information: Personal Scope
ID: 55
CONTENT:
The obligation to publish inside information under Article 4(1) of REMIT applies to market participants who possess inside information in respect of business or facilities which the market participant concerned, or its parent undertaking or related undertaking, owns or controls or for whose operational matters that market participant or undertaking is responsible, either in whole or in part. Market participants who possess inside information in respect of business or facilities of other market participants are not covered by this obligation. However, they still need to comply with the prohibition of insider trading in relation to such inside information.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Market Manipulation: Widest Personal Scope
ID: 56
CONTENT:
The prohibition of market manipulation or attempted market manipulation applies to any person, or persons acting in collaboration. Article 2(8) of REMIT defines person as any natural or legal person. Therefore, the prohibition of market manipulation (and attempted market manipulation) under Article 5 of REMIT applies to any natural or legal person, presenting the widest personal scope of REMIT application.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Data Reporting Obligation and Registration Requirements
ID: 57
CONTENT:
The data reporting obligation laid down in Article 8 of REMIT applies to two groups of entities specified in Article 8(4) and 8(5) of REMIT, respectively, that report either transaction and/or fundamental data. The registration obligation defined in Article 9(1) of REMIT applies to market participants entering into transactions which are required to be reported to the Agency in accordance with Article 8(1). More details on these obligations are provided in the Manual of Procedures on Data Reporting and Transaction Reporting User Manual.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Obligations of Persons Professionally Arranging Transactions
ID: 58
CONTENT:
The obligations to notify and to have arrangements in order to identify market abuse under Article 15 of REMIT apply to persons professionally arranging transactions (PPATs). These obligations require PPATs to establish procedures and arrangements to identify potential market abuse in transactions they professionally arrange.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Personal Scope of REMIT Prohibitions and Obligations
ID: 59
CONTENT:
The prohibition of market manipulation under Article 5 of REMIT has the widest personal scope, applicable to all legal and natural persons. In contrast, the obligation to publish inside information under Article 4(1) of REMIT applies only to a predefined group of market participants. The obligation to notify and have arrangements to identify market abuse under Article 15 is restricted to persons professionally arranging transactions. These varying scopes reflect different regulatory requirements across REMIT's provisions.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Definition and Importance of Market Participant
ID: 60
CONTENT:
Article 2(7) of REMIT defines a market participant as "any person, including transmission system operators, who enters into transactions, including the placing of orders to trade, in one or more wholesale energy markets." Understanding this concept is crucial because: (1) market participants have the obligation to disclose inside information under Article 4(1); (2) they must provide transaction records and fundamental data to the Agency under Article 8(1) and 8(5); and (3) they must register with the competent NRA if entering into reportable transactions under Article 9(1).

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Categories of Market Participants Under REMIT
ID: 61
CONTENT:
ACER considers the following persons to be market participants if entering into transactions in wholesale energy markets: Energy trading companies (electricity and natural gas undertakings); Producers of electricity or natural gas; Shippers of natural gas; Balance responsible entities; Wholesale customers; Final customers with consumption capacity of 600 GWh or more per year; Transmission system operators (TSOs); Distribution system operators (DSOs); Storage system operators (SSOs); LNG system operators (LSOs); and Investment firms under MiFID II. The crucial criterion is whether the entity enters into transactions or places orders to trade in wholesale energy markets.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Storage and LNG System Operators as Market Participants
ID: 62
CONTENT:
SSOs and LSOs are explicitly mentioned as market participants in Article 3(4)(b) of REMIT. SSOs may conclude contracts for gas supply when storage facilities experience operational problems, acquiring volumes over the spot market. LSOs may sell contracts leading to extraction or feeding of gas into/from the gas network. When engaging in such transactions, these operators are market participants required to publish inside information under Article 4(1) and report capacity and facility usage data under Article 8(5). ACER considers it best practice for SSOs and LSOs to facilitate publication of REMIT-related information on behalf of multiple market participants involved, though market participants remain ultimately responsible for publication and should maintain backup arrangements.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Interaction Between REMIT and Financial Legislation
ID: 63
CONTENT:
According to Article 1(2) of REMIT, Articles 3 and 5 (market abuse prohibitions) do not apply to wholesale energy products that are financial instruments subject to Article 9 of Directive 2003/6/EC or Article 2 of MAR. However, this exclusion applies only to Articles 3 and 5. Other REMIT articles remain applicable to all wholesale energy products, including those that are also financial instruments. For example, the obligation to disclose inside information under Article 4(1), the data reporting requirement under Article 8, and the registration requirement under Article 9 continue to apply regardless of whether the product qualifies as a financial instrument. REMIT is without prejudice to MAR, MiFID II, MiFIR, and competition law.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Example: Physically Settled Derivative on OTF (REMIT Applies)
ID: 64
CONTENT:
Situation: Potential market manipulation identified in Market Area A involving 'Market Area A Power Base Q1 OTF Future' traded on an OTF. Product characteristics: Underlying is the day-ahead electricity price of Market Area A. Final settlement price based on mean value of hourly day-ahead auction prices. Physical settlement requires delivery of 1 MW electricity at maximum voltage level during Q1 2022, with no cash settlement option. Counterparty risk managed by the organised marketplace. Assessment: This future is a derivative relating to electricity, making it a wholesale energy product under Article 2(4)(b) of REMIT. Under MiFID II Annex I Section C(6), it is carved out from the financial instrument definition because it must be physically settled and is traded on an OTF. Therefore, it is not a financial instrument, and Articles 3 and 5 of REMIT fully apply to transactions in this product.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Physically Settled Forward Contract - Natural Gas Example
ID: 67
CONTENT:
A physically settled forward contract for natural gas with the following characteristics: The seller is obligated to physically deliver 5 MW of gas into Market Area A on each delivery day of the year 2022, and the buyer must take delivery. There is no cash settlement option. The parties manage counterparty risk themselves, with no margining service in place. This contract is equivalent to a spot product with deferred delivery to a standard delivery period. Its final settlement price is based only on the price decided by market participants, not on an underlying product value. Therefore, this contract is not an electricity or natural gas derivative and is not included in the definitions of financial instruments in Section C of Annex I of Directive 2014/65/EU.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: REMIT Application to Physically Settled Forward Contracts
ID: 68
CONTENT:
According to MAR Article 3(15), a spot commodity contract means a contract for the supply of a commodity traded on a spot market which is promptly delivered when the transaction is settled, and includes physically settled forward contracts. MAR Article 3(16) specifies that spot markets encompass non-financial markets, such as forward markets for commodities. As a contract for the supply of natural gas in the Union, this contract is a wholesale energy product pursuant to Article 2(4)(a) of REMIT. Regardless of the venue where it is traded (broker MTF or OTF), this yearly forward product is not a financial instrument and the prohibitions of insider trading and market manipulation under Articles 3 and 5 of REMIT are fully applicable to transactions in this product.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Cash-Settled Derivative Future - Electricity Example
ID: 69
CONTENT:
A 'Market Area A Power Base Year Future' product with the following characteristics: Underlying is the day-ahead electricity price of Market Area A. Final settlement price is determined based on an index corresponding to the mean value of all auction prices of hourly day-ahead contracts traded for Market Area A for Base load delivery during the delivery period (every delivery day of 2022). The contract involves delivery or acceptance of 1 MW of electricity into the maximum voltage level of Market Area A during Base load hours on every delivery day of 2022. However, no physical delivery occurs; instead, cash settlement is performed. The seller (buyer) must settle in cash on the day of execution the difference between the agreed price and the higher (lower) final settlement price. The organised marketplace manages counterparty risk by ensuring initial and maintenance margins are respected.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Financial Instrument Classification and MAR Application
ID: 70
CONTENT:
The 'Market Area A Power Base Year Future' is a derivative because its final settlement price is based on the value of another product (the underlying day-ahead electricity price). No physical delivery occurs; parties settle in cash the difference between agreed and final settlement prices. As a derivative relating to electricity traded and delivered in the Union, this contract is a wholesale energy product pursuant to Article 2(4)(b) of REMIT. Additionally, as a cash-settled derivative traded on a regulated market, this future is also a financial instrument according to Annex I Section C of MiFID II. As a financial instrument admitted to trading on a regulated market, it falls within the scope of MAR under Article 2. According to Article 1(2) of REMIT, Articles 3 and 5 of REMIT do not apply to suspicious transactions in this product, which instead fall under MAR and must be scrutinised by competent financial authorities.

SECTION: NRA Responsibilities and Referral Procedures
ID: 71
CONTENT:
When an NRA assesses a case involving a financial instrument admitted to trading on a regulated market, it should refer the case to the competent financial authority and notify the Agency under Article 16(3)(a) of REMIT. However, the NRA remains responsible for assessing whether the behaviour constitutes a potential breach of Article 4 of REMIT in cases where potential insider trading is related to non-effective or non-timely disclosure of inside information.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Definition of Inside Information - Two-Step Approach
ID: 72
CONTENT:
Qualifying a specific fact as 'inside information' under REMIT requires a two-step approach. First, determine whether there is an item of information according to at least one of criteria (a) to (d) defined in Article 2(1), second subparagraph, of REMIT. Second, ascertain whether it fulfils four cumulative conditions established in Article 2(1), first subparagraph, of REMIT: it must be precise, not public, related to one or more wholesale energy products, and likely to significantly affect prices. This chapter provides guidance on what constitutes 'information' under REMIT and on the definition of 'inside information', including application of the four cumulative conditions.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Categories of Information Under REMIT Article 2(1)
ID: 73
CONTENT:
Article 2(1), second subparagraph, of REMIT specifies four categories of 'information': (a) information required to be made public in accordance with Regulations (EC) No 714/2009 and (EC) No 715/2009, including guidelines and network codes adopted pursuant to those Regulations; (b) information relating to capacity and use of facilities for production, storage, consumption or transmission of electricity or natural gas or related to LNG facilities, including planned or unplanned unavailability; (c) information required to be disclosed in accordance with legal or regulatory provisions at Union or national level, market rules, contracts or customs on the relevant wholesale energy market, insofar as likely to have significant effect on prices; and (d) other information that a reasonable market participant would likely use as part of the basis for entering into a transaction or issuing an order to trade in a wholesale energy product.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Information Related to Facility Capacity and Unavailability
ID: 74
CONTENT:
The concept of 'information' under REMIT encompasses information related to all planned or unplanned changes in capacity or output of any size at facilities for production, storage, consumption or transmission of natural gas or electricity (Article 2(1)(b) of REMIT). This specifically includes: capacity and use of production facilities including planned and unplanned unavailability; capacity and use of storage facilities including planned and unplanned availability; capacity and use of consumption facilities including planned and unplanned unavailability; capacity and use of transmission facilities including planned or unplanned unavailability; and capacity and use of LNG facilities including planned and unplanned unavailability.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Information Required to be Disclosed Under Legal and Regulatory Provisions
ID: 75
CONTENT:
Article 2(1)(c) of REMIT covers facts required to be disclosed in accordance with legal or regulatory provisions at national level, legal or regulatory provisions at the European Union level, market rules, contracts, and customs on the market. Importantly, this includes regulatory provisions at the European Union level in Regulation (EC) 543/2013 on submission and publication of data in electricity markets (referred to as 'transparency information'). This regulation establishes multiple obligations to publish facts that would constitute 'information' according to Article 2(1)(c) of REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: The Reasonable Market Participant Test
ID: 76
CONTENT:
Article 2(1)(d) of REMIT establishes that any other information a reasonable market participant would likely use as part of the basis for entering into a transaction relating to a wholesale energy product, or for issuing an order to trade in such a product, should be considered 'information' under REMIT. The Agency recommends that NRAs use the 'reasonable market participant test' to determine whether a given fact qualifies as 'information' under REMIT, but only when such facts are not already covered by Articles 2(1)(a), (b) and (c). The concept of 'reasonable market participant' may encompass different profiles (beginner, average, informed, professional) with different trading strategies (portfolio optimisation, arbitrage, speculative) covering short-term and/or long-term products.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Cognitive Elements and the Reasonable Market Participant
ID: 77
CONTENT:
The concept of 'reasonability' in the reasonable market participant test is related to the use of cognitive elements by the market participant in its trading decisions (at least partially). By contrast, a market participant that makes trading decisions based on non-cognitive elements, such as instinct or mood, should not be considered reasonable. To qualify a fact as information under REMIT, it is enough that at least one profile of reasonable market participant is likely to use the fact as part of the basis of their decision to enter into a transaction relating to a wholesale energy product, or their decision to issue an order to trade in such a product.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Indicators for the Reasonable Market Participant Test
ID: 78
CONTENT:
When using the 'reasonable market participant test', NRAs may take into consideration indicators such as: the concept of 'would be likely to use' should be distinguished from the concept of 'would like to use' – the test is not about whether there is a wish on the part of the reasonable market participant to use some type of information. Rather, the test is used to determine whether a reasonable market participant would likely consider the information relevant to their trading decisions in wholesale energy products.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: REMIT Information Criteria and Reasonable Market Participant Expectations
ID: 79
CONTENT:
The concept of 'would be likely to use' should be interpreted based on what can be reasonably expected to be published. For example, the fact that a market participant would like to use its competitors' trading plans for its own trading strategy does not mean that these plans are 'information' under REMIT, as they are not information that 'can reasonably be expected to be published' and that would likely be used by a reasonable market participant. The fact that a market participant used comparable facts (for example, at a different moment in time) as the basis for its trading decisions could be considered a proxy to further assess with an ad hoc analysis if the fact is information that would be likely to be used by a 'reasonable market participant'.

ID: 80
CONTENT:
The estimates of TSOs A and B of the available transfer capacity for each day and the available transfer capacity already reserved in the electricity interconnector between bidding zones C and D constitute information under REMIT because they relate to information required to be disclosed in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 2019/943. According to Article 50(3) thereof, TSOs shall publish estimates of available transfer capacity for each day, indicating any available transfer capacity already reserved.

SECTION: ACER Guidance: Information on Annual Maintenance of Generation Units
ID: 81
CONTENT:
Market participant A plans to perform annual maintenance on its electricity generation unit XPTO, with a total capacity of 50 MW from 01/02/2025 to 01/04/2025. This fact is information under REMIT as it constitutes information relating to the capacity and use of facilities for the production of electricity as specified in Article 2(1)(b) of REMIT. The fact that the unavailable capacity is below the 100 MW threshold included in Regulation (EC) No 543/2013 is relevant for the assessment of whether it constitutes information under Article 2(1)(c) of REMIT but not under Articles 2(1)(a), (b) and (d) of REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Definition of Inside Information Under REMIT
ID: 82
CONTENT:
Pursuant to Article 2(1), second subparagraph, of REMIT, information qualifies as 'inside information' if it fulfils four cumulative conditions: information of a precise nature, which has not been made public, which relates, directly or indirectly, to one or more wholesale energy products, and which, if it were made public, would be likely to significantly affect the prices of those wholesale energy products. It is the responsibility of market participants to ascertain whether the information they hold potentially constitutes 'inside information' according to these four cumulative conditions, and therefore needs to be made public according to Article 4(1) of REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Internal Compliance Rules for Market Participants
ID: 83
CONTENT:
In order to have an appropriate framework for the assessment of information, it is recommended that market participants have clear internal compliance rules that are adapted to their activities and to the specificities of the information they use and have access to. The best practices for internal compliance rules may include: a framework for the assessment of whether the facts at hand can be qualified as inside information, including measures on how to identify inside information and appropriately tested thresholds; an adequate workflow of information compliant with the presence of inside information, including a mapping of the flow of information and measures on how to handle inside information; and lists of insiders and/or mechanisms in place to identify insiders. The internal compliance rules should be consistent with a market participant's organisational structure and trading strategy.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Information of a Precise Nature - Definition and Assessment
ID: 84
CONTENT:
Information shall be deemed to be of a precise nature if it indicates a set of circumstances which exists or may reasonably be expected to come into existence, or an event which has occurred or may reasonably be expected to do so, and if it is specific enough to enable a conclusion to be drawn as to the possible effect of that set of circumstances or event on the prices of wholesale energy products. The precise nature of the information is to be assessed by the information holder on a case-by-case basis and depends on what the information is, as well as on the surrounding context. In that assessment, the holder of the information may take into consideration: that there is a realistic prospect that a fact will occur; that the estimation of the potential price effect of information disclosure is irrelevant for the assessment of the precise nature; and that intermediate steps in a lengthy process may be precise information.

metadata.title: Information of a Precise Nature - Definition and Assessment
metadata.original_text: Information shall be deemed to be of a precise nature if it indicates a set of circumstances which exists or may reasonably be expected to come into existence, or an event which has occurred or may reasonably be expected to do so, and if it is specific enough to enable a conclusion to be drawn as to the possible effect of that set of circumstances or event on the prices of wholesale energy products. The precise nature of the information is to be assessed by the information holder on a case-by-case basis and depends on what the information is, as well as on the surrounding context. In that assessment, the holder of the information may take into consideration: that there is a realistic prospect that a fact will occur; that the estimation of the potential price effect of information disclosure is irrelevant for the assessment of the precise nature; and that intermediate steps in a lengthy process may be precise information.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Realistic Prospect Standard for Precise Information
ID: 85
CONTENT:
Information is precise as long as there is a realistic prospect that the circumstances or events it refers to will come into existence or occur, considering all the factors existing at the time of the assessment. It is enough that there is a realistic prospect that the fact will occur to make the information related to that event precise. The calculation of the potential effect of the information on the prices of wholesale energy products is not an element to be taken into consideration in the assessment of the precise nature of the information. However, the likelihood of a significant price effect should be assessed to determine if the information is inside information under REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Example: Information on Strikes Impacting Generation Units
ID: 86
CONTENT:
Information on strikes provided to the market participant impacting workers relevant for the normal operation of a generation unit can be seen as having a realistic prospect of happening due to, for example, the existence of historical records of this information resulting in effective strikes impacting the production of this unit. Therefore, it can be considered that there is a realistic prospect of a strike happening, considering all the factors existing at the time of the assessment. This information on strikes would then qualify as precise information, despite the fact that the strike can still be cancelled and/or that there may be some uncertainty about the overall duration of the strike or other elements. Any further developments of the situation may make the prospect of the strike less realistic, but as long as they occur after the market participant assessed whether the information was precise, they should not be taken into consideration by the NRA when assessing whether the information was precise at the time the market participant received the information.

SECTION: Example: Nuclear Safety Authority Security Tests Request
ID: 87
CONTENT:
Information or request by the nuclear safety authority to the market participant of possible security tests to be run at an electricity generation unit during the first half of the year can be seen as having a realistic prospect of happening due to, for example, the existence of previous information of the same type that resulted in effective security tests impacting the production and/or availability of the unit, episodes reflecting the planning of the nuclear safety authority, or previous expressions of concerns with the operation of the unit. Therefore, it can be considered that there is a realistic prospect of the security tests impacting the production and/or availability to happen considering all factors existing at the time of the assessment. In some Member States there is an obligation deriving from the national legislation for the nuclear safety authority to publish this information on possible security tests.

SECTION: Intermediate Steps in Lengthy Processes as Precise Information
ID: 88
CONTENT:
Intermediate steps in a lengthy process that are connected to bringing about future circumstances or events may be regarded as precise information. The knowledge of such steps could constitute an advantage that could undermine the spirit and objective protected by REMIT, which is to place market participants on an equal footing and enhance market integrity in terms of information symmetry. Intermediate steps connected to bringing about future circumstances or events shall be specific enough to enable conclusions to be drawn as to the likely effect of that set of circumstances or events on the prices of wholesale energy products.

SECTION: Information That Has Not Been Made Public
ID: 89
CONTENT:
Inside information is information that has not been shared with the public and, as a consequence, creates information asymmetries between market participants. Effective disclosure to the public of market participants is the criterion that transforms non-public information into public information. Once the information becomes public, it enhances the integrity and transparency of the market, as envisaged by Recital 2 of REMIT.
