text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: ACER Guidance on Market Manipulation Prohibitions - Introduction
ID: 192
CONTENT:
Article 5 of REMIT prohibits any engagement in or attempt to engage in market manipulation on wholesale energy markets. The guidance provides direction to NRAs on applying this prohibition based on definitions in Articles 2(2) and 2(3) of REMIT. The guidance explains concepts of market manipulation and attempted market manipulation, describing their different forms and exploring elements of their definitions. It provides a list of indicators facilitating identification of potential market manipulation organized into simple signals and more complex practices combining several signals. Additional details are available in Agency Guidance Notes. The guidance identifies types of legal or natural persons falling within Article 5 scope and explains exemptions related to accepted market practices. NRAs should consider specific facts and circumstances of each case when applying these principles.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Definitions of Market Manipulation Under REMIT
ID: 193
CONTENT:
Article 5 of REMIT prohibits market manipulation on wholesale energy markets. Articles 2(2) and 2(3) define two forms: 'market manipulation' and 'attempted market manipulation'. Article 2(2) defines market manipulation as: (a) entering into transactions or issuing orders to trade that give or are likely to give false or misleading signals regarding supply, demand, or price of wholesale energy products; (b) securing or attempting to secure the price at an artificial level by a person or persons acting in collaboration, unless the person establishes legitimate reasons and conformity with accepted market practices; or (c) employing fictitious devices or deception giving or likely to give false or misleading signals. Additionally, disseminating information through media or other means giving false or misleading signals regarding supply, demand, or price constitutes manipulation when the disseminating person knew or ought to have known the information was false or misleading.

SECTION: Journalism and Artistic Expression Exceptions
ID: 194
CONTENT:
When information is disseminated for purposes of journalism or artistic expression, such dissemination shall be assessed considering rules governing freedom of press and freedom of expression in other media. However, exceptions do not apply when: (i) those persons derive, directly or indirectly, an advantage or profits from the dissemination of the information in question; or (ii) the disclosure or dissemination is made with the intention of misleading the market as to the supply of, demand for, or price of wholesale energy products.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Definition of Attempted Market Manipulation
ID: 195
CONTENT:
Article 2(3) of REMIT defines attempted market manipulation as: (a) entering into any transaction, issuing any order to trade or taking any other action relating to a wholesale energy product with the intention of: (i) giving false or misleading signals as to supply, demand, or price of wholesale energy products; (ii) securing the price at an artificial level, unless the person establishes legitimate reasons and conformity with accepted market practices; or (iii) employing fictitious devices or deception giving false or misleading signals; or (b) disseminating information through media or other means with the intention of giving false or misleading signals as to supply, demand, or price of wholesale energy products.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Core Elements: Market Manipulation vs Attempted Market Manipulation
ID: 196
CONTENT:
The core element in market manipulation (Article 2(2)) is the effect or likely effect that certain behavior has on demand, supply or prices of wholesale energy products. The core element in attempted market manipulation (Article 2(3)) is the intention behind the behavior, even if unsuccessful. For market manipulation, what matters is whether behavior gave or was likely to give false or misleading signals regarding supply, demand, or price (Articles 2(2)(a)(i), 2(2)(a)(iii), 2(2)(b)) and/or secured price at artificial level (Article 2(2)(a)(ii)). This definition includes no element of intent—whether behavior is intentional or not is irrelevant to qualify it as breach of Article 5. A mere erroneous trading activity can end up being manipulative.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Likelihood Standard and Artificial Price Levels
ID: 197
CONTENT:
According to Articles 2(2)(a)(i), 2(2)(a)(iii) and 2(2)(b) of REMIT, it is enough that behavior is likely to give false or misleading signals regarding demand, supply or price to qualify as breach of Article 5. NRAs need not demonstrate that false or misleading signals were actually sent—only that behavior was likely to give these signals. According to Article 2(2)(a)(ii), market manipulation is established when artificial price level is secured by person or persons acting in collaboration through suspicious orders or transactions. Artificial price means the price level does not correspond to what would emerge from fair and competitive interplay between supply and demand, reflecting market fundamentals. Article 2(2) does not require examination of suspected person's state of mind.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Intent Requirement and Successful Attempts
ID: 198
CONTENT:
The definition of attempted market manipulation (Article 2(3)) focuses on intent concept. Situations with evidence of intention to manipulate market but no market effects qualify as breach of Article 5 in attempted market manipulation form. NRAs need not demonstrate the attempt was successful to conclude breach of Article 5. Such situations occur when, despite manipulative intent, an order or transaction does not achieve intended results. Whether legal or natural person derives benefits from behavior is irrelevant to qualify behavior as market manipulation or attempted market manipulation. This aspect can be considered by NRAs at enforcement stage when calculating sanction amounts but should not influence qualification of behavior as breach of Article 5.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Four Main Categories of Manipulative Behavior
ID: 199
CONTENT:
Articles 2(2) and 2(3) of REMIT distinguish four main categories of behavior as manipulative: (1) giving false or misleading signals; (2) securing price at artificial level; (3) using fictitious devices, deception or contrivance; and (4) disseminating false or misleading information. For both manipulation and attempted market manipulation, the first three categories (giving false/misleading signals, securing price at artificial level, using fictitious devices/deception/contrivance) involve issuance of order or entering into transaction, representing 'on-market' behaviors. The concepts of entering into any transaction or issuing any order to trade encompass all types of actions related to orders and transactions or that are part of the processes.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Market Manipulation: Forms and Categories Overview
ID: 200
CONTENT:
Market manipulation can occur through 'on-market' or 'off-market' behaviours. On-market behaviours include issuing orders, amending/modifying existing orders, cancelling orders, and entering into transactions on wholesale energy markets. Off-market behaviour consists of disseminating false or misleading information using any communication channel to spread rumours or false news, requiring no trading activity on the market. Market manipulation can occur on any type of wholesale energy market (continuous, auction, other), involve different products, markets and trading venues, and may occur across borders, between electricity and gas markets, and across financial and commodity markets.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Market Manipulation Categories: On-Market vs Off-Market
ID: 201
CONTENT:
Market manipulation is categorized by effect type and behaviour location. On-market behaviours giving false/misleading signals constitute attempted market manipulation if likely effect, or market manipulation if real effect. On-market behaviours securing artificial price or using fictitious devices/deception/contrivance follow the same effect-based distinction. Off-market dissemination of false or misleading information requires case-by-case assessment. In certain circumstances, non-issuance of orders when a market participant is expected to issue orders can also constitute market manipulation under REMIT Article 5.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: False or Misleading Signals Under REMIT Article 2(2)(a)(i)
ID: 202
CONTENT:
Entering into any transaction or issuing any order to trade in wholesale energy products is a breach of market manipulation prohibition when these orders/transactions give, or are likely to give, false or misleading signals as to supply, demand or price of wholesale energy products. Similarly, orders placed and transactions entered into with the intention of giving false or misleading signals are prohibited as attempted market manipulation under Article 2(3)(a)(i). False or misleading signals lead other market participants to make trading decisions based on false information and may create mistrust in market integrity, negatively impacting liquidity. They can also give false price signals to energy consumers/retailers when retail contracts are indexed to wholesale energy prices.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Identifying Non-Genuine Orders and Transactions
ID: 203
CONTENT:
When assessing market manipulation, NRAs may identify suspicious orders/transactions and determine whether they send false or misleading signals by identifying non-genuine orders/transactions. Non-genuine orders/transactions might not result from genuine interest in procuring/selling a wholesale energy product at the offered price, but may be used instrumentally to achieve another purpose or result from trading mistakes. Examples include: orders placed at uneconomical price levels; erroneous orders not reflecting real buying/selling interest; orders not placed with real interest in buying/selling but with other interests (influencing behaviour, price settlements, other products, circumventing rules, benefiting other contracts, tax evasion, profit/loss sharing, circumventing accounting rules, transferring money); orders placed with no intention to execute; and buy/sell orders with volumes exceeding or falling short of buying/selling needs/interest in context of asset-backed trading portfolio.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Assessment of False or Misleading Signals: Real Effects
ID: 204
CONTENT:
To establish that suspicious orders/transactions sent false or misleading signals, NRAs should consider the state of the market before and after suspected orders/transactions, whether market developments can be imputed to them or other events, and assess measurable effects on the market. Price level, transaction volume, and order book developments must be considered. Assessment of other market participants' trading behaviour regarding issuing/changing orders after suspicious activity (adapting size/price) provides evidence of effect. False or misleading signals can affect other participants' behaviours not only in the market where signals are sent, but also in related wholesale energy markets. Where such effects are demonstrated, it is not necessary to also demonstrate that suspicious orders/transactions were likely to send false or misleading signals. Market manipulation can be established whether suspicious orders/transactions were likely to give false or misleading signals and did so, or might not have been likely but nonetheless achieved this result.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Attempted Market Manipulation: Intent Assessment
ID: 205
CONTENT:
When assessing attempted market manipulation under Article 2(3)(a)(i) of REMIT, NRAs should focus on whether orders/transactions were intended to give false or misleading signals, regardless of whether they actually gave these signals. Proof of intent is the key element for this type of breach. Articles 2(2)(a)(i) and 2(3)(a)(i) of REMIT cover different situations: the former addresses actual false or misleading signals (or likely signals), while the latter addresses intended false or misleading signals.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Example: Momentum Ignition Market Manipulation
ID: 206
CONTENT:
Market participant A on intraday electricity market with limited trading activity and low liquidity initially has only sell orders at 32 euro/MWh. A then cancels remaining sell orders and places 60 bid orders at increasing price levels (32.1-32.7 euro/MWh), knowing execution would create imbalance requiring position reversal or imbalance charge payment. Other market participants subsequently introduce new bids at higher price levels. A then cancels its 60 bid orders and introduces multiple ask orders above previously prevailing price level. After low liquidity period, increased trading activity following A's behaviour allows execution of A's ask orders. This constitutes market manipulation through false or misleading signals (momentum ignition) because: (i) the 60 bid orders are non-genuine, not resulting from genuine interest in procuring electricity but instrumental to create buy-side momentum; A's economic interest is on sell side, bids were cancelled shortly after introduction showing lack of execution interest, and execution would be uneconomical; (ii) behaviour effects other market participants—observed price increase is linked to A's behaviour with no other fundamental explanation, A's activity created market depth and liquidity generated by other participants, resulting in trading activity that would not have occurred without A's behaviour.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: High-Frequency Trading and Algorithmic Market Manipulation
ID: 207
CONTENT:
Momentum ignition behaviour is often linked to high-frequency trading, though not necessarily. Algorithms introducing and cancelling large numbers of orders on one side of the order book may be designed to mislead other trading programs. Other market participants' systems may automatically react to increased activity, interpreting it as growing demand or supply, and when reacting, they can bid up the price.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Algorithmic Market Manipulation and Intent
ID: 208
CONTENT:
When it can be concluded from the analysis of the code/design of the algorithm that the intention of the market participant was to manipulate the market, the mere fact that the algorithm is put to use on the market under such circumstances can constitute an attempted market manipulation. Trading behaviour where a market participant has an interest to sell but introduces buy orders to influence the materialisation of that selling interest could occur in speculative trading as well as asset-based trading settings.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: REMIT: Assessing Orders/Transactions Likely to Give False or Misleading Signals
ID: 209
CONTENT:
Suspicious orders/transactions that do not have any effect on market development can still be considered manipulative if the NRA establishes they were likely to do so. Article 2(2)(a)(i) of REMIT prohibits trading activity which actually gives false or misleading signals, and also any trading activity which is likely to give false or misleading signals. The likelihood should be evaluated by considering: the circumstances existing at the time of suspicious trading activity; and the characteristics of the suspicious orders/transactions.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Circumstances and Characteristics for Assessing Likelihood of False Signals
ID: 210
CONTENT:
Regarding circumstances at the time of suspicious trading activity, NRAs consider information available to market participants on demand and supply (outages, weather conditions, congestion issues, grid use and availabilities), market liquidity, price levels of relevant products, and order book composition. Regarding characteristics of suspicious orders/transactions, NRAs consider: size (percentage of average daily/hourly volumes, volume comparisons with previous periods, average transaction size); price (divergence from prevailing market prices); and timing/recurrence. Suspicious orders that are large, at diverging price levels, placed close to marking reference periods, or recurrent are more likely to give false or misleading signals. Views of other market participants and PPATs present in the market may constitute relevant evidence.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Example: Market Manipulation by False or Misleading Signals - Industrial Consumer Scenario
ID: 211
CONTENT:
Market Participant A is an industrial electricity consumer that accepted an urgent order and participates in the intraday market to cover its short position. The market trades between 41-43 euro/MWh with a deep order book. Based on previous intraday sessions, MP A expects that hitting best bids at multiple decreasing price levels until below 40 euro/MWh will trigger stop loss orders from other participants, creating downward price pressure. In the past, this strategy led to prices between 36-38 euro/MWh, allowing MP A to buy needed volumes at lower prices. MP A executes this strategy by hitting best bids at multiple decreasing price levels.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Interpretation: Industrial Consumer Market Manipulation Case
ID: 212
CONTENT:
This behaviour represents market manipulation as likely to give false or misleading signals because: (i) MP A's sell orders are non-genuine, not reflecting genuine selling interest but used instrumentally. These orders are uneconomic and inconsistent with the participant's balancing responsibility - MP A's economic interest is on the buy side, not sell side. MP A expects to lose money on these orders, betting on offsetting gains from large buy orders. By executing these orders, MP A likely increases its temporary imbalance. The orders are placed to improperly move the price. (ii) There is likelihood of false/misleading signals due to circumstances: evidence from previous sessions shows that when the market trades in narrow range 41-43 euro/MWh with deep order book filled with small volume orders, hitting best bids at multiple decreasing price levels until below 40 euro/MWh will trigger additional sell orders and downward price pressure. Characteristics: MP A placed subsequent small ask orders creating directional price movement. Trading in quick succession at decreasing price levels breaking below 40 euro/MWh was likely to induce short-term but large price movement compared to regular intraday volatility. Transactions breaking through perceived price floors or ceilings are likely to influence behaviour of other market participants.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Attempted Market Manipulation: Intention to Give False Signals
ID: 213
CONTENT:
Orders/transactions placed with the intention of giving false or misleading signals are considered manipulative under Article 2(3)(a)(i) of REMIT, regardless of whether they were likely to give these signals or actually did give them. An intended market manipulation which is unsuccessful can be characterised as attempted market manipulation prohibited under REMIT. To prove manipulative intent, NRAs may use evidence from communications (any channel), documents including trading plans and strategies, instructions on algorithm design or code, and other possible pieces of evidence.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Example: Attempted Market Manipulation Without Effects - Layering Strategy
ID: 214
CONTENT:
Market Participant A is a trading firm active on the within-day gas market using a redesigned algorithm that introduces ask orders in layers on one side of the order book and then one single large order on the bid side. The layered orders are immediately cancelled, then the loop repeats on the other side. The algorithm was designed based on conviction that layered orders will attract other market participants to adjust their order prices on the same side, narrowing the bid-ask spread and allowing more profitable transactions. On a specific day, MP A inserts 10 sell orders at different descending price levels, followed by one buy order within the bid-ask spread. A few minutes later, all orders are cancelled. Next, it inserts 10 buy orders and one sell order at different ascending price levels and cancels them again within minutes. The complete cycle is repeated several times. Liquidity is very low and no orders are executed. Other market participants do not change behaviour, no transactions occur, and price levels do not change following MP A's activity.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Interpretation: Layering Attempted Market Manipulation Case
ID: 215
CONTENT:
MP A is in breach of Article 5 of REMIT as it attempted to manipulate the market using a practice known as 'layering'. It tried to give false or misleading signals as to supply, demand, and price of the within-day product and/or to secure the price at an artificial level. The strategy failed. Nevertheless, the algorithm was designed with intention to influence demand, supply, and price of the wholesale energy product, constituting attempted market manipulation.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Securing Price at Artificial Level: Definition and Prohibition
ID: 216
CONTENT:
Entering into any transaction or issuing any order to trade in wholesale energy products is a breach of market manipulation prohibition under Article 5 of REMIT when this order/transaction secures, or attempts to secure, the price of one or several wholesale energy products at an artificial level (market manipulation under Article 2(2)(a)(ii) of REMIT). Orders and transactions are also prohibited if entered with intention of securing price at artificial level (attempted market manipulation under Article 2(3)(a)(ii) of REMIT). Market manipulation is established when an artificial price level is secured by suspicious orders or transactions. Attempted market manipulation is established when there is intention to secure price at artificial level, regardless of whether orders/transactions actually secured it. The term 'secure' refers to successfully setting/positioning the price of a wholesale energy product at a certain level, implying that a price results at least partially from actions of a market participant. For price-securing behaviour to be manipulative, the resulting price should be at an artificial level. Such behaviour may be conducted by a person or persons acting in collaboration, and may concern one or several wholesale energy products.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Artificiality of Price: Definition and Counterfactual Analysis
ID: 217
CONTENT:
The notion of 'artificiality' entails that the level of price of a wholesale energy product does not correspond to the one that would have emerged from fair and competitive interplay between supply and demand in that particular market, reflecting market fundamentals. A price resulting from particular orders/transactions is considered artificial if it deviates from the price level without any manipulation (the counterfactual price). If it were not for manipulative orders and/or transactions, other market participants would have been exposed to other price levels. An artificial price can induce other market participants to place orders or enter transactions at prices differing from those that would prevail absent manipulative behaviour, potentially leading to new price trends. Whether price is secured at higher or lower level compared to counterfactual price is irrelevant in artificiality assessment. Also irrelevant is the size of deviation from counterfactual price. An artificial price is not confused with abnormal price. A market price could evolve to extreme highs or lows (abnormal compared to usual on certain market) and still be totally justified by market fundamentals (e.g. electricity generation shortage). An abnormally high or low price justified by market fundamentals is not artificial.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Artificial Price Levels and Market Manipulation Under REMIT Article 5
ID: 218
CONTENT:
A price can be secured at an artificial level whilst still being within the bid/ask spread of previous transactions. A price can be established as secured at an artificial level irrespective of the duration of the deviation from the counterfactual price. For a wholesale energy product price to be considered fixed at an artificial level, it is not necessary that the price maintains an artificial level for more than a certain duration. Even a very short-term artificial movement of the price is sufficient to qualify as a breach of Article 5 of REMIT. Securing the price at an artificial level always qualifies as market manipulation unless the person who entered into the transaction or issued the order to trade establishes that their reasons are legitimate and that the transaction or order conforms to accepted market practices on the wholesale energy market concerned, as specified in Articles 2(2)(a)(ii) and 2(3)(a)(ii) of REMIT. The burden of proof lies on the suspected market participant to establish the legitimacy and conformity to accepted market practices of the suspected behaviour.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Example: Market Manipulation by Securing Price at Artificial Level - Natural Gas Case
ID: 219
CONTENT:
Situation: MP A is a natural gas supply company that indexed sales prices to the reference price of the day-ahead product of the last trading day of the quarter preceding delivery. On the last working day of a specific quarter, the day-ahead product was trading between 8 and 13 euro/MWh with low liquidity. MP A inserted a sell order at 32 euro/MWh three minutes before the trading session ended. In agreement with MP A, MP B inserted a matching buy order for the same price and quantity. This was the last transaction of the day. The market operator calculated the day-ahead reference price using the weighted average price of trades in the reference window, resulting in 18 euro/MWh. Without MP A's trade, the reference price would have been 11 euro/MWh. Interpretation: This behaviour, known as 'marking the reference period', represents market manipulation by securing the price at an artificial level because: (i) MPs A and B secured the price by marking the last trade and daily reference price significantly higher than observed in the reference time window, only possible due to their previous agreement. In absence of this transaction, the reference price would have been 7 euro/MWh lower, exposing other MPs to a different reference price. (ii) The price was set artificially because MPs A and B agreed via phone about timing, volume and price, executing a pre-arranged trade in collusion that allowed MP A to profit indirectly via its bilateral contracts. The reference price does not correspond to what would have emerged from fair and competitive interplay between supply and demand. The pre-arranged trade price of 32 euro/MWh was outside the observed price range (8-13 euro/MWh) despite not reflecting any change in market fundamentals.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Considerations on Reference Price Manipulation and False Signals
ID: 220
CONTENT:
The reference price may be used by price reporting agencies in their price assessments and may indirectly affect a multitude of contracts indexed to it. Other market participants may have entered into transactions at prices differing from those that would prevail in the absence of manipulative behaviour. Therefore, this behaviour not only positioned the price at an artificial level but also gave false or misleading signals on the price of other natural gas products. This behaviour fulfils the criteria for attempted market manipulation, as the orders and transactions entered by MP A and MP B at 32 euro/MWh had the intention to secure the price at an artificial level. Even if the market operator had excluded these orders and transactions from the calculation of the day-ahead reference price, MP A and MP B would still be breaching Article 5 of REMIT in the form of attempted market manipulation.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Example: Market Manipulation by Securing Price at Artificial Level - Electricity Intraday Case
ID: 221
CONTENT:
Situation: Since opening of the electricity intraday market, the product for hour 12 (11:00-12:00) traded at prices between 36 and 44 euro/MWh. All other intraday hours traded below 45 euro/MWh. Supply and demand conditions for hour 12 were similar to adjacent hours (11 and 13). In the last minute of the trading session for hour 12, MP A inserted 39 buy orders at 70 euro/MWh each for 1 MW. The orders were immediately matched with existing sell orders and represented the last trades of the session. The closing price for hour 12 was set at 70 euro/MWh. Without these transactions, it would have been 40 euro/MWh. Closing prices for hours 11 and 13 were 38 and 39 euro/MWh respectively. Subsequently, MP A informed the energy exchange that its buy orders represented a manifest error from an algorithm malfunction. However, this notification occurred outside the cancellation/annulment time window according to market rulebook. The trades were upheld and MP A suffered financial loss due to erroneous orders/trades that forced payment of imbalance charges.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Interpretation: Erroneous Orders as Artificial Price Manipulation
ID: 222
CONTENT:
This behaviour involving erroneous orders represents market manipulation by securing the price at an artificial level because: (i) MP A set/positioned the price of a wholesale energy product. Due to MP A's behaviour, hour 12 product traded at prices significantly higher than prevailing levels and diverging from adjacent hours' trading prices. The closing price of hour 12 was more than double the closing price for hours 11 and 13, a direct result of MP A's behaviour. Otherwise, the closing price would have been similar to adjacent hours. (ii) The price was set artificially because MP A's orders were erroneously submitted by the algorithm and misrepresented the demand side, unveiling an interest to buy at a price level not corresponding to the market participant's needs or interests. They created an imbalance for the market participant. The closing price of hour 12 does not correspond to what would have emerged from fair and competitive interplay between supply and demand. If not for the manipulative orders/transactions, other MPs would have been exposed to a different settlement price of 40 euro/MWh. MP A's order price levels were outside the observed price range (36-44 euro/MWh) despite not reflecting any change in market fundamentals.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Employing Fictitious Device, Deception, or Contrivance Under REMIT Article 5
ID: 223
CONTENT:
Entering into any transaction or issuing any order to trade in wholesale energy products employing a fictitious device, deception or contrivance which gives, or is likely to give, false or misleading signals regarding the supply, demand or price of wholesale energy products is considered a breach of the market manipulation prohibition under Article 5 of REMIT (Article 2(2)(a)(iii) of REMIT). Similarly, orders and transactions entered into with the intention of employing a fictitious device, deception or contrivance which gives or is likely to give false or misleading signals are prohibited as attempted market manipulation under Article 2(3)(a)(iii) of REMIT. This type of market manipulation typically does not focus exclusively on particular orders or transactions but rather covers orders placed or transactions entered into as part of a bigger scheme where 'on-market' orders/transactions build on another, potentially 'off-market', part of the scheme.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Structure and Components of Fictitious Device Schemes
ID: 224
CONTENT:
The 'off-market' part of a fictitious device strategy can be the dissemination of false or misleading information, the undertaking of actions sending misleading signals, or trading recommendations which are erroneous or biased. The rest of the scheme can also happen 'on-market' and involve other orders/transactions giving or likely to give false or misleading signals, or orders/transactions securing the market price at an artificial level. The other part of the scheme, whether 'off-market' or 'on-market', can either precede or follow the placing of orders or entering into transactions. A person engaging in or linked to such behaviour can either first disseminate false information/recommendations and then place orders or enter into transactions to benefit from potential market developments induced by the dissemination, or conversely, place orders/transactions first and then disseminate false information or recommendations. Instead of 'off-market' dissemination of false information, the same market impact could be achieved by a series of orders placed with no intention to execute them.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Market Manipulation Scenarios Under Fictitious Device Provisions
ID: 225
CONTENT:
The employment of a fictitious device, deception or contrivance will be considered market manipulation if it gives, or is likely to give, false or misleading signals to the market, and attempted market manipulation if it is intended to do so. The behaviour covers the use of any other type of deception or contrivance that would give a fictitious representation of the market reality. The considerations concerning the way orders and transactions give or are likely to give false or misleading signals regarding the supply, demand or price of wholesale energy products are fully applicable to this type of market manipulation. Market manipulation under Article 2(2)(a)(iii) or attempted market manipulation under Article 2(3)(a)(iii) of REMIT can happen in the following scenarios: if orders/transactions employing a fictitious device/deception/contrivance give false or misleading signals; or if orders/transactions employing a fictitious device/deception/contrivance are likely to give false or misleading signals.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Market Manipulation Through Fictitious Device - Definition and Criteria
ID: 226
CONTENT:
Market manipulation through the use of a fictitious device, deception, or contrivance that gives false or misleading signals to the market is prohibited under REMIT. This includes orders or transactions employing such devices intended to give false or misleading signals. The behavior must involve a fictitious device, deception, or contrivance that creates false or misleading market signals regarding the supply, demand, or price of wholesale energy products.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Case Study: Market Manipulation by Power Plant Operator
ID: 227
CONTENT:
Market Participant A (MP A) owns and operates a 300 MW power plant with high ramping capability. MP A notified the Transmission System Operator (TSO) it would not generate from morning until noon the next day (covering morning peak demand hours). Simultaneously, MP A entered into transactions with other market participants committing to deliver a large portion of its capacity for the same period. As a relevant balancing service provider, MP A participated in the balancing mechanism. Following the notification, the TSO expected a system shortage and offered payment to MP A to generate during morning peak. Once the TSO committed to remunerate MP A, MP A reversed its notification and changed its balancing mechanism orders accordingly.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Interpretation: MP A's Manipulative Behavior Analysis
ID: 228
CONTENT:
MP A's behavior constitutes market manipulation through fictitious device and deception because: (a) The notification to the TSO did not represent MP A's true expectation regarding generation, while MP A simultaneously entered into transactions it could not fulfill without operating its power plant. (b) MP A knew or ought to have known its power plant would generate, yet informed the TSO it would not, creating system imbalance and inducing the TSO to take balancing action and offer payment MP A would not have received with correct nomination. (c) MP A manipulated the market by submitting false and misleading notifications which, combined with balancing mechanism orders, employed a fictitious device and deception giving false or misleading signals regarding wholesale energy product supply.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Disseminating False or Misleading Information - Legal Framework
ID: 229
CONTENT:
Under Article 2(2)(b) of REMIT, dissemination by any means of information, including news or rumors, that gives or is likely to give false or misleading signals as to supply, demand, or price of wholesale energy products constitutes market manipulation and breaches Article 5 of REMIT. Similarly, dissemination of information with intention to give false or misleading signals is prohibited as attempted market manipulation under Article 2(3)(b) of REMIT. The term 'information' includes any type specified in Subchapter 4.2, regardless of whether publicly known, confidential, or inside information before dissemination, including rumors, false or misleading information, misleading news, wilful omission of material facts, and knowingly inaccurate reporting.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Dissemination Methods and Scope of Application
ID: 230
CONTENT:
The channel and means used to spread information is irrelevant for applying REMIT provisions. Dissemination can occur through media, internet, social media, chat rooms, or any other means. The number of persons to whom information is spread is also irrelevant. To establish market manipulation, dissemination must give or be likely to give false or misleading signals as to supply, demand, or price of wholesale energy products. This effect may result from the content of information itself and/or circumstances of dissemination, including the role and reputation of the disseminator and specific market circumstances.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Likelihood Standard and Proof Requirements for Dissemination
ID: 231
CONTENT:
The likelihood of giving false or misleading signals through dissemination is interpreted as the likelihood, on balance of probabilities, that spread of information may have such effect. There is no requirement to prove dissemination actually misled market participants. National Regulatory Authorities (NRAs) must demonstrate either a direct link between false or misleading information disseminated and elements of demand, supply, or price of wholesale energy products, or an indirect link where it is more probable than not that dissemination can affect such elements.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Knowledge Standard for Market Manipulation Through Dissemination
ID: 232
CONTENT:
For market manipulation (not attempted manipulation), dissemination is considered manipulative where the disseminating person knew or ought to have known the information was false or misleading. NRAs can prove the person knew about the false or misleading nature, or infer from the person's position, responsibilities, experience, and previous decisions that the person could not be ignorant of or ought to have known the information was false or misleading. NRAs should investigate trading activity of persons disseminating false information and persons with relationships to them, as trading preceding or following false information dissemination can reveal how the person benefits or intends to benefit from induced market developments.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Coupling of Off-Market and On-Market Manipulation
ID: 233
CONTENT:
Off-market dissemination of false information might be coupled with other on-market types of market manipulation giving false or misleading signals or securing market price at artificial level. Although dissemination occurs off-market without requiring orders or transactions, NRAs should investigate parallel trading activity to understand the full scope of manipulative conduct and its market impact.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Journalism and Artistic Expression Exception
ID: 234
CONTENT:
Under Article 2(2)(b) of REMIT, when information is disseminated for purposes of journalism or artistic expression, it should be assessed considering rules governing freedom of press and expression in other media. However, this exception does not apply where persons directly or indirectly profit from dissemination or dissemination is made with intention to mislead the market. The disseminating person must act in good faith with professionalism and conduct necessary verification of accuracy and credibility following press code principles, especially when information likely has important market impact. Failure to verify enables NRAs to question professionalism and assess that absent verification, the person ought to have known information was false or misleading.

metadata.title: Journalism and Artistic Expression Exception
metadata.original_text: Under Article 2(2)(b) of REMIT, when information is disseminated for purposes of journalism or artistic expression, it should be assessed considering rules governing freedom of press and expression in other media. However, this exception does not apply where persons directly or indirectly profit from dissemination or dissemination is made with intention to mislead the market. The disseminating person must act in good faith with professionalism and conduct necessary verification of accuracy and credibility following press code principles, especially when information likely has important market impact. Failure to verify enables NRAs to question professionalism and assess that absent verification, the person ought to have known information was false or misleading.

SECTION: Information Providers and Market Manipulation Liability
ID: 235
CONTENT:
News providers and legal or natural persons delivering and disseminating information about wholesale energy market developments, analysis, or forecasts on supply, demand, or prices of wholesale energy products may manipulate the market by disseminating information giving or likely to give false or misleading signals. The application scope of Article 5 of REMIT is not restricted to market participants but concerns any person, including information providers.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Case Study: False Information About Nuclear Power Plant Unavailability
ID: 236
CONTENT:
Company A, a specialized market information provider for electricity trading, published a newsflash on its website about an unannounced unavailability of unit 1 of Nuclear Power Plant B (1,000 MW capacity), representing 8 percent of the country's total installed capacity. This contradicted information from the plant operator stating normal operations and one-hour delayed real generation information. Company A failed to cross-check with other sources. The newsflash was shared on social media by traders expressing distress about tight supply and high prices. Two hours later, Nuclear Power Plant B published an UMM confirming uninterrupted operations and rebutting any unannounced downtime. Company A removed the newsflash the next day after communications and pressure, admitting it was materially false.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Analysis: Nuclear Power Plant Case - Market Manipulation Determination
ID: 237
CONTENT:
This behavior constitutes market manipulation by disseminating false and misleading information about significant electricity supply unavailability with direct market impact because: (a) Information about generation unit availabilities fulfills the concept of 'information' under Article 2(1)(b) of REMIT. (b) Information was disseminated through a newsflash on a specialized electricity trading information provider's website. (c) Information was false, corroborated by facility owner and other available information showing no unplanned unavailability. (d) Direct link exists between disseminated false information and electricity supply elements, as generation unit unavailability inevitably impacts potential electricity supply. (e) Dissemination likely gave false signals regarding electricity supply, considering content (unplanned outages on large power plant) and circumstances (information provider's reputation), and actually gave false signals as traders expressed concerns about tight supply and high prices. (f) Company A, a respected specialized firm, ought to have known the published information was false or misleading given relevant counter-evidence, and its processes were insufficiently robust to cross-check published information.

SECTION: 6.3. Indicators of Market Manipulation - Overview
ID: 238
CONTENT:
6.3. Indicators of market manipulation In order to identify (attempted) market manipulation under REMIT, NRAs shall take into account the non-exhaustive list of indicators included in Subchapters 6.3.1 and 6.3.2, which shall not necessarily be deemed, by themselves, to constitute (attempted) market manipulation. The list is organised into simple signals (e.g. relevant variables, actions, or diagnostic flags) and more complex types of practices that typically combine different signals.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Signals of Market Manipulation - False or Misleading Signals (Part 1)
ID: 240
CONTENT:
Signals of (attempted) market manipulation through (attempting to give) giving false or misleading signals or securing the price at an artificial level: a) the extent to which issued orders to trade or realised transactions represent a significant proportion of the daily total volume of transactions and/or orders in a specific trading session of the relevant wholesale energy product, in particular when these orders/transactions lead to a significant change in the price of the wholesale energy product; b) the extent to which issued orders to trade or realised transactions by persons with a significant buying or selling position in a wholesale energy product lead to significant changes in the price of the wholesale energy product or a related wholesale energy product; c) Whether realised transactions lead to no change in beneficial ownership of a wholesale energy product; d) the extent to which issued orders to trade or realised transactions include position reversals in a short period and represent a significant proportion of the volume of transactions in a specific trading session of the relevant wholesale energy product, and might be associated with significant changes in the price of a wholesale energy product.

ID: 243
CONTENT:

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: 6.3.2. Types of Practices - Introduction and REMIT Recitals
ID: 244
CONTENT:
6.3.2. Types of practices Recitals in REMIT identify, in a general and non-exhaustive way, some types of practices that constitute market manipulation and attempts to manipulate the market: Forms of market manipulation include placing and withdrawal of false orders; spreading of false or misleading information or rumours through the media, including the internet, or by any other means; deliberately providing false information to undertakings which provide price assessments or market reports with the effect of misleading market participants acting on the basis of those price assessments or market reports; and deliberately making it appear that the availability of electricity generation capacity or natural gas availability, or the availability of transmission capacity is other than the capacity which is actually technically available where such information affects or is likely to affect the price of wholesale energy products. Manipulation and its effects may occur across borders, between electricity and gas markets and across financial and commodity markets, including the emission allowances markets.

SECTION: Types of Practices - Guidance Framework
ID: 246
CONTENT:
In order to provide further guidance to the NRAs, based on the current experience, the Agency developed a non-exhaustive list of types of practices that could constitute, under certain circumstances, market manipulation, or attempts thereof, and are currently considered relevant for wholesale energy markets. Again, these types of practices are not conclusive and should only be regarded as a starting point when considering whether or not a behaviour gives rise to indications of a possible REMIT breach in the form of market manipulation or attempted market manipulation. Some of the below practices relate to specific types of behaviours, while others describe more general situations. It is to be noted that these types of practices can be used individually or in combination. Furthermore, these types of practices can fall under one or more of the types of market manipulation identified in Subchapters 6.2.1 to 6.2.4. The classification below is indicative only.

SECTION: Types of Practice - Wash Trades, Pre-arranged Trading, and Phishing
ID: 247
CONTENT:
Types of practice of (attempted) market manipulation through (attempting to give) giving false or misleading signals and/or securing the price at an artificial level: a) Wash trades: entering into arrangements for the sale or purchase of a wholesale energy product where there is no change in beneficial interests or market risk, or where beneficial interest or market risk is transferred between parties who are acting in concert or collusion; b) Pre-arranged trading: entering into arrangements for the sale or purchase of a wholesale energy product where the transfer of beneficial interest or market risk is only between parties who are acting in concert or collusion; c) Phishing: executing orders to trade, or a series of orders to trade, in order to uncover orders of other participants, and then entering an order to trade to take advantage of the obtained information.

ID: 253
CONTENT:

SECTION: Cross-Product Manipulation
ID: 254
CONTENT:
Cross-product manipulation involves undertaking trading or entering orders to trade on one wholesale energy product (including entering indications of interest) with a view to improperly influence the price of another (usually related) product. Examples include trading in the underlying wholesale energy product to distort the price of the derivative contract, or trading on the day-ahead/intraday market to influence the balancing market. Another example involves entering into arrangements to distort costs associated with a wholesale energy product, such as transportation cost, with the effect of fixing the price of a wholesale energy product at an abnormal or artificial level.

SECTION: Manipulative Capacity Withholding - Definition and Scope
ID: 257
CONTENT:
Actions undertaken by persons that artificially cause prices to be at a level not justified by market forces of supply and demand (including actual availability of production, storage or transportation capacity) constitute manipulative capacity withholding. This occurs when a market participant with the relative ability to influence the price or the interplay of supply and demand of a wholesale energy product decides, without justification, not to offer or to economically withhold the available production, storage or transportation capacity on the market. This includes the undue limiting of infrastructure or transmission capacities, resulting in prices that likely do not reflect the fair and competitive interplay of supply and demand.

CONTENT:
Electricity generation capacity withholding refers to the practice of keeping available generation capacity from being competitively offered on the wholesale electricity market, even though offering it competitively would lead to profitable transactions at the prevailing market prices. It can occur in two ways: via economic withholding or physical withholding. This practice may be performed by one or more market participants, acting independently or in collaboration. REMIT applies to electricity generation capacity withholding irrespective of whether competition law also applies.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Electricity Generation Capacity Withholding - Legal Analysis
ID: 259
CONTENT:
Electricity generation capacity withholding does not automatically amount to a breach of Article 5 of REMIT. A case-by-case analysis that takes into account the circumstances and specificities of the market is therefore needed. REMIT does not prohibit prices to be high, provided that they reflect a fair and competitive interplay between supply and demand. Assessment of whether behaviour involving electricity generation capacity withholding amounts to a breach of Article 5 of REMIT requires two concurrent elements: (1) whether the market participant concerned is able, in the case-specific circumstances, to influence the price or the interplay of supply and demand of a wholesale energy product by engaging in such behaviour, and (2) whether the market participant has any legitimate technical, regulatory and/or economic justification for not offering its available generation capacity or for offering it above the marginal cost.

SECTION: Trash and Cash Market Manipulation
ID: 261
CONTENT:
Trash and cash involves taking a short position in a wholesale energy product and then undertaking further selling activity and/or disseminating misleading negative information, directly or indirectly affecting the wholesale energy product with a view to decrease its price by the attraction of other sellers. When the price has fallen, the position is totally or partially closed.

When the price has risen, the position is totally or partially closed.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Persons Falling into the Scope of Article 5 of REMIT
ID: 268
CONTENT:
Article 5 of REMIT prohibits any engagement in, or attempt to engage in, market manipulation on wholesale energy markets. Contrary to some other REMIT provisions, Article 5 is drafted in general terms and is not exclusively destined to market participants. This means that the prohibition of market manipulation applies to any legal or natural person. This is consistent with the definition of market manipulation, according to which market manipulation (or attempted market manipulation) can happen off-market (without any order being placed or any transaction being entered into) through the dissemination of false or misleading information.

SECTION: Entities Likely to Give Signals on Wholesale Energy Markets
ID: 269
CONTENT:
Based on experience, the following entities (non-exhaustive list) were identified as more likely to take actions that give signals as to the supply, demand or price of wholesale energy products: legal or natural persons that are market participants; legal or natural persons that are to become market participants; legal or natural persons that manage physical assets or are under contractual obligations that can have a strong impact on the supply or demand of wholesale energy products; public authorities; persons professionally arranging transactions, publishing indexes, benchmarks or other information on prices, supply or demand; legal or natural persons using monitoring technologies to provide real-time (or quasi-real-time) information on the capacity or use of facilities for the supply or demand of wholesale energy products.

CONTENT:
Legal or natural persons delivering and/or providing information about wholesale energy market developments and analysis, or forecasts on the supply, demand or prices of wholesale energy products; legal or natural persons publishing wholesale energy price benchmarks or indexes; news providers; or any other natural or legal person that is likely to give signals as to the supply, demand or price of wholesale energy products could disseminate information that gives or is likely to give false or misleading signals to the market in breach of Article 5 of REMIT, provided they knew, or ought to have known that the information was false or misleading.

SECTION: Algorithmic Trading and Market Manipulation Liability
ID: 271
CONTENT:
Natural or legal persons involved in algorithmic trading fall equally into the scope of Article 5 of REMIT. Persons using algorithms to trade are thus responsible for the behaviour of their algorithm on the market and can be held liable for market manipulation in case the algorithm is likely to give/gives false or misleading signals or secures the market price at an artificial level, even in situations where this results from a poor design of the algorithm. The legal or natural person(s) that participate(s) in the conception or design of the algorithm can also be held liable for attempted market manipulation if the mere conception and design of the algorithm reveals a manipulative intent.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: REMIT and Competition Law - Scope Relationship
ID: 272
CONTENT:
Article 1(2) of REMIT provides that the Regulation is without prejudice to the application of European competition law to the practices covered by REMIT. In other words, the fact that REMIT is applicable to a certain situation or behaviour does not prevent the application of European competition law to the same situation or behaviour. The two legislations – REMIT and European competition law – cover different types of breaches. While REMIT prohibits market manipulation under Article 5, competition law prohibits agreements between companies which prevent, restrict or distort competition in the EU and which may affect trade between Member States (Article 101 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU)) and abuses of a dominant position (Article 102 of the TFEU).

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: REMIT vs. European Competition Law
ID: 274
CONTENT:
The sale or purchase of wholesale energy prohibited by competition law does not necessarily constitute a breach of Article 5 of REMIT. A company does not need to have or abuse a dominant position to indulge in market manipulation prohibited under REMIT, whereas being in a dominant position and abusing it are necessary conditions for the application of Article 102 of the TFEU. A breach of REMIT does not necessarily amount to a breach of competition law. However, in certain situations, the same behaviour might qualify as both market manipulation under REMIT and as a breach of European competition law, such as prearranged manipulative trading, A-B-A manipulative wash trades, and manipulative electricity generation capacity withholding. These types of practices give false or misleading signals and/or secure the market price at an artificial level in the meaning of REMIT and may also constitute a prohibited agreement or an abuse of dominant position according to competition law.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: REMIT Scope vs. Other Laws and Regulations
ID: 275
CONTENT:
According to Article 1(2), REMIT is without prejudice to the application of European competition law to the practices covered by REMIT. REMIT does not preclude the application of other laws and regulations specifically tailored to sanction money laundering, corporate fraud, and tax fraud. Some orders or transactions on wholesale energy markets may not be motivated by a real need to procure or sell energy, but rather to achieve other goals such as money laundering or fraud. If these trading activities end up being manipulative according to REMIT, they can qualify as a breach of Article 5 of REMIT. Even though these trading activities are fraudulent in nature, they do not necessarily intend to manipulate the wholesale energy markets. However, depending on their recurrence, scale, and the prices at which transactions were concluded, they could harm the integrity of the wholesale energy markets. NRAs should examine on a case-by-case basis whether they sent false or misleading signals as to the supply, demand or price of wholesale energy products and/or secured market prices at artificial levels.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Exemptions to Market Manipulation Under REMIT
ID: 276
CONTENT:
The REMIT Regulation does not provide for general exemptions to the prohibition of (attempted) market manipulation. Only Article 2(2)(a)(ii) and Article 2(3)(a)(ii) provide exemptions to the qualification of market manipulation. According to these provisions, securing (or having the intention to secure) the price of one or more wholesale energy products at an artificial level is (attempted) market manipulation, unless the person who entered into the transaction or issued the order to trade establishes that his reasons for doing so are legitimate and that the transaction or order to trade conforms to accepted market practices on the wholesale energy market concerned. Recital 14 of REMIT provides that accepted market practices (AMPs), such as those applying in the financial services sector defined by Articles 3(1)(9) and 13 of MAR, could be a legitimate way for market participants to secure a favourable price for a wholesale energy product.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Accepted Market Practices (AMPs) - Scope and Application
ID: 277
CONTENT:
The 'accepted market practice' argument can only be used in respect of the specific category of (attempted) market manipulation linked to price securing, and not in respect of other categories of market manipulation that do not provide this exemption possibility. For a price securing behaviour not to be considered manipulative, a person has to establish cumulatively that his/her reasons were legitimate and that the order or transaction conformed to accepted market practices on the relevant market. The burden of proof lies on the suspected market participant. The reasons invoked by a person to justify any order or transaction should be examined by NRAs on a case-by-case basis. AMPs accepted by financial market authorities according to MAR may also apply under REMIT, but AMPs under REMIT are not limited to these AMPs. New AMPs relating to wholesale energy markets may be established under REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Distinction Between Activities and Market Practices
ID: 278
CONTENT:
The Agency distinguishes between practices and activities carried out on wholesale energy markets. 'Activities' cover different types of operations or strategies that may be undertaken, such as arbitrage, hedging, and short selling. 'Market practices' cover the way these activities are handled and executed on the market. 'Activities' are considered too broad to qualify for the status of AMPs. Only the concrete market practices implementing these 'activities' may qualify as AMPs. For instance, an 'activity' such as hedging could be undertaken in different ways. If the hedging 'activity' in itself cannot be considered an AMP, specific practices of market participants aimed at hedging could be accepted as AMPs.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: National and Regional Responsibility for AMPs
ID: 279
CONTENT:
The decision on whether a process constitutes an AMP is a matter of national or regional specificities. AMPs are primarily the responsibility of individual NRAs, which means that a practice that a particular NRA considers an AMP may not be viewed as such by another. However, each NRA has a duty to consult with other relevant NRAs and to coordinate with the Agency prior to disclosing any market practices that they have accepted. There is also an obligation on the Agency to coordinate and publish the AMPs on its website. These will be published in a standard ACER format and a link will be provided to the national legal text once they have been recognised and have undergone the requisite national and European consultation process.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Factors for Assessing Market Practices
ID: 280
CONTENT:
NRAs should take into account the following non-exhaustive list of factors when assessing particular practices on wholesale energy markets: the level of transparency of the relevant market practice to the whole market (transparency is crucial for considering whether a particular market practice can be accepted); the need to safeguard the operation of market forces and the proper interplay of supply and demand (market practices inhibiting the interaction of supply and demand can create higher risks for market integrity); the degree to which the relevant market practice has an impact on market liquidity and efficiency (practices which enhance liquidity and efficiency are more likely to be accepted); the degree to which the relevant practice takes into account the trading mechanism of the relevant market and enables market participants to react properly and in a timely manner; the direct or indirect risk inherent in the relevant practice for the integrity of related markets; the outcome of any investigation of the relevant market practice by any NRA; and the structural characteristics of the relevant market, including its time frame, types of traded wholesale energy products, and type of market participants.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Overriding Principles for AMPs
ID: 281
CONTENT:
Overriding principles to be observed by NRAs to ensure that AMPs do not undermine market integrity, while fostering innovation and the continued dynamic development of wholesale energy markets, include: new or emerging AMPs should not be assumed to be unacceptable by an NRA simply because they have not been previously accepted by it; practising fairness and efficiency by market participants is required in order not to create prejudice to normal market activity and market integrity; a market practice that has been established as an AMP by a particular NRA shall not be considered to be applicable to other markets unless the NRAs of those other markets have accepted that practice too; and NRAs should analyse the impact of the relevant market practice when assessing whether such a practice constitutes an AMP.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Market Participants Obliged to Register
ID: 283
CONTENT:
According to Article 9(1) of REMIT, 'Market participants entering into transactions which are required to be reported to the Agency in accordance with Article 8(1) shall register with the national regulatory authority.' According to Article 2(7) of REMIT, 'Market participant' means any person, including transmission system operators, who enters into transactions, including the placing of orders to trade, in one or more wholesale energy markets. The obligation to register as a market participant under Article 9(1) of REMIT only applies to those market participants entering into transactions which are required to be reported to the Agency in accordance with Article 8(1). The requirement to register under REMIT applies to any person, legal or natural, that enters into transactions which are required to be reported. All market participants entering into transactions which are required to be reported to the Agency must register, even if a parent, subsidiary or other related undertaking is already registered or is registering. Provided they are not separate legal persons, branches of a market participant do not need to register as separate market participants. A market participant may allow a third party to submit registration information on their behalf.

ID: 284
CONTENT:
Article 9(3) of REMIT requires the Agency, in cooperation with NRAs, to determine and publish the format in which NRAs should transmit registration information on market participants to the Agency. On 26 June 2012, the Agency adopted a Decision determining the registration format to be used for the establishment of the European register of market participants. The registration format consists of 5 sections: Section 1 - Data related to the market participant; Section 2 - Data related to the natural persons linked to the market participant; Section 3 - Data related to the ultimate controller or beneficiary of the market participant; Section 4 - Data related to the corporate structure of the market participant; Section 5 - Data related to the delegated parties for reporting on behalf of the market participant. All market participants entering into transactions required to be reported to the Agency in accordance with Article 8(1) are required to provide this information.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Establishment of National Registers
ID: 285
CONTENT:
According to Article 9(2) of REMIT, each NRA shall establish a registration system by which market participants can provide registration information to that NRA no later than 3 months after the adoption of the implementing acts. NRAs are free to use whatever system they deem most appropriate for their market. The Agency is developing a system to be used to establish the European register of market participants, which will also be available to NRAs as a means of registering market participants in their own Member State. NRAs should ensure that market participants are provided with information on how to register. The Agency will make available a Registration User Manual (RUM) to NRAs to provide guidance on how the fields in the registration format should be populated. On the basis of the RUM, NRAs may provide guidance to market participants on how to register. The manual will be updated periodically based on feedback from NRAs.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: NRA Registration Requirements and Establishment Criteria
ID: 286
CONTENT:
According to Article 9(1) of REMIT, market participants entering into transactions required to be reported to the Agency shall register with the national regulatory authority in the Member State in which they are established or resident, or, if they are not established or resident in the Union, in a Member State in which they are active. According to settled case law of the Court of Justice of the European Union, a legal or natural person can be established in more than one Member State. The legal or natural person is established in the Member State(s) in which it pursues a professional activity on a stable and continuous basis. If a market participant is established in more than one Member State, the Agency would normally expect market participants to register in the Member State in which they have their primary establishment. For market participants not established or resident in the Union, such market participants may choose in which Member State to register, as long as they are active in that Member State.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Registration Submission Deadlines and Obligations
ID: 287
CONTENT:
According to Article 9(4) of REMIT, market participants must submit all Sections of the registration form (Sections 1 to 5) before entering into any transaction which is required to be reported to the Agency. In line with Article 12(2) of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 1348/2014, the reporting obligation will apply to market participants from 7 October 2015 and from 7 April 2016, according to the type of data to be reported. For market participants entering into transactions on an organised market place (OMP), the registration obligation takes effect at the latest prior to 7 October 2015. For all other market participants, the registration obligation takes effect at the latest prior to 7 April 2016, or prior to the first day they enter into transactions required to be reported. Any person who enters into a transaction required to be reported without having submitted the registration form to the relevant NRA is in breach of Article 9 of REMIT. Market participants are obliged to communicate promptly to the relevant NRA any change as regards the information provided in their registration form.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Special Registration Provisions for Early Registrants
ID: 288
CONTENT:
Market participants who registered before 17 March 2015 (before the Agency published for the first time the list of market participants in the European register) were not able to complete Section 4 (data related to the corporate structure of the market participant) of the registration form by the time of its submission to the NRA. In accordance with the Agency Decision No 01/2012, they shall provide information on Section 4 of the registration form within 3 months from the first publication of the European register. They shall update their registration form in Section 4 at the latest by 17 June 2015. Example 1: Market participant A registered before 17 March 2015 and was required to complete Sections 1, 2, 3 and 5 of the registration form before submission. Section 4 was not filled at the time of first submission as the publication of the European register occurred for the first time on 17 March 2015. After 17 March 2015, MP A has three months (until 17 June 2015) to fill Section 4 with data available at the European register. If a related undertaking (MP B) only registers after 17 June 2015, MP A will also be obliged to update data in Section 4 accordingly once MP B registration is published. MP A has an obligation to promptly update any other information provided in its registration form at any time once that change takes effect.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Registration Requirements for Later Registrants
ID: 289
CONTENT:
If a market participant (MP C) registers after 17 March 2015, it is obliged to complete all Sections (1 to 5) of the registration form with updated data at the time of submission. In Section 4 of the registration form (Data related to corporate structure), MP C is required to include all its related undertaking(s) which are registered MPs, i.e., all those that are published in the European register of MPs at the time of the form submission. If a related undertaking (MP D) registers with the relevant NRA at a later stage, MP C is also required to promptly update its registration form accordingly once MP D registration is published at the European register of MPs. In addition to the update of Section 4, MP C has an obligation to promptly update any other information provided in its registration form at any time once that change takes effect, such as if MP C chooses a new Registered Reporting Mechanism (RRM), Section 5 of the registration form needs to be updated accordingly.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: ACER Code Issuance and Timing
ID: 290
CONTENT:
As required by Article 9(2) of REMIT, each market participant registered under REMIT will be issued with a unique identifier (the 'ACER code'). The ACER code will enable market participants to report data under Article 8 of REMIT and will also be needed to provide information relating to Section 4 of the registration form (data related to the corporate structure of the market participants). According to Article 9(4) of REMIT, market participants shall submit the registration form prior to entering into transactions required to be reported to the Agency. The ACER code will be issued upon the transmission of the information in the national registers to the Agency for the first time, in accordance with the Agency Decision No 01/12. According to Article 2 of this Agency Decision, NRAs should promptly transmit the registration information to the Agency once it is submitted by the market participant, after which the Agency immediately issues the ACER code. NRAs should ensure that market participants receive the ACER code in a timely manner, and in any case before the transactions entered by the market participants are required to be reported to the Agency. This will enable market participants to fulfill their reporting obligations and ensure efficient and effective data collection by the Agency.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: ACER Code Issuance for Different Registration Phases
ID: 291
CONTENT:
The registration system will provide for automatic checks that will prevent incomplete registration forms from being submitted. For market participants registering before the Agency for the first time publishes the European register, the ACER code will be issued upon the submission of those market participants' first phase information (relating to Sections 1, 2, 3 and 5) to the relevant NRA. However, such market participants should not consider the receipt of an ACER code as a confirmation that they have completed the registration process. In order to complete the process, such market participants still need to provide the information relating to Section 4 of the registration format. For any market participant registering after the Agency for the first time publishes the European register, the ACER code will be issued upon the submission of all sections of the registration format to the relevant NRA (i.e., Sections 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5). According to Article 2 of the Agency Decision No 01/2012, NRAs shall provide promptly the Agency with the information in the national registers in electronic format, through a secure channel and using one of the following formats: CSV or XML.

SECTION: Requirement to Keep Registration Information Up to Date
ID: 292
CONTENT:
According to Article 9(5) of REMIT, market participants shall communicate promptly to the national regulatory authority any change which has taken place as regards the information provided in the registration form. It is important to recognise that registration is not a one-off event, but rather an ongoing obligation to maintain accurate and current information.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: REMIT Registration Requirements and NRA Responsibilities
ID: 293
CONTENT:
REMIT requires market participants to register with an NRA prior to entering into a transaction and to update their registration form with any changes to the information provided in accordance with Article 9(5) of REMIT. If mandatory registration information is not communicated promptly, the registration is considered incomplete. Market participants with outdated registration forms may breach Article 9 of REMIT. Although market participants bear responsibility for updating information in national registers, NRAs are encouraged to set up regular reminders (e.g., once a year) asking market participants to verify that submitted information remains correct and up to date.
