text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: The Three Roles of NRAs in the Registration Process
ID: 294
CONTENT:
NRAs undertake three key roles during registration. First, they act as a source of support for market participants seeking to register, providing users with support during the registration process and utilizing the Agency's Registration User Manual (RUM) when available. Second, NRAs transmit registration information from their national registers to the Agency promptly upon submission by market participants, after which the Agency immediately issues the ACER code. Third, NRAs ensure accuracy of registration information by establishing and maintaining up-to-date registers of market participants. NRAs should have systems in place to effectively check registration information provided by market participants to identify omissions and obvious errors, with any detected errors promptly notified to the Agency.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Registration System Accuracy and ACER Code Issuance
ID: 295
CONTENT:
The Agency's registration system provides automatic checks to prevent incomplete registration forms from being submitted. Market participants are allowed to trade without breaching Article 9 as soon as they submit complete registration forms to the relevant NRA, regardless of whether an ACER code has been issued. The Agency aims to issue the ACER code immediately upon receipt of registration information from the NRA while ensuring high accuracy in the European register of market participants. The Agency may delay publication of information transmitted by NRAs while conducting additional checks on registration information submitted by market participants. It is important to note that through the registration process, NRAs do not issue authorization or licenses to trade, and completion of registration does not constitute a 'know-your-customer' check or 'fit-and-proper' assessment.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Registration Process Steps and Timeline
ID: 296
CONTENT:
For market participants starting registration before the Agency publishes the first European register list, the process includes: (1) Submitting a registration form to the relevant NRA with information from Sections 1, 2, 3, and 5 of Agency Decision No 01/2012 before entering into reportable transactions; (2) The NRA promptly transmitting national register information to the Agency; (3) The Agency issuing a unique ACER code identifier and informing the market participant and NRA; (4) The Agency establishing a European register and publishing a list of market participants; (5) The market participant completing the second registration phase by submitting Section 4 information within 3 months of the first European register publication. Market participants registering after the first European list publication must provide all relevant information (Sections 1-5) during initial registration.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Important Registration Clarifications and Announcements
ID: 297
CONTENT:
A clear and consistent message must be given to market participants: registration under REMIT does not constitute any kind of authorization or license to trade and is without prejudice to obligations to comply with applicable trading and balancing rules. Market participants must transmit registration forms to the NRA prior to entering into transactions required to be reported to the Agency in accordance with Article 8(1) of REMIT. NRAs should encourage market participants to register in advance to facilitate smooth registration processes. The Agency will announce early in advance when it intends to publish the European register of market participants for the first time.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Introduction to Persons Professionally Arranging Transactions (PPATs)
ID: 298
CONTENT:
Chapter 8 provides guidance to NRAs concerning supervision of obligations imposed on persons professionally arranging transactions (PPATs) by Article 15 of REMIT. According to Article 15, any person professionally arranging transactions in wholesale energy products who reasonably suspects a transaction might breach Article 3 or 5 shall notify the national regulatory authority without further delay. PPATs must establish and maintain effective arrangements and procedures to identify breaches of Article 3 or 5. An important number of trades in wholesale energy markets are intermediated by PPATs. Through their role as intermediates, PPATs have exclusive knowledge of their market and clients, positioning them to monitor trading activities and identify potential REMIT breaches. REMIT imposes explicit responsibility on PPATs to monitor and contribute to integrity, transparency, and proper functioning of European wholesale energy markets.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Definition and Delimitation of PPATs
ID: 299
CONTENT:
Apart from Article 15 of REMIT, Article 8(4)(d) of REMIT and Article 2(4) of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 1348/2014 include references to PPATs. Article 8(4)(d) identifies entities that could be considered PPATs: organized markets, trade-matching systems, or other persons professionally arranging transactions. Organized market places and trade-matching systems fall under the PPAT definition, as do any other entities engaged in similar activities. The concept of 'organized market place' or 'organized market' is defined in Article 2(4) of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 1348/2014 as: (a) a multilateral system bringing together or facilitating multiple third-party buying and selling interests in wholesale energy products resulting in a contract, or (b) any other system or facility where multiple third-party interests interact to result in a contract, including electricity and gas exchanges, brokers, other persons professionally arranging transactions, and trading venues as defined in Article 4 of Directive 2014/65/EU.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Cumulative Criteria for PPAT Classification
ID: 300
CONTENT:
For an entity to be considered a PPAT subject to Article 15 obligations, it must fulfill three cumulative criteria: (1) Person: means either natural or legal person; (2) Professionally: engaged in a specified activity as part of one's normal and regular paid occupation; (3) Arranging transactions: an activity that either enables or assists third parties (buyer or seller) in a way that directly brings about a particular wholesale energy transaction, or provides a facility that facilitates third parties entering into transactions in wholesale energy products. Simply providing means by which parties can communicate is excluded from the PPAT concept. However, if a person makes arrangements beyond providing communication means and adds value to what is provided, it loses this exclusion and shall be recognized as a PPAT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: PPAT Characteristics and Distinction from Market Participants
ID: 301
CONTENT:
The main characteristic of a PPAT is its intermediary role, whether acting as principal or agent, in arranging transactions in wholesale energy products. Legal form, ownership, market type, wholesale energy product type, and number of represented parties are not relevant elements in determining PPAT status. REMIT places different obligations on PPATs and market participants, making it necessary to establish in each case whether a person acts as a PPAT or market participant. Whereas a market participant enters into transactions involving wholesale energy products, a PPAT arranges such transactions for others.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: PPAT Classification and Exclusions
ID: 302
CONTENT:
An entity may qualify as a PPAT in one transaction and as a market participant in another transaction. There are situations where a person is both a market participant and a PPAT in the same transaction. The arranging activity can comprise the whole trade lifecycle or be restricted to one or more parts of it. Some transactions may involve the participation of several PPATs and others may not involve the participation of any PPAT. Persons such as Internet service providers, e-mail service providers, messaging providers or telecommunication providers are excluded from the concept of PPAT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: PPAT Concept Application Examples
ID: 303
CONTENT:
Entities were assessed against characteristics to identify whether they fulfil the criteria to be classified as PPATs. The assessment of the existence of the three cumulative criteria has always to be done on a case-by-case basis. Energy Exchanges, Broker platforms/Brokers, Cross border capacity exchanges/platforms, Secondary capacity allocation platforms, and TSOs (or persons acting on their behalf) organising gas trades, energy balancing, capacity trading all qualify as PPATs by bringing about transactions through introducing buyer/seller or providing facilities that facilitate entering into transactions by third parties. Sleeves arranging transactions also qualify as PPATs by offering intermediary services. However, Sleeves not arranging and Communication facilities do not meet the arranging transactions criterion.

metadata.title: PPAT Concept Application Examples
metadata.original_text: Entities were assessed against characteristics to identify whether they fulfil the criteria to be classified as PPATs. The assessment of the existence of the three cumulative criteria has always to be done on a case-by-case basis. Energy Exchanges, Broker platforms/Brokers, Cross border capacity exchanges/platforms, Secondary capacity allocation platforms, and TSOs (or persons acting on their behalf) organising gas trades, energy balancing, capacity trading all qualify as PPATs by bringing about transactions through introducing buyer/seller or providing facilities that facilitate entering into transactions by third parties. Sleeves arranging transactions also qualify as PPATs by offering intermediary services. However, Sleeves not arranging and Communication facilities do not meet the arranging transactions criterion.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Duty to Notify Potential REMIT Breaches
ID: 304
CONTENT:
According to Article 15(1) of REMIT: 'Any person professionally arranging transactions in wholesale energy products who reasonably suspects that a transaction might breach Article 3 or 5 shall notify the national regulatory authority without further delay.' This obligation specifies what, whom, when and how to notify. The assumption of a reasonable suspicion lies within the responsibility of the PPAT. Although the obligation to notify relates to Articles 3 and 5 of REMIT, PPATs might become aware of potential breaches of other REMIT provisions. As a good cooperation practice, PPATs are invited to transmit all available information to the relevant NRA(s) through adequate communication channels.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Content Requirements for Breach Notifications
ID: 305
CONTENT:
The notification of a potential REMIT breach should be clear and accurate to enable the NRA(s) to understand the basic facts and should contain as much information as possible for assessment. When reporting a potential breach of Article 3 or 5, PPATs should provide information on the identity of market participant(s), timing of the potential breach, market(s) concerned and details on related transaction(s)/order(s)/behaviour(s). A Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) should contain: Type of market abuse (insider trading and/or market manipulation with subcategory identification); Details of the notifying party (name, organisation, position, contact details, notification date and time); Description of the potential breach including order(s)/transaction(s)/behaviour(s) details, product(s) involved, delivery location, delivery date, timestamps, load type, contract/transaction IDs; Description of inside information or potential inside information for Article 3 breaches; Information on potentially affected parties and products; Identification of other PPATs involved.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Additional Information for Breach Notifications
ID: 306
CONTENT:
Suspicious Transaction Reports should include: Identification of persons involved in the potential breach (name, organisation, position, contact details) and any other associated persons; Identification of relevant NRA(s) to be notified and other entities notified; Further information of significance including analysis of behaviour, spreadsheets analysing relevant transaction(s)/order(s)/behaviour(s), copies of communications with market participants or other entities, any actions already undertaken by the PPAT, estimation of market price impact, estimation of benefit from the potential breach, affected Member State(s) with supporting evidence, and any other information the PPAT considers relevant including information on events which may lead to potential breaches of other REMIT provisions.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Notification Recipients and Criteria
ID: 307
CONTENT:
According to Article 15(1) of REMIT, PPATs must notify the national regulatory authority without further delay. The PPAT should notify at least the following NRA(s): The NRA(s) in the Member State(s) of the delivery of the wholesale energy product(s); The NRA in the Member State in which the Market Participant involved in the potential breach has registered in the Centralised European Register of Energy Market Participants (CEREMP). If a single NRA meets both criteria, only that NRA should be notified. Otherwise all NRAs that meet at least one criterion should be notified. Where a PPAT notifies more than one NRA, it should inform each NRA of the other NRAs being notified. If the PPAT has already notified at least the NRA(s) fulfilling the criteria based on available evidence at notification time, the PPAT should not be held responsible for not notifying other NRAs identified later as affected.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: National Law Requirements and Transportation Contracts
ID: 308
CONTENT:
Where, in accordance with the national law of the Member State where the PPAT is incorporated and/or active, another NRA than those mentioned above shall be notified, the PPAT should notify this NRA in addition to the one(s) that should be notified per the criteria in this Guidance. For transportation contracts, the notion of delivery is to be understood as the location where the transmission service is provided. For example, if the suspicion involves orders or transactions on the capacity of an interconnector between two countries, the NRAs in both countries should be notified.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Financial Instruments and MAR Coordination
ID: 309
CONTENT:
Article 1(2) of REMIT refers that Articles 3 and 5 shall not apply to wholesale energy products which are financial instruments and to which Article 2 of MAR applies. However, if a potential breach involves wholesale energy products that are also financial instruments falling in the scope of Article 2 of MAR, the PPAT should notify the NRA(s) identified above in parallel with the relevant financial authorities, in order to promote cooperation between different investigatory authorities.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Timing of Breach Notifications
ID: 310
CONTENT:
Article 15 of REMIT provides that persons who reasonably suspect a transaction might breach Article 3 or 5 shall notify the national regulatory authority without further delay. The notion of 'without further delay' is linked to the existence of a reasonable suspicion of a potential breach of REMIT. The PPAT shall notify the NRA(s) after preliminary analysis of an anomalous event and as soon as it has reasonable grounds to suspect a potential REMIT breach. The timeliness of notification after the occurrence of an anomalous event is crucial for collecting evidence. The sooner the NRA is informed, the earlier it can collect evidence (notably communication records) avoiding destruction or deterioration.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Best Practice Notification Timeline
ID: 311
CONTENT:
To promote best practice, PPATs shall notify the NRA(s) as soon as possible once they have reasonable grounds to suspect a REMIT breach, and should usually do so no later than four weeks from the occurrence of the anomalous event. This recommendation means that PPATs should perform market surveillance routinely. Once they detect an anomalous event, they should collect evidence and conduct necessary analysis to further assess that event. This enables PPATs to assess whether there are reasonable grounds to suspect a potential breach within four weeks of the occurrence of the anomalous event, and to produce a good quality STR. This four-week period is deemed sufficient for PPATs to perform market surveillance, gather necessary information to conclude on the existence of reasonable grounds, and produce quality notifications.

SECTION: STR Notification Procedures and Timeframes
ID: 312
CONTENT:
A comprehensive notification including the elements listed in Subchapter 8.3.1 above. However, should the anomalous event be of particular complexity, or should the PPAT be unable, for other objective reasons, to conclude on the existence of reasonable grounds of suspicion within the timeframe indicated above, the PPAT should proceed with its analysis and notify the NRA(s) as soon as it has reasonable grounds to suspect a REMIT breach. The practice of delaying the submission of an STR in order to be able to incorporate further STRs cannot be reconciled with the obligation to act without further delay when the PPAT has gathered sufficient evidence to have reasonable grounds to suspect a potential breach. Arrangements and procedures in place shall entail the possibility to notify a potential breach which occurred in the past, where reasonable grounds of suspicion have arisen in the light of subsequent events or information. In such cases, the PPAT should be able to explain the delay between the day of occurrence of the anomalous event and the notification, according to the specific circumstances of the case, if requested to by the NRA. PPATs should also transmit any relevant additional information which they become aware of after the notification is originally submitted.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Secure Communication Channels for Breach Notification
ID: 313
CONTENT:
PPATs shall use secure communication channels to notify the NRA(s). As a service to NRAs, the Agency has established on its website a secure 'Notification Platform' for the notification of, inter alia, STRs by PPATs (available at: https://www.acer-remit.eu/np/home). The Notification Platform enables PPATs to fulfil their notification obligations, allowing them to directly notify, simultaneously and in a standardised manner, one or several of the 28 NRAs together with the Agency. In order to ensure legal certainty, the notifying PPAT receives an immediate confirmation of its notification. The PPATs may also choose to notify a potential breach using the secure communication channels that NRAs may have put at their disposal. In any case, NRAs should publish on their website the communication channel that PPATs should use in order to notify potential breaches. Any contact to the competent NRA(s) through any other means than the secure communication channels referred to above does not replace the submission of an STR.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Duty to Establish Effective Arrangements and Procedures
ID: 314
CONTENT:
According to Article 15(2) of REMIT: 'Persons professionally arranging transactions in wholesale energy products shall establish and maintain effective arrangements and procedures to identify breaches of Article 3 or 5.' The provisions of Article 15 of REMIT set out the responsibility of a PPAT not only to notify whenever it has reasonable grounds to suspect a potential breach, but also to proactively monitor the wholesale energy markets in which it is involved. This subchapter provides guidance on what can be expected from PPATs with regards to establishing and maintaining effective arrangements and procedures for monitoring. Given the fact that PPATs vary in size and organisational characteristics, and operate different markets (e.g. electricity, gas, spot, futures, capacity, etc.), there is no one-size-fits-all governance or organisational arrangement. As a result, while some recommendations concern basic requirements applicable to all PPATs, the way to implement the recommended measures shall take into consideration the specificities of each PPAT. In general, the effectiveness of the market surveillance activity of a PPAT, and its level of internal and external independence and integrity, depend on the organisational arrangements and procedures in place.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Governance and Conflict of Interest Management
ID: 316
CONTENT:
In establishing a governance model, the PPAT has to take into account the conflicts of interest at individual and corporate level. Individual conflicts of interest may arise when a market surveillance team member has close contacts with market participants who trade on its platform. The market surveillance team member might be inclined not to internally report an anomalous event or notify a potential breach to the NRA(s) for a number of reasons, including to avoid damaging its relationships and future career prospects with the market participants. Corporate conflicts may arise when a market surveillance team member wants to report an anomalous event/notify a potential breach regarding a market participant, while the management team does not want to, for commercial or other reasons. The market surveillance team member might be put under pressure not to report an anomalous event/notify a potential breach. The existence and the nature of corporate conflicts is affected, among other things, by the structure of control, the governance model, as well as the nature of the business activity performed by the PPAT. In order to identify and to prevent or manage conflicts of interest, it is important to consider all the steps to be undertaken by the PPAT, from detecting an anomalous event to finally notifying a potential breach to the NRA(s). Appropriate governance models, based on the assessment of the potential sources of risk within the PPAT, could mitigate the above mentioned risks by addressing how market surveillance teams are structured, how they report to the management team (internal reporting) and how they notify STRs to NRAs (external reporting).

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Market Monitoring Unit (MMU) Governance Model
ID: 317
CONTENT:
In this governance model the market surveillance team operates independently from the other parts of the PPAT. The MMU is only accountable towards an Independent Body, not involved in the daily management of the PPAT (e.g. Exchange Council, Supervisory Board) that is responsible for the supervision of the effective execution of the unit activities. Differences may exist in the structure, duties and composition of the Independent Body (for example, members may be external to the PPAT or at least some of them, including NRA representatives). In this situation, as the market surveillance team operates as a segregated unit from the other PPAT activities and does not report to the management team, the conflicts of interest at corporate level can in theory be more effectively mitigated. The composition and the duties of the Independent Body are of utmost importance in this model to ensure that the mitigation of these risks is effective and that the confidentiality of the market surveillance activities is secured. In this case the governance structure should include clear rules on the nomination of the members of the Independent Body, as well as on its duties, to adequately mitigate the individual potential conflicts of interest. Both the structure of the Independent Body and the level of segregation of the market surveillance team should also take into account potential conflicts arising from the PPAT's control structure and the types of activities carried out by the PPAT.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Market Monitoring Department (MMD) Governance Model
ID: 318
CONTENT:
In this governance model, the market surveillance team operates as any other department within the organisation, reporting to a Director who may be member of the Management Team. In this situation some consideration should be given to the reporting lines to prevent conflicts of interests. The market surveillance team should not report to a Director whose objectives or performance are evaluated based on commercial achievements rather than on the fulfilment of the mission of the market surveillance function. Appropriate arrangements, based on the nature and assessment of the PPAT's conflicts of interests, should be in place to manage the flow of confidential information (also at the Management Team level). Appropriate processes that enable the auditing of the reporting from the Market Monitoring Department to the Management Team should be in place to mitigate potential conflicts of interest. The independent body or an auditing body can take responsibilities for the supervision of these communications. The appointment of a compliance officer could also be envisaged.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Market Monitoring Committee (MMC) Governance Model
ID: 319
CONTENT:
In this governance model, the market surveillance team consists of a number of experts, working in different parts of the PPAT. The MMC is accountable towards the Management Team as a whole or to a designated Director. In the situation where the market surveillance team is organised by way of a committee, appropriate arrangements should be in place to mitigate potential conflicts of interest and to ensure the confidentiality of the data as it might flow through different parts of the organisation. The members of the MMC should not have their objectives or performance evaluated based on commercial achievements but rather on the fulfilment of the mission of the market surveillance function. Also, the members of the MMC should not simultaneously work for the teams in the PPAT with commercial responsibilities. As in the situation where a MMD is in place, due consideration should be given to the reporting lines of the market surveillance team. Appropriate processes that enable the auditing of the reporting from the MMC to the Management Team should be in place to mitigate potential conflicts of interest. The independent body or an auditing body can take responsibilities for the supervision of these flows of information. The appointment of a compliance officer could also be envisaged.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Organisational Setup for Market Surveillance
ID: 320
CONTENT:
Proper organisation of the market surveillance activity is essential for its ability to detect market abuse. This involves at least five dimensions: adequacy of resources; human resources policy; appropriate amount of human resources dedicated to market surveillance (referred to as market surveillance team); communication with other units and confidentiality. For each dimension the PPAT should be able to justify why its organisational setup is best suited for the tasks of the market surveillance team.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Resource Adequacy and Human Resources Requirements
ID: 321
CONTENT:
The market surveillance activity requires availability of some fundamental resources, which include human resources, analytical tools and data/information. The appropriate amount of resources dedicated to the market surveillance activity is dependent on the size of the PPAT. Independently from the specific requirements on these issues, the adequacy of these resources, both in terms of quantity and quality, is fundamental in order to ensure effectiveness and true independence of market surveillance. The human resources, analytical tools and data/information should be adequate to perform real-time and ex post analyses on anomalous events which are deemed relevant for the markets the PPAT operates. For example, markets with low transactions volumes might be better suited for manual supervision, but markets with high transactions volumes could benefit from automated systems. There should always be an element of human analysis in the detection of potential REMIT breaches as the most effective form of surveillance will likely be a mix of both automated and human forms.

ID: 323
CONTENT:
Internal factors, such as potential conflicts of interest at individual level, have the potential to influence the work of the market surveillance team. In order to ensure an adequate level of quality, consistency and effectiveness of the market surveillance team work, there should be a human resource policy with specific requirements for the market surveillance staff that can contribute to establish and safeguard the independence and integrity of the team. That policy can include the principles for the management of conflicts of interest (including the list of interests that need to be declared). As part of the specific requirements for the market surveillance staff, the human resource policy should develop specific incentives which are based on the accomplishment of the market surveillance function and not correlated to financial/commercial achievements.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Dedicated Market Surveillance Team Structure and Organization
ID: 324
CONTENT:
The specificities of the market surveillance function require the identification of a dedicated team. The market surveillance team will be specifically assigned to the monitoring activities, endowed with the relevant skills and able to devote the required time and operate in a timely manner. Implementation of appropriate segregation measures (e.g., Chinese walls) is critical in the creation of a dedicated market surveillance team in order to ensure the integrity and confidentiality of the information assessed.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Delegation and Outsourcing of Monitoring Functions
ID: 325
CONTENT:
PPATs belonging to a group of companies should be able to delegate their monitoring functions to another entity within the same group. In addition, PPATs should be able to outsource a part of their monitoring activity, including the analysis of orders and transactions, alerts generation for the detection of anomalous events, as well as the identification of potential breaches of Articles 3 and 5 of REMIT. However, PPATs should retain the expertise and resources necessary for evaluating the quality of the services provided and the organisational adequacy of the providers, and for supervising the outsourced services effectively and managing the risks associated on an ongoing basis. PPATs must have direct access to the relevant information related to the outsourced service and define in a written agreement their rights and obligations and those of the providers. The outsourcing agreement should allow PPATs to terminate it. In any case, PPATs shall ensure that the delegated entity complies with the organisational and procedural arrangements described in this Guidance. PPATs will remain fully responsible for the obligations stated in Article 15 and should submit themselves any STR to the competent NRA(s). Furthermore, PPATs should still be able to conduct any complementary analysis.

SECTION: Communication with Other Units and Confidentiality
ID: 326
CONTENT:
Whichever the way the market surveillance team is organised, the team itself needs to keep regular contact with other functions within the PPAT, to get access to the information needed to perform its activities. In order to safeguard the integrity of the market surveillance team, the information collected by the market surveillance team for the purpose of investigating an anomalous event shall be considered confidential and systems that restrict the access to such information shall be implemented.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Clear Definition of Market Surveillance Function
ID: 327
CONTENT:
The lack of a clear definition of the market surveillance function may undermine the ability of the market surveillance team to perform its tasks, namely through the weakening of the trust in the function. Therefore, the market surveillance team should have a clear (written) function and be trusted by the PPAT management, other PPAT employees and members/customers. Without a clear definition of the function and trust from the PPAT management, other PPAT employees and a certain authority towards PPAT members/customers, the market surveillance team can neither investigate anomalous events nor notify potential breaches of REMIT adequately. The mission of the market surveillance function should be broader than the sum of the tasks of the market surveillance team, as it should affect PPAT employees working outside of that team. These employees may jeopardise the market surveillance team's compliance efforts if they are not aware of the mission of the market surveillance function. The PPAT should have arrangements to ensure that its employees working outside of the market surveillance team are aware of the mission of the market surveillance function.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Procedural Arrangements Overview
ID: 328
CONTENT:
Procedural arrangements are key to ensuring that the PPAT fulfils its obligations under Article 15 of REMIT. This subchapter outlines guidance on the market monitoring strategy, human resources policies, communications and traceability related procedures. PPATs' procedural arrangements should be documented, including any changes or updates to them. Documentation on the compliance of the PPAT with these procedural arrangements should also be elaborated. Both kinds of documentation should be maintained for a period of at least five years.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Market Monitoring Strategy and Risk Assessment
ID: 329
CONTENT:
In order to identify potential breaches of Articles 3 or 5 of REMIT, the PPAT shall have a documented market monitoring strategy. That strategy shall be designed based on a risk assessment. The market monitoring strategy shall define thresholds for investigating alerts and include processes in place to identify potential breaches. It should also prescribe some actions to be performed by the monitoring team to further assess the anomalous events. The risk assessment shall include at least the identification of the different types of market abuse that may constitute Article 3 or 5 breaches and a graduation of the different forms of market abuse based on the expected risk of occurrence on the PPAT platform/operations. The identification of the different types of market abuse that may constitute Article 3 or 5 breaches shall take into consideration Chapters 3, 4, 5, 6, and 8 of this Guidance. The risk assessment and the market monitoring strategy shall be revised regularly. In particular, they shall be revised when there is evidence that the current strategy is not comprehensive enough and some potential breach was not detected. It shall also be revised whenever relevant changes in the markets or in the market participants' behaviour take place. Best practice should be taken into consideration when designing such strategy. The PPAT should be able to explain to the NRA, upon request, how it manages the alerts generated by the adopted system and why the adopted level of automation is appropriate for its business.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Human Resources Procedures and Conflict of Interest Management
ID: 330
CONTENT:
Conflicts of interest can have the potential to affect the integrity and focus of the market surveillance team. Therefore, the market surveillance team within each PPAT should be covered by the organisation's human resources policies and procedures, which should safeguard the independence and integrity of the market surveillance team members as well as other affected departments. The human resources policy implemented by the PPAT should have focus on conflicts of interest throughout the organisation. As part of the management of conflicts of interest, relevant employees should be required to declare potential interests that they may have in companies active in the wholesale energy markets, for example shareholdings or close family relationships. Basic background checks should routinely be carried out at the commencement of employment, covering fraud and criminal record checks. Due diligence should be applied when employing staff to work in the market surveillance team.

SECTION: Training and Harassment Prevention for Market Surveillance Staff
ID: 331
CONTENT:
Consideration should be given to potential psychological harassment of the market surveillance team by persons involved in trading-related activities, such as brokers or traders within the PPAT. A broker or trader within the PPAT could be investigated for a potential breach of REMIT and that broker or trader could then harass the market surveillance team member during the investigation. Appropriate training should be given to the market surveillance team on how to handle potential psychological harassment situations and safeguards should be in place to manage this. Members of the market surveillance team should be given appropriate training and guidance on REMIT and the practical considerations for the application of Article 15. Training should be delivered regularly according to the training map and should be updated in line with any guidance offered by the Agency and NRAs. Training on REMIT should not be restricted to the members of the market surveillance team and should be offered across the organisation where appropriate. A record of training attendance or completion should be kept and the effectiveness of training shall be assessed by the PPAT.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Communication Procedures and Information Access
ID: 332
CONTENT:
Internal policies should cover the use of data and information by the market surveillance team and should allow its members to access any information or data which may help to explain the anomalous event under investigation. The market surveillance team should also be able to request information from the market participant in relation to an anomalous event. Communication between the market surveillance team and anyone involved in an anomalous event/potential breach of REMIT should be carefully considered in order to avoid tipping off the company or person under suspicion. The market surveillance team should have and follow a policy setting the process for approaching members/customers and all communication in relation to an anomalous event/potential breach should be noted or recorded on file.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: STR Submission and Contact Protocols
ID: 333
CONTENT:
As a general rule, once an STR has been submitted to an NRA, the market surveillance team should not make contact with the member/customer in relation to that incident unless agreed with the NRA. Furthermore, under no circumstance should the market surveillance team make the member/customer aware that an STR has been submitted to the NRA. In exceptional circumstances it may be necessary for the market surveillance team or senior management at the PPAT to contact the member/customer reported in a STR and they may enforce a sanction such as suspension of trading. By its nature, this form of contact may tip the member/customer off that an investigation is being conducted, but it may be necessary in order to avoid further harm to the market. If this is to happen, engagement with the relevant NRA from the start is important.

SECTION: Cross-Market Communication and Documentation Procedures
ID: 334
CONTENT:
In circumstances where contacts between market surveillance teams of different PPATs are envisaged, for example in potential cases of cross-market manipulation, internal policies should detail procedures accordingly. Guidelines relating to what can be discussed between market surveillance teams should be clearly defined in the internal policies and all contact and decisions should be recorded so that if an STR is raised, the relevant NRA is aware of the work that has already been carried out and if it is not this can be justified. The communication policy in place should detail how staff members outside of the market surveillance function identify and/or escalate suspicions of market abuse.

DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: Decision-Making Process and Record Keeping for Anomalous Events
ID: 336
CONTENT:
The team should follow a traceable decision-making process when looking into an anomalous event. The full PPATs' decision-making process related to the qualification of an anomalous event as a potential breach (from the initial alert to the STR being raised) should be traceable and key decision points should be recorded. All transaction(s)/order(s)/behaviour(s), including related updates to them, particularly relating to an anomalous event/potential breach should be stored by the PPAT for a defined amount of time. The relevant NRA may place further retention requirements on the PPAT where appropriate. NRAs should request PPATs to maintain for a period of at least five years the information documenting the analysis carried out with regard to an anomalous event/potential breach which have been examined and the reasons as to whether or not submitting a STR. This information shall be provided to the NRA upon request. All processes and decisions made by the market surveillance team should also be recorded.

SECTION: Internal Audits and NRA Oversight
ID: 337
CONTENT:
The PPAT should conduct internal audits or hire an external auditor to review their processes at least on an annual basis and in certain circumstances an NRA may wish to conduct a visit or audit. Within the limits of their investigatory and sanctioning powers, the relevant NRAs shall enforce PPATs compliance with Article 15. Based on their competencies, and among other things, NRAs may choose to issue 'Systems and Controls Questionnaires' relating to the PPAT's Article 15 processes. They may also conduct visits to the PPAT's market surveillance teams in order to assess their surveillance and monitoring processes in practice.

SECTION: Compliance Advocacy and NRA Activities
ID: 338
CONTENT:
NRA visits and questionnaires help NRAs understand the processes that STRs have gone through to consider their next steps. The NRA may also choose to run STR Supervision Forums, focussing on best-practice sharing between the PPATs. It is at the discretion of each NRA whether to conduct visits, issue questionnaires or hold forums relating to REMIT Article 15 processes and adequate notice should be given to the PPAT ahead of any such activities. NRAs can implement peer reviews on the quality of the STRs and benchmark PPATs performance against references to improve compliance with the Article 15 requirements.

SECTION: REMIT Compliance and Penalty Regimes - Introduction
ID: 339
CONTENT:
This chapter provides considerations from the Agency on best practices that market participants could implement to ensure their compliance with REMIT and on the enforcement of the different REMIT obligations and prohibitions through national penalty regimes. The Agency is of the opinion that market participants should develop a clear compliance regime towards real time or close to real time disclosure of inside information and towards the other obligations and prohibitions of REMIT.

SECTION: Market Participant Compliance Regime Best Practices
ID: 340
CONTENT:
NRAs should consider the following best practice examples of compliance regime for market participants, taking into account the market participant's size and trading capacity: Compliance culture - the creation of a corporate culture to comply with REMIT requirements; Compliance objectives - the compliance with REMIT requirements, namely the registration, disclosure and reporting obligations and the market abuse prohibitions; Compliance organisation - the definition of roles and responsibilities in the internal organisation (e.g. responsibilities for the REMIT requirements (centralised vs. decentralised), internal vs. external reporting lines, internal vs. external interfaces, provision of resources: human / technical (IT Systems) resources).

SECTION: Compliance Risks, Programme, and Monitoring
ID: 341
CONTENT:
Compliance risks involve the identification and assessment of concrete compliance risks. The compliance programme includes the identification of concrete actions to define compliant/non-compliant behaviour. Communication of the rules and regulations to be observed includes internal communication and training concept (raising the awareness of employees) and external communication and reporting to the Agency/NRAs. Reporting processes include internal reports on compliance, reporting of infringements, and status of current processes. Monitoring improvements involve internal controls, audits, reporting lines for monitoring results, and documentation of processes and actions.

text:
DOCUMENT: 6th Edition ACER Guidance REMIT.pdf
SECTION: REMIT Penalty Regimes and Infringements
ID: 342
CONTENT:
According to Article 18 of REMIT, Member States should have laid down the rules on penalties applicable to infringements of REMIT by 29 June 2013. In order to ensure an effective implementation of REMIT, the Agency considers it important that penalties are put in place for all potential infringements of REMIT, which may consist of breaches of the market abuse prohibitions of Articles 3 and 5 of the Regulation, but also of breaches of the obligation to notify the relevant information to the Agency and the competent NRA in situations according to Article 3(4)(b) of the Regulation, the obligation to disclose inside information according to Article 4(1) of the Regulation, and the obligation to notify the Agency and the competent NRA of delayed disclosure of inside information according to Article 4(2) of the Regulation.

text:
DOCUMENT: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
SECTION: Guidance Note Series and Scope
ID: 1
CONTENT:
This series of Guidance Notes complements the ACER Guidance by providing in-depth information on specific types of behaviour prohibited by Article 5 of REMIT which constitute market manipulation or attempted market manipulation. The Agency aims to provide greater clarity and share insights on the general framework of assessment that NRAs shall use to determine whether specific behaviour could constitute a breach of REMIT. The Guidance Notes include frequent examples and indicators related to specific behaviours but are not exhaustive. The evolving nature of trading strategies does not allow identification of all types of behaviour and indicators. Therefore, circumstances may exist that this Guidance Note does not cover but which may still constitute market abuse under REMIT. The Agency will update the Guidance Notes as necessary. NRAs should take into account specific facts and circumstances of each case. This Guidance Note is without prejudice to the interpretation which the Court of Justice of the European Union may give to the application of Article 5 of REMIT.

text:
DOCUMENT: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
SECTION: Introduction to Layering and Spoofing
ID: 2
CONTENT:
The Agency aims to clarify the application of REMIT in the context of trading behaviours associated with layering and spoofing. This Guidance Note describes a general framework promoting consistent approach to NRA assessment of these behaviours and assists NRAs in reviewing suspicious behaviours and deciding whether investigation and enforcement procedures need to be undertaken. The scope does not include specific tools for investigation of possible cases. Layering and spoofing refers to issuing by a market participant of one large or multiple non-genuine orders to trade on one side of the order book, in order to enter into one or multiple transactions on the other side of the order book. These behaviours influence expectations of other market participants regarding supply, demand, and/or price of wholesale energy products, allowing a market participant to benefit from better conditions than would have prevailed in the absence of these behaviours.

text:
DOCUMENT: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
SECTION: Market Dynamics and Integrity Concerns
ID: 3
CONTENT:
On organised market places such as energy exchanges and electronic trading venues, misrepresentation of the order book via layering or spoofing is facilitated by the fact that the order book for continuous trading displays unveiled interest of buyers and sellers in an anonymised manner. By issuing non-genuine orders, a single market participant can alter the order book visible to other market participants. Layering and spoofing in wholesale energy markets undermines confidence in market signals. If market participants are unsure whether the order book reflects market fundamentals, they may lose confidence in market integrity and transparency, and even withdraw from it. As a result, competition would be adversely affected, to the detriment of all market participants and final consumers of energy.

text:
DOCUMENT: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
SECTION: Advanced Manifestations and Related Behaviours
ID: 4
CONTENT:
Layering and spoofing can occur through colluding market participants, including colluding traders acting on behalf of the same or different market participants. They can be performed in combination with other manipulative behaviours, such as wash trades. They can have far-reaching consequences when used to manipulate reference prices such as closing prices or index prices. By allowing unprecedented trading speed, algorithms can facilitate implementation of new layering and spoofing behaviours and other behaviours involving use of non-genuine orders in wholesale energy markets, particularly in issuing and cancellation of orders. There are other behaviours that may show similar patterns to layering or spoofing but do not fully adhere to them. These behaviours may also constitute market manipulation under REMIT but are beyond the scope of this Guidance Note. The Agency selected layering and spoofing as the subject of this Guidance Note because several potential REMIT breaches assessed by NRAs in recent years can be associated with this behaviour.

text:
DOCUMENT: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
SECTION: Document Structure and Economic Concepts
ID: 5
CONTENT:
This Guidance Note is divided into five Sections. Section 1 is an introduction. Section 2 explains the economic concepts of layering and spoofing and explores their main components. Section 3 explains why layering and spoofing constitute a breach of REMIT. Section 4 presents indicators that may help identify suspicious trading behaviour in the context of layering and spoofing. Section 5 provides conclusions and highlights the most important insights. Layering consists of issuing multiple non-genuine orders to trade at different price levels (layers) on one side of the order book, in order to enter into one or multiple transactions on the other side of the order book. Spoofing consists of issuing a single large or multiple non-genuine orders at the same price level on one side of the order book, in order to enter into one or multiple transactions on the other side of the order book.

source: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
text:
DOCUMENT: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
SECTION: Common Elements of Layering and Spoofing
ID: 6
CONTENT:
Both layering and spoofing exhibit two common elements: (i) the issuing of non-genuine orders on one side of the order book in order to (ii) enter into transactions on the other side. Layering and spoofing require issuing of non-genuine orders on one side of the order book. A market participant issues these orders to influence other market participants' behaviour, for example by creating the impression that there is stronger selling or buying interest at decreasing or increasing price levels than there actually is. Non-genuine orders are issued in order to enter into transactions at better conditions (price or volume) on the other side of the order book. Non-genuine orders can be issued within or outside the bid-ask spread. In more liquid markets, orders are typically issued outside the spread (not at the best price level), as this makes them less likely to be executed. In less liquid markets, where the risk of execution is lower, it is more likely that non-genuine orders are issued as the best bids or asks.

source: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
text:
DOCUMENT: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
SECTION: Timing and Cancellation of Non-Genuine Orders
ID: 7
CONTENT:
In most cases, non-genuine orders are cancelled shortly after entering into one or multiple transactions on the other side of the order book. However, non-genuine orders may remain in the order book after the genuine transaction (not cancelled), or be cancelled at a later or earlier stage. Layering and spoofing imply entering into one or multiple transactions or at least the intention to enter into one or multiple transactions on the other side of the order book. The transaction(s) should be executed after issuing of non-genuine orders on the opposite side of the order book. A genuine order can be issued either before or after issuing the non-genuine ones, while the transaction(s) should occur within a period that allows the non-genuine orders to influence the behaviour of other market participants.

text:
DOCUMENT: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
SECTION: Example 1: Layering the Sell Side to Buy Electricity at Lower Prices
ID: 8
CONTENT:
Situation: Market Participant A wants to buy 300 MW on the electricity intraday market (for Hour 10) at an advantageous price, lower than 28 euro/MWh, which is the best ask when it enters the market and the price of the last transaction. T1: Before MP A enters the market, the best and only ask is 400 MW at 28 euro/MWh by MP B, while the best and only bid is 100 MW at 21 euro/MWh by MP C. If MP A wants to buy 300 MW, the best price available is 28 euro/MWh. T2: MP A issues two ask orders: 200 MW at 27 euro/MWh and 100 MW at 26 euro/MWh, with the latter becoming the best ask. The bid-ask spread is narrowed by 2 euro/MWh compared to T1. T3: MP B reacts to changes in the order book and updates the price of its ask order to 25 euro/MWh. T4: MP A issues two additional ask orders: 50 MW at 24 euro/MWh and 20 MW at 23 euro/MWh, with the latter becoming the best ask. The bid-ask spread is further narrowed by 2 euro/MWh.

text:
DOCUMENT: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
SECTION: Example 1 Continued: Transaction Execution and Order Cancellation
ID: 9
CONTENT:
T5: MP B reacts by updating the price of its 400 MW ask order to 22 euro/MWh. T6: MP A issues a bid order of 300 MW at 22 euro/MWh. It matches with the ask order of MP B, resulting in a transaction of 300 MW at 22 euro/MWh. T7: Shortly after the execution, MP A cancels all four of its previously issued ask orders. A chronological representation of the order book shows the sequence of events from T1 to T7. The order book displays prices in euro/MWh and quantities in MW. Bid orders are shown in green and underlined; ask orders are shown in red. Orders from MP A are represented with an exclamation mark. This behaviour constitutes layering, as it encompasses the two elements described in the economic concepts: issuing of non-genuine orders on one side of the order book and entering into transactions on the other side.

source: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
text:
DOCUMENT: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
SECTION: Layering Strategy Example - Non-Genuine Orders and Market Manipulation
ID: 10
CONTENT:
MP A issues two ask orders in T2 and two in T4 at different price levels, reducing the initial bid-ask spread from 7 to 2 euro/MWh. These orders create four new price layers on the sell side of the order book visible to other MPs, representing 370 MW of apparent additional supply. MP A cancels the unexecuted ask orders immediately after buying electricity and ends the session without reinserting orders or attempting to sell, showing lack of interest in trading on that side. The ask order at 23 euro/MWh is particularly close to the last price with higher execution risk after the transaction. MP A uses these ask orders to change perception of supply and price of the Hour 10 product by layering the sell side with lower price levels, creating an impression of strong selling interest, competing sellers, and downward price tendency. MP B's behavior in T3 and T5 is a reaction to the false market representation created by MP A's non-genuine ask orders.

text:
DOCUMENT: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
SECTION: Genuine Transaction Execution and Price Benefit
ID: 11
CONTENT:
In T6, MP A effectively buys 300 MW at 22 euro/MWh instead of 28 euro/MWh (the best ask in T1 when MP A entered the market). This transaction reflects MP A's genuine interest and is performed at a price better than could have been achieved without layering behavior. The price of the last transaction before MP A entered the market was 28 euro/MWh. The genuine bid order may be issued as a standing order prior to non-genuine orders, with MP A potentially using an iceberg bid order to hide genuine interest (e.g., 300 MW order with 100 MW visible and 200 MW invisible).

text:
DOCUMENT: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
SECTION: Risk Management Considerations in Layering Strategies
ID: 12
CONTENT:
MP A may delete non-genuine ask orders before execution of genuine bid orders to reduce execution risk and limit impact on credit limits. In T4, MP A could have cancelled the 200 MW and 100 MW ask orders after MP B's reaction in T3 created a new layer on the ask side. To limit potential loss from unwanted execution, MP A could use two strategies: (i) issue best ask orders at decreasing volumes (20 MW in T4 compared to 200 MW in T2), and (ii) react immediately to unwanted execution by cancelling remaining ask orders and buying 320 MW at 25 euro/MWh. In this alternative scenario, despite partial execution of non-genuine orders, MP A still benefits: saves EUR 900 buying 300 MW at 25 instead of 28 euro/MWh, loses EUR 40 selling 20 MW at 23 euro/MWh and buying back at 25 euro/MWh, resulting in EUR 860 net benefit.

source: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
text:
DOCUMENT: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
SECTION: Advanced Layering and Spoofing Techniques
ID: 13
CONTENT:
Beneficial transactions can occur in order books other than where non-genuine orders were entered. Orders can be issued in the same trading venue but on different bidding zones, assuming zones are coupled with sufficient available transmission capacity. Two-leg strategies involve layering and spoofing in different directions during trading sessions depending on changes in MPs' trading interests. Layering strategies can be combined with spoofing. Iceberg orders divide total order amount into visible portion (seen by market participants) and hidden portion (not visible). When visible part is fulfilled, a new part of hidden portion of same size becomes visible. These strategies can be performed in combination to enhance market manipulation effects.

text:
DOCUMENT: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
SECTION: REMIT Article 5 Assessment - Overview of Market Manipulation Definition
ID: 14
CONTENT:
Section 3.1 analyzes layering and spoofing against the definition of market manipulation and attempted market manipulation outlined in REMIT. Recital 13 of REMIT provides examples of market manipulation including placing and withdrawal of false orders. Article 5 of REMIT specifies that any engagement in or attempt to engage in market manipulation on wholesale energy markets is prohibited. Article 2 of REMIT provides definitions of market manipulation and attempted market manipulation. Articles 2(2) and 2(3) of REMIT distinguish four categories of market manipulation or attempts through: (i) false/misleading signals; (ii) price positioning; (iii) orders/transactions involving fictitious devices/deception; and (iv) dissemination of false or misleading information.

text:
DOCUMENT: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
SECTION: Layering and Spoofing Classification Under REMIT Categories
ID: 15
CONTENT:
Depending on case specificities, layering and spoofing can fall under one or both of the first two REMIT categories. They give or are likely to give false or misleading signals regarding supply or demand status in the order book, falling under market manipulation (Article 2(2)(a)(i) of REMIT), or intend to do so falling under attempted market manipulation (Article 2(3)(a)(i) of REMIT). They secure or attempt to secure wholesale product prices at artificial levels (price positioning), falling under market manipulation (Article 2(2)(a)(ii) of REMIT), or intend to do so falling under attempted market manipulation (Article 2(3)(a)(ii) of REMIT). By design, layering and spoofing behaviors create through non-genuine orders the likelihood of sending false or misleading signals regarding supply, demand or price of wholesale energy products, as other MPs likely assume orders are genuine and react accordingly.

text:
DOCUMENT: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
SECTION: Market Manipulation Characteristics and Price Artificial Level Effects
ID: 16
CONTENT:
Layering and spoofing behaviors are likely to secure price formation process of wholesale energy products at artificial levels and may create false impressions of price volatility. Whether layering and spoofing secure prices at artificial levels depends on specific circumstances and market characteristics during their use. Taking into consideration Recital 13 and Article 2 of REMIT, as well as layering and spoofing characteristics, these behaviors always amount to market manipulation under Article 5 of REMIT. NRAs can identify market manipulation in layering and spoofing forms by assessing: (i) the pattern of orders and transactions, and (ii) that orders issued on one side of order book are non-genuine.

text:
DOCUMENT: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
SECTION: Pattern Assessment for Identifying Layering and Spoofing
ID: 17
CONTENT:
The pattern should encompass issuing one or multiple non-genuine orders to trade on one side of order book, followed by entering into one or multiple transactions on the other side. Non-genuine orders should be issued at prices/volumes at least likely to trigger reactions from other MPs. This pattern is usually repeated but can be one-off. In case of repetition, the pattern of issuing non-genuine orders and entering into transactions is deployed several times in cycles. Non-genuine orders are unlikely to be genuine if three cumulative criteria are met: (a) one or multiple orders are issued before entering into transactions on the other side; (b) same orders are cancelled (totally or partially) shortly after entering into transactions on the other side; and (c) cumulative volume of orders on one side is disproportionate to transaction volume on the other side.

text:
DOCUMENT: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
SECTION: Non-Genuine Order Assessment and Indicators
ID: 18
CONTENT:
If not all three criteria (a) to (c) are met, NRAs shall use indicators in Section 4 to further assess probability of orders being non-genuine. An order can still be non-genuine even if not cancelled in situations including: the order expires shortly after entering into transactions; potential loss from non-genuine order execution is small compared to potential benefit from genuine order execution; market trading speed results in non-genuine order execution before MP can cancel; MP amends non-genuine orders to price levels making them less likely to be executed; MP intends to conceal non-genuine nature of orders; or non-genuine orders are left in order book to attract orders from other MPs and continue trading at advantageous prices.

source: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
text:
DOCUMENT: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
SECTION: Risk Management and Profit Considerations in Market Manipulation
ID: 19
CONTENT:
Engaging in layering and spoofing poses risks for MPs. Changes in market fundamentals may lead to non-genuine order execution and/or inability to enter intended transactions, representing losses for involved MPs. To reduce unwanted execution risk, MPs layering market may issue most aggressive non-genuine orders last and remove them first. Whether the MP achieved overall trading profit is not relevant to determine if behavior constitutes market manipulation, as manipulative character is not linked to MP profit or loss. However, evidence of undue profit caused by behavior may strengthen market manipulation case and influence fine amounts imposed by NRAs.

text:
DOCUMENT: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
SECTION: Legitimate Trading Strategies vs. Market Manipulation
ID: 20
CONTENT:
Isolated elements of layering and spoofing behaviors may be part of legitimate trading strategies. MPs may be active simultaneously on sell and buy sides under specific circumstances, such as when providing market-making services wanting to take advantage of market price volatility or managing different portfolios in completely segregated ways. MPs may issue orders at varying price levels reflecting different willingness to buy or sell at diverse prices. MPs may cancel large order volumes simultaneously, particularly when market fundamentals change. These legitimate activities must be distinguished from manipulative layering and spoofing behaviors through comprehensive pattern and intent analysis.

text:
DOCUMENT: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
SECTION: False or Misleading Signals Under REMIT Article 2(2)(a)(i)
ID: 21
CONTENT:
Pursuant to Article 2(2)(a)(i) of REMIT, entering into any transaction or issuing any order to trade which gives or is likely to give false or misleading signals as to supply of, demand for, or price of wholesale energy products constitutes market manipulation. Layering and spoofing behaviors are by design likely to give false or misleading signals to market regarding supply of, demand for, or price of wholesale energy products due to reliance on orders that do not directly reflect true interest of market participants.

text:
DOCUMENT: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
SECTION: Non-Genuine Orders and Market Manipulation Basics
ID: 22
CONTENT:
Non-genuine orders induce other market participants (MPs) to change their perception of the market and adapt their trading behaviours in a way that benefits the manipulative MP's real interest. By issuing a series of non-genuine ask orders at gradually decreasing price levels, a MP is likely to create an impression of substantial selling interest and availability of supply at those price levels. As a result, other MPs may act on the basis of this information, changing their own ask orders by decreasing their price. The higher the number and/or volume of the non-genuine orders, the higher the potential to create a misleading signal of the supply of, demand for and price of the relevant wholesale energy product. The repetition of the layering and spoofing behaviours exacerbates the misrepresentation of the order book and can trigger other MPs into entering into transactions that they otherwise would not have considered.

text:
DOCUMENT: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
SECTION: Assessing Trading Behaviour and Spoofing Effects
ID: 23
CONTENT:
An assessment of the trading behaviour of other MPs with regard to the issuing and/or changing of their orders (e.g. by adapting the size and/or price) after the issuing of non-genuine orders may provide additional evidence with regard to the effect of the behaviour of the concerned MP. Spoofing can give misleading signals about the demand for wholesale energy products. In spoofing scenarios, a MP with a selling interest can create a false impression of a strong demand that drives the price upwards on a day-ahead continuous market.

text:
DOCUMENT: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
SECTION: Example 2: Spoofing Case Study - Natural Gas Market
ID: 24
CONTENT:
In this example, MP A has a selling interest and creates a false impression of strong demand that drives the price upwards on a day-ahead continuous gas market. Initial market state (T1): The last transaction was at 23 euro/MWh. Other MPs have 50 MWh/h bid and ask orders. The best bid order is priced at 23 euro/MWh and the best ask order at 26 euro/MWh (spread of 3 euro/MWh). T2: MP A issues a bid order of 200 MW at 22 euro/MWh, becoming the second best bid. T3: MP A issues a 50 MW ask order at 25 euro/MWh, becoming the best ask. T4: MP B lifts MP A's ask order at 25 euro/MWh as a reaction to the large bid. The orders are matched and transaction is executed. T5: 10 seconds later, MP A cancels the 200 MWh/h bid order (visible for mere seconds, while MP A's other orders were visible for 10 minutes). This pattern is repeated several times.

text:
DOCUMENT: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
SECTION: Example 2 Analysis: Spoofing Pattern and Non-Genuine Orders
ID: 25
CONTENT:
This trading behaviour is market manipulation under REMIT in the form of spoofing due to two cumulative elements: (i) Pattern of orders and transactions: MP A issues a single large order (200 MW in T2, four times larger than average market order) at 22 euro/MWh on the buy side, and issues an order to enter transaction on the sell side (50 MWh/h ask order at 25 euro/MWh in T3). The prices and volumes triggered a reaction from MP B. The large order created perception of more demand than supply. MP B reacted by lifting MP A's ask order in T4, believing the new large demand could absorb available supply. The pattern repeated several times. (ii) Non-genuine order on buy side: The bid order of 200 MW at 22 euro/MWh is non-genuine as it meets three cumulative criteria: issued before transaction on other side (T2 before T4); cancelled quickly after transaction (10 seconds later); cumulative volume (200 MWh/h per sequence) disproportionate to transaction volume on that side (50 MWh/h per sequence). MP A manipulated the market by sending false and misleading signals about demand and price using spoofing behaviour.

text:
DOCUMENT: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
SECTION: Price Positioning and Artificial Price Levels
ID: 26
CONTENT:
Pursuant to Article 2(2)(a)(ii) of REMIT, entering into any transaction or issuing any order to trade in wholesale energy products which secures, or attempts to secure, the price of one or more wholesale energy products at an artificial level, amounts to market manipulation. The issuance of non-genuine orders as part of layering and spoofing behaviours has the potential to push the price of a wholesale energy product either upwards (by issuing non-genuine orders on the buy side) or downwards (by issuing non-genuine orders on the sell side). Such a price is therefore secured at an artificial level. This applies regardless of whether non-genuine orders are issued at prices within or outside the bid-ask spread.

source: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
text:
DOCUMENT: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
SECTION: Layering and Price Movement Mechanisms
ID: 27
CONTENT:
Layering multiple ask orders at prices lower than prevailing ones is likely to induce other MPs to align their orders in the same direction. Other MPs wanting to remain competitive try to offer a better (lower) price to the market. As a consequence, the best ask order (lowest revealed price at which a MP is willing to sell) is likely to move downwards, which can lead to transactions at this new lower price level. When a non-genuine order is issued outside the bid-ask spread, it can still influence other MPs by providing misleading signals about demand/supply balance. It can induce other MPs to enter transactions at prices differing from those that would prevail without non-genuine orders. By creating a cumulative position on the buy side with non-genuine bid orders, a MP sends a signal of substantial demand. As a result of this false representation, potential buyers may be induced to raise their bid prices.

text:
DOCUMENT: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
SECTION: Artificial Price Movements and REMIT Breaches
ID: 28
CONTENT:
Non-genuine bid/ask orders, as part of layering or spoofing behaviour, are always likely to induce an artificial short-term movement of the price on the bid/ask side, which may vanish with order cancellation. In other instances, momentum induced by non-genuine orders may lead to a new price trend in the market. Even a short-term artificial movement of the transaction price is sufficient to be qualified as a breach of Article 5 of REMIT, in both layering and spoofing scenarios. Layering can position the price of a wholesale energy product at an artificial level through systematic order placement and cancellation patterns.

source: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
text:
DOCUMENT: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
SECTION: Example 3: Layering Case Study - Electricity Futures Market
ID: 29
CONTENT:
In this example, layering consists of two legs. In the first leg, MP A secures an artificially high price; in the second leg, an artificially low price. First leg initial state (T1): When MP A enters the electricity Future Calendar Y+1 contract market, there are two orders: one ask order at 20.5 euro/MWh and one bid order at 20.1 euro/MWh, each representing 100 MW. Last transaction was at 20.1 euro/MWh. T2: MP A issues 30 MW ask order at 20.4 euro/MWh, just below best ask (20.5 euro/MWh). T3: MP A issues 50 MW bid order at 20.2 euro/MWh, just above best bid (20.1 euro/MWh). T4: MP A issues another 50 MW bid order at 20.3 euro/MWh, just above best bid. T5: MP B lifts MP A's 30 MW ask order at 20.4 euro/MWh, entering transaction. T6: MP A cancels two 50 MW bid orders within milliseconds of transaction and seconds after issuance. At first leg end, MP A has short position valued at EUR 5.36 million (30 MW sold at 20.4 euro/MWh).

source: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
text:
DOCUMENT: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
SECTION: Example 3: Second Leg and Profit Realization
ID: 30
CONTENT:
Second leg of layering behaviour: T7: MP A issues 30 MW bid order just above best bid at 20.2 euro/MWh. T8: MP A issues 50 MW ask order below best ask at 20.4 euro/MWh. T9: MP A issues another 50 MW ask order just below best ask at 20.3 euro/MWh. T10: MP C hits MP A's 30 MW bid order at 20.2 euro/MWh. Transaction is executed. T11: MP A cancels two 50 MW ask orders within milliseconds of transaction and seconds after issuance. On other days, MP A's orders typically present in order book for two minutes. At second leg end, MP A closes short position and makes profit of EUR 52.56 thousand (30 MW bought at 20.2 euro/MWh and sold at 20.4 euro/MWh). This demonstrates how layering secures prices at artificial levels through coordinated order placement and rapid cancellation.

source: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
text:
DOCUMENT: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
SECTION: Example 3 Analysis: Layering Pattern and Non-Genuine Orders
ID: 31
CONTENT:
This trading behaviour is market manipulation under REMIT in the form of layering due to two cumulative elements: (i) Pattern of orders and transactions: In first leg, MP A issues two bid orders (T3 and T4) at increasing price levels (20.2 and 20.3 euro/MWh), significantly reducing initial bid-ask spread and creating two new price layers on buy side. MP A also issues ask order (30 MW) on sell side (T2), lifted by another MP in T5. The bid orders triggered reaction from MP B, issued as best bids, creating perception of more demand than supply. MP B entered transactions at prices that would not have prevailed without these bid orders. Pattern repeated symmetrically on other side. In second leg, MP A issues two ask orders (T8 and T9) at decreasing price levels (20.4 and 20.3 euro/MWh), significantly reducing bid-ask spread and creating two new price layers on sell side. MP A also issues bid order (30 MW) on buy side (T7), hit by another MP in T10. The ask orders triggered reaction from MP C, issued as best asks, creating perception of more supply than demand. MP C entered transactions at prices that would not have prevailed without these ask orders.

text:
DOCUMENT: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
SECTION: Example 3: Non-Genuine Orders Criteria
ID: 32
CONTENT:
The two bid orders of 50 MW at 20.2 euro/MWh and 20.3 euro/MWh and the two ask orders of 50 MW at 20.4 euro/MWh and 20.3 euro/MWh are non-genuine, as they meet three cumulative criteria: (i) the orders are issued before entering into transaction on the other side of the order book; (ii) they are cancelled quickly after entering into transaction on the other side; and (iii) the cumulative volume of the orders is disproportionate to the volume of the transaction(s) on that side of the order book. These characteristics demonstrate the systematic nature of the layering manipulation strategy.

text:
DOCUMENT: ACER Guidance Note Layering and Spoofing.pdf
SECTION: Market Manipulation Through Layering and Spoofing - Case Example
ID: 33
CONTENT:
The other side of the order book (the bids in T3 and T4 before T5 and the asks in T8 and T9 before T10); (ii) they are cancelled quickly after (milliseconds later) the entering into the transaction on the other side of the order book; and (iii) the cumulative volume of the orders (100 MW for each sequence) is disproportionate to the volume of transactions on the other side of the order book (in total 30 MWh/h for each sequence). In the first leg, MP A moves the market price from 20.1 to 20.4 euro/MWh. In the second leg, it repeats the behaviour on the other side of the order book and moves the market price from 20.4 to 20.2 euro/MWh. In both cases, MP A secured the price of the Future Calendar Y+1 contract at an artificial level twice.
